The Zuri Programming Language

by the Zuri Project

Zuri is a programming language for building complete applications, and it comes with the tools and libraries those applications need. The runtime, the web server, the template engine, the data formats, the cryptography and the toolchain were designed together and ship as a single binary. You don't have to assemble a stack of third-party packages before you can start on a real program. When you do want outside code, package management and vendoring are built into the language, so you don't need extra tools for that either.

The standard library is large. Templates, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, WebSockets, TLS, JSON, YAML, CSV, compression, cryptography, image decoding and drawing, HTML parsing, date arithmetic with the IANA time zone database, and concurrency on OS threads are all included, and each is available with a plain import.

The tools are part of the same binary. zuri fmt formats your code, zuri test runs your tests, and zuri lsp provides completion, navigation and diagnostics in your editor. zuri install and zuri publish manage packages on Nyssa, a package registry that any Zuri installation can host, and zuri bundle packages a finished program so it can run on machines that do not have Zuri installed, even as a single executable.

Zuri is dynamically typed, but it checks more than most dynamic languages do. Parameter types you declare are checked when the function is called, classes are sealed, a function can't be silently redefined, and names that start with an underscore are private to the module that declares them. Your code runs as bytecode at first. When part of it runs often enough, a JIT compiler turns that part into machine code while the program keeps running.

This book teaches the language, starting with your first line of code and ending with a complete web application. The output shown below each program is the output it actually produced.

Introduction

Welcome! Open a terminal next to this page and let's get started.

This book teaches you Zuri. It starts with installing the language and printing a line of text, and it ends with a task-board web application that stores its data on disk, renders HTML from templates, serves a JSON API and runs behind several layers of middleware. The chapters in between cover everything you need to get from the first program to the last.

What Zuri Looks Like

Here is a complete program. Don't worry about understanding all of it yet. Read it the way you'd read a paragraph in a language you're learning, and see how much of it makes sense.

If you've programmed before, most of this will look familiar. A few things are worth pointing out now, because you'll see them again as soon as Chapter 3:

  • var declares a variable, and class declares a class.
  • The constructor is named @new. Methods whose names start with @ hook into the language's own syntax. Chapter 6 lists all of them.
  • self refers to the current instance, and you always read a field through it. You write self.balance, never just balance.
  • '${...}' inserts the value of an expression into a string.
  • echo prints a value followed by a newline.
  • raise raises an error. Chapter 7 explains how to catch one.
  • Blocks are written with braces, and every control flow statement needs them.

What Comes With Zuri

When you install Zuri, you get its whole toolchain as well. Each tool is a subcommand of zuri, and each one is covered somewhere in this book:

Command What it does Where
zuri Starts the interactive REPL Chapter 1
zuri run Runs a script, a package or a directory Chapter 1
zuri init Creates a new project Chapter 1
zuri fmt Formats Zuri source code Chapter 1
zuri test Runs a project's tests Chapter 23
zuri migrate Applies and rolls back database migrations Chapter 17
zuri lsp Runs the language server that your editor talks to Chapter 29
zuri doc Builds a documentation site (like this book) from Markdown, and an API reference from doc comments Chapter 30
zuri install Adds packages to a project and records them in a lockfile Chapter 27
zuri publish Publishes a package to a registry Chapter 27
zuri serve Runs Nyssa, your own package registry Chapter 27
zuri bundle Packages a program to run on machines without Zuri Chapter 27
zuri upgrade Updates Zuri to a newer release Chapter 27

Projects and packages can add their own commands too. Appendix I shows how.

Who This Book Is For

Chapters 1 through 6 assume only that you know how to open a terminal. If Zuri is your first programming language, start at the beginning and take your time. Each idea is explained before it's used, and the examples are short enough to type in yourself.

If you already know Python, JavaScript, Ruby, Go or Java, you can skim Chapters 3 to 5. Read Appendix H first, though. It lists the places where Zuri behaves differently from the language you know, even when the syntax looks the same, and those are the places where you're most likely to get stuck.

How This Book Is Organized

Getting started, Chapters 1 and 2. You'll install the language, run some code, create and format a project, and then build a small command-line application from start to finish, so you've seen what a real program looks like before we go through the language piece by piece.

The language, Chapters 3 to 8. Variables, types, operators, control flow, strings, numbers, collections, functions, closures, type annotations, classes, inheritance, decorated methods, error handling and modules. These chapters are best read in order.

The world outside your program, Chapters 9 to 13. Files, binary data and byte streams, isolates and concurrency, sockets and networking, and a tour of the standard library.

The large modules, Chapters 14 to 20. Wire for templates, HTTP for clients and servers, Imagine for images, SQL for databases, Mail for sending and receiving email, env for configuration, and args for parsing the command line. Each of these modules is big enough for a chapter of its own, and you'll probably come back to them as a reference.

Going deeper, Chapters 21 to 24. Reflection and the compiler API, how Zuri runs your code and how to make it faster, how to test it, and how to debug a program that isn't doing what you expected.

The capstone project, Chapter 25. A single application, built in seven steps, that uses most of what the book has covered.

Interoperability, Chapter 26. Calling C and Rust libraries, and letting them call back into Zuri.

Sharing and shipping, Chapter 27. Installing and publishing packages, the lockfile, bundling a program so it runs where Zuri isn't installed, and running Nyssa, the package registry, for your team or for the public.

Talking to other programs, Chapter 28. JSON-RPC, for calling methods in another program and handling its calls over any kind of connection.

Tools, Chapters 29 and 30. The language server and how to set up your editor to use it, and building documentation with zuri doc.

Appendices. Keywords, operators and precedence, decorated methods, built-in functions, the methods of every built-in type, an index of the standard library, the error hierarchy, notes for readers coming from other languages, and how to write your own commands. The appendices are meant for looking things up, while the chapters are meant to be read.

How to Read It

Keep the REPL open while you read. You can paste any of the short examples straight into it, and one of the quickest ways to understand a rule is to break it deliberately and read the error message.

The chapters build on each other. When a chapter mentions something that's covered later, it links to it, but you can keep reading without following the link. When a chapter introduces something you'll need again later, it tells you.

Conventions

Commands that you type in a shell are shown with a $ prompt, followed by their output:

When the file name matters, code that belongs in a file is shown with the name above it:

Sessions in the REPL use %> for the first line of input and .. for each continuation line, which is what the REPL itself prints:

All of the examples in this book were run to check that they behave as described.

Let's get started.

Chapter 1 · Getting Started

Getting Started

Before we get to the language itself, this chapter covers three things: installing Zuri, running a file, and using the interactive prompt.

The prompt is more useful than it might sound. It prints the value of any expression you type, which makes it the quickest way to find out what something returns. You'll want to check that often over the next few chapters.

1.1 · Getting Started

Installation

You can install Zuri with a single command. The installer downloads the right release for your machine, verifies it, and adds zuri to your PATH. Releases are available for:

  • Linux on x86-64 and ARM with the GNU C library 2.28 or later (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu). This includes Debian 10, Ubuntu 20.04, RHEL 8, Amazon Linux 2023 and newer versions of each.
  • Linux on x86-64 and ARM with musl, such as Alpine (x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, aarch64-unknown-linux-musl)
  • macOS on Intel and Apple silicon (x86_64-apple-darwin, aarch64-apple-darwin)
  • Windows on x86-64 (x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)

You can also build Zuri from source with Cargo, as described at the end of this page.

Linux and macOS

The installer downloads the archive for your machine and checks it against the checksum published with it. Next, it runs the new zuri once to make sure it reports the expected version. Only then does it move the files into ~/.zuri/runtime, so a failed or tampered download can't replace a working installation. The installer links zuri into ~/.zuri/bin, which is also where globally installed tools put their launchers, and adds that directory to your PATH in your shell's startup file. That's .zshrc for zsh, .bashrc for bash (.bash_profile on macOS), config.fish for fish, and .profile for any other shell.

On Linux distributions that use musl, the installer picks the musl build, which runs on a plain Alpine system without any extra packages. It loads shared libraries the same way Alpine's own programs do. That's what allows ffi to open them, and it's also why the build needs the musl loader to be present. The musl build doesn't run on Linux systems that use the GNU C library.

To pass options to the installer, put them after sh -s --:

Option What it does
--version <version> Installs the given release instead of the newest one
--prerelease Includes pre-releases when looking for the newest release
--no-modify-path Leaves your shell's startup files unchanged

Windows

In PowerShell:

The Windows installer performs the same checks and installs Zuri into %USERPROFILE%\.zuri\runtime. It adds that directory to your user PATH, along with %USERPROFILE%\.zuri\bin, where globally installed tools put their launchers. Any terminal you open afterwards will have both, and so will the terminal the installer ran in.

On Windows, the options are parameters. To use them, run the installer as a script block:

-Version, -Prerelease and -NoModifyPath work like the options described above.

Checking the Installation

The %> is the Zuri prompt. Type .exit and press the ENTER key to leave it.

zuri --version prints the same build information without starting a session, which makes it the better choice in scripts and CI jobs. zuri --help also lists every command that the runtime can run from the current directory:

Where Zuri Is Installed

Both installers put everything under ZURI_HOME. Unless you set that variable, it's the .zuri directory in your home directory:

runtime contains the executable, with copies of the libs and cmds directories next to it. The two need to stay together. Most of the standard library is written in Zuri, and the runtime finds it by looking for a libs directory next to the executable. cmds works the same way for the commands that come with the runtime.

Running an installer again installs over the existing copy. zuri upgrade does the same thing from inside an installation, as described in Bundles and Upgrades. To remove Zuri, delete ~/.zuri/runtime and the zuri link in ~/.zuri/bin, and remove the line the installer added to your shell's startup file.

If you set ZURI_RELEASES_URL, both installers and zuri upgrade read the list of releases from that address instead, for example from a mirror. The listing has to use the same format that GitHub does. If GITHUB_TOKEN is set, it's sent along with requests to GitHub's API, which gives you a higher rate limit.

Downloading a Release Manually

Each release on the releases page has one archive per platform, named zuri-<version>-<target>.tar.gz (or .zip on Windows), and a .sha256 file next to it. Verify the archive against the checksum, unpack it, and add the zuri executable it contains to your PATH. Keep the libs and cmds directories next to the executable.

Building From Source

To build Zuri, you need Cargo, Rust's package manager. If you don't have Rust installed, you can get it from rustup.rs. It only takes a minute, and it installs cargo for you.

cargo patch-crates prepares the few dependencies that Zuri builds with its own changes. You need to run it once after cloning the repository, and again only when one of those changes is updated. The build tells you when that happens.

The first build compiles a large number of native dependencies, so expect it to take a few minutes. Later builds are incremental and much faster.

When the build finishes, you'll have an executable at target/release/zuri, with copies of the libs/ and cmds/ directories next to it, arranged the same way as in a release.

Adding a Build to Your PATH

The simplest approach is to leave the binary and its two directories where they are and create a symlink to the binary:

This works because the runtime resolves symlinks before it looks for libs. Copying only the binary somewhere else doesn't work.

If you want to keep the directories somewhere else, set ZURI_ROOT to the directory that contains them:

ZURI_ROOT takes priority over the directory next to the executable. This is useful when you're working on the standard library itself and want a build to pick up your changes right away:

Debug Builds

A plain cargo build produces target/debug/zuri. This build keeps the runtime assertions that the optimized build removes, which makes it useful when a program does something you didn't expect. The trade-off is that it runs more slowly. Both builds can run everything in this book.

1.2 · Getting Started

Hello, World!

Create a directory, put one file in it, and run it.

Create a file called main.zu. The runtime looks for the .zu extension when it resolves imports, so it's a good habit to use it from the start.

Then run it:

That's the entire program. You don't need a main function, imports or any boilerplate. A Zuri file is a script, and the code at its top level runs when you run the file.

A Closer Look

echo is a keyword, not a function. Instead of echo(...), you write echo followed by an expression. It prints the value followed by a newline.

Strings can be written in single or double quotes, and both mean the same thing. Most Zuri code uses single quotes, and double quotes for strings that contain an apostrophe.

There's no semicolon at the end. A statement ends at the end of the line. You can use a semicolon to put two statements on one line, but that's rarely done.

echo and print

There's also a print() function. It's worth knowing how it differs from echo now, because the difference can catch you out later.

echo adds a newline and print() doesn't, and print() accepts any number of arguments. Use echo for output that someone will read in a terminal, and print() when you're building up output piece by piece.

Running a Directory

run accepts a directory as well as a file. When you give it a directory, it looks for an index.zu file inside and runs that:

If there's no index.zu, it tells you:

The module system uses the same rule for packages, which we'll look at in Chapter 8. A directory with an index.zu can be either run or imported.

If you leave out the path, run runs the current directory. This is the usual way to start a project:

Any arguments after the path are passed to your program, not to zuri, so a script can read its own flags the same way it would anywhere else:

Chapter 20 explains how to read them.

Rerunning on Every Change

While you're working on a program, the --watch flag (or -w for short) keeps it running and restarts it from the beginning whenever one of its files changes:

The watched files are the entry file, every module it imports, the Wire templates it renders, and the project's project.toml and .env files. Zuri discovers modules and templates as the program runs, so a module that's only imported partway through is watched from the moment it's loaded. Files the program writes itself, such as logs, databases and uploads, don't trigger a restart.

Watch mode writes its own messages to standard error, so you can still pipe the program's output somewhere else. If the program exits, watch mode waits for the next change. If it fails to start because of a mistake in the code, it's started again as soon as you fix the mistake. Press Ctrl+C to stop both the program and watch mode.

The flag has to come right after run. Anything after the path is passed to the program, so zuri run . -w passes -w to your program instead.

Starting a Project

Everyone starts with a single file, but once you have a second one you'll want some structure. zuri init creates the layout for a new project:

When you run it in a terminal, it asks for the project's name, its starting version and its author, and suggests an answer for each. Press Enter to accept the suggestion. When there's nobody to answer, such as in a script or a CI job, it uses the suggested answers automatically. You can also ask for that explicitly with --yes.

Here's what it creates:

The project runs, and its tests pass, before you've written any code:

The root index.zu does two jobs:

The import re-exports everything that app declares, so another project can import myproject and use all of it. The if statement starts the application, but only when this file is the one being run. __root__ is the file that zuri was started with, and __file__ is the file that contains the line. When the project is imported, main() isn't called. This is how Zuri writes a main guard, and you'll see it in every runnable package.

app/index.zu contains the application itself. Whatever it exports, the project exports:

project.toml describes the project for any tool that reads it:

The name is taken from the directory and the author from git config. A git repository is created as well, unless the directory is already inside one. Run zuri init --help to see the other options. Each question that init asks can also be answered with a flag:

If you run init in a directory that already contains files, it adds the files that are missing and doesn't overwrite anything. If the directory already contains a project, init stops without changing it.

Chapter 8 covers packages and re-exports in detail, and Chapter 25 builds this layout into a full application.

Formatting

zuri fmt formats Zuri source code in a single, consistent style: two spaces per indentation level, one statement per line, explicit blocks where they belong, conventional spacing, and lines longer than 80 columns broken at sensible points. Line breaking follows the rules of the Dart formatter. A list of arguments or items stays on one line if it fits, and otherwise goes one item per line. A list or dictionary that contains another one is always expanded, as rooms is below. When a call has a single function or collection among its arguments, only that argument is expanded, as in each(items, @{. The layout depends only on the code, so it doesn't matter where you broke lines inside an expression. Blank lines between statements are kept.

Here's a file written in a hurry:

If you give zuri fmt a directory, it formats every .zu file in it, except for packages the project has installed. With no path, it formats the current directory. Formatting never changes what a program does. Before writing a file, the formatter parses its own output and checks that the code and all of its comments are unchanged. If it can't format a file that way, it leaves the file alone.

With --dry-run, nothing is written. The formatter lists each file that would change and exits with status 1 if there are any, which is what you want in a commit hook or a CI job:

Your editor uses the same formatter through the language server, for a whole file or a selection. Chapter 29 explains how to set that up.

Commands

If the first word after zuri isn't run, it's treated as the name of a command rather than a path:

A command is either a .zu file or a directory with an index.zu, inside a cmds directory. A project keeps its own commands in .zuri/cmds, so either of these will run as zuri greet:

If both exist, the directory is used. This means that when a command grows too big for one file, the directory takes over as soon as you add its index.zu. Until then, the directory isn't a command and the file is still used.

The commands that come with the runtime live in the cmds directory next to the executable, and they take priority over a project's own commands. Everything after the command name is passed to the command unchanged, including flags.

If a name doesn't match any command, zuri reports an error instead of guessing:

A command describes itself in its doc comment, using two tags. zuri --help uses them to list every command it can find:

If a description doesn't fit on one line, continue it on the lines below, indented:

Two flags don't run anything at all. zuri --help prints the list shown above, and zuri --version prints the build information:

Both also have short forms, -h and -v.

1.3 · Getting Started

The REPL

If you run zuri without any arguments, you get an interactive prompt:

REPL stands for read-eval-print loop, and the print part is what makes it so handy. At the top level of the REPL, the value of any expression that isn't nil is printed for you, so you don't need echo just to look at a value:

Notice that var name = 'Zuri' didn't print anything. A declaration isn't an expression, and nothing is printed for values that are nil. That's why list.append(4) and echo x don't print their output twice.

Values are only printed automatically at the top level. If you type a loop, its body doesn't print anything on each iteration:

Use echo inside a block when you want to see a value.

Multi-line Input

When what you've typed isn't a complete statement yet, the prompt changes from %> to ... If a line ends with an unclosed brace, press Enter and keep typing:

The same goes for an unclosed bracket or parenthesis, an unfinished string, or a block comment. The REPL reads your input the same way the compiler does, so a bracket inside a string or a quote inside a comment doesn't count. The REPL works out when your input is complete, so you never have to tell it.

Definitions Persist

Variables, functions and classes that you declare at the top level stay defined for the rest of the session, because the whole session shares one namespace:

If you declare a name again at the top level, the new declaration replaces the old one instead of raising an error. That way, you can keep retyping a function until you get it right.

Leaving the REPL

Type .exit. In a terminal, this is the only way to end the session.

Ctrl+C and Ctrl+D don't exit. Both print an interrupt message and give you a new prompt:

Use Ctrl+C to throw away a line you've only partly typed. The line is discarded and you get a fresh prompt.

As far as the rest of the language is concerned, the whole session is a single program. Handlers registered with os.at_exit() run when the session ends, and os.set_exit_code() sets its exit status.

Piped Input

When standard input isn't a terminal, zuri reads the session from standard input instead. It doesn't show a banner or a prompt, only the session's output, and it stops when the input ends:

Otherwise, it behaves as though you'd typed the input yourself. Expressions are printed, declarations stay defined, statements can span several lines, and .exit ends the session early. When a line fails, its error is reported and the session continues, so the exit status is still 0. If you want a program to stop at its first error, use zuri run instead.

Syntax Highlighting

In a terminal, the REPL highlights your input as you type. Keywords are colored and everything else is left plain, so a misspelling such as retrun or whiel is easy to spot before you press Enter, because it doesn't change color.

The highlighter knows about string literals. A keyword inside quotes is just text, so it isn't colored:

Here, return stays plain because it's part of the string.

The REPL also shows a grayed-out suggestion to the right of the cursor when what you've typed matches an earlier line in your history. Press the Right Arrow key to accept it.

Highlighting and suggestions only appear in a terminal. If you pipe input into zuri or redirect its output, you get plain text, so a session saved to a file contains no escape codes.

Other Dot Commands

.help reminds you that you can press Tab for completions.

.credits opens the project's license in a pager. Press q to return to the prompt. In a piped session, the license is printed instead.

Tab completes both commands, as well as every keyword in the language.

History

Use the Up and Down arrow keys to move through previous lines, and Ctrl+R to search backward through them. History is saved to a history.txt file next to the zuri executable, so it's kept between sessions.

What the REPL Is Good For

Each line is compiled and run separately, which makes the REPL a good fit for quick questions like these:

  • What does this method return? 'a,b,,c'.split(',')
  • Is this value truthy? !!(-1)
  • What type is this value? typeof(x)
  • Does this syntax parse the way I expect? Type it in and see.

It's not a good place to write a program, since you can't go back and edit line four. Once you have more than a few lines, put them in a .zu file and run that instead. That's what the next chapter does.

Chapter 2 · Getting Started

Programming a Bookmark Keeper

In this chapter we'll build a small but useful program: a command-line bookmark keeper. It asks for a title and a URL, saves them to a JSON file, and lets you list, search and delete bookmarks later.

Along the way, you'll use variables, functions, lists, dictionaries, loops, branches, string methods, files, JSON and error handling. We won't explain any of them in depth here, because that's what Chapters 3 to 8 are for. The goal of this chapter is to show you a complete, working program before we look at each part in detail.

Try typing the code in yourself instead of copying it. Making mistakes is the quickest way to learn what the error messages mean.

Setting Up

Create main.zu and start by importing the modules we'll need:

There are three things to notice here. import loads a module and binds it to a name, and you use a dot to reach what's inside it. var declares a variable. And the top level of a .zu file is ordinary code that runs from top to bottom.

Asking for Input

The io module has a readline() function, which prints a prompt and waits for the user to type a line:

The returned value contains exactly what the user typed, including any spaces, so you'll almost always call .trim() on it:

trim() is a method of strings. In Zuri, every value has methods, including numbers, booleans and nil, and you call them with a dot.

Storing One Bookmark

A bookmark has a title, a URL and some tags. The natural way to represent that is a dictionary, which is a set of keys, each with a value.

Square brackets create a list, which is an ordered sequence of values. Curly braces create a dictionary. You read a value from a dictionary with a dot, just as you do with a module:

Zuri has a shorthand that you'll use all the time. When a key has the same name as the variable that holds its value, you only need to write the name once:

This creates the same dictionary as { title: title, url: url }, but it's shorter and easier to read.

Many Bookmarks

A single bookmark is a dictionary, so a collection of bookmarks is a list of dictionaries:

Saving to Disk

The json module converts Zuri values to text and back. file() opens a file, and 'w' opens it for writing.

def declares a function. The parameters don't need types, although you can add them (see Chapter 5). The body is a block, and in Zuri, blocks always use braces.

The second argument to json.encode() is called compact. It defaults to true, which puts everything on one dense line. Passing false gives you indented output instead, which is easier to read if someone opens the file:

Loading the File Safely

Reading the file is where a real program has to think about what might go wrong. The file might not exist yet. Or it might exist but contain invalid JSON because someone edited it by hand. Neither case should crash the program.

This code introduces two new things.

The first is ${...} inside a string. This is called interpolation: the expression inside the braces is evaluated, and its value is inserted into the string. Interpolation works in both single-quoted and double-quoted strings.

The second is catch. Zuri doesn't have try. Instead, you wrap the code that might fail in catch { ... } and handle the error in as error { ... }. If nothing goes wrong, the handler doesn't run. If something does, error is an object with message, type and stacktrace properties.

There's no finally either. Code after the catch statement runs whether or not there was an error, which covers most of the things finally is normally used for.

Adding a Bookmark

Now we can put these pieces together:

The line that builds the tags uses three new ideas.

cond ? a : b is the conditional operator. If cond is truthy, the result is a. Otherwise, it's b.

split(',') splits a string into a list at each comma.

map() calls a function on every element of a list and returns a new list of the results. @(t) { return t.trim() } is an anonymous function, written as @ followed by a parameter list and a body. You can also write it as def(t) { ... }, but @ is the shorthand, and it's what most Zuri code uses for short functions.

There's an even shorter form. When the body is a single expression whose value you want to return, you can use => instead of the braces and the return:

These are three ways of writing the same function. Chapter 5 covers all of the forms and when to use each one.

Notice also that the code uses or instead of ||. Zuri's logical operators are and, or and !.

Printing a Bookmark

join is a method of the string, not of the list. It reads naturally: take this separator and use it to join the items in that list.

Listing and Searching

each() calls your function once for every element, passing the value first and the index second. This order surprises some people. It's the same for lists, dictionaries and strings.

Searching is a filter combined with a test:

filter() keeps the elements for which your function returns true. some() checks whether a condition is true for at least one element, and it stops as soon as it finds one.

Removing a Bookmark

to_number() converts a string to a number, bookmarks[position] gets an element of a list by its index, and remove_at() removes the element at a given position and moves the remaining elements down.

The bounds check is necessary. Reading past the end of a list raises an error, and an error that isn't handled ends the program.

The Main Loop

The last piece is a loop that reads a command and decides what to do with it:

using is Zuri's multi-way branch statement, and each branch starts with when. It compares the value against each when and runs the first branch that matches. The default branch handles everything else. When a branch's body is a single short statement, it can stay on the same line, which keeps a dispatch table like this one easy to read. Longer bodies need a block.

Unlike switch in C, there's no fall-through, so you don't need break. One branch runs, and then the statement is finished.

The Complete Program

Here's what a session looks like:

Summary

You've just written a program with persistent state, user input, error handling and a command loop, in about a hundred lines, using only what comes with Zuri.

Along the way, you've seen var, def, if/else, while, using/when, catch/as, return, lists, dictionaries, the dictionary shorthand, string interpolation, the conditional operator, anonymous functions and a number of built-in methods.

The next six chapters explain each of these in detail.

Chapter 3 · Learning the Language

Common Programming Concepts

Every language gives you a way to name values, a set of types for those values, operators for combining them, and statements that control what runs next. This chapter covers how Zuri handles each of these.

If Zuri is your first language, read the sections in order, since each one only relies on the ones before it. If you've programmed before, pay close attention to Operators and Control Flow. That's where syntax you already know behaves differently in Zuri.

Reserved Words

First, the words you can't use as names. Zuri reserves 31 keywords:

They're all lowercase, and each one is explained somewhere in this book. Appendix A lists them all, with a one-line summary and a link for each.

A few words are not on the list, and it helps to know that now:

  • print isn't a keyword. It's an ordinary built-in function, so you could even shadow it with a variable of your own. echo, on the other hand, is a keyword.
  • There are no function, int, string or bool keywords. Type names are ordinary identifiers, which is why you can use them in annotations without them being reserved.
  • There's no try, finally, switch, case, new, this, public or private. Zuri uses catch, using, when, a direct call to the class, self, and a leading underscore instead.

3.1 · Learning the Language

Variables and Constants

A variable is a name for a value. In Zuri, you declare one with var, and from then on the name refers to whatever value you last assigned to it.

That's really all there is to it. The rest of this section covers the details: which names are allowed, what happens if you leave out the value, where a name is visible, and what const adds.

Declaring Variables

A var without an initializer holds nil, the value that means "nothing here yet":

You can declare several names in one statement by separating them with commas, and each one can have a value or not:

This is useful when the names really do belong together, such as the three components of a color or the lower and upper bounds of a range. When they don't, it's better to avoid it, because one long line of declarations is harder to read than three short ones.

var is a declaration, not an expression. It doesn't have a value, so you can't write if var x = f() or echo var y = 1. Declare the variable first, then use it.

Naming Rules

A name can contain letters, digits and underscores, but it can't start with a digit. firstName, first_name and _first_name are all valid, and they're three different names.

Zuri code uses the same naming conventions everywhere, and the standard library follows them too:

Kind of name Convention Example
Variable, function, method snake_case read_line, total_count
Class PascalCase Account, HttpClient
Constant SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE MAX_RETRIES
Anything private Leading underscore _cache, _retry()

The leading underscore is more than a convention. A name that starts with _ is private, and the compiler enforces it. Another file can't access module._helper, and code outside a class can't access instance._field. Chapter 6 and Chapter 8 explain what this means for classes and modules.

You can't use any of the 31 keywords listed in the previous section as names. If you try, you'll get a syntax error at the declaration.

Reassignment

Zuri is dynamically typed. A variable holds a value rather than having a type, so you're allowed to assign a different kind of value to the same name:

Just because you can doesn't mean you should, though. If a name holds a number on one line and a list twenty lines later, nobody reading the code can predict what it holds. Use a second variable instead.

Assignment is an expression, and its value is the value that was assigned. This means you can chain assignments:

Compound Assignment

Each arithmetic and bitwise operator has an assignment form, which applies the operator to the variable's current value and stores the result back in the variable:

The full set is +=, -=, *=, /=, //=, **=, %=, &=, |=, ^=, ~=, <<=, >>= and >>>=. Each one does the same thing as the corresponding binary operator, but updates the variable in place.

Compound assignment works with anything you can assign to, not only plain variables:

Increment and Decrement

++ and -- add or subtract one in place:

There are two rules to remember. First, both are postfix only. ++n is a syntax error, because the operator has to come after the name.

Second, when n++ is used inside a larger expression, it updates n and then evaluates to the new value:

If you're used to C, Java or JavaScript, this is the opposite of what you'd expect. In those languages, j++ gives you the old value, but in Zuri it gives you the new one. The easiest way to avoid any confusion is to use ++ only as a statement of its own, or in the update clause of an iter loop, where its value isn't used:

const

const declares a name that can't be reassigned:

Assigning to it is caught when the file is compiled, before any code runs:

A const has to be given a value when it's declared, so const K on its own doesn't compile. A constant without a value would just be nil forever.

const is enforced in local scopes, meaning inside functions, methods and blocks. At the top level of a module, const declares an ordinary module-level variable, and reassignment isn't checked. Use it inside code where the check is useful, which is where you might otherwise be tempted to reassign the name.

Constants Aren't Frozen

const prevents you from rebinding the name, but it doesn't affect the value. A constant list is still a list, and lists can still be changed:

items = [4] would be an error, but items.append(3) isn't. If you need a collection that can't be changed, give out a copy instead of relying on the declaration.

Scope

Every block is a scope. Braces open a new scope, and any name declared inside it disappears when the block ends:

Inside the block, the inner x hides the outer one. This is called shadowing, and it's allowed on purpose, so that a short block can use a short name without worrying about what that name means outside the block.

Function bodies, loop bodies, if branches and bare { ... } blocks all behave this way. So does the initializer of an iter loop, whose variable belongs to the loop:

After the loop, i no longer exists, and reading it is an error. That's what you want. Using a name that doesn't exist is a mistake, and Zuri reports it instead of quietly giving you nil.

One Declaration per Scope

You can shadow a name in an inner scope, but you can't declare the same name twice in the same scope:

The exception is the top level of a script or module. There, a second var a rebinds the existing global instead of raising an error. That's what lets you retype a declaration in the REPL while you're experimenting.

Functions Follow the Same Rule

A def is scoped the same way as a var. A function declared at the top level of a file creates a module-level name. A function declared inside another function is local to that function, and nothing outside can see it:

The first call works because helper is local to outer. The second one fails, because outside outer that name was never defined.

Chapter 5 covers this in more detail.

3.2 · Learning the Language

Data Types

Zuri has ten built-in types. typeof() tells you which one a value is:

In addition, there are function, class, instance, module, file and ptr values, which you get by declaring or opening things rather than by writing a literal.

number

A number is an IEEE 754 double-precision value. There's no separate integer type, so 1 and 1.0 are the same value:

is_int() checks whether a number's value is a whole number. It doesn't matter whether it was written with a decimal point:

Doubles can represent integers exactly up to 2^53. Beyond that, precision is lost:

There are five ways to write a number literal:

Underscores can be used as digit separators, but only in decimal literals. 1_000_000 and 1_0.5_5 are fine, while 0xdead_beef and 0b1010_1010 aren't. See Numbers for the full rules.

The special values behave as the IEEE standard specifies:

Numbers have methods, so math can be written from left to right:

You can call a method directly on a literal. The parentheses around (-3) are needed because a method call binds more tightly than the minus sign, so -3.abs() would negate the result instead of the number. Numbers explains this rule in full.

bigint

When 2^53 isn't big enough, add an n suffix to the literal to get an arbitrary-precision integer:

Bigints never lose precision and never overflow. They're slower than numbers, and the two types don't mix automatically, so you convert between them explicitly with to_bigint() and to_number(). Chapter 4 covers them in detail.

bool

A bool is either true or false. Every value in Zuri is either truthy or falsy, which determines how if, while, and, or, ! and ? : treat it. These are the falsy values:

Value Why it's falsy
false It's false
nil No value
0, 0.0, -0.0 Zero
NaN Not a number
0n Bigint zero
'' Empty string
bytes(0) Empty byte buffer

Everything else is truthy, including negative numbers, [], {} and '0'.

This has two consequences that are easy to miss.

A position of 0 is falsy. index_of() returns -1 when it doesn't find anything, which is truthy, and 0 when the item is first, which is falsy. So if list.index_of(x) { ... } gets both cases wrong. Compare the result explicitly instead:

An empty list is truthy. [] and {} are objects, and all objects are truthy. Use is_empty() instead:

nil

nil represents the absence of a value. An uninitialized var holds nil, a function that ends without returning anything returns nil, and reading a missing dictionary key with get() gives you nil.

nil is falsy, but it still has a to_string() method:

Calling any other method on nil raises a TypeError, which is usually the error you want to see in that situation.

string

This section is a quick overview. Strings covers quoting, escape sequences, interpolation, concatenation, repetition and regular expressions in detail.

Strings can be written in single or double quotes, and both mean the same thing:

Either kind can span several lines:

The escape sequences are \0, \a, \b, \f, \n, \r, \t, \v, \\, \', \" and \${ (for a literal ${), along with \xNN for a byte, \uNNNN for a code point, and \UNNNNNNNN for a code point outside the Basic Multilingual Plane:

A backslash followed by any other character is left as it is, backslash included.

Interpolation

${...} inside a string evaluates the expression and inserts the result. It works with both kinds of quotes, and the expression can be anything:

To write a literal ${, put a backslash in front of it:

Strings as Sequences

Indexing a string gives you a one-character string. Negative indexes count from the end:

s[a,b] is a slice, from index a up to but not including b. You can leave out either side, so s[,3] is the first three characters and s[3,] is everything from index three onward.

+ concatenates strings and * repeats them:

list

A list is an ordered sequence that can grow, written in square brackets. Its elements can be of any type, including other lists:

Lists support indexing and slicing just like strings, including negative indexes. Chapter 4 covers their forty methods.

dict

A dictionary maps keys to values and remembers the order in which keys were inserted:

A key written as a bare word is treated as a string, so { host: ... } and { 'host': ... } are the same dictionary. Keys can also be numbers, and they can be computed:

Dot access and bracket access do the same thing. Use a dot when the key is a fixed name, and brackets when the key is computed or isn't a valid identifier.

When a key has the same name as the variable that holds its value, you can write the name once:

range

a..b represents the integers from a up to but not including b:

A range is a value in its own right, not just loop syntax. You can store it in a variable, pass it to a function, and call methods on it:

bytes

A bytes value is a fixed-size buffer of 8-bit values, used for binary data. bytes(n) creates a buffer of n zero bytes, and bytes(list) creates one from a list of numbers between 0 and 255:

Bytes are printed as hexadecimal values in parentheses, so you can always tell them apart from lists. Chapter 10 covers them in full.

Checking Types

typeof() gives you the name of a type. The is_* functions give you a boolean instead, and there are fifteen of them:

To check whether a value is an instance of a class, use instance_of(value, SomeClass), which also checks parent classes. Chapter 6 covers this.

3.3 · Learning the Language

Operators

Arithmetic

Operator Meaning Example
+ Addition 2 + 3 is 5
- Subtraction 5 - 2 is 3
* Multiplication 4 * 3 is 12
/ Division (always floating point) 7 / 2 is 3.5
// Floor division 7 // 2 is 3
% Remainder 7 % 3 is 1
** Exponentiation 2 ** 10 is 1024

/ never truncates. 7 / 2 is 3.5 even though both operands look like integers, because Zuri has only one number type. If you want an integer result, use //.

// rounds toward negative infinity, and the result of % has the same sign as the left operand:

% also works with numbers that aren't whole: 7.5 % 2 is 1.5.

Comparison

Operator Meaning
== Equal
!= Not equal
< <= > >= Ordering (numbers only)

== compares numbers, strings, lists and dictionaries by value, and everything else by identity. A class can change how its instances are compared by defining @eq.

== never converts types, so a string is never equal to a number.

The ordering operators only work with numbers. Comparing two strings with < raises a TypeError. Use compare() instead, which returns -1, 0 or 1:

Logical Operators

Zuri uses words for these:

Operator Meaning
and True when both sides are truthy
or True when either side is truthy
! Negation

and and or short-circuit, and they return one of their operands rather than a boolean:

That's why var name = given or 'anonymous' works. Keep in mind that 0, NaN, '' and false are all falsy, so only use this idiom when none of those are valid values.

The Conditional Operator

cond ? a : b evaluates cond, and then evaluates only one of the two branches.

Bitwise Operators

Operator Meaning
& And
| Or
^ Exclusive or
~ Not
<< Left shift
>> Arithmetic right shift (keeps the sign)
>>> Logical right shift (fills with zeros)

Bitwise operators work on the integer value of a number, and on bigints.

Concatenation and Repetition

When one side of + is a string, + concatenates, and a number on the other side is converted to a string:

With lists, + concatenates and * repeats:

Dictionaries don't support +. Use extend() instead.

If you use an operator with types it doesn't support, you get a TypeError that shows the exact combination of types:

Classes can define what + and the other operators do for their instances. That's covered in Chapter 6.

Member Access, Indexing and Slicing

Syntax Meaning
x.name A member of an object, dictionary or module
x[key] Index with a computed key
x[a, b] Slice from a up to but not including b
x[, b] Slice from the start
x[a, ] Slice to the end
a..b A range

Negative indexes count back from the end, for both strings and lists.

Precedence

The table lists operators from highest to lowest precedence. Operators on the same row have equal precedence and associate from left to right, except for **, which associates from right to left.

Level Operators
1 Literals, (...), [...], {...}, self, parent
2 ..
3 . () []
4 ++ --
5 **
6 ! - ~ (unary)
7 * / // %
8 + -
9 << >> >>>
10 &
11 ^
12 |
13 < <= > >= == !=
14 and
15 or
16 ? :
17 = and the compound assignment operators

** follows the usual mathematical convention. It binds more tightly than multiplication and more tightly than a unary operator in front of it, and it groups from the right:

2 * 3 ** 2 means 2 * (3 ** 2), 2 ** 3 ** 2 means 2 ** (3 ** 2), and -2 ** 2 means -(2 ** 2). The exponent can have its own sign, so 2 ** -1 doesn't need parentheses. To raise a negative number to a power, write (-2) ** 2.

.. binds very tightly, to primary expressions only. 1 + 2..5 is parsed as 1 + (2..5), so put parentheses around a range whose endpoints are expressions.

Operators Zuri Doesn't Have

There's no in operator for checking membership, so use contains() instead. There's no optional chaining with ?. and no null coalescing with ??, but or handles the most common case. There's also no comma operator, and you can't use += on a member that doesn't exist yet.

3.4 · Learning the Language

Comments and Doc Blocks

Line Comments

A # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line:

Block Comments

/* ... */ can span as many lines as you like, and block comments nest:

Nesting matters for two reasons. You can comment out a section of code that already contains a block comment, and it works as you'd expect. But it also means that an unmatched /* inside a comment turns the rest of the file into a comment.

Doc Blocks

A block comment that starts with /** is a doc block. The parser keeps doc blocks in the syntax tree instead of throwing them away, which is how the zuri module can read a file's documentation without needing a separate parser. Put a doc block directly above the thing it documents:

The standard library uses these tags:

Tag Meaning
@param {type} name: description Describes one parameter
@returns type Describes the return value
@throws ErrorClass Names an error the function can raise
@note Something the caller needs to know
@default The default value of a parameter

Two habits from the standard library are worth copying. Document the default value of every optional parameter, and describe what happens in edge cases, such as an empty input, a length of zero or a value that's out of range. If a caller would otherwise have to find something out by trial and error, put it in the doc block.

Doc blocks aren't only for people reading the source. Because the parser keeps them, programs can read them too. zuri.parse() returns each doc block as a DocBlock node placed just before the declaration it documents, which is all you need to build a simple documentation generator in a few dozen lines. Chapter 21 shows how.

Writing Good Comments

A good comment explains why the code does something. The code itself already shows what it does:

3.5 · Learning the Language

Control Flow

Control flow is how a program decides what to run next. You might want to run some code only when a condition is true, keep running it until a condition becomes false, or run it once for each item in a collection. Zuri has seven statements for this, and this section covers all of them.

Blocks and Single Statements

Every control flow statement has a body, which is either a block in braces or a single statement:

Both forms are valid. if, else, while, do, for and the when branches of a using statement all accept either one.

The exception is iter. Its body has to be a block, because otherwise the semicolons in its header could be confused with the statement that follows:

The standard library and the examples in this book use braces for every body except short when branches. With braces, it's easy to turn a one-line body into a three-line one later, and the structure of nested statements is easier to see. This is only a convention, though, so use whichever form reads better in your code.

if / else

There's no elif. else if is simply two keywords, which works because the body of an else can itself be an if statement.

The condition can be any expression. It's checked for truthiness, so it doesn't have to be a bool:

This is convenient, but it's also the most common source of bugs in new Zuri code, because a perfectly valid 0 is falsy. Look at the table in Data Types again before you write if count or if position.

The Conditional Expression

? : is the expression version of if. Instead of choosing between two statements, it chooses between two values:

Conditional expressions can be nested, and they can span several lines. When you split one across lines, ? and : can go at the end of a line or at the start of the next one. Putting each operator at the start of its branch makes the structure easier to follow:

Use ? : when you need a value, and if when you want to do something. A conditional expression whose branches only exist for their side effects is harder to read than the if statement it replaced.

while

while checks its condition before each pass, so the body might not run at all:

do / while

do runs the body once before it checks the condition, so the body always runs at least once. This is useful when the condition depends on something the body computes:

The condition was false from the start, but the body still ran once.

iter

iter is the counting loop. Its header has three clauses separated by semicolons: an initializer, a condition and an update.

The initializer runs once. The condition is checked before each pass, and the update runs after each pass. A variable declared in the initializer belongs to the loop and doesn't exist after the loop ends.

The initializer can declare several variables, and the update can contain several expressions, separated by commas. The updates run in the order they're written:

All three clauses are optional:

iter ; ; { ... } loops forever, but while true is easier to read.

You can spread the header over several lines, which helps when the condition is long:

for / in

for loops over an iterable, such as a list, a dictionary, a string, a range, a byte stream, or an instance of any class that implements the iterator protocol.

With one variable, you get each value:

With two variables, you get the key first and the value second:

For a list, the key is the index. For a dictionary, it's the key, and for a string, it's the position of the character. Dictionaries are iterated in insertion order, as is anything else whose order is preserved.

Ranges don't include their upper bound:

The expression after in is evaluated only once, before the first pass. If you call a function there, it's called once, not once per element:

Chapter 6 shows how to make your own classes work with for by defining @key() and @value().

break and continue

continue skips to the next pass, and break exits the loop completely:

Both apply to the innermost loop, and Zuri doesn't have loop labels. To exit a nested loop, you can use a flag:

Or, more often, you can move the nested loop into a function and return from it:

The second version is better. Its name says what it's looking for, and there's no flag to keep in sync.

using / when

using compares one value against several possible values:

When a when lists several values, any one of them can match, so this when matches 'B' or 'C'. The first branch that matches runs, and then the statement ends. There's no fall-through, so you don't need break.

Matching uses the same equality as ==. That means using works with numbers, strings and booleans, and compares instances by identity, or with @eq if their class defines it.

default is optional. If nothing matches and there's no default, nothing happens:

A when branch can use a block when it needs more than one statement:

Use using whenever you need to choose between many outcomes based on one value. A chain of else if statements that compares the same variable again and again does the same job with more code.

assert

assert checks a condition and raises an AssertError if it's false:

The optional second argument is the message for the error:

Use assertions for things you believe are already true, meaning conditions that should never happen. Don't use them to check input that might really be wrong. Raise a ValueError for that instead. Chapter 7 explains the difference in more detail.

return

return exits the current function. It returns the value you give it, or nil if you don't give it one:

A function that reaches its closing brace without a return returns nil. There are no implicit returns, so the last expression in a function body isn't its return value.

return can only be used inside a function. At the top level of a script, it's a syntax error, because there's nothing to return from.

Chapter 4 · Learning the Language

Text, Numbers and Collections

Chapter 3 introduced the built-in types and showed how the operators work with them. This chapter goes into detail on the five types you'll use every day: strings, numbers, lists, dictionaries and ranges.

All five have one thing in common. In Zuri, behavior belongs to the value itself. Instead of len(x) or str.upper(x), you write x.length() and x.upper(). This is true for numbers as well, and the math functions are all available as methods:

Because the methods are called on the value, you can chain them, and a chain reads from left to right in the order the work happens:

Each section in this chapter covers the methods you should know by name, the ones whose behavior might surprise you, and the most common mistakes. Appendix E has the complete list, generated from the same documentation that ships with the runtime.

4.1 · Learning the Language

Strings

A Zuri string is UTF-8 text. Indexing, slicing and length() all work in characters rather than bytes, so a string of emoji behaves the way you'd expect.

You'll probably work with strings more than any other type, so this section starts with how to write them (quoting, escape sequences and interpolation) before moving on to what you can do with them.

String Literals

A string literal is written in single or double quotes:

The two styles are identical. Unlike in some other languages, they don't mean different things. Both process escape sequences, both support interpolation, and both can span several lines. The only difference is which quote character ends the string:

Choose whichever one saves you from escaping. A string that contains an apostrophe is easiest to write in double quotes, and one that contains a double quote is easiest in single quotes:

Most Zuri code, including the whole standard library, uses single quotes by default and switches to double quotes when the content needs it.

Multi-line Strings

A string literal can contain newlines directly. There's no special triple-quoted syntax and no line continuation character:

Everything between the quotes is part of the string, including indentation. If you indent a long string inside a function, the leading spaces on each line end up in the string too. For that reason, code that builds indented text is usually better off assembling it with join() than writing one long literal.

Escape Sequences

A backslash starts an escape sequence. These are all of them:

Escape Produces
\0 The null character, U+0000
\a The alert (bell) character, U+0007
\b Backspace, U+0008
\t Horizontal tab, U+0009
\n Line feed, U+000A
\v Vertical tab, U+000B
\f Form feed, U+000C
\r Carriage return, U+000D
\\ A single backslash
\' A single quote
\" A double quote
\${ A literal ${, with no interpolation
\xNN The byte with the hexadecimal value NN
\uNNNN The code point U+NNNN
\UNNNNNNNN The code point U+NNNNNNNN

The three numeric forms take exactly the number of hex digits shown (two, four and eight), and the digits can be uppercase or lowercase:

\u covers code points up to U+FFFF. Anything higher, such as emoji, most historic scripts and mathematical alphanumerics, needs \U with eight digits. Pad the value with leading zeros to fill them.

Unknown Escape Sequences

A backslash followed by a character that isn't in the table above is not an error, and it isn't silently removed either. Both the backslash and the character stay in the string:

The first line comes through unchanged. \d and \w aren't escape sequences, so both backslashes are kept, and that's why you can write regular expressions as ordinary strings.

The second line doesn't. \t is an escape sequence, so C:\temp becomes C: followed by a tab and emp. \n is an escape sequence too, so \notes becomes a newline followed by otes. That's two silent substitutions in a single path. The rule is simple but easy to forget: unknown escape sequences are left alone and known ones aren't, and nothing in the way you write them tells you which is which.

Windows paths and regular expressions are where this usually causes trouble. In both, double the backslashes:

Escaping Quotes

You only need to escape the quote character that would otherwise end the string:

Escaping the other quote character doesn't do anything useful. Since it isn't a known escape sequence, the backslash stays in the result:

That's another reason to pick the quote style that lets you write the text without escaping anything.

Interpolation

${...} inside a string evaluates the expression between the braces and inserts its text into the string:

Interpolation works with both quote styles, and it's how most Zuri code builds strings. Two sections from now, we'll look at +, which does the same job with more punctuation.

Using Any Expression

The braces can contain any expression, not just a variable name. Arithmetic, method calls, indexing, comparisons and conditional expressions all work:

Look at the third line. The quotes inside ${...} are the same quote character that started the string, and it still works. That's because the expression inside the braces is read as code, not as part of the text. You don't need to switch quote styles or escape anything to put a string literal inside an interpolation.

Nested Interpolation

A string literal inside ${...} is an ordinary string literal, so it can contain interpolations of its own, nested as deeply as you like:

This is more useful than it might sound. It lets a conditional inside a string produce formatted text instead of a single word, which you'll need often in messages meant for people to read:

There are three levels of interpolation here: the outer message, the branch that chooses between a count and "nothing new", and the branch that chooses between singular and plural. Each level is an ordinary string literal in an ordinary expression, and each one uses single quotes. The quotes never clash, because the expression inside ${...} is read as code.

Nesting is also handy inside a callback, where the inner string builds one piece of a larger result:

Deep nesting gets hard to read quickly. When a line like the message above becomes difficult to follow, move the inner parts into local variables on the lines before it. Both versions work the same way.

How Values Are Displayed

Interpolation displays a value the same way echo does:

You can't write a dictionary literal directly inside ${...}, because its closing brace would end the interpolation:

Assign it to a variable first, as in the example above. List literals don't have this problem, because ] and } are different characters.

There's one important exception that catches almost everyone at least once. Interpolating a class instance doesn't call its to_string() method:

You have to call the method yourself. The same applies to 'text ' + p. Neither interpolation nor + will call a method for you to get the text. If you want to_string() to run, call it. echo is the exception, through @to_string(), which is covered in Decorated Methods.

Writing a Literal ${

A backslash in front of ${ prevents interpolation, and the backslash itself is removed:

The escape sequence is a backslash, a dollar sign and a {. \\ is a separate escape sequence, so \\${x} gives you a backslash followed by the value of x. Anywhere else, \$ is an unknown escape sequence and keeps its backslash, which is how a regular expression can match a literal dollar sign:

A $ on its own has no special meaning, so you only need to escape the exact sequence ${:

Combining Strings

Concatenation with +

+ joins two strings together:

When one side is a string, the other side is converted to text first. This works whichever side the string is on, and for all built-in types:

Look at the second line again. 5 + 'n' gives '5n'. It's not an error, and it's not arithmetic. A string on either side turns the whole expression into concatenation. Keep this in mind when a value comes from a source you don't control:

The first line is string concatenation and the second is arithmetic, and nothing in the expression tells you which one you'll get. When a value needs to be a number, convert it as soon as it enters your program.

The one type that doesn't convert in a useful way is a class instance:

Concatenating the instance directly would give you <instance of Point>, for the same reason as with interpolation: Zuri doesn't call to_string() for you.

Concatenation or Interpolation?

Both produce the same string, so choose whichever is easier to read:

Interpolation is usually better when there's more than one value to insert. The literal text stays in one piece, you don't end up with lots of quotes, and you can't accidentally lose a separator between two + signs. Use + when you're joining just two pieces, or when one of them is a variable that already holds a complete string.

Repetition with *

* repeats a string a given number of times:

The second line shows why this operator is useful. Separators, horizontal rules, indentation and padding each become one short expression instead of a loop.

Here are the exact rules for the count:

  • A count of 1 returns the string unchanged.
  • A count of 0 returns an empty string.
  • A negative count also returns an empty string instead of raising an error.
  • A fractional count is truncated toward zero, so * 2.7 repeats the string twice.

Watch out for the negative case. '-' * (width - label.length()) quietly produces nothing when the label is longer than the width, and there's no error to tell you. When the count is calculated, clamp it:

Unlike +, the order matters for repetition. The string has to be on the left:

Building a String From Many Pieces

When you have more than a few pieces, neither operator is a good fit. Collect the pieces in a list and call join():

join() is a method of the separator, not of the list. It converts each element to text as it goes, so a list of numbers can be joined just as easily as a list of strings:

join() also puts the separator only between elements, never at the beginning or end. That's exactly the part that hand-written loops tend to get wrong for the last item.

Inspecting Strings

index_of() returns -1 when there's no match. It accepts an optional second argument that sets where the search starts.

last_index_of() searches from the end instead, which is what you want when the separator you care about is the last one:

Both methods take a second argument, and in both cases it limits where a match can start. Together, they split a string at an index: for any n, index_of(str, n) finds the first match at or after n, and last_index_of(str, n) finds the last match at or before n.

There's also a set of methods that test character classes. Each one returns true when every character in the string matches:

The full set is is_alpha, is_alnum, is_number, is_lower, is_upper and is_space, along with is_empty.

Changing Case

capitalize() converts the first character to uppercase and the rest to lowercase. title() does the same for every word.

When you compare text entered by users, use case_fold() instead of lower(). Case folding is the Unicode operation designed for case-insensitive matching, and it handles cases that simple lowercasing gets wrong:

Trimming and Padding

Called without an argument, all three methods remove whitespace: spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, vertical tabs and form feeds. If you pass a string, they remove any of the characters in it, in any order, so '-=hi=-'.trim('-=') gives hi.

lpad and rpad take a target width and an optional fill character, which defaults to a space. If the string is already as wide as the target or wider, it's returned unchanged.

Splitting and Joining

join is a method of the separator, not of the list. to_list() splits a string into single characters. lines() splits on newlines, and handles both \n and \r\n.

Replacing Text

replace() replaces every occurrence. The pattern can be a regular expression, and the replacement can refer to capture groups with $1, $2 and so on:

The optional third argument turns off regular expression handling, so a pattern that would otherwise be treated as a regular expression is matched literally, delimiters and all:

When the replacement depends on what was matched, use replace_with(), which calls a function for each match:

Regular Expressions

Zuri uses PCRE2 for regular expressions, the same engine used by PHP, R and many other tools. It's the full library, not a subset, so named groups, backreferences, lookahead, lookbehind, atomic groups, possessive quantifiers, conditionals and recursion all work as the PCRE2 documentation describes.

This section explains how to write a pattern in Zuri, which methods accept patterns, what each modifier does, and the few places where Zuri behaves differently from what you might expect. It doesn't teach regular expression syntax itself, but any PCRE or Perl reference applies as it is.

Writing a Pattern

A pattern is an ordinary string. Its first character must be a non-word character, and the same character closes the pattern. Any modifier letters go after the closing delimiter:

A non-word character is anything other than a letter, a digit or an underscore. A forward slash is the usual choice, and it's what every example in this book uses, but you can pick a different delimiter. That's useful when the pattern itself contains a lot of slashes:

Because a pattern is a string, Zuri's own escape rules are applied to its backslashes first. In practice, this rarely causes problems, because \d, \w, \s, \b and \S aren't escape sequences in strings and are passed through unchanged. The exceptions are the letters that are escape sequences: \t, \n, \r, \f, \v, \a, \b, \0, \x and \u. \t and \n mean the same thing in both strings and patterns, so they're harmless. The one that will catch you out is \b, which means a word boundary in a pattern but a backspace in a string:

Whenever a pattern needs \b, write it with a double backslash.

Plain Strings Are Matched Literally

All of the methods in this section also accept a plain string, which they treat as a literal substring rather than a pattern:

The first call replaced the single period. The second call compiled . as a pattern, where it means "any character", so it replaced all three characters.

The only thing that decides this is whether the string looks like a delimited pattern. If you're working with text from elsewhere that might happen to look like one, pass false as the third argument to replace() to turn off pattern handling:

With false, the delimiters are matched as ordinary characters.

Methods That Accept Patterns

There are exactly five:

Method What it does with the pattern
match(pattern) Returns the first match and its groups, or false
matches(pattern) Returns every match, grouped by capture group
replace(pattern, with, use_regex) Replaces every match
replace_with(pattern, callback) Replaces every match with the result of a function call
split(pattern) Splits the string at every match

All the other methods, such as contains(), index_of(), count(), starts_with(), ends_with() and trim(), only accept literal strings. If you pass them something that looks like a regular expression, they search for those exact characters:

All three calls searched for the six-character string /[0-9]/, which doesn't appear in a1b. If you need a pattern in a case like this, use match() instead.

match() and matches()

match() finds the first match and returns it in a dictionary under the key 0. When nothing matches, it returns false, not nil:

Both false and nil are falsy, so if s.match(p) { ... } works as expected. Comparing the result with nil doesn't, and that's the most common regular expression mistake in Zuri code.

The dictionary also contains the pattern's capture groups, each under its number, and named groups under their names as well. A group that doesn't take part in the match is nil:

matches() finds every match and groups the results by capture group. Key 0 holds the full matches, key 1 holds the matches for the first group, and so on. Each value is a list, and the lists line up with each other:

In the second result, the first match is a1, with groups a and 1, and the second match is b2, with groups b and 2. Read down each list, not across them.

When nothing matches, matches() returns {0: []} instead of false. Since the two methods behave differently here, check the result of matches() by calling is_empty() on key zero:

Capture Groups in a Replacement

In replace(), you refer to a capture group with $1, $2 and so on:

Don't write ${1}. The braced form is Zuri's own string interpolation, and it's evaluated before replace() sees the string. The expression 2 evaluates to the number two, so by the time the replacement string reaches replace(), it's already '2, 1':

Always use the plain $1 form. This is one of the few places where Zuri's interpolation syntax clashes with another syntax, and when it goes wrong, there's no error to warn you.

Named Groups

Named groups are supported in patterns, because PCRE2 supports them:

However, the results are keyed by position, not by name. A group's name documents what it's for and lets a backreference such as \k<first> refer to it, but it doesn't change the keys in the result. To find the group you want, count the groups.

Computing the Replacement

When the replacement depends on what was matched, replace_with() calls a function for each match:

The function receives the full match first, then one argument for each capture group, then the position of the match, and finally the whole string being searched. You only need to declare the arguments you use, because extra arguments are ignored:

Splitting on a Pattern

split() accepts a pattern, which lets you split on "one or more of something" instead of an exact separator:

Modifiers

Modifier letters go after the closing delimiter, in any order and combination. For example, /[a-z]+/mi is both multi-line and case-insensitive.

Modifier Effect
i Case-insensitive matching.
m Multi-line mode: ^ and $ match at the start and end of every line, not just the start and end of the string.
s Dot-all mode: . also matches newlines.
x Extended mode: whitespace in the pattern is ignored unless escaped, and # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line.
u Unicode mode: \d, \w, \s and similar classes match Unicode characters instead of only ASCII.
U Ungreedy mode: quantifiers are lazy by default, and a ? after one makes it greedy.
A Anchored mode: a match is only accepted if it starts exactly where the search started.
J Allows two capture groups in the same pattern to have the same name.

Here's each of them in use:

Compare the last two results. The pattern matched when the text was at the start of the string and failed when it wasn't, which is what A is for. Without A, the second one would have matched at position one.

u deserves a closer look too. Without it, \w only matches ASCII, so é isn't a word character. With it, Unicode properties apply, and é is a word character. Matching is always done per character rather than per byte, so positions are correct on text with multi-byte characters, with or without u.

Differences From PCRE2

PCRE2's D (dollar end only) modifier has no effect in Zuri. $ always matches before a trailing newline as well as at the very end of the string, and you can't change that. The D letter is accepted rather than rejected, so a pattern that uses it still compiles and runs. It just doesn't do anything.

The same goes for any other modifier letter that Zuri doesn't recognize. It's accepted and ignored instead of raising an error. That means a typo in a modifier goes unnoticed, so keep it in mind if a pattern behaves as though one of its flags isn't set.

All the other modifiers in the table are supported and behave as the PCRE2 documentation describes.

Invalid Patterns

If PCRE2 can't compile a pattern, Zuri raises an error that includes the pattern and PCRE2's own explanation:

Patterns are compiled once and then reused, so using the same pattern repeatedly in a loop has no extra cost after the first time.

Converting Strings

to_number() accepts an optional base. ord() takes a string of exactly one character and returns its code point, and chr() converts a number back into a character.

to_number() Never Fails

This is the one conversion rule you should memorize. to_number() never raises an error, and it never returns NaN. It reads the first number in the string, and if the string doesn't contain a number at all, the result is zero:

Look at the last three lines. Anything around the number is ignored, so '12abc' gives 12, the spaces in ' 7 ' don't matter, and only the first number is read, however many follow it.

This can work for you or against you. '3 apples' giving 3 is usually what you want, but '2026-09-16' giving 2026 usually isn't. A number starts at a digit, or at a sign or decimal point immediately before a digit, so '-5' is negative five, while 'a - 42', where the sign is separated from the digits, is 42.

Since there's no error to catch and no special value to check for, an empty form field and a field containing '0' give you the same number, and so do 'eighty' and '0'. When the difference matters, check the text before you convert it:

is_number() is stricter than its name suggests. It's only true for a string made entirely of digits, so '3.5' and '-5' both fail. For anything other than unsigned integers, a regular expression is the more reliable check.

Iterating Over a String

Strings are iterable, one character at a time, and you can use the same four approaches that work for lists.

for, One Character at a Time

This is the approach to use by default. Each ch is a one-character string, not a code point number. Use ord() if you need the number.

for With Two Variables, for the Position

The key comes first and the value second. For a string, the key is the position of the character.

iter, When You Need Control Over the Position

s[i] indexes by character rather than by byte, so this works correctly on text that isn't ASCII. Use iter when you need to skip ahead, go backward, or look at s[i + 1] inside the loop.

each(), With a Function

As with the other types, the function receives the value first and the index second. Note that this is the opposite of the order used by for.

each_line() and lines(), for Line-Based Text

each_line() calls a function once for each line, and lines() gives you all of the lines as a list, so you can loop over them, filter them or count them. Both split on \n and \r\n, so they work with files written on any platform.

Comparing Strings

== compares two strings by value, which is nearly always what you want:
