The ordering operators are different. <, <=, > and >= only work with numbers, and using one to compare two strings raises a TypeError. Use compare() instead, which returns -1, 0 or 1:

A three-way result like this is what a sort comparison function needs. compare() compares strings by code point, so the result is stable and doesn't depend on the locale.

Strings Are Immutable

Every method in this section returns a new string. None of them change the string in place:

It's important to keep this in mind, because it leads to the most common string mistake of all:

The first trim() call created a trimmed string and then threw it away. Assign the result to a variable, or chain another call onto it.

Because strings are immutable, you never need to copy one before passing it somewhere. Nothing you pass a string to can change the string you still have.

Example: Parsing a Configuration File

Here's a small parser that uses most of what this section has covered. It takes key = value configuration text and turns it into a dictionary, skipping blank lines and comments and accepting any spacing around the =.

A few things in this code are worth pointing out. lines() handles both \n and \r\n, so the same code can read a file written on Windows. The result of index_of() is compared with -1 explicitly rather than tested for truthiness, because 0 is falsy and 0 is a valid position. And every value starts out as a string, because the input is text. to_number() is how you turn it into a number.

4.2 · Learning the Language

Numbers

Zuri has a single number type, number, which is a 64-bit IEEE 754 double. Whole numbers and fractions are the same type. What usually matters is whether a particular value happens to be a whole number.

Number Literals

There are five ways to write a number literal, and they all produce the same type:

0b is binary, 0c is octal and 0x is hexadecimal. The letters in a hexadecimal literal can be uppercase or lowercase, so 0xff and 0xFF are the same number. Note that octal uses 0c, not the 0o that some other languages use.

The exponent form uses e or E, and the exponent can be negative. 1e3 is 1000, and the part before the e doesn't need a decimal point. The exponent is only a way of writing the literal, though. The value doesn't remember it, so 6.02e23 prints in full decimal form.

Digit Separators

Underscores between digits are ignored, which makes long numbers easier to read:

Separators only work in decimal literals. 0xdead_beef and 0b1010_1010 are syntax errors.

Literals That Aren't Allowed

A literal needs a digit on both sides of the decimal point, so neither of these parses:

Write 0.5 and 5.0 instead. The second case matters more than you might think, because 5. is also how a method call on a literal begins, as you'll see two sections from now.

Math Methods

Everything you'd normally find in a math library is available as a method on the number:

log() is the natural logarithm. There are also log1p() and expm1(), which are more precise for values close to zero.

All of the trigonometric functions are available: sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan and atan2, along with the hyperbolic sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh and atanh.

Calling a Method on a Literal

You can call a method directly on a number literal, without parentheses or a temporary variable. This works in every base, with or without a decimal point:

The one case that needs parentheses is a negative literal. A method call binds more tightly than unary minus, so the minus applies to the result of the call instead of the number:

-3.abs() means -(3.abs()), which is -3. When the number is negative, put it in parentheses, or assign it to a variable first so the question doesn't come up:

The same goes for any expression you want to call a method on. Wrap it in parentheses, because otherwise the call only applies to the last part of the expression.

Rounding

trunc() and int() both remove the fractional part, rounding toward zero.

round() rounds halves away from zero:

fixed() rounds to a given number of decimal places and returns a number:

fraction() returns the digits after the decimal point as a whole number:

Sign, Magnitude and Comparison

sign() returns -1, 0 or 1.

Bases and Characters

chr() converts a code point into a one-character string, and 'A'.ord() does the reverse.

Special Values

NaN is falsy, like zero, so var x = a / b or fallback replaces the NaN from 0 / 0 with the fallback. Use is_nan() when you need to tell NaN and zero apart.

As the IEEE standard requires, NaN isn't equal to itself, so x == x is false only when x is NaN.

Other Methods

factorial() works on small integers, and to_string(), to_bool() and to_bigint() convert numbers to other types.

The math Module

Constants are defined in the math module, since a constant doesn't belong to any particular number:

The module also defines LOG_2, LOG_10, LOG_2_E, LOG_10_E, ROOT_2, ROOT_3 and ROOT_HALF.

Bigints

When 2^53 isn't big enough, use a bigint. To write one, add an n suffix:

Bigints have arbitrary precision. They never overflow, and they never lose a digit.

They also never mix with numbers automatically:

Convert between them explicitly, in whichever direction you need:

Converting to number loses precision once you go past 2^53, which is exactly why bigints exist. Converting the other way is always exact.

Type annotations keep the two types separate as well. bigint is a type name alongside number and int, and it only accepts bigints:

The number theory methods are where bigints really earn their keep:

modpow(exponent, modulus) is the operation that public-key cryptography is built on, and it's computed without ever calculating the full power. modinv returns the modular multiplicative inverse.

There are also nth_root(), cbrt(), bit(), set_bit(), trailing_zeros(), is_zero(), is_even(), is_odd(), abs(), sign(), max(), min() and pow(), as well as bin(), oct() and hex().

Use a bigint when you need exact values beyond 2^53, for example in cryptography, for money stored in cents, for factorials, or for identifiers that have to survive a round trip unchanged. For everything else, such as measurements, coordinates, counters and ratios, use a number.

4.3 · Learning the Language

Lists

A list is an ordered sequence of values. It can hold values of any type, including other lists, and it grows and shrinks as you add and remove elements.

Lists have 40 methods, which fall into six groups: reading, searching, adding and removing, ordering, transforming and iterating. This section goes through them in that order. Throughout, keep an eye on whether a method changes the list you call it on or returns a new one. Zuri's lists have both kinds of methods, and you can't tell which is which from the name.

Reading Elements

Indexing

Indexes start at zero, and negative indexes count back from the end:

l[-1] is the last element, which saves you from writing l[l.length() - 1] all the time.

Using an index that's out of range raises an error instead of returning nil:

get() can return a fallback value, but only if you give it one. With just one argument, get(i) raises an error in the same way as l[i]:

Slicing

l[a, b] returns a new list with the elements from a up to but not including b:

You can leave out either bound. l[, b] starts at the beginning, and l[a, ] goes to the end. Negative bounds count from the end, as they do for indexes.

Slices check their bounds in the same way as indexes. If a slice goes past the end, it raises an error instead of returning what it can:

Since a slice's upper bound is exclusive, length() is always a valid upper bound. l[0, l.length()] is the whole list, and l[3, 3] on a three-element list is an empty list rather than an error.

String slicing follows the same rule, which is why Strings uses s[split_at + 1, s.length()] to mean "the rest of the string" instead of using some large number.

A slice is a copy, so changing one doesn't affect the other:

Nested Lists

A list can contain other lists, and you can chain indexes to reach into them:

grid.length() counts the rows, not the individual elements. There's no two-dimensional index syntax. grid[1, 0] is a slice from row one to row zero, so it's empty.

Combining Lists

Concatenation with +

+ combines two lists into a new one and leaves the original lists unchanged:

That's how + differs from extend(). a + b creates a third list, while a.extend(b) changes a in place and returns it. Use + when you want to keep the original lists, and extend() when you're adding to an existing list.

Repetition with *

* repeats a list a given number of times:

[0] * 5 is the usual way to create a list of a fixed size filled with a starting value, so you don't need to write a loop for it.

The count works the same way as it does for strings. Zero or any negative number gives an empty list, and a fractional count is truncated.

There's one trap to watch for. Repetition copies the elements, so when an element is itself a list, every copy refers to the same list:

A single assignment changed every row, because there's really only one row. To build nested lists, use a loop or map() instead:

Comparing Lists

== compares lists by value, element by element, however deeply they're nested:

Both the order and the length have to match. To compare two lists as sets, sort copies of them first, or use the set module described in Chapter 13.

Searching

index_of() returns -1 if the value isn't in the list. last_index_of() searches from the end:

Both methods take a second argument that limits where a match can be, so together they split the list at an index. index_of(x, n) finds the first match at or after n, and last_index_of(x, n) finds the last match at or before n. Both compare by value, so you can search a list of dictionaries using a dictionary literal.

Adding and Removing Elements

These methods change the list in place:

Method Effect
append(v) Adds v to the end
insert(v, at) Inserts v at the given position
extend(other) Appends every element of another list
pop() Removes and returns the last element
shift() Removes and returns the first element
remove(v) Removes the first element equal to v
remove_at(i) Removes the element at position i
delete(from, to) Removes an inclusive range and returns how many elements were removed
clear() Removes every element

Note that delete() takes a from and a to position, both inclusive, and returns the number of elements it removed, not the list.

Sorting and Reversing

Take a close look at those two methods. sort() changes the list and returns it. reverse() returns a new list and leaves the original unchanged. This difference is the most common cause of list bugs in Zuri code.

To sort by something else, pass a comparison function. It receives two items and returns a negative number if the first item should come first, a positive number if the second should come first, or zero to keep their current order:

You can't subtract strings, so to compare text in a comparison function, use compare(), which returns exactly what a comparison function needs: people.sort(@(a, b) => a.name.compare(b.name)).

Transforming Lists

All of these methods return a new list and leave the original unchanged:

compact() removes nil elements:

reduce() combines the elements of a list into a single value. If you don't give it an initial value, it starts with the first element:

partition() splits a list in one pass, and returns the matching elements first:

Finding Elements

Testing Every Element

some() stops at the first element that matches, and every() stops at the first one that doesn't.

Iterating Over a List

There are four ways to visit every element, and each one suits a different situation. Choose based on what you need inside the loop.

for, When You Only Need the Values

This is the default choice. Use it whenever the position doesn't matter.

for With Two Variables, When You Also Need the Index

With two variables, you get the key first and the value second, and for a list the key is the index. There's no need to call length() or keep a counter yourself.

iter, When You Need to Control the Position

iter takes more typing, so it's only worth using when you don't simply move forward one element at a time, for example when going backward, stepping by two, comparing each element with its neighbor, or changing the index inside the loop.

each(), When You Already Have a Function

each() takes a function, which makes it easy to combine with other methods. You can chain it after map() or filter() without a temporary variable, and you can pass it a function you've already defined by name.

Pay attention to the argument order. each() passes the value first and the index second, which is the opposite of for. All of the list callbacks in this chapter, including map, filter, find, some and every, take (value, index), so there's only one rule to remember. for loops over key and value pairs, while each calls a function with each value and also tells it the position.

break and continue work in for and iter loops, but not inside an each() callback. There, return only ends the current call, not the whole iteration. If you need to stop early, use a loop instead, or find() or some(), which stop by themselves.

Combining

zip() pairs up the elements of two lists. zip_from() takes a list of lists and zips all of them together.

Lists Are Passed by Reference

Assigning a list to another variable doesn't copy it:

Use clone() when you need a separate copy. The copy is shallow, which means any nested lists inside it are still shared.

Replacing the top-level 3 only changed the copy. Appending to the nested list changed both, because both lists refer to the same inner list. If you need a deep copy, copy each level you care about yourself.

Summary: Which Methods Change the List

You'll probably want to refer back to this table.

Changes the list Returns a new list
append, insert, extend map, filter, find_all
pop, shift, remove, remove_at unique, compact, take
delete, clear reverse, clone, zip, zip_from
sort partition

sort() is the one that trips people up. It's in the left column, but it also returns the list, so var sorted = items.sort() sorts items too. If you need both the original order and the sorted order, clone the list first:

Example: A Simple Report

Here's a small report generator. It takes a list of records, drops the incomplete ones, groups the rest, and prints a summary. It uses filter, map, reduce, sort and each together, which is how you'll usually see them.

east doesn't appear in the report at all, rather than appearing with a total of zero. Its only record was filtered out before anything was added up, so the key was never created. That's usually what you want in a report. If it isn't, add every region to the dictionary first.

Two other details are worth pointing out. totals.get(r.region, 0) provides a starting value for a key that doesn't exist yet, which is what lets the dictionary act as an accumulator. And totals.to_list()[0] gets the keys (to_list() returns the keys and the values as two parallel lists), which are then sorted so the report always comes out in the same order, regardless of the order the records arrived in.

4.4 · Learning the Language

Dictionaries

A dictionary maps keys to values and remembers the order in which the keys were added.

A key written as a bare word is a string, so { name: ... } and { 'name': ... } are the same. Keys can also be numbers:

A key written as a bare identifier is always taken literally, as that name. To compute a key, write it as an expression that the parser can't mistake for a name. In practice, that means wrapping it in parentheses:

Assigning with brackets is often clearer:

Shorthand Keys

When a key has the same name as the variable that holds its value, you only need to write it once:

{ name, age } means exactly the same as { name: name, age: age }. This is especially common in functions that build a result from local variables they've just computed, and Zuri code uses the shorthand whenever the names match.

Nesting

A value can be another dictionary or a list, nested to any depth. You can chain accesses to reach nested values:

You can mix dot and bracket access freely, because they do the same thing. Use a dot when the key is a fixed identifier, and brackets when it's computed, contains punctuation or is a number.

Reading Values

Dot access and bracket access do the same thing:

Reading a key that doesn't exist raises a PropertyError. Use get() if the key might be missing:

Without a fallback value, get() returns nil for a missing key.

Writing Values

Assigning with a dot, with brackets or with set() all do the same thing, and all three create the key if it doesn't exist yet. add() is another name for set().

To remove a key:

remove() returns the value that was stored under the key.

clear() removes every key.

Merging Dictionaries

extend() changes the dictionary it's called on, and when both dictionaries have the same key, the value from the argument wins. Dictionaries don't support +.

Transforming Dictionaries

compact() removes entries whose value is nil.

All of these callbacks receive the value first and the key second, the same order that list callbacks use.

Iterating Over a Dictionary

All of the approaches below visit the entries in insertion order, which is the order in which keys were first added, not the order in which they were last updated.

for With Two Variables

You get the key first and the value second. This is what you'll want nearly every time.

for With One Variable Gives You the Values

This is worth pointing out, because in several other languages the equivalent loop gives you the keys. In Zuri, a single variable always receives the values, whatever you're iterating over.

iter Over the Keys, When You Need an Index

A dictionary doesn't have positional indexes of its own, so iter loops over the list of keys instead. Use this when you need to number the output or look ahead to the next key.

each(), With a Function

The callback receives the value first and the key second. That's the opposite of for, but it's the same as every other each() in the language.

Iterating Over Only the Keys or the Values

keys() and values() both return an ordinary list, so everything in Lists applies. You can sort, filter or reduce them. Sorting keys() is how you get output in a predictable order, whatever order the keys were added in.

Converting Dictionaries

to_list() returns two parallel lists, one of keys and one of values, rather than a list of pairs. find_key() searches by value and returns the first key that holds it.

Dictionaries of Functions

A dictionary value can be a function, which turns the dictionary into a dispatch table: a set of named behaviors that you can choose between at run time by looking up a name. This is what you use in Zuri instead of eval(), so it's worth getting to know well.

The three entries are equivalent. The first is a named function, the second is an arrow function, and the third is an anonymous function with a body.

Calling a Stored Function

This surprises a lot of people, so let's start with it. You can't call a stored function with a dot in one step:

A dot followed by a call looks for a method of the dictionary itself, such as length(), keys() or get(), not for a value stored under that key. Dictionaries don't have a method called plus, so the call fails.

There are two ways that do work. You can read the function into a variable first:

Or you can use brackets and call the result:

Use the bracket form when the key is computed, which is the whole point of a dispatch table:

Avoid Keys That Are Method Names

When you use a dot call, the dictionary's own methods take priority over its keys. If you store a function under add, keys, get, length or the name of any other method, the call will succeed but do the wrong thing:

d.add(1, 2) called the dictionary's own add() method, which is another name for set(). So it stored the key 1 with the value 2 and returned nil. No error was raised, and the only sign that something went wrong is the extra key in the output.

Two habits will keep you out of trouble: use bracket calls for dispatch tables, and don't use method names as keys. Appendix E lists all of the names that dictionaries already use.

Example: A Command Dispatcher

A dispatch table usually consists of a table of handlers, a lookup with a fallback, and a call:

commands.get(args[0], _unknown) does most of the work. If the key exists, you get its handler. If it doesn't, you get the fallback. That means you don't need a separate contains() check or a branch for the error case.

The important thing is that only the handlers in the table can ever run. Whatever the user types, it selects one of the four functions you wrote, or the fallback. That's the difference between a program that handles input and a program that executes it, and it's why Zuri doesn't have eval(). Chapter 21 explains the reasoning.

Storing Methods

zuri.reflect.bind_method() stores an instance's method in a table while keeping the instance attached to it:

The bound method remembers its instance, so calling it through the table updates the counter it came from.

Comparing Dictionaries

== compares dictionaries by value, and the order of the keys doesn't matter:

A dictionary remembers its insertion order when you iterate over it, but two dictionaries with the same entries in a different order are still equal. This is the opposite of lists, where order is part of what makes two lists equal.

Dictionaries Are Passed by Reference

As with lists, assigning a dictionary to another variable shares it rather than copying it. clone() gives you a shallow copy.

Dictionaries or Classes?

A dictionary is a good fit for data with a variable set of keys, such as configuration, a parsed JSON document or a set of HTTP headers. When the keys are fixed and there's behavior attached to them, use a class instead. Chapter 6 covers the difference.

Example: Analyzing a Log

Dictionaries are well suited to counting, grouping and indexing. This example does all three with a list of log lines. It counts how many times each level appears, groups the messages by level, and builds an index that maps each request ID to the line that mentions it.

There are four habits here that are worth copying.

counts.get(level, 0) + 1 is the usual way to count. Because get() has a fallback, you never have to check whether the key exists before adding to it.

if !grouped.contains(level) { grouped[level] = [] } is the usual way to group. You have to write it out, because get() would return a new default list each time instead of one you can keep appending to.

grouped.ERROR and by_request.a1 read keys with a dot, which works because both keys are valid identifiers. If a key were computed or contained unusual characters, you'd need brackets, as in by_request['b2'].

Finally, the order is preserved throughout. counts lists INFO, WARN and ERROR in the order those levels first appeared, not in alphabetical or random order.

4.5 · Learning the Language

Ranges and Iteration

Ranges

a..b creates a range, which represents the integers from a up to but not including b.

.. binds more tightly than a method call, so you can call a method on a range directly without parentheses:

You only need parentheses when the bounds are themselves expressions, because .. only accepts primary expressions: (n * 2)..(n * 3).

Property accesses and method calls are expressions too, so 0..self.size and 0..items.length() mean (0..self).size and (0..items).length(). If you want the bound to be the property instead of applying it to the range, write 0..(self.size) and 0..(items.length()).

This is a consequence of the previous rule. .. has to bind more tightly than . so that 1..10.step(3) creates a range with a step, and once it does, 0..self.step(5) can't mean the instance's own step method. The parentheses make it clear which one you mean, because the compiler has no way of guessing.

range() returns the distance between the two bounds.

A range is a value in its own right, not just loop syntax. You can store it, pass it to a function and return it:

Counting Down

If you write the larger bound first, the range counts down:

The same rule applies in both directions: the first bound is included and the second isn't.

Steps

step() returns a new range with the given step size. get_step() returns the step, which is 1 by default.

to_list() turns a range into a list with a step of one, and ignores any step you've set:

Checking Whether a Value Is in a Range

within() checks a value against the bounds, including both of them. It works the same way regardless of direction, so 10..1.within(10) and 1..10.within(10) give the same answer:

This is different from iteration, which leaves out the upper bound. If you want to know whether a loop over the range would visit a particular number, compare it against lower() and upper() yourself.

Iterating Over a Range

With one variable, for gives you the values. With two, it gives you the position first and the value second:

The position always counts from zero, wherever the range starts. That's what makes it useful: 3..6 gives the values 3, 4 and 5 at positions 0, 1 and 2.

loop() takes a callback instead. It respects both the step and the direction:

An iter loop doesn't need a range at all. Its three clauses can express everything a range can, and more, since the step can be any expression:

Use a range with for when the bounds are what matter, and iter when the way you step through the values matters more.

Iterable Types

You can use for ... in with:

  • Lists, which give the index and the value
  • Dictionaries, which give the key and the value, in insertion order
  • Strings, which give the position and the character
  • Bytes, which give the index and the numeric value of the byte
  • Ranges, which give the position and the value
  • Any class that defines @key() and @value()

is_iterable() tells you whether a value can be iterated over:

The Iterator Protocol

There's nothing magic about for. Under the hood, it's a loop that makes two method calls.

For for value in thing, Zuri evaluates thing once, and then repeats these steps:

  1. key = thing.@key(key), starting with key set to nil
  2. If key is nil, stop
  3. value = thing.@value(key)
  4. Run the body

In other words, @key(previous) returns the key that comes after the previous one, or nil when there are no more, and @value(key) returns the value stored under that key.

All of the built-in types implement this protocol, and your own classes can too, as Chapter 6 shows.

Because the expression after in is evaluated only once, this is safe:

The function is called once, not once for every line.

Chapter 5 · Learning the Language

Functions

A function is a named piece of behavior with a list of parameters and a result. You've been calling functions since Chapter 1. This chapter is about writing your own.

In Zuri, functions are values. You can put one in a list, pass it to another function, return it from a function, store it in a dictionary, and call whatever you get back:

That's what makes map, filter, reduce, the callbacks throughout the standard library and the route handlers in Chapter 15 possible.

Look closely at those two calls. operations.twice reads the function from the dictionary, and then you call the value you read. You can't write operations.twice(5) in one step, because a dot followed by a call looks for a method of the dictionary, and dictionaries don't have a method called twice. Either read the function into a variable first, as above, or use brackets and call the result: operations['twice'](5).

This chapter covers how to declare functions, the different ways to write anonymous functions, how closures capture the variables around them, and the optional type annotations that ask the runtime to check arguments for you.

5.1 · Learning the Language

Defining Functions

Declaring a Function

A function declaration is def, followed by a name, a parameter list in parentheses and a block. You don't declare a return type, you don't need a forward declaration, and there's no separate signature.

A function without a return statement returns nil:

There are no implicit returns. The last expression in a function body isn't its return value, so if you want to return something, use return.

Argument Counts Aren't Checked

If you call a function with fewer arguments than it declares, the missing parameters are nil. If you call it with more, the extra arguments are ignored:

This is deliberate. It's how optional parameters work, since there's no syntax for default values in a parameter list. Instead, you set the default in the function body:

Watch Out for or in Defaults

Because the default comes from or, any argument that's falsy gets replaced by the default, even when it was passed on purpose. In Zuri, the falsy values include 0, NaN, '' and false:

The caller asked for no indentation and got two spaces. When a falsy value is a valid input, check for nil explicitly instead:

Use or for a default when a falsy value can only mean the argument is missing, as with a name, a path or a list. For numbers and booleans, use == nil.

If you want the runtime to reject a missing argument instead of using a default, add a type annotation to the parameter. Type Annotations explains how.

Variadic Functions

If the last parameter starts with ..., it collects all of the remaining arguments into a list:

There are three things to be clear about when it comes to what a variadic parameter receives.

It's always a list, even when no arguments were passed. count() gives you [], not nil, so you can safely call items.length() without checking first.

It collects arguments, not their contents. If you pass a list, that's one argument, and it ends up as a list nested inside the variadic list:

... marks a parameter, not an argument, so count(...list) doesn't parse. To call a function with a list of arguments, use apply():

If a function is meant to accept a collection, though, it's simpler to take the list as an ordinary parameter and avoid both.

Named parameters are filled first. A variadic parameter can come after named ones, and it receives whatever arguments are left over:

The variadic parameter has to be last. def mid(a, ...rest, b) is a syntax error, because there'd be no way to decide how many arguments rest should take.

A typical use is a function that formats any number of values:

Where a Function Is Visible

A def is scoped the same way as a var. At the top level of a file, it creates a module-level name. Anywhere else, it creates a local in the enclosing block, which goes away when the block ends:

A helper defined inside a function belongs to that function. Code outside the function can't call it, and it can't interfere with anything outside the function either.

This works in any block, not only in function bodies:

Helpers That Call Each Other

Helpers declared in the same block can call each other, in either order:

even refers to odd before odd is declared. This works because the compiler reserves a slot for every def in a block before it compiles any of them. The declaration isn't moved, though. Until the def line itself runs, the slot holds nil, so calling a helper from a line above its declaration raises an error.

A helper can also call itself:

Helpers Are Closures

A nested def is a closure over the local variables around it, and it can outlive the call that created it:

An anonymous function assigned to a var does the same job. It's usually the better choice when the helper is a single line, or when you're passing it straight to something else:

Use whichever reads better. A def gives the function a proper name in stack traces and can call itself without an extra var, while an anonymous function is shorter.

One Declaration per Name

Declaring two functions with the same name in the same scope is a compile error:

A different parameter list doesn't make it a different function. Zuri doesn't support overloading, so each name refers to exactly one function.

If you want one function to handle different kinds of input, make the extra parameters optional and check them in the body, as the greeting parameter above does.

The check applies per scope, just like it does for var. A function declared inside another function is a separate declaration in a separate scope, so the compiler allows it, and it shadows the outer function for as long as its scope lasts:

wrapper's own render is local to wrapper. It handles every call made inside that function and disappears when the call ends, leaving the module-level render unchanged.

Classes follow the same rule for their methods:

The only exception is the REPL. Typing a def again there replaces the previous version, because fixing what you just typed is exactly what the REPL is for.

Declaration Order

A function has to be declared before any top-level line that calls it:

Declarations aren't hoisted. They run in order, like everything else.

Inside a function body, this rule doesn't apply, because names are resolved when the call runs, not when the code is compiled. That's why mutual recursion works without a forward declaration:

is_even refers to is_odd before is_odd exists. That's fine, because the name is only looked up when is_even(10) runs, and by then both declarations have run.

Helpers nested inside a function get the same freedom in a different way, because their slots are all reserved before any of their bodies are compiled. Either way, what matters is that every declaration has run before the first call is made.

Functions as Values

A function is a value, so you can pass it around, store it and return it:

Function Metadata

Every callable value has these four methods:

arity() counts the declared parameters, including the variadic one, so for a variadic function, the arity is a minimum rather than an exact requirement.

Anonymous functions are named according to the order in which the compiler found them:

A method read from an instance keeps its instance, and counts it as a parameter:

hello() doesn't declare any parameters, but arity() returns 1, because the instance counts as the first parameter.

call()

call() calls a function with the arguments you pass to it:

call() takes the arguments one by one, just like a normal call. It doesn't spread a list, so add.call([2, 3]) passes a single argument, which is a list. It's useful when you only have the function as a value, such as a handler from a dictionary or a method from zuri.reflect, and the normal call syntax would be awkward to read.

Checking Whether Something Can Be Called

is_callable() returns true for anything you can call, including classes, since calling a class creates an instance. is_function() is narrower. It returns true for a def, an anonymous function or a built-in function, and false for a class.

Example: A Text Pipeline

Here's a small pipeline builder that uses most of this section: functions as values, a variadic parameter, a default value and a returned closure.

There are four things to notice.

pipeline() takes its stages as a variadic parameter and returns a closure over them, so each call returns a new function built for those particular stages.

Calling pipeline() without any arguments still works, because the variadic parameter is an empty list rather than nil, and a for loop over an empty list simply doesn't run.

The third stage is wrapped in @(t) => truncate(t, 12), because truncate takes two parameters while each stage takes only one. In languages with a spread operator, you might use that instead.

Finally, limit = limit or 20 is safe here only because 0 isn't a sensible limit. If it were, you'd need the == nil form instead.

5.2 · Learning the Language

Anonymous Functions and Closures

Syntax

There are two parts of an anonymous function that you can vary independently: how it starts and how its body is written. That gives you a small grid of options rather than a list to memorize.

The start. def is the keyword, and @ is its shorthand. They mean the same thing.

The body. A block in braces returns a value with return. An arrow returns the single expression that follows it.

When there are no parameters, you can also leave out the empty parentheses:

All eight forms create the same thing. Here's when to use each:

  • @(x) => expr for a callback that's a single expression. This is what most Zuri code uses, including the standard library.
  • @(x) { ... } when the body needs more than one statement.
  • def(x) { ... } when the function is long enough that you want it to look like the declarations around it.
  • @ => expr for a thunk, a value that's computed when it's needed and takes no arguments.

Here are the two most common forms as you'd typically see them:

The arrow form doesn't use return, because the expression is the return value. Mixing the two up is a mistake the compiler won't always catch. @(x) => return x doesn't parse, but @(x) { x } parses fine and returns nil.

Anonymous functions accept variadic parameters and type annotations in the same way as named functions:

The real error message contains a number instead of the N shown here. Anonymous functions are named @anonN, numbered in the order the compiler finds them in the file. This helps when one shows up in a stack trace, but don't rely on the number, because adding another anonymous function earlier in the file changes the numbers of all the ones after it.

Closures

A function keeps the variables it uses from its surroundings, and keeps them alive even after the enclosing function has returned:

a and b each have their own n, because each call to make_counter() created a new one.

Closures Capture Variables, Not Values

A closure captures the variable itself, not a copy of its value at that moment:

That's what makes accumulators work, and it's also why closures over loop variables can be surprising. If you want each iteration to capture its own value, declare a new variable inside the loop body:

captured is a new variable on each pass through the loop, so each closure gets its own.

Closures Over Parameters

Parameters are captured in the same way, which is the basis of partial application:

Recursive Anonymous Functions

An anonymous function doesn't have a name it can use to call itself. Assign it to a variable first:

The variable is captured by reference, so by the time the body runs, factorial has been assigned.

Comparing Functions

Functions are compared by identity, so two functions written separately are never equal, even if their bodies are identical.

Example: A Rate Limiter

Closures are most useful when a function needs to remember something between calls without storing it in a global variable. Here's a rate limiter. It returns a function that answers the question "am I allowed to do this now?", and it keeps its own count where nothing else can get at it.

The three functions share a single used variable, because they all closed over the same variable in the same call to make_limiter. Calling make_limiter again would create a second, independent set of three.

This is the closest you can get to a private field in Zuri without writing a class. A caller has no way to read or change used except through the three functions you gave them.

5.3 · Learning the Language

Type Annotations

Zuri is dynamically typed, but you can annotate parameters with types. An annotated parameter is checked on every call, and if the argument doesn't match, Zuri raises a TypeError that names the parameter and its position, and says what was actually passed.

Type Names

Name Accepts
any Anything, including nil
bool true or false
number Any number
int A number with no fractional part
bigint An arbitrary-precision integer
string A string
bytes A byte buffer
list A list
dict A dictionary
range A range
file A file handle
function A named or anonymous function
callable Anything that can be called, including classes
iterable Anything for can loop over
type A class
ClassName An instance of that class or one of its subclasses

Any other name is treated as the name of a class.

number and bigint are separate types in annotations, just as they are everywhere else. A parameter annotated as bigint rejects 10, and one annotated as number rejects 10n:

If a function really does accept either one, write bigint|number, and convert the value inside the function with to_bigint().

Annotated Parameters Are Required

A plain annotation makes the argument required. Leaving it out raises a TypeError, because the parameter receives nil:

That's how you get argument checking in a language that otherwise lets you call any function with any arguments.

Optional Parameters

To allow nil, put a ? in front of the type:

?any is the same as having no annotation at all, which is what unannotated parameters get.

Union Types

To accept several types, separate them with |:

The ? goes at the front and applies to the whole union, as in ?string|number.

Classes and Subclasses

A class name accepts instances of that class and of any class that inherits from it:

The name means the same as it would inside the function body, so the class can be declared in the same file, imported, or stored in a variable that the function can see:

This makes error handling easier to read, since all of the built-in errors are subclasses of Error:

Where You Can Use Annotations

You can annotate the parameters of a def, a method or an anonymous function.

The same syntax also works on var declarations and class fields:

An annotation on a variable describes what you intend to store in it, but it isn't checked at run time, so nothing stops you from putting a string in count. What it does is document the declaration and give tools something to work with. A linter, an editor's completion engine or a type checker can read the annotation, know what belongs in the variable, and flag an assignment that you'd otherwise have to spot by eye.

Annotate declarations for people and tools, and annotate parameters for the runtime.

When to Use Annotations

Annotations are optional, and a program that doesn't use them at all is perfectly normal Zuri. The real question is where they're most useful.

Annotate at the boundaries of your code. A function that receives data from outside your program, such as a request handler, a file parser or a public function in a module that other people import, is where a value of the wrong type first shows up. An annotation there replaces a confusing failure deep in the call stack with a clear error at the point where the bad value came in:

Notice how the work is divided. The annotation catches the wrong type, and the explicit check catches the wrong value. An annotation can never do the second job, because 70000 is a perfectly valid number.

Use annotations instead of manual type checks. If a function starts with if !is_string(x) { raise TypeError(...) }, it's doing by hand what an annotation does in one word, and the annotation gives a better error message:

Annotating internal helpers is up to you. A private function that's only called from three places in the same file, all of which you can see, gains less from annotations. Add them if they document something that isn't obvious, and leave them out if they don't.

Keep in mind that an annotation isn't a replacement for validation. text: string guarantees that you have a string, but not that the string is a valid email address, a correctly formatted date or a non-empty name. That's what the validate module is for, which is introduced in Chapter 13.

Chapter 6 · Learning the Language

Classes and Objects

A dictionary holds data. A class holds data together with the behavior that goes with it, under a name that you can check for and inherit from.

Three facts about Zuri classes come up throughout this chapter, so it's worth knowing them from the start.

The constructor is called @new. Methods whose names begin with @ are called decorated methods, and each one connects the class to part of the language's own syntax, such as construction, arithmetic, comparison, iteration or JSON encoding. There's a fixed set of them, and Decorated Methods covers them all.

Fields are accessed through self. Inside a method, self refers to the instance. A bare balance doesn't mean self.balance, and you don't declare self as a parameter either.

Classes are sealed. A class's fields and methods are fixed when the class is declared. Nothing at run time can add a new field to an instance or a new method to a class, and trying to do so raises an error instead of silently creating it. That rules out a whole category of bugs, since a misspelled field name is an error rather than a new field. It also rules out monkey patching, a technique that some languages depend on but Zuri doesn't support.

Zuri has single inheritance: a class can have at most one parent, which you write with <. There are no interfaces, mixins or abstract keyword. The following sections show what to use instead.

Sealed doesn't mean a class can never change, though. A separate declaration written with > instead of <, called a class extension, can add methods to an existing class, even one you didn't write. Class Extensions explains how.

6.1 · Learning the Language

Defining a Class

  • class Name { ... } declares a class. By convention, class names use PascalCase.
  • var inside the class body declares a field, with an optional default value. A field without a default starts out as nil.
  • A plain name(params) { ... } declares a method. Methods don't use the def keyword.
  • @new is the constructor.
  • self refers to the current instance.

Creating an Instance

To create an instance, call the class. There's no new keyword:

If the class doesn't have an @new method, calling it without arguments gives you an instance with every field set to its default value.

The Constructor

@new is the constructor. It runs once, when the class is called, and its job is to put the new instance into a usable state, as Account's constructor did above.

Constructors Are Optional

A class without an @new method is created with no arguments, and each field gets its declared default:

If you pass arguments to a class that has no @new, they're ignored rather than rejected, as they would be for a function.

Constructors Can Declare Fields

self.x = value inside @new declares a field. This is the only place in the language where an assignment creates a member, and it exists so that a constructor doesn't have to repeat every field as a var line above it:

distance was never declared with var, but it's still a real field.

This only works in the body of @new itself. If a constructor delegates its setup to a helper method, the fields that helper assigns have to be declared:

If you remove the var ready line, setup() raises undefined field 'ready'.

Constructor Arguments Aren't Checked by Default

@new is a function, so the usual rules apply: missing arguments are nil, and extra arguments are ignored. A constructor that assumes it received an argument fails later, somewhere confusing:

If you annotate the parameter, the error is raised at the call instead, and it tells you what's wrong:

Constructors are the most valuable place in a program to add annotations, because an object that's built incorrectly usually fails somewhere else entirely.

Validating in the Constructor

A constructor can raise an error. When it does, nothing is returned to the caller, so an object that can't be valid never exists:

This is worth doing whenever a class has an invariant, a condition that should always be true for its instances. The other methods can then rely on it instead of checking it again.

@new Can't Return a Value

Calling a class always gives you an instance of that class. A return in @new ends the constructor early, but it doesn't change what the caller receives:

If you need a call that might return something else, such as a cached instance, a subclass or nil for invalid input, write a static factory method and call that instead.

Methods

A method is a name(params) { ... } declaration inside the class body. Methods don't use the def keyword:

deposit returns self, which is what makes the chained calls work. Returning self from a method that modifies the object is a common pattern in Zuri.

Inside a method, you have to use self to access a field or call another method. There's no implicit receiver:

Writing just name there would look for a local or global variable, not a field.

Fields Must Be Declared

A class's fields are fixed when the class is declared, which has two consequences.

First, assigning to a field that was never declared is an error:

Second, as described above, self.x = value inside @new does declare a field, so that constructors don't have to repeat themselves:

Again, this only applies in the body of @new itself. If a constructor calls a helper to do its initialization, the helper's fields have to be declared with var:

Without the var line, the assignment in setup() raises undefined field 'from_helper'.

Static Members

static attaches a field or method to the class itself instead of to each instance:

Static methods don't have a self:

Use the class name to refer to the class instead.

Static fields are the only part of a class that can change. The set of members is sealed, but the values of static fields aren't.

Duplicate Members

If you declare the same method twice in one class, Zuri reports an error instead of quietly keeping the second one:

The same is true if you declare two classes with the same name in one module.

Classes or Dictionaries?

dict class
Keys Any, added at any time Fixed when the class is declared
Access d.key or d['key'] obj.field only
Missing member get() returns a fallback Error
Behavior None Methods
Cost of reading a member Hash lookup Array index

Use a dictionary for data whose shape you only find out at run time, such as parsed JSON, HTTP headers or a configuration file. Use a class when you know the shape in advance and want to attach behavior to it.

6.2 · Learning the Language

Inheritance

To make a class inherit from another, use <:

A subclass inherits all of its parent's fields and methods. Zuri only supports single inheritance, so a class can have at most one parent.

Pay attention to the direction of the arrow. class Circle < Shape creates a new class based on Shape. Reversing it to class Anything > Shape means something else entirely: it adds methods to Shape itself and doesn't create a class at all. See Class Extensions.

Specifying the Parent Class

A class is a value like any other, so the parent doesn't have to be a plain name declared in the current file. Any expression that starts with a name works, which lets you build on a class from another module:

Property access, indexing and calls all work the same way, so a parent taken from a registry (class Store < backends['redis']) or returned by a function (class Store < chosen_backend()) is just as valid as a name. The expression is evaluated once, at the point where the class is declared.

The only rule is that the expression has to start with a name. That's what stops the { that opens the class body from being read as the start of a dictionary.

parent

parent has two related uses.

parent(args) calls the parent class's constructor. That's the parent('circle') line in Circle above. Call it first in @new, before the subclass sets up anything of its own. If you call it later, the parent's constructor overwrites what you've just assigned, and if you don't call it at all, the parent's fields are never initialized.

parent.method(args) calls the parent's version of a method that this class overrides:

Look at what happened there. parent.describe() ran Shape's version of describe, which calls self.area(), and that call went to Square's area. Method calls are always resolved on the actual object, not on the class where the calling code was written.

Overriding Methods

To override a method, declare it again in the subclass. You don't need a keyword, and there's no way to prevent a method from being overridden.

describe() above shows the most useful version of this: a parent method written in terms of a method that the child class provides. Shape.area() raises NotImplementedError, so a subclass that forgets to override it gets a clear error:

That's how you write an abstract method in Zuri. There's no abstract keyword, because you don't need one.

Subclasses Without a Constructor

If a subclass doesn't declare @new, it uses its parent's constructor:

Checking a Class's Ancestors

instance_of() checks the entire inheritance chain:

typeof() returns the name of the most specific class, as a string:

Deep Hierarchies Cost Nothing

Inheritance chains have no cost at run time. Looking up a method on a class four levels deep is the same operation as looking it up on a class with no parent, because each class's method table is complete as soon as the class is declared. Design the hierarchy however your problem needs.

Alternatives to Interfaces

Zuri has single inheritance and no interfaces, but the two patterns below cover what you'd use an interface for in other languages.

A base class that raises an error. When every subclass needs to provide a particular method, declare it in the base class and raise an error from it:

describe() calls self.area(), and self is the actual instance, so the subclass's version runs. That's all there is to dynamic dispatch in Zuri. You don't need to declare anything or mark methods as virtual.

A parameter annotated with the base class. A type annotation that names a class accepts any of its subclasses, so you can use it to say "any kind of Shape":

Checking the Type of a Value

There are two built-in functions for checking an instance's type, and they answer different questions.

instance_of(value, Class)

instance_of() answers the question "can I treat this as a Class?", and it checks the whole inheritance chain to find out:

Ellipse is two levels below Shape, and the result is still true. There's no limit on depth, because the check follows the parents until it finds a match or reaches the top. A sibling class, such as Circle compared with Square, gives false, because siblings share an ancestor but neither descends from the other.

It never raises an error because of the first argument. Anything that isn't an instance of the class just gives false, including values that aren't instances at all:

This means it's safe to use as a check on a value you know nothing about, without calling is_instance() first.

A class isn't an instance of itself. If you pass the class instead of an object, the result is false:

This catches people out when a variable might hold either one. Circle is a class and Circle() is an instance, and only the instance is a Shape.

The second argument has to be a class, and here it does raise an error if it isn't:

The most common version of this mistake is passing the class name as a string. Pass the class itself instead.

A class stored in a variable works, because the check uses the value, not the name you wrote:

So does a class accessed through a module:

How the Error Hierarchy Uses It

All of the built-in errors inherit from Error, so instance_of() lets a single handler tell them apart:

This is how the "handle one kind of error and re-raise the rest" pattern in Error Handling works, as well as the mapping from domain errors to HTTP status codes in Chapter 25.

typeof(value)

typeof() answers a different question: "what exactly is this?" For an instance, it returns the name of its actual class, and it never mentions the parent classes:

Look at the third line. typeof() on the class itself returns class, not Circle. The class is a value of type "class", and typeof() reports the type, not the class's name.

Which One to Use

Question Use
Can I treat this as a Shape? instance_of(x, Shape)
Which exact class is this? typeof(x)
Is this an instance of any class? is_instance(x)

Use instance_of() by default, because it takes inheritance into account. Code that checks typeof(x) == 'Circle' breaks as soon as someone subclasses Circle, since an instance of the subclass is a perfectly good Circle, but the string comparison says it isn't.

Type Annotations Use the Same Check

Annotating a parameter with a class name performs the same test as instance_of() on every call, and gives a better error message:

Use an annotation when the answer decides whether the function should run at all, and instance_of() when the answer decides which branch to take.

6.3 · Learning the Language

Decorated Methods

A method whose name starts with @ is a decorated method. The runtime calls it for you when a particular piece of syntax is used with an instance of your class. This is how a class can support construction, arithmetic, comparison and iteration without any special syntax of its own.

Apart from that, decorated methods are ordinary methods. They can be inherited, overridden and called by name.

@new: Construction

You've already seen this one. It runs when the class is called and receives the arguments, and it's the only place where self.x = value can declare a new field.

Arithmetic

Define a method for the operator you want, and the operator works with your instances:

Here's the full set of arithmetic decorators:

Decorator Operator
@add +
@sub - (binary)
@mul *
@div /
@floordiv //
@mod %
@pow **
@neg - (unary)

Bitwise and Logical Operators

Decorator Operator
@and &
@or |
@xor ^
@lshift <<
@rshift >>
@urshift >>>
@not ~

@not is bound to ~, the bitwise complement. ! is logical negation, and you can't override it. An instance is always truthy, so !instance is always false.

Comparison

Decorator Operator
@eq == and !=
@lt <
@lte <=
@gt >
@gte >=

Each Operator Is Defined Separately

Operators aren't derived from each other. Defining @lt doesn't give you >, and defining @add doesn't give you += with your instance on the other side:

Define every operator you want to support. @gt is usually a single line, as the Version example above shows.

The Other Operand Isn't Checked

A decorated method is an ordinary method, and its parameter is an ordinary parameter, so nothing guarantees that the other operand is an instance of the same class:

Compare those two results. With the instance on the left, @add ran and failed inside your own method with a confusing message. With the instance on the right, the operator was never passed to your class at all, because a decorated method only handles the case where its own instance is the left operand.

Annotate the parameter to fix the first error message, and treat the second case as a rule of the language:

Equality

@eq defines == for your class, and != is always the opposite of ==:

@eq only runs when the value on the right is also an object, such as a string, a list or another instance. p == nil, p == 5 and p == true are compared in the usual way without calling it, so a check for nil always behaves the same, whatever the class defines. @eq has to return a bool, and returning anything else raises a TypeError. Without @eq, two instances are only equal if they're the same object.

using also uses @eq for matching, since it compares values the same way == does.

@eq only affects ==. Lists and dictionaries compare the instances they contain by identity, and so do contains(), index_of() and dictionary keys:

Iteration

Together, @key and @value make a class work with for ... in. They take the most care to get right of all the decorated methods, so they have their own section: Making a Class Iterable.

Decorator Called by Signature
@key for ... in @key(previous)
@value for ... in @value(key)

@to_json

json.encode() calls @to_json() on an instance and encodes whatever it returns:

Without @to_json(), there's nothing for the encoder to work with. With it, you decide exactly what gets sent, which makes it the right place to leave out things like a password.

@to_string

@to_string() controls what echo and print() display for an instance:

It applies wherever the instance appears in the output, including inside lists and dictionaries, as a key or as a value. Without it, an instance is displayed as <instance of Money>. @to_string() has to return a string, and returning anything else raises a TypeError.

to_string()

to_string() doesn't have an @ because it isn't a decorated method. It's a regular method that every value already has, and a class can override it to give its instances a plain string form.

Nothing calls it for you. String interpolation and + show an instance as <instance of Money>, so call to_string() inside the interpolation yourself. A class that defines both usually implements one in terms of the other:

This is the convention the standard library follows: to_string() returns the value as text, and @to_string() controls how the instance looks when you print it.

Keep both methods fast and free of side effects, because error messages, logging and debugging all rely on them.

6.4 · Learning the Language

Encapsulation and Class Immutability

Private Members

A field or method whose name starts with _ is private. You can access it through self or parent, but nowhere else:

Code outside the class that tries to access it doesn't compile:

The check happens at compile time rather than at run time, so it has no cost, and you can't get around it by building the name dynamically.

A subclass can access its parent's private members, through self for fields and through parent for methods:

Modules follow the same underscore convention: a module member whose name starts with _ can't be imported by name. Chapter 8 covers modules.

Classes Are Sealed

Once a class has been declared, its structure can't change. You can't add a field or a method to the class, and you can't add one to an instance either:

In practice, this means a misspelled field name is reported as an error where you wrote it, instead of creating a new field that quietly hides the one you meant. Every field of a class is declared in one place, which is @new.

The values of static fields can change, but the set of static fields can't.

Accessing Fields by Name

Four built-in functions read and write fields by name:

setprop(obj, name, value) writes a field, and delprop resets it to nil. Both return false if the class doesn't have the field, because neither function can create one.

These functions ignore the underscore rule on purpose. They exist for serializers, debuggers and test helpers, whose whole job is to look inside objects. Regular code shouldn't use them.

The zuri module goes further and provides a complete reflection API for classes, functions and modules. Chapter 21 covers it.

Designing With Sealed Classes

Sealed classes lead to two good habits.

Declare every field in the class, even the ones the constructor sets. self.x = value inside @new declares a field for you, but a var line at the top of the class body documents it for the next person who reads the code. It's also required as soon as a helper method does the assigning instead.

Represent optional state as a field that holds nil, not as a missing field. Fields can't be missing, so a var cached_result that starts out as nil is the way to do it.

Example: A Bounded History

Privacy is most useful when a class has an invariant to protect. Here's a bounded history buffer. It keeps the last n entries and nothing more, and a caller has no way of breaking that from outside.

Four design decisions make this work.

The list is private, so nothing outside the class can append to it and skip the trimming. history._entries.append('x') doesn't compile.

entries() returns a copy. Otherwise, the caller would have the real list and could grow it past the limit. The fourth line of output shows that this doesn't happen. Returning a private, mutable collection is the most common way encapsulation breaks down.

The invariant is set up in the constructor. _limit is validated once, so record() never has to check whether it's sensible.

The class is sealed, so history.limit = 999 is an error, rather than a second field that's ignored while _limit keeps working.

6.5 · Learning the Language

Making a Class Iterable

You can loop over an instance of any class with for ... in. All it takes is two decorated methods. You don't need to declare an interface, return an iterator object or keep any state between passes.

This section explains the protocol, the two forms it usually takes, what happens when part of it is missing, and the rules that keep a custom iterator well behaved.

How It Works

There's nothing magic about for value in thing. Zuri evaluates thing once, and then repeats these steps:

  1. key = thing.@key(key), starting with key set to nil
  2. If key is nil, stop
  3. value = thing.@value(key), and run the body

So the two methods answer two different questions:

  • @key(previous) answers "given the last position, what's the next one?" It receives nil on the first call, and it must return nil when there's nothing left.
  • @value(key) answers "what's stored at this position?"

The loop doesn't keep track of its position itself. The key is the position, which is why @key receives the previous key each time.

A Counting Example

If you trace through it once, the protocol becomes much less abstract. @key(nil) returned 3, so the first value is @value(3), which is 30. Next, @key(3) returned 2, then @key(2) returned 1, and finally @key(1) returned nil, which ended the loop.

Notice that the key and the value really are different here. The key counts down from three, and the value is ten times the key. If you use two loop variables, you get both:

Wrapping a Collection

More often, the class wraps a list and the key is an index. The structure is always the same, with three checks:

Each of the three checks in @key is needed:

The check for an empty collection comes first. Without it, @key(nil) would return 0 for an empty stack, and @value(0) would read past the end.

previous == nil starts the iteration, with 0 as the first index.

previous >= length() - 1 ends it. Using >= instead of == means the loop still ends if the collection gets shorter partway through.

An empty collection doesn't fail. The loop just runs zero times:

What You Get

Once you've defined both methods, is_iterable() returns true for your class, and you can use it anywhere for works:

Both Methods Are Required

for calls @key and then @value. If you only define one of them, you get an error that names the missing one:

A class that defines neither fails on @key:

Rules to Keep in Mind

A nil key always ends the loop. So if nil could be a valid key in your collection, you can't use those keys directly. Use indexes instead, and look up the real key in @value.

The instance is evaluated only once. for x in build_thing() calls build_thing() a single time, before the first pass, so @key and @value are always called on the same object.

Neither method should change anything. They're called on every pass, in a loop you don't control, and if @key has a side effect, the loop's behavior depends on how many times something asked for the next key.

The iteration order is whatever @key returns. There's no rule that you have to count upward or visit every element. Countdown goes backward, and a class could just as easily skip, filter or repeat elements.

6.6 · Learning the Language

Class Extensions

An extension adds methods to an existing class. It's written with > instead of <, and it's different from inheritance. Inheritance creates a new class based on an existing one, while an extension changes the existing class directly.

Account now has two more methods. No new class, subclass or wrapper object was created. a is still the same Account instance, and it now responds to shout() and initials() as well as the methods declared in the class itself.

< Compared With >

They're easy to tell apart if you think of the arrow as pointing to where the methods end up.

Inheritance Extension
Syntax class Child < Parent class Anything > Target
Creates A new class Nothing; it modifies Target
Affects existing instances No Yes
Can declare fields Yes No
Can declare @new Yes No, because it doesn't hold fields
Methods are Ordinary methods static, with the instance as a parameter
self inside a method The instance Not available

Rules for Extensions

The compiler enforces four rules, and its error messages tell you exactly what's wrong.

The Name Is Only a Label

The name of an extension is never bound to anything. It's there so the declaration reads like any other declaration, and so error messages have something to refer to:

Name an extension after what it adds, such as AccountExtras, ShapeFormatting or NodeDebugging. The name isn't used anywhere else in your code.

Every Method Must Be static

Here, static doesn't mean that the method is attached to the class instead of its instances. It means that the method is compiled without an implicit receiver, so self doesn't exist inside it. The instance is passed as an ordinary argument instead.

Extensions Can't Add Fields

An extension adds behavior, never state. A class's fields are fixed when the class is declared, and nothing can add one later, not even an extension. If your extension needs to store something, keep it in the module that declares the extension, keyed by something that identifies the instance.

The Target Must Already Exist

The target is evaluated when the extension is declared, so it has to be a name that's already bound to a class:

The name doesn't have to be a plain identifier. Any expression that starts with an identifier works, so you can name a class from another module directly through that module:

Built-in types aren't classes you can refer to, so you can't extend string, list, number or the other built-in types. You can extend Error and any class that the standard library exports.

The Instance Parameter

An extension method receives the instance as its first parameter, and you can call that parameter whatever you like:

r.scaled(3) passes r as reading and 3 as factor. All the arguments at the call site come after the instance, as they would for an ordinary method.

Since argument counts aren't checked, the instance parameter is optional. A method that doesn't need the instance can simply leave it out:

There's No self

Use the instance parameter instead: write t.n, not self.n.

Private Members Are Still Private

An extension counts as code outside the class, so the underscore rule applies to it in full:

This is the most important limitation of extensions. They can add behavior built from a class's public members, but they can't reach inside it. You can't use an extension to get around encapsulation.

Replacing an Existing Method

If an extension method has the same name as an existing method of the class, it replaces that method:

Read that example carefully. g was created before the extension was declared, and calling greet() on it afterwards runs the new version. The new method doesn't shadow or wrap the old one. The class's method table itself has changed, and every instance of the class sees the change, whenever it was created.

This is true however much the original method has already been used. Here, we build an eight-level tree, call the original count() four thousand times, and then replace it:

After four thousand calls to the old method, the next call runs the new one. Replacement always takes effect, and there's no warm-up state, cached lookup or earlier result that can keep the old method alive after the extension runs.

Decorated Methods

An extension can add decorated methods, which is how you add operators, iteration or a string form to a class you didn't write. The instance still comes first, followed by the decorated method's own parameters:

@add(a, b) receives the left operand as a and the right operand as b. @key(box, previous) receives the instance and then the previous key, which is the argument @key would normally take on its own.

Extension Methods Are Instance Methods

static in the declaration describes how the method is compiled, not where it ends up. The methods are added to instances:

Call the method on an instance, as in Item().label().

Extensions and Inheritance

There's one interaction between the two that you need to know about, and it depends on when each declaration runs.

An extension changes the target class's method table, and a subclass copies its parent's methods when the subclass is declared. So a subclass only gets an extension's methods if the extension was declared first:

Car was declared after the extension, so it inherited doubled. If you move the class Car declaration above the extension, Car().doubled() raises undefined property 'doubled' on instance of 'Car', while Vehicle still has the method.

Declare extensions before any subclasses that should inherit them. In practice, that means at the top of a module, or in a module that's imported at the top.

Extending a subclass never affects its parent:

Extensions Apply Everywhere

This is what makes extensions powerful, and it's also why you should use them sparingly. An extension isn't limited to the module that declares it. It changes the class throughout the whole program, starting as soon as the declaring module runs. For an imported module, that's as soon as it's imported.

main.zu never refers to the definition of label. Importing extras, for whatever reason, even one that has nothing to do with Shape, added a method to a class declared in a third file, and the instance created before the import got the method too.

This has two consequences.

An import can change behavior you didn't ask it to change. If a module extends a class you use, the change affects your code as well, and nothing at your call site tells you.

Two extensions that define the same method conflict without any warning. The last one to run wins, so which one wins depends on the order of the imports:

When to Use an Extension

Extensions solve a problem that inheritance can't: adding behavior to a class whose instances are created somewhere you don't control. A subclass only helps if you're the one calling the constructor.

Good reasons to use one:

Adding a view or format to a domain class. For example, a to_string(), a @to_json or a summary() method. This is presentation code that doesn't belong in the model, added by the module that needs it.

Adding an operator or iteration to a standard library class, so that it works with syntax it wasn't originally written for.

Instrumenting code while debugging. You can replace a method with one that logs its calls, and then delete the extension when you're done, without touching the original file.

Reasons to think twice:

It's invisible at the call site. Nothing about account.shout() tells you that shout is defined in a different file from Account. Someone searching the class body won't find it.

It applies everywhere, as described above.

An ordinary function is usually enough. shout(account) is a plain function, it's obvious where it's defined, and it can't conflict with anything. Use an extension when you really need a method, either because the syntax requires one, as with decorated methods, or because callers only have the instance and nothing else.

Chapter 7 · Learning the Language

Error Handling

Things go wrong. A file is missing, a number arrives as text, or a server on the network stops responding. Zuri handles all of these with one mechanism: an Error object that you raise with raise and handle with catch. There's no try, no finally and no checked exceptions.

This chapter covers raising errors, the three forms of catch, what an error contains, the built-in error classes, writing your own, and what to use instead of finally.

Raising Errors

raise only accepts an instance of Error or one of its subclasses. Raising a plain string or number is itself a TypeError:

This is a small inconvenience, but it means that every error has a type, a message and a stack trace, because there's no way to raise anything else.

If an error isn't caught, the program ends and prints a message, an excerpt of the source code and a stack trace:

Catching Errors

The code in the catch block runs. If anything inside it raises an error, execution jumps to the handler, with the error assigned to e. If nothing raises an error, the handler doesn't run.

There are three forms of catch, and each one behaves differently.

catch { ... }, with nothing after it, discards the error and continues:

Only use this when the failure really doesn't matter.

catch { ... } as e, without a handler block, assigns the error to a variable that's still available after the statement. If nothing went wrong, e is nil:

Use this form when the recovery code doesn't belong inside a handler, for example when you want to check several things one after another.

catch { ... } as e { ... } is the full form, and the one you'll use most often.

What an Error Contains

  • message is the error message.
  • type is the name of the error's class, as a string.
  • stacktrace is a list of stack frames, starting with the innermost one. Each frame names a file, a line and a function.

The stack trace is recorded where the error was raised, not where it was caught, so it always points to where the error started, however many frames it passed through:

There are three frames: inner, middle and the top level of the script. Printing the stack trace is often the quickest way to find out how the program got to a certain point, especially in code you didn't write.

Built-in Error Classes

Each of these is a class, and they all inherit from Error:

Class Raised when
Error The base class, for general failures
TypeError An operation received a value of the wrong type
ValueError The type was right, but the value wasn't
NumericError An arithmetic operation failed
ArgumentError A function received the wrong number of arguments
NotImplementedError A method that should have been overridden wasn't
RangeError An index or bound was out of range
AccessError A permission or access check failed
AssertError An assert failed
PropertyError Code read a member that doesn't exist
UndefinedError Code read a name that isn't defined
ModuleNotFoundError An import couldn't be resolved

Since they all inherit from Error, catching Error catches all of them, and a parameter annotated as Error accepts any of them.

Defining Your Own Errors

Create a subclass of Error and give it whatever information the caller needs:

There are two things to get right. Call parent(message) so that the base constructor sets message and records the stack trace. And set self.type, so that the class name appears in logs and in the message for an uncaught error.

Catching Specific Errors

catch catches every error raised inside its block. To handle one kind of error and let the others through, check the error and raise it again if it isn't the kind you want:

instance_of() checks the whole inheritance chain, so checking against Error matches every error, while checking against HttpError only matches that branch of the hierarchy.

Replacing finally

Code after the catch statement runs whether or not the block raised an error, because the handler either recovers from the error or raises it again:

That covers the most common case. But if the handler raises the error again, or the block contains a return, the code after the statement is skipped. So if a resource has to be released either way, release it in the handler as well:

Using as e Without a Handler
