The version above calls handle.close() twice, once in the handler and once after the statement, because those are two different ways out. The third form of catch, as e without a handler block, combines them into one:

The only difference is the missing { ... } after as e, but it changes the control flow, not just the layout. Without a handler, there's nothing to jump to, so an error raised inside the block is stored in e, and execution continues on the next line. Both paths, the one that raised an error and the one that didn't, now run the same code afterwards:

This way, close() is written once and always runs, and then you decide explicitly whether to raise the error again. It's the nearest thing Zuri has to finally, built from ordinary statements rather than a separate construct:

Line Purpose
catch { ... } as e Runs the block and records any error, without jumping
handle.close() Cleans up, whichever path was taken
if e { raise e } Passes the error on, unchanged

There are two things to keep in mind.

e is nil when nothing went wrong, so if e { raise e } is all you need to decide what to do. When there's no error, the cleanup runs and the function continues as normal.

Raising e itself again keeps the original stack trace, which points to the line that actually failed rather than to your raise statement. Only wrap it in a new error when you have something to add, as shown in Nesting and Re-raising.

Use the form with a handler when you need to handle the error, and this form when you only need to clean up afterwards.

return Inside catch

A return inside a catch block or its handler returns from the enclosing function, just as it would anywhere else:

Errors Raised by Handlers

A handler can raise an error, and an outer catch will see it:

assert or raise?

assert raises an AssertError when its condition is falsy. The message is optional.

Here's how to decide between them. Use raise for things that can happen, such as a missing file, a number that doesn't parse or a network timeout. The caller is expected to deal with these. Use assert for things that should never happen, such as an invariant that your own code is responsible for keeping. If an assertion fails, the program has a bug. It doesn't mean something outside the program went wrong.

Good Practices

Keep the catch block small. It should contain only the operation that might fail, so that the handler doesn't accidentally catch a mistake somewhere else:

This block is too wide. A failure inside render() would be reported as a parsing failure:

This is better. Only the call that might fail is inside the block:

Notice that var data is declared outside the block. A catch block is a scope like any other, so a variable declared inside it no longer exists once the statement ends.

Write error messages that include the value that caused the problem:

Whoever reads that message is trying to work out what went wrong from a single line in a log file. Give them the number.

Catching Inside a Loop

A catch inside a loop body handles a single iteration and lets the rest of the loop continue. Use this when you're processing a batch of items and some of them are allowed to fail:

If you put the catch outside the loop instead, the first failure ends the whole loop. That's the right choice when one bad item makes the rest pointless, and the wrong choice when it doesn't. Where you put the block is how you make that decision, since there's no flag for it.

Nesting and Re-raising

A catch inside a handler works like any other catch. You can use this to turn a low-level failure into an error that makes sense to your caller:

The caller now gets an error that's in terms it understands. Include the original message, as shown above, so the details aren't lost along the way.

Raising the same error again, instead of a new one, keeps the original stack trace, which points to the line where the error first happened:

This is the pattern for handling one kind of error and letting all the others through. Use it whenever a handler might otherwise hide a bug along with the failure it was meant to catch.

Example: Loading a File

Here's everything in this chapter in a single function: a loader that validates its input, separates the failures a caller can do something about from the ones it can't, and closes the file it opened whatever happens.

There are four things worth pointing out.

Every failure the caller might reasonably handle is reported as a single error type, StoreError, so the catch on the calling side needs one branch instead of three.

The message always includes the path. A log line that says "file is corrupt" without saying which file can cost someone an hour.

handle.close() is called on both paths: once in the handler before the error is raised again, and once after the block. There's no finally to do this for you, and forgetting the call in the handler is the most common way Zuri code leaks resources.

Finally, the check on the file's contents at the end uses raise, not assert. A file on disk with the wrong contents is a problem with the outside world, not a bug in this function.

Chapter 8 · Learning the Language

The Module System

A module is a .zu file. It runs at most once per program, it has its own global namespace, and nothing it declares is visible anywhere else until another file imports it.

That's all there is to the model. The rest of this chapter covers the syntax and the rules for finding modules.

Importing a Module

import name makes the module available under that name. Use a dot to access what's inside it.

Importing Specific Members

The members you name are bound directly, and the module name itself isn't bound.

{ * } imports every public member:

Renaming a Module

This is useful when the module's name is long, or when it would clash with another name.

as renames the module, not a member. You can't rename individual names in a member list, so import math { PI as pi } doesn't parse. If you want to use a different name for something you've imported, assign it yourself:

Calling a Module Directly

If a module contains a function with the same name as the module, you can call the module itself. set declares a function called set, so calling the module calls that function:

The short form is usually preferred. wire(), date(), log(), hash(), enum() and compress() work the same way, and so do your own modules: once you've imported a greet.zu that contains def greet(name), you can call it as greet('Ada'). A class with the same name as its module can be called in the same way.

The call relies on the name the module is bound to, so it stops working if you rename the module. The function is still available as a member:

The name still refers to a module, not a function. typeof() confirms this, and a method that expects a function needs the member itself:

Calling a module that doesn't have a matching function raises a TypeError.

Relative Imports

A path that starts with . or .. is resolved relative to the directory of the file that contains the import, and Zuri never looks for it anywhere else.

Each .. goes up one directory, so .. .. goes up two, and .. .. .. goes up three. You can also write the dots together, as in ....shared.config, which means the same thing: every two dots in a row go up one directory. zuri fmt keeps whichever form you used.

Each part of the path is resolved the same way as a bare name: Zuri tries name.zu first, then name/index.zu. So import .helpers finds either helpers.zu or helpers/index.zu, and import .models.user finds models/user.zu or models/user/index.zu, where models is a directory in both cases.

You can't tell from the import which of the two it found, and that's what allows a module to grow into a package. If you split helpers.zu into helpers/index.zu and a few other files, every import .helpers keeps working without changes.

Inside a package, always import a sibling module with import .sibling, not with the full path from the project root. If you write import myapp.models.user inside myapp/models/, Zuri searches the library path for it and won't find anything.

Re-exporting Imports

Imports are private by default. If a.zu imports b.zu, a third file that imports a can't see what's in b through it.

To re-export a module, put @ in front of its path:

Everything that util.zu exports is now part of this module's public API as well. All three forms of import accept the prefix:

This is how a package's index.zu builds a public API from several private files:

util's members are re-exported, while deep_slug is imported for this file's own use and stays private.

Private Members

A member whose name starts with _ is private to its module and can't be imported by name:

{ * } skips private members as well. If something is an implementation detail, give it a leading underscore and the module system will keep it private.

Packages

A directory that contains an index.zu is a package. Importing the directory runs its index.zu:

The same rule applies to zuri run pkg on the command line, which is why a package can be run as well as imported.

Resolving Bare Names

For an import with no leading dot, such as import http, Zuri looks in these places, in order:

  1. .zuri/libs/http in the project
  2. $ZURI_ROOT/libs/http, or libs/http next to the zuri executable, which is the standard library
  3. A built-in native module named http
  4. $ZURI_HOME/libs/http, the packages installed for your user, which are in ~/.zuri/libs unless you set ZURI_HOME to something else

At each step, http.zu is tried first, and then http/index.zu.

The project is the nearest directory containing a project.toml, found by searching upward from the script given to zuri run, or from the working directory for a command or the REPL. A program run from anywhere inside a project imports that project's packages, and a program that isn't in a project uses .zuri/libs in the working directory. The project is found once, when the program starts, so changing directory while it runs doesn't change where imports come from.

zuri install puts packages in .zuri/libs, and Packages and Nyssa covers it in full. The first step in the search is also what makes vendoring possible. A file you put in .zuri/libs/ takes priority over a standard library module with the same name:

Modules Run Only Once

A module's top-level code runs the first time the module is imported, and never again. Every later import of the same file gets the same module object:

There's one line of output for three imports. Modules are identified by their canonical file path, so two different relative paths to the same file refer to the same module.

That makes a module's top level the natural place for setup that should happen exactly once, such as opening a connection pool, reading a configuration file or registering handlers.

Circular Imports

Circular imports work. A module is registered before its body runs, so when b.zu imports a.zu while a.zu is still loading, b gets the partly loaded module instead of looping forever:

The output shows the catch: b finished loading before a did, so anything b reads from a at its top level doesn't exist yet. Reading it inside a function is fine, because by the time the function runs, a has finished loading.

If a module fails while it's loading, it's removed from the cache instead of being left half loaded, so a later import really does try again.

Module Variables

Every module automatically has two variables:

__file__ is the canonical path of the module itself. __root__ is the entry file the program was started with, and it's the same in every module. Use them to find files relative to your source code, rather than relative to whatever directory the user ran the program from:

Both are also defined in the REPL, with placeholder values in place of a real file:

In the REPL, they're different from each other, so the __root__ == __file__ check below is false at the prompt. A REPL session is never the entry point of a program.

Running a Module as a Program

Since __root__ is the entry file and __file__ is the current one, comparing them tells a module whether it's being run as the program or imported by something else:

When imported, the same file is a library with no side effects, and when run directly, it's a command-line program. Put the argument parsing and the entry point behind that check, and everything else above it.

These two variables describe which file this is, so they aren't exported. A wildcard import copies every public name from the module it imports, but __file__ and __root__ are always left out:

That's what makes the __root__ == __file__ check reliable in every file, even in a file that uses a wildcard import of a sibling module.

Organizing a Project

A small program can be a single file. Beyond that, a good structure is one package for each area of responsibility, each with an index.zu that re-exports its public members:

Run it with zuri run myapp. The capstone project in Chapter 25 uses exactly this layout.

A Complete Package

Here's the smallest complete example of that structure: three files, one package and one public entry point.

There are four things to notice.

greet/index.zu is what import .greet loads. A directory with an index.zu is a package, and importing the directory runs that file.

The @ in import @.english is what re-exports the module. Without it, greet.english wouldn't be accessible outside greet/index.zu, although greet() itself would still work, which is often what you want.

Both submodules define hello, and they don't clash. Each one lives in its own namespace and is accessed through its own module name. That's the reason to use import @.english here rather than import @.english { * }.

_shout can't be accessed from outside. Writing greet.english._shout(x) anywhere else is a compile-time error, not a run-time one:

The leading underscore is the only way to declare something private, and it's checked before the program runs.

Chapter 9 · Working with the World

Files and the Filesystem

Two things handle most of the work with files. The built-in file() function gives you a handle to a single file, and the os module covers everything else: directories, paths, globs, temporary files and environment variables.

Opening a File

file(path) opens a file for reading by default. The second argument sets the mode:

Mode Meaning
r Read. The file must exist.
w Write. Creates the file, or truncates it if it exists.
a Append. Every write goes to the end. Creates the file if needed.
r+ Read and update. The file must exist.
w+ Read and update. Creates the file, but does not truncate it.
a+ Read and append. Creates the file if needed.
x Write. Creates the file, and fails if the path already exists.
x+ Read and write. Creates the file, and fails if the path already exists.

Add b to any mode to open the file in binary mode, as in 'rb', 'wb' or 'ab'.

Use x when two programs might try to create the same file at the same time. Checking whether the file exists and creating it happen in a single step, so exactly one program succeeds and all the others fail. That's what a lock file needs.

Creating a handle doesn't touch the disk. Nothing happens until you read, write or call open().

Reading an Entire File

read() without an argument opens the file, reads all of it and closes it again. It's the one-line way to get a file's contents, and it's what you'll want most of the time.

In text mode, you get a string, decoded as strict UTF-8. In binary mode, you get bytes.

Reading in Chunks

read(length) reads up to that many bytes and leaves the handle open, so you can call it again. This is how you process a file that's too large to fit in memory all at once:

Reading six bytes at a time is only for demonstration, and in real code you'd read tens of kilobytes at a time. What matters is the pattern: open the file once, read until you get an empty result, then close it once.

Note that chunks end wherever the byte count runs out, not at the end of a line. If a chunked reader needs complete lines, it has to keep the end of each chunk and join it to the start of the next one.

Reading Lines

To process text one line at a time, the simplest approach is to read the whole file and split it:

lines() handles both \n and \r\n, and it drops the empty string that a trailing newline would otherwise produce at the end.

Writing to a File

Like read(), write() opens the handle if it's closed, writes the data, flushes it and closes the handle again. One call writes one complete file.

Closing automatically has an important consequence. If you call write() twice on a closed handle in w mode, each call truncates the file, so only the second write is kept. When you need to write more than once, open the handle yourself:

The explicit open() call keeps the handle open for both writes. Without it, each write() would open the file, truncate it, write to it and close it, and only second line would be left.

If the handle is already open, write() writes at the current position, so the code above does what it looks like it does.

puts() writes without opening or closing the handle at all. The handle has to be open already, and puts() is the method to use inside a loop.

Reading and Writing at a Specific Position

seek(offset, whence) takes 0 for the start of the file, 1 for the current position and 2 for the end. The io module has names for these values:

tell() returns the current position.

Getting Information About a File

stats() returns a dictionary of information about the file on disk:

size is in bytes. mtime, atime and ctime are times in seconds since the epoch, which you can pass straight to the date module. mode is the raw word that holds the permissions and the type of entry, and the stat module helps you make sense of it:

S_ISREG, S_ISDIR, S_ISLNK and the other functions like them each check for one kind of entry. file_mode() formats the permission bits the same way ls -l does.

Managing Files

File handles also have truncate(length), chmod(mode), set_times(access, modify) and symlink(target).

Closing Files

read() and write() clean up after themselves, but you're responsible for closing anything you opened with open(). The cleanest way to make sure it happens is a catch that closes the file on the way out:

For cleanup that has to happen however the program ends, rather than however a single block ends, register a handler with os.at_exit():

Handlers run in reverse order of registration. They run whether the program reached the end of its script, called os.exit() or stopped because of an uncaught error. If a handler raises an error, the error is reported on standard error and the remaining handlers still run, so one failed cleanup can't stop the others.

Directories

The three arguments are the path, the permission bits, and whether to create any missing parent directories. It returns false if the directory already existed.

If the second argument to remove_dir is true, it removes the directory and everything in it.

Listing Files and Globbing

The examples in this section work on a real directory tree, so let's create one first:

read_dir() lists the contents of a directory:

There are three things to notice here. First, . and .. are included, so a loop over the result usually needs to skip them. Second, the recursive form returns nested entries as paths relative to the directory you listed, not as bare names, so you can use them directly. Third, entries are sorted by name, and each directory's contents come immediately after the directory itself, so the listing is the same on every machine and file system.

glob() is usually what you really want:

* matches within a single part of a path, while ** matches across parts. The second argument is the base directory, and the results are relative to it.

Compare those two results carefully, because the difference often catches people out. *.txt found the file at the top level but not the nested one. **/*.txt found the nested file but not the top-level one, because **/ means "in a subdirectory". Neither pattern finds both.

To match files at any depth, glob for ** and filter the results:

** on its own matches every entry at every depth, including directories, which is why the filter on the second line is needed. glob() uses read_dir() internally, so its matches come back in the same sorted order.

Clean up when you're done:

Paths

All of the path functions just manipulate strings, except where noted:

real_path() resolves symbolic links, and the path has to exist. abs_path() doesn't require that. expand_user() replaces a leading ~ with the home directory. path_contains(base, candidate) checks whether one path is inside another, which is the check you need before serving a file that a user asked for by name. On Windows, both path_contains() and relative_path() ignore case, the same way Windows does when it looks up names.

Temporary Files

Both functions create the file or directory and return its path. You're responsible for removing them when you're done.

Environment Variables

get_env() accepts a fallback value. environ() returns all of the environment variables as a dictionary.

Finding Files Relative to Your Code

The current working directory is wherever the user ran zuri from, which isn't necessarily where your source code is. Use __file__ instead:

Do this in every module that reads a file stored next to it. Otherwise, your program will only work when it's run from the project root.

Watching for File Changes

An os.Watcher is notified by the operating system as files change. It doesn't poll the files repeatedly. Instead, it uses each platform's own notification mechanism: inotify on Linux, FSEvents on macOS, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows, and kqueue on the BSDs. FSEvents only allows about one watched directory for every twelve files a process can have open, so on macOS, the first watcher raises the process's soft limit on open files as far as the hard limit allows.

add() accepts either a directory, which is watched along with everything inside it, or a single file. next() waits for the next event. It takes a timeout in milliseconds and returns nil if nothing happened in that time. Each event's kind is one of the following:

  • 'create': something now exists at path.
  • 'modify': the file at path was changed in place.
  • 'remove': nothing exists at path anymore.
  • 'rescan': the operating system dropped some events, so anything might have changed.

A rename is reported as a 'remove' of the old path and a 'create' of the new one. Reading a file is never reported.

A watcher can also follow a child process. When the process exits, the watcher reports it alongside the file changes:

A for loop over a watcher keeps waiting for events until the watcher is closed. Signal handlers still run while it waits, so pressing Ctrl+C is the usual way to stop one:

zuri run --watch is built on top of this.

Example: Counting Words

Here's a complete function that counts the words in every text file in a directory tree:

There are four things in that function worth pointing out.

glob('**', root) returns paths relative to the root, so you have to join each one to the root before you can open it. Forgetting to do that is the most common mistake in code that uses globs.

The .md file doesn't appear in the result, because text_files() filtered it out. That's the filtering that ** can't do by itself.

split('/\W+/') splits on a regular expression, which is why no punctuation ends up in the keys: world, and hello! became world and hello. A plain split(' ') would have kept the punctuation.

And counts.get(word, 0) + 1 provides a starting value for keys that don't exist yet. Without the fallback, the first time each word appeared would raise an error.

Further Reading

Binary files, byte streams and the io module's in-memory files are covered in Chapter 10. Reading files over the network is covered in Chapter 12. Appendix E lists every method of a file handle.

Chapter 10 · Working with the World

Binary Data and Streams

Text is easy to work with, but protocols, file formats, images and checksums aren't text. This chapter covers the four tools Zuri provides for working with binary data: the bytes type, the struct module, io.BytesIO and the compress module.

The bytes Type

bytes is a mutable buffer of 8-bit values.

bytes(n) creates a buffer of n zero bytes. bytes(list) creates one from a list of numbers, each between 0 and 255. Calling to_bytes() on a string gives you its UTF-8 encoding.

Bytes are always printed as hexadecimal values in parentheses, so you can't mistake them for a list.

Reading Bytes

Indexing gives you a number, and slicing gives you bytes. to_string() decodes the bytes as UTF-8, and to_list() returns them as a list of numbers.

index_of() and last_index_of() both return -1 if the byte isn't found, and both take a second argument that limits where a match can be, so you can search either side of a given index.

Slicing

b[a, b] returns a new byte buffer with the bytes from a up to but not including b:

The rules are the same as for lists. You can leave out either bound: b[, n] starts at the beginning, and b[n, ] goes to the end. Negative bounds count back from the end, so b[-2, ] is the last two bytes.

Be careful with the difference between indexing and slicing, because for bytes they return different types:

An index gives you the numeric value of a single byte, while a slice of length one gives you a byte buffer that contains that byte. Writing b[0] when you meant b[0, 1] is the most common mistake here, and instead of an error where you slice, it shows up later as a number where bytes was expected.

Slices Check Their Bounds

A slice that goes past the end raises an error instead of returning as much as it can:

Because the upper bound is exclusive, length() itself is always a valid upper bound, and an empty slice is allowed:

An empty byte buffer is printed as ().

Slices Are Copies

Slicing creates a new buffer, so writing to the slice doesn't change the original:

This matters when you're parsing a buffer. If you take a header out with frame[0, 4], you can change it freely, and the frame you're reading from stays the same. It also means that slicing in a loop makes a copy every time. A parser that works through a large buffer should keep track of an offset and slice each field once, rather than slicing off the rest of the buffer at every step.

Slicing Before Decoding

This is the usual approach when a buffer contains text of a known length:

to_string() decodes the entire buffer it's called on, so the slice is what limits how much is decoded. If you slice in the middle of a multi-byte character, the result isn't valid UTF-8. Decode whole characters, or keep the leftover bytes for the next read.

Slices Can't Be Assigned To

You can read a slice, but you can't write to one:

Assign one index at a time instead, or rebuild the buffer with extend(). You can assign to a single index, and the value must be a valid byte:

This is different from bytes([300]), which wraps the value around instead of raising an error. Creating a buffer is lenient, but assigning to one isn't.

Changing Bytes

Unlike reverse() on a list, bytes.reverse() changes the buffer in place. So do append, extend, pop and remove.

dispose() frees the buffer's memory immediately instead of waiting for the garbage collector, which can be useful when you've just finished with a very large buffer.

Splitting Bytes

split() takes a bytes delimiter, not a number:

Iterating Over Bytes

A byte buffer is iterable, and every form of iteration that works with lists also works here. Each value you get is always a number between 0 and 255, never a one-character string.

With two variables, you get the index first and the value second:

Use iter when you're decoding a structure and the position determines what comes next, for example when you read a two-byte length, skip that many bytes, and then read the next field:

each() takes a function, which receives the value first and the index second, as it does everywhere else:

If you want characters rather than numbers, convert the buffer first. b.to_string() decodes the whole buffer as UTF-8, and b.to_list() gives you the numbers as an ordinary list.

Binary Files

Add b to the file mode to read the file as bytes instead of a string. Writes then accept bytes too:

Reading a file that isn't valid UTF-8 without the b raises an error instead of silently inserting replacement characters. That's the behavior you want, because a decoding failure tells you something.

struct: Packing and Unpacking

struct converts between Zuri values and a fixed binary layout. A format string is a series of fields separated by /, each written as CODE[COUNT][:NAME].

unpack() returns a dictionary, using the :NAME you gave each field as its key. Fields without a name are numbered:

When a single name has a count greater than one, the keys are numbered:

Format Codes

Strings:

Code Size Meaning
a count String padded with NUL bytes
A count String padded with spaces
Z count String padded with NUL bytes and NUL-terminated, as in C
h / H ceil(count/2) Hex string, low or high nibble first

Integers. The letter determines the width and the byte order:

Code Size Meaning
c / C 1 Signed / unsigned 8-bit
? 1 Boolean
s / S 2 Signed / unsigned 16-bit, native byte order
n / v 2 Unsigned 16-bit, big endian / little endian
i l / I L 4 Signed / unsigned 32-bit, native byte order
N / V 4 Unsigned 32-bit, big endian / little endian
q / Q 8 Signed / unsigned 64-bit, native byte order
J / P 8 Unsigned 64-bit, big endian / little endian
u / U 16 Signed / unsigned 128-bit, little endian

Floating-point numbers:

Code Size Meaning
f / g / G 4 Float: native / little endian / big endian
d / e / E 8 Double: native / little endian / big endian
w / W 2 Half precision: little endian / big endian

Padding:

Code Meaning
x Writes count NUL bytes without using an argument
X Moves back count bytes
@ Moves to the absolute position count

n, N and J use network byte order, which is what almost every network protocol needs.

A count of * means "all of the rest".

Precision

Zuri numbers are doubles, so they can only represent integers exactly up to 2^53. All of the 64-bit and 128-bit codes (q, Q, J, P, u and U) automatically return a bigint when the unpacked value is outside that range, instead of silently losing digits. When packing, they accept either a number or a bigint.

Other Functions

calcsize(format) returns the size in bytes of a format that doesn't contain *. pack_into(buffer, offset, format, ...) and unpack_from(format, buffer, offset) work on an existing buffer at a given position, which lets you build one large frame without creating and concatenating a new buffer for each field.

io.BytesIO

BytesIO is a file-like object stored in memory. It has the same interface as the handles returned by file(), so anything that accepts a file also accepts a BytesIO:

The constructor takes a bytes value to start from and a mode. BytesIO has read, gets, write, puts, seek, tell, flush, close and stats, so a function written for files works in memory without any changes.

This is where it's useful. You can test a function that writes a file without touching the disk, and you can parse an in-memory buffer with code that was written for streams.

Compression

The compress module has a submodule for each format, and each submodule has compress() and decompress() functions:

The available formats are deflate, zlib, gzip, zstd, lz4, bzip2 and brotli. zlib is also re-exported at the top level, so compress() and compress.decompress() use zlib:

Use gzip when another program needs to read the data, zstd when you want the best balance of compression ratio and speed, lz4 when speed is all that matters, and brotli for text that you'll serve over HTTP.

Archives

compress.tar and compress.zip read and write archives, and compress.checksum provides crc32() and adler32():

Hashing and Encoding

base64 lets you send binary data through channels that only accept text:

hash provides the digest algorithms:

Each function takes an optional last argument, as_bytes. Pass true to get raw bytes instead of a hex string.

The available algorithms are md2, md4, md5, sha1, sha224, sha256, sha384, sha512, the sha3 family, shake128 and shake256, blake2b512, blake2s256, ripemd160, whirlpool and gost. Each one has an hmac_ version as well, and there's also pbkdf2() for key derivation. hash(algorithm, data) lets you choose the algorithm by name at run time.

To store passwords, use bcrypt instead of any of these. A fast hash is the wrong tool for passwords, and Chapter 13 covers the right one.

Example: A Length-Prefixed Frame

Most binary protocols consist of a header followed by a payload. Here's a complete round trip:

calcsize() tells you where the header ends, slicing splits the frame in two, and the compressed flag takes up a byte of its own, so the receiver never has to guess whether the payload is compressed.

Chapter 11 · Working with the World

Concurrency with Isolates

Zuri's concurrency model rests on one rule: nothing is shared.

An isolate is an operating system thread that runs its own complete VM. It has its own heap, garbage collector, register stack and module namespace. Two isolates never hold a pointer to the same object, so there are no data races to think about, no locks to take, and no pauses in one thread caused by memory allocation in another.

Values are copied when they're passed between isolates. The copy is exact: cycles are preserved, objects that appear more than once in the same value are still shared within the copy, and class instances arrive as instances of the same class.

Spawning an Isolate

spawn(fn, ...args) queues the call and immediately returns an Isolate handle. join() waits for the isolate to finish and returns its result. You can call join() more than once, and it returns the same value each time.

What You Can Spawn

You can spawn any function: a top-level def, a helper declared inside another function, an anonymous function or a bound method. Anything the function captures goes with it, including the modules it uses:

Modules aren't copied the way lists are. Instead, the isolate loads the same module itself and uses its own copy. That works because the top level of a module consists of declarations that run once, and the result is cached. Be careful with a module that depends on live state in the current process, since the isolate gets a fresh copy of the module, not yours.

There are still two things you can't spawn. You can't use a native function or a class as the spawn target directly, so wrap it in a def. And a resource handle, such as an open socket or file, is moved rather than copied, so the side that passed it no longer has it.

Once a worker grows beyond a few lines, it's better to put it in a module of its own:

That's the structure the rest of this book uses. A worker referred to by name is looked up in the isolate's own namespace, so nothing about it needs to be reconstructed.

An import inside the function body also works, and runs inside the isolate:

Arguments are copied, not shared. If an isolate changes a list it was given, it changes its own copy:

The isolate saw two elements, while the caller still has one. That's the whole concurrency model in a single example: you can't write a data race, because nothing is shared.

Running Several Isolates at Once

Spawn a list of isolates, then join them:

isolate.map() does the same thing in a single call:

wait_all(tasks, timeout) waits for all of the tasks to finish, and wait_any(tasks, timeout) returns as soon as one of them finishes.

Task Status

A spawned task is in one of two states, and there are several methods that let you check on it without blocking.

Method Returns Blocks?
join(timeout) The result Yes
try_join() The result, or nil if it isn't ready No
is_done() Whether the task has finished No
status() 'pending' or 'done' No
name() The task's name, or nil No

If a task's own result could be nil, a nil from try_join() is ambiguous, so check is_done() as well when it matters.

You can call join() more than once. The second call returns the same value immediately.

Naming Tasks

spawn() creates an unnamed task. spawn_named() gives the task a name, which appears in diagnostics:

Give a name to any task that runs for a long time. When a program gets stuck, it's much easier to find the problem if each task can tell you what it is.

Timeouts Are in Seconds

All timeouts in the isolate module are measured in seconds, and fractions are allowed:

This applies to join(), send(), recv(), select(), wait_any(), wait_all() and shutdown().

This is worth emphasizing, because the net module uses milliseconds for its timeouts. socket.set_read_timeout(5000) is five seconds, but channel.recv(5000) is an hour and twenty minutes. It's common to use both modules in the same program, and mixing them up doesn't produce an error. A timeout that never fires just looks like the program has hung.

If you leave out the timeout, the call waits forever. That's a good default when the other side is code you control, and a bad one when it isn't.

Cancelling a Task

cancel() asks a task to stop, but it doesn't force it to.

What happens next depends on what the task is doing:

If it's blocked in a channel operation, a join(), a wait_* call or a select(), the call is interrupted within about 50 ms and raises an IsolateCancelledError.

If it's running ordinary code, nothing is interrupted. The task's function has to check for cancellation and return by itself:

isolate.is_cancelled() is the module-level function that a worker calls to check its own status. task.is_cancelled() is the method that the code that spawned the task calls to find out whether cancellation was requested. It returns true from the moment cancel() is called, whether or not the task noticed:

That output isn't a contradiction. The worker in this example doesn't check for cancellation, so it finished normally. is_cancelled() tells you that cancellation was requested, not what the task did about it. A loop that never checks for cancellation can't be stopped.

Put the check at the point where the loop starts its next pass, and keep it cheap. Checking once per pass of an outer loop is usually enough, and checking inside the innermost calculation isn't worth the cost.

Passing Values Between Isolates

Arguments, results and messages sent over channels all cross between isolates in the same way: everything is copied. Nothing is shared, and no reference survives the trip.

Copies Are Exact

A copy isn't a shallow snapshot. Cycles are kept, objects that appear more than once in a value are still shared within the copy, and class instances arrive as instances of the same class, with their methods:

Look at the last line. pair contained the same list twice, and on the other side it still does: appending through back[0] is visible through back[1]. The copy kept the structure of the sharing as well as the values.

What Can't Be Passed

A few kinds of value are tied to the isolate that created them. Trying to send one raises an error instead of quietly producing something broken:

The error message lists what can be passed, which is the more useful part. The case you'll run into most is an open file. A file handle refers to a position in a file descriptor owned by the current process, and there's no way to copy that. Send the path instead, and let the worker open the file itself.

Costs

Spawning is cheap. A task is a small record of the function and a copy of its arguments, pushed onto a queue that the thread pool works through, so queueing a hundred thousand tasks is perfectly reasonable.

What isn't free is the copying. Passing a large list to an isolate copies the whole list, once for every spawn. When a worker needs a lot of data, give it a description of the work instead, such as a path, a range of indexes or a query, and let it read the data itself:

Errors in Isolates

An uncaught error inside an isolate is raised at the join() call as an IsolateError, which carries the original error's message and the stack trace from inside the worker:

Nothing is lost. You get the failure in a place where you can deal with it, along with enough information to track it down. Notice the form of the message: the IsolateError wraps the worker's own error instead of replacing it, so e.message still names the ValueError and the line it came from.

If nobody joins a task, an error in that task has nowhere to go. scope(), described below, exists to prevent that.

Channels

A channel is a queue with a fixed capacity that can be shared between isolates. One side sends values and the other receives them, and like everything else, the values are copied on the way:

Read the loop condition carefully, because it's easy to get wrong. recv() returns nil both when someone sent a nil and when the channel is closed and empty, so the end of the stream is when you get nil and is_closed() is true. If you only checked for nil, the loop would stop early when a real nil was sent. If you only checked is_closed(), it would stop before the queue was empty.

channel(capacity) limits the size of the queue, which gives you backpressure automatically. A producer that sends faster than its consumer can receive blocks on send(), instead of letting the queue grow without limit.

Method Behavior
send(value, timeout) Blocks while the channel is full
recv(timeout) Blocks while the channel is empty
try_recv() Returns immediately, with nil if the channel is empty
close() Stops further sends. Pending values can still be received, after which recv() returns nil
is_closed() Whether the channel has been closed
length() How many values are waiting

You can see all of these behaviors from a single isolate, which makes it easy to understand how a channel works before you add a second one:

Look at the last four lines together. After close(), the queue still drains: recv() returned the buffered b before it started returning nil. Once a closed channel is empty, it keeps returning nil instead of raising an error. Only send() raises.

Closing a channel twice does no harm. try_recv() on an empty channel returns nil immediately and never blocks.

Waiting on Several Channels

select() waits on several channels at once and tells you which one produced a value:

It returns [channel, value], so you can find out where the value came from by comparing the first element with the channels you passed in. The second argument is a timeout in seconds, like every other timeout in this module. See Timeouts Are in Seconds, because the net module does the opposite.

Use this for a consumer that gets input from more than one producer, such as work on one channel and shutdown signals on another, without polling either one.

Broadcasting

A channel delivers each value to a single receiver. A broadcast delivers each value to every subscriber:

subscribe() returns an ordinary Channel, so everything in the channel table applies to it, including recv(), try_recv(), length() and the same backpressure.

Subscribers Only See Later Values

Values aren't replayed. A subscriber that joins late misses everything that was sent before it subscribed:

This matters when subscribers are being set up at the same time as the producer starts. Either subscribe everything before anything is sent, or accept that a consumer that starts later will begin partway through the stream.

Unsubscribing, and Sending With No Subscribers

unsubscribe(channel) removes one subscriber. Sending when there are no subscribers isn't an error, and the value is simply thrown away:

A removed subscriber stops receiving new values right away, but its channel keeps any values that were already queued:

So unsubscribing doesn't throw away what a consumer hasn't read yet. It only stops new values from arriving.

Closing a Broadcast

close() closes the broadcast and every channel it handed out. Subscribers receive what's left in their channels and then get nil, and send() raises an error:

Backpressure Applies to Each Subscriber

The capacity you give broadcast() is the capacity of each subscriber's channel. If a subscriber stops reading, its own buffer fills up, and once it's full, send() blocks. So one slow consumer holds up the producer, and therefore every other subscriber too.

If you can't let a slow consumer do that, give the broadcast a larger capacity, or have the slow consumer copy values into its own queue so that only it falls behind.

Channel or Broadcast?

Use a channel when each piece of work should be done once, by whichever worker is free. Use a broadcast when every consumer needs to see every event. Shutdown signals, configuration changes and progress updates are broadcasts, and jobs are channels.

Scopes

A scope owns the tasks spawned through it, and doesn't return until all of them have finished:

scope(body) calls body with a scope object, waits for everything spawned through that object, and returns whatever the body returned.

Scopes Wait Whether or Not You Join

Joining inside the body is how you collect results, but it isn't what makes the scope wait. The scope waits either way:

Neither task was joined, and the scope still didn't return until both had finished. children() returns the Isolate objects in the order they were spawned, and s.spawn_named() works just like the module-level function.

One Failure Stops the Whole Group

This is the main reason to use a scope. If you never join the result of a plain spawn(), any error it raises is silently lost. A scope raises it instead:

When a task fails, the body's return value is discarded and the error is raised by scope() itself. Use a scope whenever work is split across several tasks and all of them have to finish, and succeed, before the next step can start.

Waiting on Several Tasks

There are three helper functions for waiting on tasks, and they return different things:

wait_all(tasks, timeout) returns the results, in the same order as the tasks you passed, not the order in which they finished.

wait_any(tasks, timeout) returns the Isolate that finished first, not its result, so you still need to call join() on it. That way you can tell which task finished first.

map(fn, items, timeout) spawns one task for each item and collects the results. It's wait_all with the spawning done for you.

All three raise an IsolateTimeoutError if the timeout expires, and all three pass on a failure from any of the workers:

The whole call fails as soon as one element fails. If it's acceptable for individual items to fail, spawn and join the tasks yourself and wrap each join() in a catch, as the example at the end of this chapter does.

Spawning From Inside an Isolate

There's no restriction on nesting. A worker can spawn its own tasks and join them, and they run on the same thread pool:

This is mostly worth knowing as a warning, which the next section explains: nested tasks that wait on each other are the quickest way to run out of threads.

The Thread Pool

Each isolate doesn't get a thread of its own. Isolates run on a fixed pool of operating system threads, which by default has one thread per CPU core:

Setting the Pool Size

configure(threads) changes the size of the pool, but it only works before the pool has been created, which means before the first spawn. It returns whether it changed anything:

If you call it after a spawn, it returns false and does nothing. It doesn't raise an error, so a configure() call placed after some initialization code that already spawned a task won't have any effect. Put it at the very top of your entry file.

The size is a maximum, not a fixed number of threads. A new thread only starts when an isolate is waiting to run and every existing thread is busy, so a generous pool size for occasional bursts costs nothing when there's no burst. started_count() tells you how many threads the pool has started so far:

Why the Pool Size Matters

A pool with one thread per core can deadlock, and when it does, the program just hangs without reporting an error.

Here's how it happens. A task that blocks, whether on join(), recv() or a socket read, keeps its thread busy while it waits. If every thread is held by a task that's waiting for work that has no free thread to run on, nothing can make progress.

This is most likely with these three patterns:

  • A server and a client that talk to each other in the same process
  • Nested spawns where the parent task joins its child
  • A pipeline with more stages than there are threads

Size the pool for the number of tasks that might be blocked at the same time, not for the number of cores. Blocked threads don't compete for the CPU, so having too many costs very little, while having too few can stop the program completely.

Monitoring the Pool

active_count() returns how many tasks are running, and queued_count() returns how many are waiting for a thread. If the queued count keeps growing, the pool doesn't have enough threads.

shutdown(timeout) lets the pool finish its work and then stops it. Most programs never need to call it. It's there for long-running processes that want to release their threads without exiting.

Memory Use While Waiting

A pool thread keeps its isolate's heap from one task to the next, and garbage collection runs as the program allocates memory. A thread that's waiting doesn't allocate anything, so waiting threads collect garbage on their own. Once a thread has waited for one second, whether for its next task or inside recv(), select(), join(), wait_any() or wait_all(), it collects its garbage, and the memory is returned to the operating system. The main thread does the same in those calls. As a result, a task that built and then discarded a large data structure leaves the process at its normal working size rather than at its peak.

A wait of one second or less returns before that happens, and a heap that has grown by less than 4 MB since its last collection of this kind is left alone, so a loop that makes many short waits doesn't pay for it.

Error Types

This module raises three types of error, and each one means something different:

Error Raised when
IsolateError A worker raised an error or panicked, or an operation was invalid, such as sending on a closed channel. A panic that escapes from a Rust library called through ffi ends the process instead; see Rust in Depth.
IsolateTimeoutError A timeout expired before the operation finished
IsolateCancelledError A blocking call was interrupted by cancel()

All three inherit from Error, so a plain catch catches all of them, and you can use instance_of() to tell them apart.

The difference matters because each one calls for a different response. A timeout usually means you should retry or give up. A cancellation means you should shut down quietly. And an IsolateError that carries a worker's failure means something went wrong in your own code, and the message tells you what.

Example: Processing a Batch

This example spreads a computation across several tasks, collects the results, and reports a failure without losing the other results:

Three things make this work.

Every task is spawned before any of them are joined. Spawning all of them in one loop and joining them in another is what lets the work run in parallel. If you joined inside the first loop, the tasks would run one after another and you'd gain nothing.

Each number is stored alongside its task. The pool can finish the tasks in any order, and a plain list of results wouldn't tell you which input each result belongs to.

And the catch surrounds a single join(), so the one bad input produces one failed entry instead of ending the whole batch. If you moved it outside the loop, the first failure would take the other four results with it.

Choosing an Approach

Splitting work and collecting the results: use isolate.map(), or scope() when one failure should stop the whole group.

A pipeline: connect the stages with channels, run each stage in its own isolate, and give every channel a capacity so that backpressure reaches all the way back to the source.

Sending events to several consumers: use a broadcast, with one subscriber for each consumer.

A server: http.serve() sets all of this up for you, with one isolate per worker, a limited backlog, and connections handed out as they arrive. Chapter 15 covers it.

No concurrency at all: concurrency costs a copy every time a value crosses between isolates, and a lot of care every time you join. If a single-threaded loop finishes in time, it's the better program.

Chapter 12 · Working with the World

Networking

The net module is Zuri's socket layer. It covers TCP, UDP, Unix domain sockets, TLS, DTLS, address parsing and polling. The http module is built on top of it and provides a client and a server for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.

Every example in this chapter runs a server in an isolate and a client in the main program, which lets you test network code without needing two terminals. Chapter 11 explains isolates.

TCP

A TcpStream can be either end of a connection. bind() and accept() make it a listener, and connect() makes it a client. accept() blocks until a client connects, unless the listener is in non-blocking mode, in which case it returns nil when nobody is waiting.

There are three important things in this pair of files.

The server is in its own file. It has to be, because echo_server uses net, and a function that uses an imported module can't be spawned from the file that imported it. In server.zu, net is resolved inside the isolate instead of being captured from the caller. Chapter 11 explains this rule and the alternative.

Binding to port 0 asks the operating system for a free port, and local_address() tells you which one it chose. That's the right way to write a test, and the right way to run several servers in one process. The port is sent back to the main program through the channel, since the main program can't know it in advance.

The shutdown(net.Shutdown.WRITE) call is required here. read_as_string() keeps reading until the other side stops writing. Without a half-close from the client, the server would keep waiting for more of the request while the client waits for the response. That's a deadlock, and it looks just like a hang. Shutdown has READ, WRITE and BOTH.

Reading From a Socket

Method Behavior
read(length) Reads up to length bytes, whatever has arrived so far
read_exact(length) Reads exactly length bytes, waiting for them if necessary
read_all() Reads everything until the other side closes, as bytes
read_as_string() The same, decoded as UTF-8
peek(length) Looks at incoming bytes without consuming them

It's normal for read() to return fewer bytes than you asked for, and it isn't an error. That's what read_exact() is for.

Writing to a Socket

write(data) writes as much as it can and tells you how much it wrote. write_all(data) keeps writing until everything has been sent, and it's almost always the one you want.

Socket Options

Timeouts in this module are in milliseconds, unlike the isolate module, which uses seconds. It's easy to mix them up in a program that uses both.

Set a read timeout on every socket that talks to the network. If a socket has no timeout and the other side never responds, the thread using it never gets control back.

set_nodelay(true) turns off Nagle's algorithm, which is what you want for a request and response protocol where latency matters more than the number of packets.

set_non_blocking(true) makes a read or write that can't proceed fail instead of waiting. For a non-blocking socket watched with a net.Poller, try_read(length) and try_write(data) report this as a result instead of an error. try_read() returns nil when nothing has arrived, and try_write() returns how many bytes the socket accepted, which is 0 when it has no room. TlsStream has both methods, plus try_flush() for data it has encrypted but not yet sent.

UDP

The second line uses a placeholder because the real value is different every time. bind('127.0.0.1:0') asks the operating system for any free port, and it picks a different one each run.

receive_from(length) returns the bytes of the datagram. To find out who sent it, use peek_from(length), which returns { data, address } without consuming the datagram. So a responder peeks, reads and then replies.

If a datagram is larger than the buffer you provide, it's truncated and the rest is discarded. Make the buffer large enough for the largest message your protocol sends.

UDP sockets also have connect() to set a fixed peer, set_broadcast(), and join_multicast_v4() and join_multicast_v6().

Unix Domain Sockets

A Unix domain socket is identified by a path on the file system instead of an address on the network. It's the usual way for two programs on the same machine to communicate when one of them is a server. Databases, message brokers and system daemons nearly all listen on one.

There's no port that can clash with another program, and no way to reach the socket from another machine. And because the socket is a file, the file system decides who can connect. A socket inside a directory that only one user can access can only be reached by that user, which is more secure than binding to the loopback address and trusting everyone on the machine.

pair() returns two sockets that are already connected to each other, with no path and nothing left on disk:

A server binds to a path and accepts connections on it, just as a TcpStream binds to an address:

There are two differences from TCP, and both are because the socket is a file. First, bind() fails if the path already exists, even if it was left behind by a process that crashed, so a server that expects to be restarted should delete a stale path first. Second, closing the socket frees the file descriptor but doesn't delete the file, because by then another process might have bound the same path, and deleting it would break that process.

net.is_supported() returns false on Windows, where Unix domain sockets aren't available. On Windows, every call raises an error, but the module itself still exists, so a program that can fall back to TCP should check is_supported() rather than catch an error.

Addresses

resolve() converts a host name into addresses:

It returns a list because a name can have several addresses, and the result depends on the machine. A host with IPv6 configured returns addresses for both families, while one without IPv6 returns only [127.0.0.1:80]. Don't assume that an address is at a particular position in the list, or that it belongs to a particular family.

net.ip provides IpAddress, Ipv4Address and Ipv6Address for parsing, comparing and classifying addresses, which you'll need before you trust an X-Forwarded-For header.

TLS

net.tls wraps an existing TCP connection in TLS:

A TlsStream has the same methods for reading and writing as a TcpStream, so code written for one works with the other.

On the client side, tls.TlsStream.connect(socket, config, hostname) performs the handshake and verifies the server's certificate. config.add_ca_pem() adds a trusted certificate authority, and config.require_client_cert(true) turns on mutual TLS. Once the handshake has finished, peer_certificate() returns the other side's certificate.

net.dtls provides the same thing over UDP.

Polling

net.poll waits on many sockets at once without needing a thread for each one. It's the right tool when you have thousands of connections that are mostly idle, and the wrong tool when you have just a few busy ones. In that case, using an isolate per connection is simpler and faster.

Accepting Connections Without Blocking the Thread

accept() on a blocking listener waits inside the runtime, and nothing else on that thread can run while it waits. A signal handled with os.on_signal() isn't delivered, and a flag telling the server to stop isn't checked, until a connection happens to arrive. On an idle server, that might never happen, which is why pressing Ctrl+C on one can seem to do nothing.

net.Acceptor is an accept loop that doesn't have this problem. It switches the listener to non-blocking mode and waits on a poller instead. next() returns a connection when there is one, and returns nil when its interval passes without a connection arriving. That gives the loop a chance to check anything else it needs to.

The interval only affects how quickly a stopped server notices that it should stop, not how quickly a connection is handled, because a new connection ends the wait immediately. It doesn't add any delay while connections are arriving either, because next() tries accept() first and only uses the poller when there's nothing waiting.

This makes a server that you can stop with Ctrl+C:

The handler returns true to show that it has handled the signal. If a handler returns a falsy value, it declines the signal, and the process is terminated by the signal as it would be if no handler were registered.

http accepts connections this way in both HttpServer.listen() and http.serve(), and so do the SMTP and IMAP servers in mail. A server built on any of these can already be stopped with Ctrl+C.

Above the Socket Layer

So far, everything has been about sending bytes over a socket. Most programs need a protocol on top of that, and the standard library provides two.

http is a complete HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 client and server, with routing, middleware, cookies, multipart uploads, static files, server-sent events and WebSockets. It's big enough to need its own chapter, which is Chapter 15. Here's the shortest possible example:

net.tls wraps a TcpStream in TLS, as shown above, for protocols other than HTTP, such as a mail client, a database driver or a custom binary protocol.

Here's a rough guide to which layer to use:

If you're writing Use
A web API, or a client for one http
A server that browsers connect to http
A client for an existing protocol that isn't HTTP net.tcp, plus net.tls if the protocol is encrypted
A protocol of your own net.tcp and struct
Service discovery, telemetry or games net.udp
Anything that waits on many sockets at once net.poll
A server that has to stop on Ctrl+C net.Acceptor

Example: A Length-Prefixed Protocol

This example implements a request and response protocol of the kind net is designed for. Each message is a four-byte big-endian length, followed by that many bytes of JSON. Most binary protocols follow this pattern, and it's worth writing one by hand at least once.

The framing is the important part. TCP is a stream of bytes with no message boundaries. One write_all() might arrive as three reads, and three writes might arrive as one. Calling read_exact(4) and then read_exact(length) restores the boundaries, which read() on its own wouldn't do, because it returns whatever has arrived. That's why the table above lists both methods.

The end of the conversation is also worth looking at. read_exact() raises an error when the stream ends before all of the expected bytes have arrived, and that's exactly what happens when the other side closes the connection cleanly between messages. Catching the error and returning nil turns a closed connection into the loop's normal exit, rather than a crash.

Notice also that both sides share framed.zu. If you implement a protocol twice, once for each side, the two implementations will eventually disagree.

One last detail that's easy to miss: the reply key is reply, not echo. echo is a keyword, so it can't be used as a bare dictionary key, and { echo: x } is a syntax error. If you need that exact name, quote it: { 'echo': x }.

Other Submodules

net.poll tells you which sockets you can read from right now without a thread for each socket, which is how one isolate can serve many connections. It accepts a UnixStream as well as a TcpStream or a TlsStream. net.addr and net.ip parse, format and classify addresses with methods such as is_private(), is_loopback() and is_multicast(), which you'll need before trusting an address a client sent you. is_global() answers the question a server should ask before connecting to an address provided by someone else, such as a URL to fetch: is the address on the public internet, or in one of the ranges that the IANA registries reserve, from loopback and private ranges to carrier-grade NAT and documentation prefixes? net.dtls is TLS over UDP.

Appendix F lists all of the submodules.

Chapter 13 · Working with the World

A Tour of the Standard Library

The standard library comes with every installation. There's nothing to add to a manifest, no package manager to run and no dependencies to resolve, so import json works in a file you created ten seconds ago.

This chapter looks at what's available, grouped by what you'd use it for, with a working example of each module. It's an overview rather than a reference. Appendix F is the index, every module has doc comments in libs/, and the three largest modules have their own chapters: Wire, HTTP and Imagine.

Read through it once to see what exists. You don't need to remember the details. The point is that six months from now, when you're about to write something by hand, you'll remember that it's already in the standard library.

Data Formats

json

encode(value, compact, max_depth) produces compact output by default. parse(path) reads and decodes a file, and dump(value, file) writes one. A class that defines @to_json() controls how its instances are encoded.

yaml

Anchors, aliases, tags, documents with several parts and block scalars are all supported.

toml

parse() and dump() treat a document as data. edit() treats it as a file someone wrote by hand. The Document it returns is written back byte for byte until you change it, and a change only affects the line it's on.

That's what you need when a program edits someone else's configuration file: the comment is kept, and so is the spacing on the line that changed.

csv

Reader and Writer stream large files, Dialect configures separators and quoting, and sniff_dialect() guesses the dialect from a sample.

struct

For binary layouts, covered in Chapter 10.

base64, convert

convert handles conversions between number bases that you'd otherwise write by hand, and also has helpers for hex, binary, octal and Unicode.

Text and Markup

html

A parser that follows the WHATWG HTML standard, a full DOM and CSS selectors:

The DOM supports traversal, changes and serialization, so you can use this one module for scraping, as a template backend or to sanitize HTML.

wire

Templates, with directives written as HTML attributes instead of a second syntax mixed into your markup:

Everything is escaped by default, and escaped correctly for where it appears. A value in an attribute, in a URL and in a <script> block each need a different kind of escaping, and Wire knows which is which because it parses your template's structure instead of treating it as plain text.

Chapter 14 covers Wire in full.

url

encode(), decode() and parse_query() handle percent-encoding.

mime

detect(file) identifies a file's type by looking at its contents instead of trusting its extension, which is the check you want for uploaded files.

colors

ANSI colors for terminal output, and conversions between all the color spaces you're likely to have a value in:

colors.text(value, color, background) wraps a string in the escape codes:

The conversions are what let the same code work on a terminal that can't display the colors you asked for. A true-color value is converted to the nearest of 256 colors, and a 256-color value to the nearest of 16. hex(), rgb(), hsl(), hsv(), hwb(), cmyk() and xyz() each take a color in their color space and return the escape sequence for it.

Time

date

The format codes are single letters: Y for a four-digit year, m for a zero-padded month, d for a zero-padded day, H for the hour on a 24-hour clock, i for minutes, s for seconds, l for the name of the weekday, F for the name of the month, and jS for the day with an ordinal suffix.

localtime() and gmtime() return the current time, and from_time(seconds) converts a Unix timestamp. The module includes the IANA time zone database, so from_timezone('Europe/London', ...) handles daylight saving time changes correctly.

Cryptography and Identity

hash

Digests and HMACs, covered in Chapter 10.

bcrypt

Password hashing, which is a different problem from computing a digest:

Use bcrypt for passwords and hash for everything else. needs_rehash() tells you when a stored hash was created with a lower cost than you now require.

crypto

RSA signatures and HKDF key derivation.

uuid

Versions 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 are all available. v4 is the random version you'll usually want, and v7 is ordered by time, which makes it a better choice for database keys.

jwt

Signing, verifying and decoding JSON Web Tokens, with a JWKS client for keys that rotate.

Validation and Structure

validate

A schema builder with a fluent API:

check_or_raise() raises an error instead of returning the result. extend(), only() and except() build one schema from another, which is how you keep a schema for creating a record and a schema for updating it in sync.

types

Type checks, one for each type, as an alternative to the built-in is_* functions:

Each one answers a question and returns a boolean, and none of them convert anything. types.int(4.2) is false because 4.2 isn't an integer, not because converting it failed.

types.of() is the same as typeof(). digit(), alpha() and char() check the content of strings in ways the built-in functions don't, and instance(value, Class) checks the whole inheritance chain.

When you want to convert a value rather than check it, use the methods on the value itself: to_number(), to_string(), to_bigint(), to_list() and to_bytes().

set

Union, intersection, difference and subset checks, with insertion order preserved.

enum

Pass a dictionary instead of a list to choose the values yourself.

array

Typed numeric arrays with a fixed width, from Int8Array to Uint64Array, plus FloatArray and DoubleArray. They store values at their declared width instead of as doubles, which matters for memory use and for working with binary formats.

The Operating System

os

Processes, the file system, paths and environment variables, covered in Chapter 9.

os.exec(command) runs a shell command and returns its output. os.spawn(command, args, options) starts a process that you can communicate with. os.on_signal(name, handler) installs a signal handler. os.at_exit(handler) registers cleanup code that runs however the program ends, and os.set_exit_code(code) sets the exit status without ending the program right away.

env

Configuration: a .env file loaded into the process environment, and values read back out already converted to the right type. Covered in Chapter 19.

Variables that are already set in the environment aren't changed, so the file provides defaults and the deployment environment can override them.

io

Standard streams, terminal control and in-memory files:

io.TTY puts the terminal into raw mode, reads individual key presses and moves the cursor, which is what an interactive program needs. io.BytesIO is the in-memory file described in Chapter 10.

io.capture(body) collects everything body writes to standard output instead of printing it. That includes echo, print() and io.stdout:

Captures can be nested, and capture_begin() and capture_end() do the same thing manually, for when the body might raise an error and you still want its output. This is how the tests in Chapter 23 check what a function prints, and how output from passing tests is kept out of the report.

test

Test suites, matchers, mocks, snapshots and reports, covered in Chapter 23.

stat

The S_IS* functions for the mode value returned by file().stats(), plus a function to format it:

S_ISREG, S_ISDIR, S_ISLNK, S_ISCHR, S_ISBLK, S_ISFIFO and S_ISSOCK each check for one kind of entry. S_IMODE(mode) removes the type bits and keeps the permissions, and file_mode(mode) formats the whole value the way ls -l does.

args

A command-line parser with subcommands, typed options, automatic --help and output that wraps to the terminal width. Covered in Chapter 20.

The help text is generated from the same declarations that parse the arguments, so the two can't get out of sync.

log

A Logger attaches structured fields to every record, a child() logger inherits the fields of its parent, and transports send the records to the console, to a file or to a destination you write yourself.

isolate

Concurrency, covered in Chapter 11.

ffi

Calling C and Rust code. ffi loads shared libraries, reads their C headers or Rust source files as declarations, calls their functions with checked conversions, and turns Zuri functions into callbacks. It can also link static libraries into loadable ones.

Covered in Chapter 26.

Networking

net

TCP, UDP, Unix domain sockets, TLS, DTLS, addresses and polling, covered in Chapter 12.

http

An HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 client and server, with routing, middleware, WebSockets, server-sent events, multipart uploads, static files and a reverse proxy. It's introduced in Chapter 12, covered in full in Chapter 15, and used throughout Chapter 25.

rpc

JSON-RPC 2.0, the protocol for calling methods in another program, for both the calling side and the answering side. A service answers calls with handlers, either behind an http route or on a connection. A client calls a service over HTTP. An endpoint, which can run over a WebSocket, a socket, a child process's standard streams or a pipe between isolates, both answers and makes calls, so either side can call the other at any time. rpc.serve() gives each connection to a listening socket its own endpoint, over TCP, TLS or a Unix domain socket.

Covered in Chapter 28.

Databases

sql

A single API for relational databases, whichever one you use. sql defines what a database adapter has to provide, and supplies everything that's the same across databases: parameters, transactions and savepoints, cursors, connection pools, introspection and a single error hierarchy. It comes with adapters for SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL, and switching between them means changing the connection string. On top of that, db.schema changes tables using one description that works for every database, sql.migrate applies versioned migrations, and sql.model gives each table a class.

Covered in Chapter 17.

Mail

mail

Email messages, and the three protocols used to send and receive them, all written in Zuri from the socket up. mail.message() builds a message from text, HTML and attachments and works out the MIME structure for you, and mail.parse() reads a message back in. mail.smtp sends mail, mail.imap reads mail where it's stored, and mail.pop3 downloads it. The server side is included too: an SMTP server that uses your own handlers to decide what to accept, and an IMAP server that serves messages from a mail store. One store keeps mail on disk in Maildir format and the other keeps it in memory. mail.dkim signs outgoing mail and verifies incoming mail.

Covered in Chapter 18.

Compression

compress

deflate, zlib, gzip, zstd, lz4, bzip2 and brotli, plus tar and zip archives and checksum for CRC32 and Adler-32. Covered in Chapter 10.

Graphics

imagine

Creating and editing images in an RGBA buffer, with drawing functions, text in a built-in stroke font, filters, color space conversion, and reading and writing the common image formats.

Almost every method returns an image, so you can chain operations. Image.open(path) decodes an existing file, working out the format from the file's contents instead of its extension:

Decoding and encoding are done in native code. Everything in between, including filters, drawing and color conversion, is ordinary Zuri code that you can read and extend in libs/imagine. Chapter 16 covers it in full.

The Language Itself

zuri

Lexing, parsing, compiling and reflection, all available from Zuri code:

Chapter 21 covers it in full.

math

Mathematical constants. Everything else is a method of number, as described in Chapter 4.

Learning More

The source code for every module is in libs/, and every public function has a doc comment describing its parameters, their default values and its edge cases. Reading libs/set.zu is a quicker way to learn the set module than any summary, and the standard library is written to be readable.

Chapter 14 · The Big Modules

Wire

Wire is Zuri's built-in template engine. Unlike most template languages, Wire doesn't add its own syntax on top of your markup. Every Wire feature works through attributes on ordinary HTML elements, so anything a designer already knows about HTML still applies, and every valid HTML5 document is already a valid Wire template.

A Wire template is compiled once into a small tree of instructions, instead of being interpreted again on every render. It's parsed with the same WHATWG-conformant parser that the html module uses. One consequence is worth knowing from the start: Wire understands your markup as structure, not as text. It knows that one interpolation is inside a paragraph, another is inside an href and a third is inside a <script> tag, and it escapes each one correctly for where it is. A value passed to a template can never become new markup by accident. If you want that, you have to ask for it explicitly.
