Introduction

Wire and Blade

If you've used Laravel's Blade, PHP's best-known template engine, a lot of Wire will feel familiar, even though the syntax is different. Both engines compile templates instead of interpreting them on every request, both let you extend a base layout and override named sections of it, and both escape everything by default, so displaying a user's name can never let that user run a script in someone else's browser.

Where Wire differs from Blade is in how it handles control flow. Blade adds its own directive syntax on top of plain text (@if, @foreach, {{ }}), which a template author has to learn as a second language on top of HTML. Wire expresses everything as attributes on the HTML you'd be writing anyway:

In practice, this means you can give a Wire template to a designer who has never seen Zuri, and they can still read it. It's just HTML with some attributes they can look up. It also means every Wire template is valid HTML5, can be opened directly in a browser to check its structure, and can be processed with the html module's tools (html.format(), a linter, a selector query) without any special handling for Wire.

Your First Template

Here's the smallest possible Wire template, rendered from a string:

{{ name }} is an interpolation. It evaluates the expression name using the variables you passed in and writes the result into the page, escaped correctly for wherever it appears. Everything else in this chapter builds on that idea, along with a few attributes starting with x- that control whether an element is rendered and how many times.

Rendering Templates

Templates From Files

For anything more than a quick snippet, you'll want to keep templates in files. Create a Wire instance, point it at a directory, and render templates by their path:

The first argument to render() is a path relative to the root. If the path doesn't name an existing file, .html is added automatically, so 'pages/home' finds pages/home.html. A path that already has an extension, such as 'pages/home.wire', is tried exactly as given first. set_extension() changes the extension that's tried when none is given.

Note A Wire instance is meant to be created once, configured, and reused for the lifetime of your program, usually at startup, in the same place you configure the rest of your application. Rendering doesn't change the instance, so it's safe to render from several places at once.

Templates From Strings

render_string() renders a template passed directly as a string, without touching the file system. Apart from that, it behaves exactly like render(), with the same directives, escaping and filters, and any x-include or x-extend in the string is still resolved relative to the configured root.

The third argument names the source in error messages, and defaults to <source>. It's worth passing when the string came from somewhere with its own identity, such as a database row or a file you'd already opened for another reason:

render_string() isn't cached, since there's no file path to use as a cache key. Use render() for anything you render more than once.

The Template Root

Every path, whether it's passed to render() or written in an x-include or x-extend in a template, is resolved inside the configured root directory and nowhere else. This isn't just a convention. The loader enforces it every time it resolves a path, and it matters for security, not only for keeping things organized.

The root directory doesn't have to exist yet. create_root() creates it and tells you whether it needed to:

Wire never creates this directory by itself. If you make a typo in the root path, you should get a "template not found" error, not an empty folder created somewhere unexpected.

Displaying Data

You've already seen the basic form. {{ expression }} evaluates whatever is between the braces and writes the result into the page:

expression doesn't have to be a variable name. It can be a full expression, which is covered in its own section below, so all of these are valid:

Escaping Data

Every interpolation is escaped for the place where it appears, and you can't turn this off from inside a template. If name contains <b>Ada</b>:

the result is:

That's exactly what you want when name came from a form field, a database column or anywhere else outside your control. Wire isn't guessing here. Because it compiles a parsed document instead of joining strings together, it always knows exactly what kind of place an interpolation is in, and applies the escaping that place needs:

Where the interpolation is What happens
Text between tags &, < and > are replaced with entities
An ordinary attribute (title, alt, data-* and so on) & and " are replaced with entities
href, src, action and other URL attributes The URL scheme is checked as well
<script>, or an on* event handler attribute The value is encoded as JSON
<style> Any character outside a set that's safe in CSS is removed

That's a much stronger guarantee than simply replacing special characters. A value placed in an href can't sneak in a javascript: URL, and a value placed in a <script> block can't break out of its string literal, close the tag early or start a comment, even though none of those attacks need <, > or &.

Rendering Raw Markup

Escaping everything by default is the right choice, but sometimes you really do have markup, such as the output of another render or a snippet you built yourself and trust, and you want to write it out as markup. The raw filter lets you do that:

You can also mark a value as safe in your Zuri code before passing it to the template, with wire.safe():

Warning raw and wire.safe() tell Wire that the value is safe to write without escaping where it appears. If you use either one on anything a user submitted, such as a comment, a profile or a search query, you reopen the cross-site scripting hole that the rest of Wire is designed to close. Only use them on markup that your own code produced.

If you want to display markup as text, for example to show a literal <script> tag in a code sample, a plain interpolation already does that. You don't need to do anything extra.

Wire and JavaScript Frameworks

Wire uses {{ }} for interpolation, which is the same delimiter that many JavaScript template libraries use, including Vue, Angular, Handlebars and Mustache. If a Wire template contains inline script that a browser-side framework is supposed to process, put a % in front of the braces so that Wire leaves them alone:

%{{ produces the literal text {{, and %{! does the same for template function calls. If you find you're escaping braces all the time because most of a template belongs to a client-side framework, consider moving that part into its own file and serving it as is, without Wire.

The Expression Language

Everything between {{ and }}, as well as everything you pass to x-if, x-for, x-attr and the other directives below, is written in Wire's own small expression language. It's intentionally not a full copy of Zuri: there's no assignment, no way to declare anything and no way to access global variables. A template describes a page, and the logic that decides what goes on the page belongs in the code that calls render(), not in the template.

Literals

Looking Up Values

Reading a variable that wasn't passed in gives you nil instead of an error, and reading a key from nil also gives you nil. That lets you safely reach into an optional value without checking it first:

If user has no profile, this renders nothing instead of failing three levels down. Use x-if when the difference between "empty" and "missing" affects what you display.

Note A template can never read a name that starts with an underscore, in the same way that Zuri treats _field as private. If you need a value like that in a template, expose it through a public accessor in your Zuri code.

Operators

When either side of + is a string, it concatenates instead of raising an error:

?? and or look similar but do different things, and mixing them up is the most common mistake people make with Wire:

  • ?? checks whether the value was passed in at all, and only uses the fallback for nil.
  • or checks whether the value is worth displaying, using Wire's own rules for truthiness, and uses the fallback for anything falsy: nil, false, an empty string, an empty collection or the number 0.

Use ?? when zero is a valid value that you want to display, and or when you only want to show something if there's actually something to show.

Truthiness

x-if, x-not, and/or, !/not and ? : all follow Wire's own rules for what's truthy and falsy. These rules differ from Zuri's in one place, on purpose, to make templates easier to write:

Value In Wire
nil, false Falsy
0, NaN Falsy
Any other number, including negative numbers Truthy
An empty string Falsy
A non-empty string Truthy
An empty list or dictionary Falsy
A non-empty list or dictionary Truthy
Anything else Truthy

The difference is empty collections. Zuri treats [] and {} as truthy, but Wire treats them as falsy, so x-if="results" hides a section when a search returns nothing.

Calling Functions

You can call a value that's been registered as a global directly:

There's also an older syntax for calling a function that takes no arguments. It's been kept from Wire's first version because it reads well on its own:

This is exactly the same as writing:

Use {{ fn() }} in new templates. {! !} is there for templates that already use it, and for the few cases, such as a build stamp or a feature flag, where a function with no arguments reads a little better without the parentheses.

Filters

A filter transforms the value to the left of a |, much like a Unix pipe:

The value being filtered is always the filter's first argument, and anything in parentheses comes after it. truncate(150) above calls the truncate filter as truncate(post.body, 150).

Chaining Filters

Filters are applied from left to right, and the output of each one is passed to the next:

The = Argument Shorthand

For a filter that takes exactly one argument, name=value is a shorter way of writing name(value):

This is the same as:

This syntax was kept for consistency with Wire's first version, and it reads well for a short comparison. The form with parentheses works everywhere, and it's the only option once a filter needs more than one argument.

Available Filters

Escaping

Filter What it does
raw Marks the value as markup, so it isn't escaped at all.
escape / e Escapes the value for a different context from the one it's being written into. Takes 'text' (the default), 'attribute', 'url', 'script' or 'style'.

Text

Filter What it does
upper Converts the value to uppercase.
lower Converts the value to lowercase.
title Capitalizes the first letter of every word.
capitalize Capitalizes only the first letter and leaves the rest unchanged.
trim Removes all leading and trailing whitespace, including spaces, tabs and newlines.
truncate(length, suffix?) Shortens the value to length characters, adding suffix ('…' by default) only if something was removed.
replace(search, replacement?) Replaces every occurrence of the literal string search. It never uses a regular expression. replacement defaults to an empty string.
lpad(width, fill?) Pads the value on the left to width characters with fill, which is a space by default.
rpad(width, fill?) Pads the value on the right.
repeat(count) Repeats the value count times.
nl2br Escapes the text and then replaces line breaks with <br>. Returns markup.
line_breaks Another name for nl2br.
strip_tags Removes all HTML tags and keeps only the text. It parses the HTML properly rather than using pattern matching.
slug Converts the value to lowercase words separated by hyphens, safe to use in a URL.
url_encode(reserved?) Percent-encodes the value for use in a URL, as url.encode() does. Reserved characters such as /, & and # are kept unless reserved is false, which you need for a single value in a query string: ?q={{ query|url_encode(false) }}.
json Encodes the value as JSON.
json_script(id?) Wraps the value's JSON encoding in a <script type="application/json"> tag, with an optional id, so that a script on the page can read it. Returns markup.

Numbers

Filter What it does
abs Returns the absolute value.
round(places?) Rounds to places decimal places (0 by default), with halves rounded away from zero.
floor Rounds down to the nearest whole number.
ceil Rounds up to the nearest whole number.
number_format(places?, point?, separator?) Adds thousands separators and a fixed number of decimal places, as in 1,234,567.89. Pass point and separator to use another convention, such as 1.234.567,89.
filesize(binary?) Formats a number of bytes in a readable way, such as 1.4 MB by default, or 1.3 MiB when binary is true.

Collections

Filter What it does
length The number of items. Works on strings, lists, dictionaries and bytes. The length of nil is 0.
first The first item, or nil if there isn't one.
last The last item.
join(glue?) Joins the items into a single string with glue (an empty string by default) between them.
sort(key?) Sorts in ascending order. key sorts a list of dictionaries or instances by one of their fields.
reverse The items in reverse order, or a reversed string.
unique Removes duplicates, keeping the first occurrence of each.
keys A dictionary's keys, in insertion order.
values A dictionary's values, in insertion order.
slice(start, end?) The items from start up to but not including end. Negative positions count from the end.
sum(key?) Adds up the items. key adds up one field of a list of dictionaries or instances.
split(separator?) Splits a string into a list. By default, it splits on any run of whitespace.

Choice

Filter What it does
default(fallback) / alt Returns fallback when the value is falsy, and the value otherwise.
empty Whether the value is empty. Unlike falsiness, a number is never empty, not even 0.
is(expected) Whether the value equals expected.
not(expected) Whether the value differs from expected.

Dates

Filter What it does
date(format?) Formats a date.Date, a Unix timestamp or a date string that can be parsed, using the same format codes as Date.format(). The default format is 'Y-m-d H:i:s'.

Writing Your Own Filter

See Custom Filters below.

Conditionals

x-if, x-elif, and x-else

x-if renders an element, along with everything inside it, only when its expression is truthy:

If user.is_admin is falsy, the whole <p>, tag and contents, is left out of the page completely. No empty element is left behind.

Add more conditions with x-elif, and end the chain with a plain x-else:

Exactly one of these elements is rendered. Only whitespace and HTML comments are allowed between the elements in a chain, so any real content in between ends the chain. An x-elif or x-else without an x-if before it is rejected when the template compiles, rather than silently ignored:

x-not

x-not is simply the opposite of x-if. It renders the element when its expression is falsy, and it can't be part of a chain:

x-if="!condition" and x-not="condition" mean the same thing. x-not exists because it often reads better as a guard clause.

Loops

x-for repeats an element once for each item in whatever its expression evaluates to, which can be a list, a dictionary, a string or a range:

Notice that the element itself is repeated, not just its contents. The example above produces a separate <li> for each post, not one <li> containing all of them. x-value names the variable that holds the current item on each pass. If you don't need to refer to the item by name, leave it out.

An optional x-key gives you the position (for a list) or the key (for a dictionary):

Every kind of collection can be iterated over:

A missing or empty collection simply renders nothing, so you don't need to wrap a loop in an x-if:

The loop Variable

On each pass, Wire makes a loop variable available, with these fields:

Field Value
loop.index The position, counting from 1
loop.index0 The position, counting from 0
loop.first true on the first pass
loop.last true on the last pass
loop.length The total number of items
loop.even true on the 2nd, 4th, 6th and later even-numbered passes, counted by loop.index
loop.odd true on the 1st, 3rd, 5th and later odd-numbered passes
loop.key The current key or index, whether or not x-key is also used
loop.value The current value, whether or not x-value is also used
loop.parent The loop variable of the enclosing loop, in a nested x-for

Nesting Loops

x-loop renames the metadata variable for a particular x-for, so you can refer to both the inner loop's loop and the outer loop's loop at the same time:

Without x-loop, the inner loop's loop hides the outer one inside the inner loop. If you'd rather not rename anything, use loop.parent instead:

Looping Without a Wrapper Element

Sometimes you want to repeat several elements together without wrapping them in a real element, or without adding any element at all. Put the directive on a <template> element instead of on the element you want to repeat:

<template> is the one HTML element the parser accepts unchanged wherever it appears, including inside a <head>, a <table> or a <select>. Wire removes the <template> itself from the output and keeps only its contents, once for each pass. You can also use it to apply x-if to a group of elements without choosing one of them to carry the attribute:

Content and Attributes

x-text

x-text replaces an element's children with the value of its expression, escaped as plain text. It's useful when the element already has other attributes and you don't want to write the value twice:

This is the same as:

Anything written inside the element in the source is thrown away. It's only there to show what would appear on the page without JavaScript.

x-html

x-html is the unescaped version of x-text. It replaces the element's children with the value of its expression, written as markup instead of text:

Note the |raw. x-html still expects a value that's been marked as safe, just like an ordinary interpolation does. x-html only changes where the markup goes, replacing the element's contents instead of appearing inline in the text. It doesn't turn off escaping by itself. The warning about untrusted input applies here just as it does to the raw filter.

x-attr

x-attr takes a dictionary of names and values and adds them to the element as attributes:

In that dictionary:

  • true produces an attribute without a value, such as required, just as if you'd written required yourself.
  • false and nil leave the attribute out completely, instead of writing it with an empty value or the text "false".
  • Any other value is written as the attribute's value, escaped according to what the attribute means. As always, a URL attribute is checked as a URL.

This lets you turn a boolean into a real HTML boolean attribute without writing a conditional expression everywhere you need one:

An attribute set by x-attr overrides one written directly on the same element, so you can write a sensible default and only override it when you need to:

Comments

In a Wire template, an ordinary HTML comment is a note for the server. It never appears in the rendered page, and nothing inside it is evaluated. That means you can safely leave notes for other people who maintain the template without sending them to the browser:

If you really do want a comment to reach the browser, such as a conditional comment or a build stamp that a deployment script checks for, turn comments back on for that Wire instance with set_comments(true).

Including Templates

<include path="..." /> renders another template in its place. You can also write it as a directive, <template x-include="...">, which means exactly the same thing. The element forms in this chapter (<include>, <extend>, <declare> and <define>) are shorthand. They're rewritten into the directive form before the template is parsed, which is why they work correctly inside a <head> or a <table>, where the parser would otherwise move or drop an element it doesn't recognize.

This is the same as:

The path is resolved inside the template root, just like the path passed to render().

By default, an included template can see every variable that the surrounding page can see. It doesn't have a separate scope:

This renders correctly even though user was never passed to the partial explicitly.

Passing Data to an Include

x-with adds variables for the included template, in addition to the ones it already inherits:

only hides the surrounding scope completely, so the partial only sees what x-with gives it. This turns a plain partial into something more like a component, with a defined interface:

Includes as Components

Anything you write inside an <include> tag is passed to the included template as a named region called content, which the template declares with <declare name="content">:

The result is:

The content inside the <include> tag keeps the scope it was written in, which is the page's scope, not the partial's. That's why {{ orders|length }} above can read a variable from the page, even though x-only wasn't used and the card component never refers to orders.

Computed Include Paths

A path is read as literal text, with {{ }} interpolation allowed inside it. It isn't an expression, so x-include="header" refers to a file called header, not to a variable with that name:

This resolves to a different file on each render, depending on current_theme. Everything after path="themes/" up to the next {{ is taken literally.

Template Inheritance

Includes are for small, reusable pieces such as a navigation bar, a footer or a badge. For the overall structure of a page, meaning the parts of the layout that every page on your site shares, template inheritance works better. Includes combine pieces, while inheritance lets a base layout define the shape of a page once, so each page only fills in the parts that are different.

Defining a Layout

A base template marks the regions that a page can fill in with <declare name="...">:

Notice that footer already has some content inside its <declare> tag. That's the default, which is rendered when a page doesn't define that region.

Extending a Layout

A page states which layout it extends with <extend base="...">, and fills in regions with <define name="...">:

Rendering pages/dashboard.html produces the complete layout, with head and content replaced by what the page defined, and footer left as the layout's own default. The layout and the page are both rendered with the same variables that were passed to render(), so there's no separate scope that you need to pass values through.

Everything inside an <extend> has to be inside a <define>. The base template owns the structure of the page, and a page's job is only to fill in the regions the layout offers, not to add markup of its own outside them. A template can only extend one base template.

Default Slot Content

A region that a page doesn't define keeps whatever the layout put inside its <declare> tag:

A <declare> tag with nothing inside it, like head in the layout above, simply renders nothing when no page defines it.

x-super

<super />, or its directive form <template x-super></template>, renders whatever the region it's in would have shown if this definition hadn't replaced it. That lets a page add to a region instead of repeating all of it:

This renders the layout's own copyright line, followed by the extra privacy link, without the page needing to know or repeat what the layout's default footer said.

Multi-Level Inheritance

A template that extends a base can declare regions of its own, which lets another template extend it in turn. This is how you'd usually structure a site with a general layout and several layouts for specific kinds of page, such as a blog post or a product page:

Rendering pages/post.html follows the whole chain. It extends layouts/article.html, which extends layouts/app.html, and the final page is assembled from all three.

Overriding a Definition

Defining the same region twice in one template is nearly always a mistake, for example two people editing the same file, or a copy and paste that was never cleaned up. So Wire rejects it at compile time, unless you mark the second definition with override to show that it's intentional:

Without override on the second definition, this template fails to compile with a clear message that names the region and both locations, instead of silently keeping whichever definition came last.

Security

Why Everything Is Escaped by Default

Part of a template engine's job is to stop values that came from outside your program, such as a form submission, a query string or another user's profile, from turning into markup, a script or a link, unless you explicitly say they're safe. Wire does this by default rather than as an option you have to enable. As soon as escaping is something you have to remember to turn on, the templates where someone forgot are the ones that get exploited.

Every interpolation is escaped for the place where it appears (see the table earlier in this chapter), and there's no template setting that turns this off. The only way around it is the explicit and easy-to-spot raw filter or x-html directive. That's the right amount of friction between displaying a value and trusting it as unescaped markup.

URLs Are Checked, Not Just Escaped

Attributes that a browser treats as URLs, such as href, src, action and several others, get more than entity escaping. Their scheme is checked against an allowlist, and a scheme that isn't allowed is replaced with about:blank instead of being written out:

If profile_link were javascript:alert(document.cookie), the rendered href would be about:blank, not the script URL. A URL without a scheme, which includes every relative link, absolute path and protocol-relative URL, is always allowed, because none of them can refer to a handler.

The default allowlist includes http, https, mailto, tel and a few others, and it deliberately leaves out javascript, vbscript, data and file. If your application needs another scheme, such as a custom app: handler, use set_url_schemes() to replace the list.

srcset and ping each contain a list of URLs, and every URL in the list is checked in the same way. Descriptors such as 2x and 640w, and the separators between entries, are kept exactly as written.

Scripts and Stylesheets

A value interpolated inside a <script> element, or inside an event handler attribute such as onclick, is encoded as JSON instead of just being escaped. This happens automatically, with no filter needed:

This renders the whole user value as a JSON literal, quotes included. Keep this in mind, because it changes how you write the script around it: don't put your own quotes around the interpolation.

In a <style> block, any character outside a conservative set that's safe in CSS is removed rather than escaped. No escape sequence would stop the HTML tokenizer from reading a < while it looks for </style>, so the only safe option is to remove the character.

The Template Root Is a Sandbox

Every path, whether it was passed to render() or written in an x-include or x-extend inside a template, even one built from an interpolated value, is resolved inside the configured root. If it resolves anywhere else, including through .. segments or symbolic links, it's rejected:

If theme ever came from something a request controls, a loader without this check would let an attacker read any file the process can access. Wire's loader treats the root as a strict boundary instead, so the worst a malicious value can do here is fail to find a template.

Extending Wire

Custom Filters

register_filter() adds a new filter, or replaces an existing one with the same name. The value being filtered is always the first argument, followed by any arguments the template passes:

An argument that the template leaves out is nil, which is why words == nil ? 25 : words above provides a default instead of requiring the template to pass a value every time.

When a filter returns a plain value, that value is escaped like any other interpolation. A filter that produces markup should return wire.safe(), and from then on it's responsible for what's inside, just as raw and x-html are.

Globals

register_global() makes a value available to every template, without passing it to render() each time:

A variable with the same name passed to render() takes priority over a global. A global is a default, not a fixed value, so a page can still override site_name if it needs to.

Custom Elements

For the rare cases that the directives can't handle, register_element() takes over an HTML tag name and passes every element with that name to a Zuri function instead of writing it out:

The function receives the Wire instance and a dictionary that describes the element: its tag name, its attributes (already rendered and escaped), its rendered children and the scope it was written in. Return wire.safe(markup) to write markup, any other value to write it as escaped text, or nil to write nothing. Directives still work on a custom element as you'd expect, so <icon x-if="..." /> behaves the way it looks. This feature is meant for markup that really does have to be generated by code, where a partial and x-include aren't enough. Try an include first. It's easier for the next person to read, and they won't have to go looking for the Zuri function behind it.

Configuration

You can pass every setting to the Wire constructor at once, or set each one later with its own method:

Option / method Default What it controls
root / set_root(path) ./templates The directory that every template path is resolved inside.
extension / set_extension(ext) .html The extension tried when a path doesn't name an existing file. Must start with ..
compact / set_compact(bool) false Removes text between tags that's only whitespace.
comments / set_comments(bool) false Whether HTML comments appear in the rendered output.
auto_reload / set_auto_reload(bool) true Whether a cached template is checked against its file before each render, and read again if the file has changed.
url_schemes / set_url_schemes(list) See above Which URL schemes href, src and similar attributes can use.

root() returns the configured root as an absolute path, and create_root() creates the directory if it doesn't exist yet, returning whether it had to.

Compiling and Caching

The first time a template is used, render() compiles it into a tree of instructions and keeps the result for later. Parsing and resolving directives happen once per template, not once per request, and every later render just walks the tree.

When auto_reload is on, which is the default, each render compares the file's modification time and size with the cached values and recompiles the template if either has changed. That costs one file system stat per template per render, which is cheap and exactly what you want while you're editing templates. Once you're running under load and no longer editing templates, turn it off with set_auto_reload(false). A long-running process can then call clear_cache() to pick up a new deployment.

Under zuri run --watch, a template change does more than reload the template. Changing any template the program has rendered restarts the program, just as changing its code does, because Wire tells watch mode about every template file it reads.

compile(path) compiles a template without rendering it and returns the compiled result, or raises an error if the template has a mistake in it. That makes it useful for checking a whole directory of templates at startup, so that a broken template is caught before the first request that would use it:

Error Handling

Every error that Wire raises is a wire.WireError, and each one includes the template path and the line and column of the tag that caused it. That means catching the base class is enough to handle any template failure in one place, whether you turn it into a 500 page, log it with context or do something else your application needs:

Three more specific error classes, all subclasses of WireError, tell you what kind of problem occurred:

Error Raised when
wire.TemplateSyntaxError A template doesn't compile, for example because of an unknown directive, an invalid expression or a broken inheritance chain. It's always raised the first time the template is used, not on a later render.
wire.TemplateNotFoundError A path doesn't name a file, or resolves to somewhere outside the template root.
wire.RenderError Something went wrong because of the values a template received, for example iterating over something that can't be iterated, a filter rejecting its input, or a chain of includes that never ends.

A variable that was never passed in is not an error. It renders as nothing and counts as falsy, by design, so you can write an optional section without guarding every field it uses.

Full Directive Reference

These are all the directives Wire understands. Any other attribute starting with x- fails to compile, because Wire reserves the whole prefix. That way, a typo such as x-fi is caught as soon as the template compiles, rather than silently doing nothing.

Directive Takes Meaning
x-if Expression Renders the element only if the expression is truthy. Starts a chain.
x-elif Expression Continues an x-if chain.
x-else (nothing) Ends an x-if chain.
x-not Expression Renders the element only if the expression is falsy. Can't be part of a chain.
x-for Expression Repeats the element once for each item.
x-value Name Names the value on each pass.
x-key Name Names the key or index on each pass.
x-loop Name Renames the loop metadata variable.
x-text Expression Replaces the children with escaped text.
x-html Expression Replaces the children with unescaped markup.
x-attr Expression (dictionary) Adds attributes to the element.
x-include Path Renders another template in place of this element.
x-with Expression (dictionary) Adds variables for an include.
x-only (nothing) Hides the surrounding scope from an include.
x-extend Path Makes this template extend the named base template.
x-slot Name Declares a region that an extending template can replace.
x-define Name Replaces a region of the base template.
x-override (nothing) Allows a region that's already been defined to be defined again.
x-super (nothing) Renders the definition that this one replaces.

Five elements are shorthand for the directives above, and they're rewritten before the template is parsed:

Element Equivalent to
<include path="p" /> <template x-include="p"></template>
<extend base="p">…</extend> <template x-extend="p">…</template>
<declare name="n">…</declare> <template x-slot="n">…</template>
<define name="n">…</define> <template x-define="n">…</template>
<super /> <template x-super></template>

Cheat Sheet

Further reading: the html module that Wire's parser and serializer are built on, and the date module for the format directives the date filter accepts.

Chapter 15 · The Big Modules

HTTP

The http module is Zuri's HTTP stack. It contains a client, a server and the building blocks they share. It supports HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, over plain connections or TLS, and it's designed to be exposed directly to the internet.

That last point is a deliberate design decision. Many language runtimes include an HTTP server that's fine for development, but expect you to put a reverse proxy in front of it in production to terminate TLS, serve static files, compress responses, enforce request limits and speak HTTP/2 to browsers. All of those features are built into this module.
