Code blocks in this chapter that list several calls together are reference listings, not programs. They show the form of each call, not a sequence to run. Anything shown as a complete program runs as written. The PostgreSQL and MySQL examples need a database server, so they're shown but not run.

Following Along

Most of the examples below use a small database of posts and their authors. This creates it:

From here on, the examples assume that this file exists in the working directory.

Introduction

A database library usually ties a program to a single engine. Its functions are named after that engine, its placeholders follow that engine's syntax, and its errors use that engine's error numbers, so switching to another database means rewriting every call.

sql keeps the parts that are the same for every engine in one place, so you write a statement once:

If you change the first line to postgres://localhost/app or mysql://localhost/app, the rest runs unchanged. On PostgreSQL, the ? becomes $1, because that's what PostgreSQL expects, and on MySQL it stays ?, because that's what MySQL expects. An insert that asks for its new ID gets a RETURNING clause on PostgreSQL, because PostgreSQL has no "last insert ID" and the other two do. A duplicate key is reported as a UniqueViolation by all three.

What sql doesn't do is pretend that the engines are the same. They differ on auto-incrementing keys, on which functions are available and on a lot of other SQL. sql translates what it can and is explicit about the rest.

Connecting to a Database

open() takes a connection string and returns a Connection.

The scheme selects the adapter. A string without a scheme is treated as a SQLite file path, since it can't be anything else. MySQL and MariaDB use the same protocol, so either scheme can connect to either server, and the connection is described by the adapter for whichever server it found.

You can also pass options as a dictionary, which is how you set anything an adapter supports beyond what fits in the connection string:

Or you can pass them alongside a connection string, in which case they're merged with, and override, the values in the string:

Close a connection when you're done with it. A catch block makes sure that happens, even if the code in between raises an error:

A connection belongs to the isolate that opened it and can't be passed to another isolate. An isolate that needs to use the database opens its own connection or its own pool.

Running Queries

query() runs a statement and reads its entire result:

A result is iterable, so in the most common case, that's all you need:

There are shorter forms for the most common kinds of result:

exec() is for statements you run for their effect rather than for rows:

And exec_script() runs several statements at once, which is what a schema file contains:

Parameters

Values are bound by the database engine and never inserted into the text of the statement. That's what keeps a value from being treated as SQL, and it's your entire defense against SQL injection.

Use ? for positional parameters:

Or use :name for named parameters, where the order doesn't matter and you can use the same name more than once:

sql rewrites these into whatever form the adapter expects: $1 and $2 for PostgreSQL, ?1 and ?2 for SQLite, and ? unchanged for MySQL, which already uses that form. The scanner recognizes when a ? or a : isn't a placeholder, so none of these are changed:

PostgreSQL uses ? as a JSON operator, so to write a literal one, use ??:

Never build a statement by joining strings around a value, even when the value looks safe. The two forms above cover every case where a value varies. When an identifier varies, quote it through the driver instead of interpolating it:

Rows, Columns and Types

A row is a dictionary keyed by column name, which is why you can write post.title.

Two columns with the same name collapse into one entry in a dictionary, so keep that in mind before you select id from both sides of a join. Give one of them an alias to fix it, or use tuples() if you can't.

Values are converted like this:

Zuri Database
nil NULL
bool A boolean, where the engine has one, and 0 or 1 otherwise
number An integer if the value is a whole number, and a float otherwise
bigint A 64-bit integer, for values too large for a double
string Text
bytes A blob
date.Date A timestamp
sql.Time A TIME interval, on engines that have one
sql.Decimal An exact decimal
list, dict JSON

Not every engine has all of these types. PostgreSQL has a real boolean type and MySQL doesn't, so a true written to MySQL is read back as 1. Use db.supports() to find out about this kind of difference instead of guessing. Each engine's section below describes where it differs.

An integer that's too large for a double is returned as a bigint instead of being silently rounded:

SQLite stores five kinds of value and doesn't record what you meant, so a boolean is stored as 1 and would be read back as the number 1. What SQLite does keep is the type each column was declared with, and the adapter uses that to convert values when it reads them:

A column without a declared type is an expression, and its value is returned exactly as it was stored.

Exact Decimals

A number is a double, which can only store 0.1 approximately. That isn't good enough for money, so sql.Decimal stores a value exactly:

PostgreSQL's numeric, MySQL's DECIMAL, and SQLite's DECIMAL and NUMERIC columns are read and written as Decimal values. SQLite stores a decimal as a double, which holds 15 significant digits exactly, so a decimal column in SQLite can hold at most 15 digits, and table.decimal() rejects a larger precision on SQLite. An aggregate such as sum() doesn't have a declared type, so its result is returned as a number.

CRUD Helpers

Four methods on a connection let you work with rows without writing any SQL. insert(), update(), delete() and find() take a table name and dictionaries, build the statement for whichever engine you're connected to, and bind every value as a parameter.

They exist because the statements they replace are the ones least worth writing by hand. Those statements are repetitive, they differ between dialects in small ways that only show up in production, and building them by joining strings is how SQL injection gets in. Anything more complex than a simple list of conditions is still written in SQL, and you can mix the two freely on the same connection.

Inserting Rows and Getting Their IDs

insert() takes a table name and a dictionary, and returns the ID of the new row:

This method hides the biggest difference between the engines. SQLite and MySQL report the ID of the row that was just inserted, but PostgreSQL doesn't, so an insert that needs the ID has to ask for it with a RETURNING clause that names the primary key. MariaDB supports both and uses RETURNING. insert() does whichever applies, and finds the primary key by asking the schema rather than assuming it's called id.

If you want a column other than the key to be returned, name it:

Inserting Several Rows at Once

Several rows can be inserted in a single statement, which is split up so that no statement binds more parameters than the engine allows:

Every row must have the same columns. A row with a different set of columns raises an error instead of being filled in with nulls, because a missing column and a null value mean different things.

Finding Rows

find() returns a ResultSet, count() returns a number, and find_one() returns the first matching row as a dictionary:

If find_one() doesn't find a match, it returns nil. That's a valid answer rather than a failure, so no error is raised:

Writing Filters

The type of a condition's value determines what it means. A plain value means equality, a list means IN, an empty list matches nothing, and nil means IS NULL rather than = NULL, which no row would ever match.

Several conditions in the same dictionary are combined with AND. There's no way to express OR, so that's usually the first thing you'll need to write in SQL:

Passing nil as the whole filter matches every row. You have to ask for that explicitly, rather than it happening because a dictionary turned out to be empty. That's what prevents a filter built from user input from turning into an UPDATE without a WHERE.

Ordering, Limits and Pages

order is a list of column names, each optionally followed by asc or desc, and they're applied in the order given:

limit and offset are numbers of rows, and together they define a page. A page beyond the end of the results is empty rather than an error:

The limit and the offset are written into the text of the statement instead of being bound as parameters, because not every engine allows a parameter in those positions. That makes them the only part of a generated statement that isn't a parameter, so each one is validated before it's added:

Updating and Deleting Rows

update() and delete() return the number of rows they changed:

They interpret a filter in exactly the same way as find(), including nil, which means that passing nil updates or deletes every row.

Raw SQL Fragments

When you need to use something that isn't a plain value, sql.raw() marks a fragment of SQL to be used exactly as written:

A Raw value is accepted anywhere a column or a value is, which lets you use an aggregate or a subquery without giving up the helpers:

raw() is exactly as dangerous as it sounds. A fragment built from anything a user provided is a SQL injection vulnerability. Only build fragments from literals, and keep values in parameters, where they belong.

Using the Helpers in a Transaction

A Transaction has all of the same methods, and they work the same way. A read inside a transaction sees what that transaction has written, even though nobody else has committed it yet:

Rolling back undoes those changes, and a transaction that has already been committed rejects these calls, just as it rejects everything else.

Limitations of the Helpers

The helpers only support a simple list of equality conditions. There are no joins, no OR and no expression trees, because SQL is a better language for those than any chain of method calls. For a query that needs one, use query() or fetch_all() on the same connection, alongside the helpers.

Transactions

With the closure form, the transaction is committed when the body returns and rolled back when it raises an error, so there's no way to leave a transaction open by accident:

A failure undoes everything in the transaction:

A transaction() called inside another one becomes a savepoint, so a helper that opens a transaction works the same way whether it's called on its own or as part of a larger piece of work. Only the outermost transaction commits, and a failure inside an inner one only undoes that inner piece:

On SQLite and PostgreSQL, schema changes are part of the transaction, so if a series of create table statements fails halfway through, nothing is left behind. MySQL and MariaDB commit any open transaction on every create, alter and drop, so on those engines, a transaction() whose body changes the schema raises a TransactionError when it tries to commit. db.supports('transactional_ddl') tells you which behavior applies, so a program that migrates its own schema can run each change inside a transaction where that works, and on its own where it doesn't.

You can request an isolation level. If an engine can't provide the level you ask for, it says so instead of quietly giving you a weaker one:

Level Support
sql.READ_UNCOMMITTED MySQL supports it. PostgreSQL accepts it, but gives you read committed.
sql.READ_COMMITTED Supported everywhere
sql.REPEATABLE_READ Supported everywhere, and the default on MySQL
sql.SERIALIZABLE Supported everywhere

begin() starts a transaction that you commit or roll back yourself, for a transaction that doesn't fit inside a single block. The closure form is safer, so use it when you can.

Streaming Large Results

query() builds the entire result in memory. That's fine for the hundreds of rows most queries return, but not for the millions that some return. stream() reads the same result one row at a time:

Reading to the end closes the cursor. If a loop stops early, the cursor isn't closed, so any loop that might break needs to close it:

take(n) reads a batch of rows at a time, for work that naturally happens in batches:

On PostgreSQL, this uses a server-side portal, and on MySQL a server-side cursor. Both fetch rows in batches, whose size you can set with { batch: n }. On SQLite, the engine itself computes rows as they're requested, so only the current row is held in memory.

A server-side cursor keeps its connection busy while it's open, because the server is partway through sending the result. If you run another statement on that connection before the cursor has been read to the end or closed, an error is raised, so the two exchanges can't get mixed up.

Prepared Statements

Compiling a statement is the expensive part of running it, so a statement that runs in a loop should only be compiled once:

The placeholders are translated once, when the statement is prepared, so the loop doesn't do any string processing at all. A prepared statement has the same query and fetch methods as a connection.

A prepared statement belongs to the connection that prepared it. Closing the connection also closes the statement and any cursor still open on it, and using either of them afterwards raises a ClosedError.

Connection Pools

Opening a connection is expensive. For PostgreSQL and MySQL, it involves a TCP connection, a TLS handshake and an authentication exchange, all before the first statement runs. A server that opened a new connection for every request would spend most of its time connecting.

Used like this, the pool takes a connection, runs the statement and returns the connection to the pool. When several statements have to run on the same connection, as they do in a transaction, with_connection() holds onto one connection and releases it however the block ends:

transaction() on the pool does the same thing in a single call.

Setting Meaning
max The maximum number of connections to open. The default is ten.
min The number of connections to open in advance. The default is none.
idle_timeout How long an idle connection is kept
max_lifetime How long a connection is kept before it's replaced
validate_on_acquire Whether to check that a connection still works before handing it out
on_connect A function to run on each new connection

Keep a pool as small as your workload allows. Connections have a cost on the database side too, and a pool that's larger than the database can usefully handle just moves a queue from your application into the database, where it's harder to see.

A pool belongs to the isolate that created it, which has two consequences. An isolate that needs database access creates its own pool. And a call never waits when the pool is empty, because nothing else could release a connection while the call is running, so running out of connections is reported as an error rather than waited out.

Errors

Every error is a sql.SqlError. Catch that to handle anything that can go wrong with a database, and use the subclasses to handle particular kinds of error differently.

The error classes are the same on every engine, and that's the point. A unique constraint violation is SQLSTATE 23505 on PostgreSQL, error number 1062 on MySQL and extended result code 2067 on SQLite. None of these numbers mean anything to the other engines, so code that checked for any of them would stop working as soon as you changed adapters.

The engine's own information is kept rather than thrown away. code holds the code the engine reported, sqlstate holds the five-character SQLSTATE code where there is one, and query holds the statement that failed:

SerializationError and DeadlockError are the two errors worth retrying. Both mean that the engine abandoned a transaction to keep its guarantees, and running the whole transaction again usually succeeds.

Schema Introspection

db.schema tells you what's in the database. The queries it runs are completely different for each engine, but the results have the same structure.

Every method takes an optional schema name. PostgreSQL has schemas inside each database, and finds the default through search_path. MySQL calls a database a schema and has no level above it, so naming a schema there names a database. SQLite has neither, and ignores the argument.

Each column is described in the same way, whichever engine you're using:

indexes() and foreign_keys() describe the rest of the table:

This is also what makes insert() portable. On an engine without a "last insert ID", the insert needs a RETURNING clause, and the column to return is the table's primary key, which is looked up here.

One thing to watch for when moving a schema between engines: MySQL parses a references clause on a column and then ignores it, so a foreign key declared that way exists on the other two engines but not on MySQL. If you declare it at the table level instead, it exists on all three.

Creating, changing and dropping tables, using one description that works for every engine, is covered in Changing the Schema.

Switching Databases

This module promises that a program can switch between engines by changing its connection string. Here's a program that shows it:

The same report() function runs against PostgreSQL or MySQL if you open a different connection, and prints the same list.

Three things had to be written separately for each engine, and they're the three things that really are different:

  • The connection string, which is the whole idea.
  • An auto-incrementing key, which isn't part of standard SQL. PostgreSQL uses serial, MySQL uses auto_increment, and SQLite uses integer primary key.
  • Any SQL that only one engine supports. sql doesn't parse or rewrite statements beyond their placeholders, so a PostgreSQL array operator, a MySQL on duplicate key update or a SQLite json_extract is passed through unchanged.

db.supports() lets a program ask about a feature instead of assuming:

SQLite Features

db.native() gives you the adapter underneath, which is where the engine's own features are.

A SQLite database is a file, except for :memory:, which isn't. An in-memory database belongs to the connection that opened it, so a second connection to :memory: opens a second, empty database, not another handle to the same data.

Foreign keys are enforced. By default, SQLite doesn't enforce them, separately for each connection, for compatibility with databases created before it supported foreign keys. A database that declares foreign keys almost certainly wants them enforced, so the adapter turns enforcement on. Pass foreign_keys: false to turn it off.

SQLite doesn't have a timestamp type, so a date.Date is stored as ISO 8601 text in UTC, whatever time zone offset it had. Text in that format sorts and compares in chronological order, so order by and < on such a column agree with the clock. When a date is read back, it represents the same moment, in UTC.

Functions Written in Zuri

A function you register on a connection runs inside the database engine, once for each row, and you can use it anywhere an expression is allowed:

An aggregate is written as a fold. step is called once for each row, with the accumulator and the row's arguments, and returns the next accumulator. finish turns the final accumulator into the value for the group.

A collation defines an ordering for text, and you use it with collate:

A function must not use the connection it was registered on. SQLite is in the middle of running a statement when it calls the function, and using the connection again would cause a deadlock. If the function raises an error, the error is passed back out and raised again, with its own class, once the statement has finished.

Blobs, Backups and Hooks

A large value read with a select arrives all at once. A blob handle opens a single cell and lets you read parts of it:

The cell must already exist and already be the right size, because SQLite can't make a blob larger this way. That's what inserting zeroblob(n) is for.

Copying the database file with file system tools is only safe when nothing is writing to it. SQLite's own backup copies the database page by page and notices when the source changes during the copy:

The hooks report what the engine is doing:

PostgreSQL Features

The adapter uses version 3 of the PostgreSQL wire protocol, over TCP or a Unix domain socket, with optional TLS.

A host that starts with a slash is a socket directory, as it is in libpq, and the socket inside it is named after the port. So /var/run/postgresql with port 5432 means /var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432. A path that already names the socket file is used as it is. TLS isn't used over a socket, because there's nothing in between to protect against, so sslmode is ignored in that case.

sslmode controls how TLS is used: disable never uses it, prefer uses it when the server supports it, and require always uses it and fails if the server refuses. Only require verifies the server's identity.

Statements are sent using the extended query protocol, which compiles them on the server and binds values rather than substituting them into the text. Values are sent in the server's own binary format whenever the adapter has a codec for the type, and as text otherwise, so even a type it doesn't know about arrives in readable form instead of as raw bytes.

numeric columns are read as sql.Decimal values, arrays as lists, jsonb as dictionaries, and timestamps as date.Date values.

Listening for Notifications

LISTEN and NOTIFY are PostgreSQL's built-in publish and subscribe mechanism. A connection that has run LISTEN channel receives a message whenever anyone runs NOTIFY channel.

Notifications arrive in between other messages, so a connection that's busy running statements collects them along the way, and poll() returns whatever has built up.

Adding Support for a Type

If your database defines its own types, you can tell the adapter how to handle them:

Until you do, columns of that type are read as text, which is correct, if not especially convenient.

MySQL Features

The adapter implements the MySQL client/server protocol directly, over TCP or a Unix domain socket, with optional TLS, and doesn't depend on any client library. MariaDB uses the same protocol, and the same adapter works with it.

A socket option names a socket, and so does a host that starts with a slash. Unlike with PostgreSQL, the path names the socket file itself, not the directory it's in:

TLS isn't used over a socket, because there's nothing in between to protect against. The connection is treated as private, which lets caching_sha2_password and sha256_password send the password directly instead of encrypting it with the server's public key.

A statement without values is sent as text, which takes one round trip. A statement with values is prepared, so the values are sent in the server's binary format instead of being written into the SQL, and quoting is never an issue. Compiled statements are kept and reused, so a query that runs in a loop is only compiled once.

MySQL leaves ? as it's written, and it reports the ID of an inserted row instead of returning it, so insert() reads the reported ID instead of adding a RETURNING clause. MariaDB differs in two ways that affect the SQL generated by the layers above: it supports RETURNING, and it doesn't have a JSON type. Which behavior applies depends on the server, not the scheme, so for a MariaDB server reached through mysql://, db.driver_name() returns 'mariadb' and db.supports('json') returns false.

How Column Types Are Read

DECIMAL columns are read as sql.Decimal values, JSON as lists and dictionaries, DATE, DATETIME and TIMESTAMP as date.Date values, and TIME as sql.Time values.

MySQL doesn't have a boolean type. BOOLEAN is another name for TINYINT(1), so a value written as true is read back as 1, and db.supports('booleans') returns false to reflect that.

BLOB and TEXT have the same type in the protocol, and the only way to tell them apart is the column's collation, which the adapter checks. A binary column is read as bytes and a text column as a string. BIT and GEOMETRY are read as bytes, because Zuri has no natural way to represent them. SET is read as the comma-separated text that the server stores, not as a list, because a list written back would be encoded as JSON and the column would silently stop matching.

MySQL writes a missing date as zeros, but 0000-00-00 isn't a date in any calendar, so it's read as nil.

TIME Values Are Durations

A TIME column ranges from -838:59:59.999999 to 838:59:59.999999. It's a duration rather than a time of day, so it can be negative and can be longer than 24 hours, and neither of those would survive being read into a date.Date. sql.Time holds it instead:

Time zones

A DATETIME doesn't store a time zone, and a TIMESTAMP is converted to and from the session's time zone. That means the session's time zone determines what a timestamp means, and if it were left to the server's configuration, the same database could give different results on two different machines.

The adapter sets the session's time zone to UTC when it connects. Every timestamp is then read in UTC, and a date.Date that's written back is converted from whatever offset it has. To keep the server's own setting, pass nil as time_zone, or pass the name of the time zone you want to use:

Authentication

The supported methods are caching_sha2_password, which is the default from MySQL 8.0 onward, mysql_native_password, sha256_password, mysql_clear_password and MariaDB's client_ed25519.

Two of these need the actual password, rather than proof of it, the first time an account authenticates. Over TLS, the password is sent as is. Over an unencrypted connection, it's encrypted with a public key that the server sends first, so it can never be read in transit. mysql_clear_password has no such fallback, so it's rejected on any connection that isn't private, because it sends the password without any protection.

TLS

sslmode controls how TLS is used:

Mode Meaning
disable Never use TLS.
prefer Use TLS when the server supports it, without verifying the server's identity. This is the default.
require Always use TLS, without verifying the server's identity.
verify Always use TLS, and verify the server's certificate and host name.

MySQL's own names are accepted too. DISABLED, PREFERRED and REQUIRED mean what they say, and VERIFY_CA and VERIFY_IDENTITY both become verify. That makes VERIFY_CA stricter here than in the MySQL command-line client, which checks the certificate but not the host name. The difference can only ever cause a connection to be refused, never cause a server to be wrongly trusted.

ssl_ca names a certificate authority to trust, and ssl_cert and ssl_key provide a client certificate.

Compression

The protocol can compress everything after the handshake:

Compression is worthwhile for large results over a slow network, but costs more than it saves over a local socket, so it's off unless you turn it on. Packets that are too small to benefit are always sent uncompressed, which the protocol allows.

Sending a File to the Server

With LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE, the server names a file and the client sends it. The file is read from the machine the program is running on, but the server chooses which file, so a malicious or compromised server could ask for any file the process can read. For that reason, it's refused unless you provide a reader:

The reader decides what can be sent, which is where that decision belongs. When a request is refused, the server still gets an answer, so the connection can still be used afterwards instead of waiting for a file that will never arrive.

Statements With Several Results

A stored procedure sends one result set for each select inside it, followed by an OK packet. query() returns the first result set and reads the others, because leaving them unread wouldn't discard them. They would be returned to the next statement, which would then get this statement's rows.

The body of a stored routine contains semicolons, and exec_script() splits a script at every semicolon. So send a create procedure statement through exec() as a single statement, not through exec_script().

Accessing the Adapter

Writing Your Own Adapter

An adapter for another engine implements four classes: a Driver that reads a connection string and opens a connection, a DriverConnection that runs statements, a DriverStatement and a DriverCursor.

Everything above the adapter comes for free, including connection pools, transactions and savepoints, the CRUD helpers, placeholder translation, cursors, the error hierarchy and models. The adapter only has to provide access to the engine.

Schema changes and migrations need one more thing: how the engine writes table definitions. An adapter provides this by subclassing sql.DdlAdapter, which already writes standard SQL, and overriding whatever the engine does differently, such as type_name() for each column type and key_definition() for an id() column. It then returns an instance of that class from its driver's ddl() method. A driver that doesn't provide one rejects schema changes with a NotSupportedError.

The base classes raise NotImplementedError for anything that hasn't been implemented, so an unfinished adapter fails exactly where the gap is. An engine that really can't support a feature raises NotSupportedError instead. The two errors are deliberately different: the first means the adapter is unfinished, and the second means the engine has a genuine limitation.

Design Limits

Rows are dictionaries. A connection returns rows, never objects. Models are provided by sql.model, which is built on top of sql and only loaded by programs that use it.

It doesn't write joins for you. The CRUD helpers support a simple list of equality conditions, and models support their own columns and associations. Anything beyond that is written in SQL.

It doesn't translate SQL. Placeholders are rewritten, but statements aren't parsed, so a function that only one engine supports still only works on that engine.

It doesn't hide differences by guessing. When an engine can't do what was asked, you get a NotSupportedError that names the adapter and the feature, instead of an approximation you didn't ask for.

Module Reference

The standard library reference documents every class and method. Here's an overview of the module:

Function Description
sql.open(dsn, options) Opens a connection
sql.pool(dsn, options) Opens a connection pool
sql.register(driver) Registers an adapter
sql.drivers() Lists the registered adapters
sql.raw(fragment) Marks SQL to be used exactly as written
sql.Decimal(text) Creates an exact decimal
sql.time(h, m, s) Creates a signed duration, like a value in a TIME column
sql.parse_time(text) Reads a duration from text
sql.blueprint Table definitions that work for every engine
sql.migrate Versioned schema changes, and the Migrator that applies them
sql.model Models: Model, Query and the errors they raise

Methods of a Connection:

Method Purpose
query, exec, exec_script Run statements
fetch_one, fetch_all, fetch_value, fetch_column Read results
stream, prepare Create a cursor or a compiled statement
insert, insert_many, update, delete, find, find_one, count Run the common statements without writing SQL
transaction, begin, in_transaction Work with transactions
schema Introspection, plus create_table, alter_table, rename_table and drop_table
model Query a model's rows
driver, driver_name, capabilities, supports Describe the engine
native The adapter underneath
ping, close, is_closed Manage the connection itself

Methods of a Transaction:

Method Purpose
query, exec Run statements
fetch_one, fetch_all, fetch_value Read results
insert, insert_many, update, delete, find, find_one, count The same helpers a connection has
schema, model The connection's schema and models, inside the transaction
commit, rollback, is_finished End the transaction
connection, nested The connection it's running on, and whether it's a savepoint

17.1 · The Big Modules

Changing the Schema

db.schema can change a database as well as describe it. You describe a table once, in Zuri, using a Blueprint, and the adapter turns that description into the right statements for its engine. The same description creates the same table on SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB.

  • Creating a Table
  • Column Types
  • Columns Are Required by Default
  • Keys and Indexes
  • Changing a Table
  • Renaming and Dropping Tables
  • How Changes Are Applied
  • How SQLite Rebuilds a Table
  • SQL for a Specific Engine

Creating a Table

create_table() passes a Blueprint to its body, and creates the table when the body returns. If you annotate the body's table parameter with its type, as below, your editor can complete the blueprint's methods:

Every column method returns the column, and so does every modifier, so you can describe a column in a single chain. timestamps() adds created_at and updated_at columns, each defaulting to the time the row was inserted.

If you pass { if_not_exists: true } as a third argument, a table that already exists is left exactly as it is, indexes included. A library that creates its own table every time it starts would pass this.

Column Types

Each type holds the same kind of value on every engine, stored in whatever way suits that engine best:

Method SQLite PostgreSQL MySQL and MariaDB
id() integer primary key autoincrement bigint generated by default as identity bigint auto_increment
integer(name) integer integer int
big_integer(name) bigint bigint bigint
small_integer(name) smallint smallint smallint
float(name) real double precision double
decimal(name, p, s) decimal(p, s) numeric(p, s) decimal(p, s)
string(name, n) varchar(n) varchar(n) varchar(n)
text(name) text text longtext
boolean(name) boolean boolean tinyint(1)
date(name) date date date
datetime(name) datetime timestamp with time zone datetime(6)
time(name) time time time(6)
binary(name) blob bytea longblob
json(name) json jsonb json
uuid(name) char(36) uuid char(36)

string() has a length of 255 characters if you don't specify one. An id() value is never reused, even after the row with the highest ID is deleted. On SQLite, a decimal() can hold at most 15 significant digits, which is the most a double can store exactly, and a larger precision raises NotSupportedError there. references(name, table) creates a big integer column that refers to another table's id(), along with its foreign key.

The modifiers are:

exact() makes a text column compare values byte by byte on every engine, so 'Ada' and 'ada' are different values, and so are 'é' and 'e'. SQLite already compares this way. On PostgreSQL, the column gets the "C" collation, and on MySQL and MariaDB, utf8mb4_bin, because their default collations treat uppercase and lowercase letters as equal, and on MySQL, accented and unaccented letters too. Use it for a column that holds keys, where two values that only differ in case must not clash.

Columns Are Required by Default

Every column is NOT NULL unless you call nullable(). That way, if a program forgets to provide a value, the database reports an error instead of storing a null that nobody intended:

Keys and Indexes

A key or index on a single column is a modifier on that column. A key or index on several columns is declared on the table:

Indexes, unique indexes and foreign keys are named after their table and columns, such as posts_author_id_index, posts_slug_unique and posts_author_id_foreign. You can pass a second argument to choose a different name. Because the name is predictable, you can drop an index by its columns just as easily as by its name. A name longer than 63 characters, which is the longest PostgreSQL allows, is shortened and ends with a hash of the full name, so it stays unique.

Foreign keys are always written as table constraints. MySQL parses a references clause on a column and then ignores it, so a key declared that way would exist on the other engines but not on MySQL. Declared on the table, it exists on every engine.

The actions a foreign key can take when the row it refers to is deleted, or has its key changed, are 'cascade', 'restrict', 'set null', 'set default' and 'no action'. The last one is what a key does if you don't specify an action.

Changing a Table

alter_table() describes changes on a blueprint and applies them in the order you describe them:

A column described in alter_table() is added to the table. change() turns the description into a change to an existing column instead. The column takes the type, nullability, default and comparison you describe, whatever it had before, so you need to describe the column in full, including nullable() where it applies. The column's indexes are kept.

Here's what else an alteration can do:

Dropping a column also drops every index, unique index and key that it's part of, on every engine. A required column without a default can only be added to an empty table, because there'd be nothing to fill the existing rows with. On a table that has rows, the engine reports a NotNullViolation.

Renaming and Dropping Tables

A renamed table keeps its indexes under their existing names, and foreign keys that refer to it are updated to follow it. If another table refers to a table through a foreign key, dropping it is rejected on every engine, instead of deleting the rows that refer to it as well:

How Changes Are Applied

A change made outside a transaction is applied as a single unit. On SQLite and PostgreSQL, that means it runs in a transaction of its own, so if the third step of an alteration fails, the first two are undone as well. MySQL and MariaDB commit every statement that changes a table's definition, whatever transaction is open, so on those engines each statement is permanent once it has run.

A change made inside a transaction becomes part of it, and on engines that support it, it's rolled back along with the transaction:

How SQLite Rebuilds a Table

SQLite's ALTER TABLE can add and rename columns, but not much else. For anything more, such as changing a column, adding or dropping a key, or dropping a column that an index or key uses, the adapter follows the procedure in SQLite's own documentation. It creates a new table with the changed definition, copies the rows across, drops the old table and renames the new one to take its place. It then recreates the indexes and triggers and carries over the sequence behind the id() column. The new definition is based on the table's own create table statement, with only the changed parts rewritten, so everything else it declared, including checks and collations, is kept.

Dropping the old table deletes its rows first, and when foreign keys are enforced, that delete triggers the on delete action of every table that refers to it. With enforcement on, a rebuild would therefore delete every row that refers to the table. So a rebuild only runs with enforcement turned off, which SQLite only allows outside a transaction. A change made outside a transaction turns enforcement off for its own duration, and checks every foreign key before it commits, and sql.migrate does the same for every migration. A rebuild requested inside a transaction while foreign keys are enforced raises a NotSupportedError instead of putting the rows at risk:

SQL for a Specific Engine

A blueprint covers what every engine can do. For a feature that only one engine has, such as a PostgreSQL extension or a partial index, write the statement in SQL and run it where it applies:

Statements run this way are part of the same change as the blueprint's statements, including its transaction.

17.2 · The Big Modules

Migrations

A database's schema changes along with the program that uses it, and every copy of the database, whether it belongs to a developer, the test suite or production, has to make the same changes in the same order. A migration is one of those changes, stored as a file. It's applied to each database once and recorded there, so any copy of the database can be brought up to date from wherever it is.

sql.migrate applies migrations from a program, and zuri migrate applies them from the command line. Both read the same files and keep the same record.

  • Writing a Migration
  • Running Migrations
  • Batches and Rolling Back
  • Checking What's Applied
  • How a Migration Runs
  • When a Migration Fails
  • Several Processes at Once
  • Migrating When a Program Starts
  • The Migrations Directory

Writing a Migration

A migration is a Zuri file in a directory of migrations. Its name starts with a version, which is a sequence of digits, followed by a description made of letters, digits and underscores. zuri migrate new creates one, using the current time as its version:

Each name you give creates a separate migration, in the order you give them, so zuri migrate new create_posts add_slug_to_posts creates two.

A migration exports up(db), which makes the change, and down(db), which undoes it. db is the Transaction the migration runs in, or the Connection itself when it runs outside a transaction, which always happens on MySQL and MariaDB, and can happen anywhere for a migration that asks for it. Its type is Transaction|Connection, and you describe the change with db.schema and its blueprint, once, for every engine the program runs against:

With the types written out, your editor can complete db. with the methods that transactions and connections share, and table. with the blueprint's methods. zuri migrate new includes the types for you.

If the name has the form create_<table>, the new file starts out creating that table, as above. Any other name starts with empty up() and down() functions. A migration can also change data, using the same methods a connection has:

Running Migrations

zuri migrate finds the project by looking for the nearest directory above the working directory that contains a project.toml, and uses its migrations directory. It gets the database from --database, or from DATABASE_URL in the environment or the project's .env file:

In a program, Migrator does the same thing:

Migrator accepts a directory, which is migrations by default, and a table to keep the record in, which is zuri_migrations by default. The table is created the first time it's needed.

Batches and Rolling Back

All the migrations applied in a single run share a batch number. Rolling back without any options undoes the whole of the latest batch, however many migrations that is, starting with the newest:

Both directions accept a limit. steps counts migrations, and to names a specific migration:

Before the first migration is rolled back, every migration that's about to be rolled back is checked. Each one must still have its file, with a down() function, or nothing is rolled back at all.

Checking What's Applied

status() lists every migration, from both the files and the record, along with its state:

State Meaning
applied Recorded, and the file is unchanged since it ran
changed Recorded, but the file has changed since it ran
missing Recorded, but the file no longer exists
pending A file that hasn't been applied to this database yet

A changed migration has already run in its earlier form, and editing it doesn't change anything in a database where it has run. That database has whatever the old file did. To make a further change, write a new migration. zuri migrate status reminds you of this when it finds a changed migration.

How a Migration Runs

Each migration runs in its own transaction, together with the row that records it. On SQLite and PostgreSQL, a migration that fails partway through leaves nothing behind and isn't recorded. MySQL and MariaDB commit every statement that changes a table's definition, so on those engines, a migration runs outside a transaction and is recorded once it has finished, and a migration that fails partway through leaves the statements before the failure in place.

On SQLite, foreign key enforcement is turned off while a migration runs, so that a change that rebuilds a table can't delete the rows that refer to it. Every foreign key is checked before the migration commits.

A migration that has to run outside a transaction, as PostgreSQL's create index concurrently does, can say so:

When a Migration Fails

A failure stops the run at that point. The migrations before it stay applied, and the failed one and those after it stay pending, ready for the next run once you've fixed the problem:

Several Processes at Once

If two processes migrate the same database at the same time, as happens when two copies of a server start together, each migration is still applied only once. On PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, a run holds a lock provided by the engine, and a second run waits for the first one to finish before it looks for pending migrations. On SQLite, each migration takes the write lock when it starts. Either way, each migration checks the record again once it holds the lock, so a migration that another process applied in the meantime is skipped.

Migrating When a Program Starts

A program that manages its own database can bring it up to date when it starts. Nyssa, the package registry that zuri serve runs, does exactly this:

Because the migrations directory is found relative to __file__, it moves with the program wherever it's installed.

The Migrations Directory

Every .zu file whose name starts with a version followed by an underscore is a migration. Migrations run in order of version, compared as numbers, and then by name, so 9 comes before 10. Two files with the same version are rejected. A .zu file whose name starts with _ isn't a migration. It holds code shared by several migrations, which they import with import ._tables. Files that aren't Zuri files are ignored.

17.3 · The Big Modules

Models

sql works with rows, and a row is a dictionary. That's the right shape for a report or a script, but not for the core of an application, where a post is something with rules: it must have a title, it belongs to an author, and its slug is derived from its title. sql.model gives each table a class. Instances of the class, called records, can save, validate and delete themselves, and can load the records they're associated with.

  • A First Model
  • Declaring a Model
  • Records
  • Assigning Input
  • Validation
  • Hooks
  • Queries
  • Associations
  • Transactions
  • Casts
  • Records as Output
  • Design Limits

A First Model

A model is a class that extends Model. Its fields are the columns of its table:

db.model(Post) starts a query over the model's rows. Methods that use the database, such as save(db) and delete(db), take the connection to use as an argument. A record never holds onto a connection itself, so it's saved inside whichever transaction the calling code opened, and a record that's kept after its connection has gone back to a pool can't write through a connection that now belongs to someone else.

Declaring a Model

Every field the class declares, apart from those that start with _, is a column with the same name. Everything else about the model goes in a static define() method, which receives a definition object to describe the model on:

A model's table name is its class name in snake case, made plural using the regular rules of English, so Post becomes posts, BlogPost becomes blog_posts, Category becomes categories and Address becomes addresses. If a word has an irregular plural, set the table name with table().

define() runs once, the first time the model is used, not when the class is declared, so it can refer to models declared later in the same file. Its description is checked against the class at that point. An association without a field to load into, or a cast on a field that isn't a column, raises a ModelError the first time the model is used. A model's primary key is a single column.

Records loaded from the database are created without any arguments, so a model's own @new mustn't require any. If it accepts attributes, it should pass them on with parent(attributes).

Records

Calling the class creates a record, using a dictionary of attributes if you pass one. create() on a query creates a record and saves it:

Saving a new record inserts it. Any column that's still nil is left out of the insert, so the database fills in its default, and those columns are then read back, so the record holds what was actually stored. Saving a record that's already stored only writes the columns that have changed since it was loaded, and writes nothing if none have. That way, a column that another process changed in the meantime isn't overwritten when you save a different column.

A list or dictionary that's changed in place counts as a change. A deleted record keeps its values, and saving it again inserts it as a new row. key() returns the value of the primary key, whatever the column is called.

Assigning Input

fill() assigns attributes from a dictionary, such as one provided by a form or a request body. It only assigns fillable columns, which are the columns the model lists with fillable(), or if it doesn't list any, every column except the primary key and the timestamps. A key that isn't fillable raises a ModelError, so a request can't set a record's primary key, or any other column it was never meant to change, just by sending an extra field.

The second argument lists the keys to use and ignores the rest. Use it with input that contains more than the record should accept:

Validation

A model validates itself before every save, using validate rules, uniqueness checks and its own validate() method. A record that fails validation isn't saved, and save() raises a RecordInvalid error:

RecordInvalid is a validate.ValidationError, and its errors are the same { field, message } list that form validation reports, so the code that responds to an invalid form with a 422 can respond to an invalid record in the same way. is_valid(db) runs the checks without saving, and errors() returns what the last check found.

A uniqueness check reports a value that's already taken along with the other failures. However, only a unique index in the database can stop two records that are saved at the same moment from getting the same value, so a unique column should have a unique index in the database as well.

Hooks

A model can override any of these methods to run code at that point in a record's life cycle. Each one receives the connection or transaction the record is using:

Hook Runs
before_validate(db) Before the record is validated
validate(errors) While it's validated, to add failures of the model's own
after_validate(db) After it's validated, whatever the result
before_save(db) Before it's written, whether it's new or not
before_create(db) Before a new record is inserted
after_create(db) After it's inserted, once it has its key
before_update(db) Before a stored record's changes are written
after_update(db) After the changes are written
after_save(db) After it's written, whether it's new or not
before_delete(db) Before it's deleted
after_delete(db) After it's deleted
after_load() When a record is created from a row

If a model defines any hooks, saving and deleting run inside a transaction, or a savepoint if a transaction is already open, so anything a hook writes is undone along with everything else if something fails. A hook can raise an error to stop the save or the delete:

A model's methods share a namespace with the hooks and with every method a record has, so a model shouldn't declare a method with one of those names for any other purpose. A field can have the same name as any of them.

Queries

db.model(Post) returns a Query. Every method that narrows a query returns a new query and leaves the original unchanged, so you can keep a query and build on it in several different directions:

where() with a dictionary works the same way as the conditions for the CRUD helpers: a value matches itself, nil matches null, a list matches any of its values, and an empty list matches nothing. Anything other than a dictionary is a fragment of SQL, with a ? for each value. The fragment is wrapped in parentheses when it's added, so an or inside it stays inside it. All conditions must be true. where_not() excludes matching rows, and a row whose column is null counts as excluded by any value, since null isn't equal to anything.

Here's what a query can do with the rows it matches:

A query is iterable, so for post in query reads every record. update() and delete() change every matching row in a single statement without creating records, so no validation or hooks run. update() sets the updated timestamp unless you provide a value for it.

A scope is a reusable part of a query. You declare it with scope() and apply it with query.scope(name, argument).

Associations

There are four kinds of association, which cover the ways tables can refer to each other:

Declared as Means The key is
belongs_to('author', Author) This record holds another record's key author_id in this table
has_one('profile', Profile) Another record holds this one's key, and there's at most one author_id in the other table
has_many('posts', Post) Other records hold this one's key author_id in the other table
belongs_to_many('tags', Tag) A join table holds both keys post_id and tag_id in post_tag

Each name is also the field the association is loaded into, which the class has to declare. Keys are named after the class name in snake case, followed by _id, and the join table is named after both class names in alphabetical order. You can use options to choose different names:

Associations are only loaded when you ask for them. include() loads them along with the records, using one query per association however many records there are, and a dotted name loads an association of an association:

A field that holds an association is nil until the association is loaded. load() loads an association onto a record you already have and returns the record, and query.load(records, names) loads associations onto a list of records, using one query per association. related() returns a query over the records an association refers to, so you can narrow it further instead of loading all of them.

When you assign a record to a belongs_to field, the key that refers to it is set when the record holding it is saved, and the assigned record has to be saved first. attach(), detach() and sync() link records through a belongs_to_many association's join table, and accept either records or keys.

Transactions

tx.model(Post) runs a query inside a transaction, and a record saved with the transaction is saved inside it:

Casts

Most values are read back as the type they were stored as. A cast makes sure a field has the same type on every engine, even where the engines differ, by converting it as it's read:

Cast The field holds
bool true or false, converted from a bool, a number, '0', '1', 'true' or 'false'
integer A whole number
number A number
decimal A sql.Decimal
string Text
json A list or dictionary, decoded from JSON text if necessary
date A date.Date, converted from ISO 8601 text if necessary

MySQL doesn't have a boolean type and returns 1, and MariaDB stores JSON as text, so a model that runs on either of them should cast those columns, for example with cast('published', 'bool') and cast('settings', 'json'). Null stays nil under every cast, and a value that can't be converted is left as it was read instead of being lost.

Records as Output

to_dict() returns a record's columns, except for the ones listed with hidden(), along with every association that has been loaded, converted to dictionaries as well. json.encode() writes a record as its to_dict(), so a record passed to a response doesn't include something like a password hash:

Two records are equal if they belong to the same model and have the same primary key. A record that hasn't been saved yet is only equal to itself.

Design Limits

Associations are loaded explicitly. An association is only loaded by include() or load(), never just by reading its field, so a loop over records never silently runs a query for each record.

Each query creates its own records. If two queries read the same row, you get two separate records for it, which are equal (==) to each other. Nothing is cached between queries, so a record always reflects what the database held when it was read.

Joins are written in SQL. Conditions cover a model's own columns, and related() and include() cover associations. For a join, a union or a window function, write the SQL yourself and pass it to from_sql(), which creates records from whatever the query selects.

Tables are created by migrations. A model maps an existing table. Migrations and Changing the Schema are how you create and change tables.

Chapter 18 · The Big Modules

Mail

The mail module is Zuri's email stack. It covers the message format, the three protocols used to move messages around, and the servers for two of them. It's written in Zuri from the socket up, and it works with real mail servers.

Email is older than almost everything it runs on, and it shows. A message is text with a block of headers, a format defined in 1982 and extended ever since to carry anything that isn't ASCII, which by now is most of what people send. Sending a message uses SMTP, reading messages where they're stored uses IMAP, and downloading them uses POP3. That's three protocols, one format and a lot of accumulated history, and a program shouldn't have to know about almost any of it.

That's the idea behind this module's design. You describe what's in a message, and the module works out the rest: which parts it needs, how they nest, which encoding each header and body needs, and what has to be escaped so that a line containing a single dot doesn't end the message early. Your program says who a message is from and what it says. It doesn't need to know about Content-Transfer-Encoding.
