Following Along

Most of the examples below build on the same message. Here it is:

None of this uses the network. Building and reading messages is completely separate from sending and receiving them, so a program that only needs to create or parse a message never opens a socket.

Introduction

The three protocols do quite different jobs.

SMTP moves a message from wherever it was written to a server that will take responsibility for it. That's all it does. It has no concept of folders, read messages or searches. A message goes in, and it's either accepted or it isn't.

IMAP is for reading mail where it's stored. The mail stays on the server, the client works with it there, and two devices looking at the same mailbox see the same thing. Almost everything a mail client does uses IMAP.

POP3 is for downloading mail. It offers a numbered list of messages and a way to remove them. It's the wrong protocol for reading mail on several devices, but the right one for a program whose job is to move everything in a mailbox somewhere else.

The module covers the client side of all three protocols, and the server side of the two where a server is worth having. There's no POP3 server, and that's intentional: a POP3 server is an IMAP server with almost everything removed, so mail.imap is the one to run.

Building a Message

mail.message() creates a message. You set its contents one call at a time, and each call returns the message, so you can chain them together:

A new message starts with a Date header, set to the time it was created, and a MIME-Version header. It gets its Message-ID when it's sent, because that's when the domain it belongs to is known.

Addresses

Every method that sets addresses accepts text, an Address, or a list of either:

add_to() keeps any recipients that are already there, so you can call it in a loop. set_to() replaces them. There's the same pair of methods for Cc and Bcc.

Bcc is removed from the message before it's passed to a server, after the recipients have been taken from it. That's the whole point of a blind copy, and it's easy to get wrong if you do it yourself.

A display name that contains characters a header can't hold is encoded for you, and a name that contains a comma is quoted:

When you read them back, you get the name, not the encoded form:

mail.parse_address_list() parses an entire header, including the comments and groups that RFC 5322 allows but nobody remembers:

The members of a group are returned along with the other addresses, since a program sending mail cares about who the recipients are, not how they were grouped. Use mail.parse_address_groups() if you need to keep the grouping.

Text, HTML, or Both

Text on its own makes a plain text message, and HTML on its own makes an HTML message. Both together make a multipart/alternative message, with the plain text first, because a mail client that understands both is supposed to show the last one it can display:

Setting the text again replaces it, wherever it is in the message, instead of adding a second copy. The structure of the message follows from its contents, so it stays correct as the contents change.

Outgoing text is written as UTF-8, or as US-ASCII if that's all it needs. Asking for any other character set raises an error, because the module can't encode into it, and a header that claimed otherwise would be wrong.

Attachments

An attachment is an object in its own right. You build it the same way as a message and pass it to attach():

The media type was taken from the file name. The message became a multipart/mixed message, with its previous contents as the first part. That only happens once, however many files you attach.

Method Purpose
set_filename(name) The file name to offer the file under
set_content_type(type) The media type, when the file name isn't enough to tell
set_disposition(kind) attachment by default, or inline
set_cid(id) The identifier the HTML uses to refer to it
set_encoding(name) The transfer encoding. If you don't set it, it's chosen based on the data.
set_description(text) A description that some mail clients show next to the file

Attaching a file from disk takes one call:

Both the name and the media type are taken from the path, unless you say otherwise. A file name with characters that a header can't hold is encoded as RFC 2231 describes, split across several lines if it's long, and read back in one piece at the other end.

Images in HTML

An image that the message displays, rather than offers as a download, is attached like any other file and referred to by an identifier:

embed() returns the reference to use in an <img> tag, and rearranges the message into a multipart/related structure, which tells the mail client that the two belong together. The HTML ends up as the first part, which marks it as the one to display.

Custom Headers

For any header that the other methods don't cover, use set_header():

The value is written exactly as you give it. If a header needs encoding, you have to encode it first. The methods for addresses and the subject do this for you, because those are the headers where people most often get it wrong.

add_header() keeps any existing header with the same name instead of replacing it, which is what a header such as Received needs.

Replies and Threads

A reply is an ordinary message with two extra headers. Getting them right is what puts the reply in the same conversation in a mail client:

references() on the original message returns the chain it already belongs to, so adding the original's own identifier extends the thread instead of starting a new one.

Reading a Message

mail.parse() takes the raw bytes and returns the message tree:

Nothing is decoded until you ask for it. Reading the subject of a message with a 20 MB attachment costs no more than reading the headers, which makes it reasonable to parse every message in a mailbox and only look at some of them.

The Message Tree

A part is a message too. It has headers and a body, and its body can contain more parts. The same class represents both, so the code for walking through a message and reading a standalone one is the same.

walk() returns the whole tree, starting with the outermost part. parts() returns one level of it, and find_part() returns the first part of a given type anywhere in the tree.

Finding the Body

Most programs want the text, wherever it is in the message:

Both methods return nil if the message has no such part, which isn't the same as an empty part. An attachment that happens to be text/plain isn't mistaken for the body. A part that says it's an attachment, or that has a file name without saying either way, is skipped.

Incoming Attachments

body_bytes() decodes the transfer encoding, so both base64 and quoted-printable return the original bytes. text() goes one step further and also applies the character set.

Character Sets

A header that contains anything outside ASCII stores it in encoded form, using one of two encodings. Reading a header through the module decodes both:

Whitespace between two adjacent encoded words is removed, which is what allows a long subject to be split across several encoded words without adding spaces that weren't there. Anything that isn't a well-formed encoded word is left exactly as it is, including text that just happens to start with =?.

A message body declares its character set in the Content-Type header. The character sets that messages are likely to use are all supported: UTF-8, US-ASCII, the ISO 8859 Latin sets 1 and 15, windows-1252, and UTF-16 in either byte order. A character set the module doesn't know is read as UTF-8, which keeps any ASCII text in it intact instead of throwing away the part that would have been readable.

Sending Mail

mail.send() opens a connection, sends a single message and closes the connection again:

That's all you need to send mail from a program that sends one message at a time.

Creating Your Own Client

A program that sends many messages should keep one connection open for all of them, because opening a connection involves a handshake and an authentication exchange:

quit() ends the session politely and closes the connection. close() just closes it, which is what you should do when something has gone wrong and the conversation is no longer in a state the server would understand.

Scheme Port Meaning
smtp:// 587 Submission, with TLS negotiated over the connection
smtps:// 465 TLS from the first byte

Port 25 is for one server relaying mail to another, not for a program submitting mail, so it isn't used by default. Specify it explicitly if that's really what you're doing.

The Envelope

What the server is told and what the message says are two separate things. Unless the options say otherwise, the envelope is taken from the message: the sender from From, and the recipients from To, Cc and Bcc combined, with duplicates removed.

The first example is what a mailing list does: the message says who wrote it, and the envelope says where bounces should go. The second one delivers to an address that the headers don't mention at all, which is how a blind copy actually works.

An empty sender is the null path, which is the sender used for bounce messages, so that a bounce can't itself bounce:

TLS

By default, a client connects, reads the server's capabilities and negotiates TLS before it sends anything that needs protecting:

tls What happens
require Negotiates TLS, and refuses to continue without it. This is the default.
prefer Negotiates TLS if the server offers it
disable Doesn't ask for TLS

smtps://, imaps:// and pop3s:// perform the TLS handshake before the first byte instead, so tls has no effect with them.

Whatever tls is set to, a mechanism that sends the password itself is never used on a connection that isn't encrypted. If the server offers nothing else, the client raises an error instead of sending the password. This can't be configured, and it's the one place where the module won't do what it's told.

To trust a certificate that the system doesn't, pass a TLS configuration:

Authenticating

Put the credentials in the options, and the client chooses the strongest mechanism that both sides support:

If you provide a token, a token-based mechanism is chosen. To use a specific mechanism instead of letting the client choose, pass mechanisms. How the choice is made is described in Authentication Mechanisms.

A username and password in the connection string also work, which is convenient when the string comes from configuration:

Server Capabilities

If a message is larger than the server says it accepts, it's rejected before it's sent instead of after it's been uploaded, which matters when the message is the reason the connection is slow.

If the server supports CHUNKING, send() can send the message in pieces without escaping anything:

If the server supports SIZE, 8BITMIME or DSN, those extensions are used automatically. If it doesn't, the message is still sent.

Handling Failures

If the server rejects something partway through a transaction, it's left holding half of one. send() cancels the transaction before raising an error, so the connection can still be used for the next message, instead of the server responding with 503 to everything that follows. This is easy to forget if you do it yourself:

Every message after the failed one is still sent.

Reading Mail with IMAP

IMAP keeps mail on the server. A client opens a mailbox, searches it, and fetches the messages it needs:

Opening a Mailbox

select() opens a mailbox for reading and writing. examine() opens it read-only, which also means that reading a message doesn't mark it as read. close_mailbox() closes the mailbox and removes any messages marked as deleted, while unselect() closes it without removing them.

uidvalidity is how a server tells clients that its message numbering has been reset. A client that remembers message identifiers between sessions has to check it, because if it has changed, every identifier the client remembers now refers to something else.

To list the mailboxes that exist:

* matches anything, including the separator between levels of the hierarchy. % matches anything except the separator, which lets you list a single level. status() asks what's in a mailbox without opening it, which is how a client can show unread counts for a dozen folders without selecting each one:

You give and get mailbox names in the form a person would read them. IMAP writes names in a modified version of UTF-7, so Entwürfe is sent as Entw&APw-rfe and Tom & Jerry as Tom &- Jerry. The client converts names for every command that names a mailbox. After enable(['UTF8=ACCEPT']) on a server that supports it, names are sent as UTF-8 instead, and enabled lists what the server agreed to turn on. encoding.encode_mailbox_name() and decode_mailbox_name() perform the same conversion, for a program that talks to the server in some other way, such as through run().

Searching

The search criteria are IMAP's own, and they read almost like English:

The second argument asks for unique identifiers instead of positions. A position is only valid until something is removed from the mailbox and every message after it is renumbered. An identifier stays valid after the connection closes, and it's what a program that runs more than once should remember. Pass true unless you're going to use the numbers straight away.

Fetching Only What You Need

Fetching every message just to show a list of them is exactly the mistake IMAP was designed to prevent:

The envelope contains the addresses and the date, already parsed by the server. No message bodies were sent over the network at all.

What to ask for What you get
ENVELOPE The addresses, subject and date
FLAGS What has been done to the message
RFC822.SIZE The size of the message
INTERNALDATE When the server received it
BODYSTRUCTURE The structure of the message, part by part
BODY.PEEK[HEADER] The block of headers
BODY.PEEK[] The whole message
BODY.PEEK[2] A single part of it

BODYSTRUCTURE is the one worth knowing about. It describes what the message is made of without sending any of it, so a client can choose to fetch the text and leave a large attachment on the server:

section is the number you use to request that part on its own.

fetch_headers() is a shortcut for requesting the block of headers, and fetch_message() is a shortcut for requesting the whole message:

Reading a message doesn't mark it as read unless you ask for that. A program working through a mailbox shouldn't change what a person sees the next time they open it.

Flags

A flag records what has been done to a message:

\Seen, \Answered, \Flagged, \Deleted and \Draft have defined meanings. A server can allow other flags, and lists them in the mailbox's permanent_flags.

mark_deleted() only marks messages. Nothing is removed until you call expunge():

expunge() returns the positions of the removed messages, highest first, because each removal renumbers every message after it, and that's the order in which they have to be applied.

Moving, Copying and Removing

move() uses the server's own MOVE command if it has one. Otherwise, it does what MOVE was invented to replace: it copies the message, marks it as deleted and expunges it. Either way, the message ends up in one place.

create(), delete(), rename(), subscribe() and unsubscribe() do what their names say.

Adding a Message to a Mailbox

append() adds a message to a mailbox without sending it anywhere, which is how a sent message gets into the Sent folder:

The flags are the ones to store it with, and \Seen is the usual choice for a message the account sent itself. The last argument is the internal date, and if you don't provide it, the time of arrival is used.

Waiting for New Mail

idle() waits for the server to report something, instead of asking repeatedly:

A server might drop a connection that has been idle for too long, which is why the wait has a time limit and the loop starts it again. The default is 25 minutes, which is what RFC 2177 recommends.

noop() does the same thing without waiting. It gives the server a chance to report any changes, and stops the connection from becoming idle at all.

Collecting Mail with POP3

POP3 hands over the mail and forgets about it. There's no searching and there are no folders, just a numbered list of messages and a way to remove them:

list() returns every message with its size and, if the server provides one, an identifier that stays valid after the session ends. The message number doesn't. It's only valid until something is removed and the remaining messages are renumbered.

Nothing is actually removed until you call quit(). delete() only marks messages, and reset() removes all the marks. If a connection drops partway through, the mailbox is left exactly as it was, which protects you from a program that fails in the middle. It also means that closing the connection without calling quit() is how you cancel a run.

top() fetches the headers and the first few lines of the body, which is enough to decide whether the rest is worth fetching:

If the server's greeting offers APOP, it's used instead of sending the password, and if the server supports SASL, those mechanisms are preferred over both. USER/PASS is the last resort, and it's only used over TLS.

Running an SMTP Server

SmtpServer implements the protocol but has no policy of its own. Handlers decide what to accept:

The Handlers

Handler Called with When
on_connect The session A connection opens, before the greeting
on_auth The session and the credentials A client authenticates
on_mail The session and the sender A transaction starts
on_rcpt The session and a recipient Once for each recipient
on_data The session and the message The whole message has arrived
on_close The session The connection closes, however it was closed
on_error The error and the session Something inside the server failed

The session holds what's known so far: who connected, whether the connection is encrypted, who authenticated, the sender, and the recipients accepted so far. session.state is an empty dictionary where your handlers can store anything, and it lasts as long as the connection.

Rejecting Mail

A handler that returns nothing accepts. A handler that returns a code and a message rejects with that code and message:

A handler that raises an error indicates a failure on the server's side, not a bad message, so the sender is told 451 and asked to try again later. This distinction matters, because a database that's temporarily down shouldn't cause mail to bounce.

Rejecting in on_rcpt is the most useful option. It tells the sender straight away which address is wrong, while it's still connected and can do something about it, instead of accepting the message and then sending a bounce to an address that might not exist either.

The null sender, which is what bounces are sent from, reaches on_mail as an empty string rather than an address. If you reject mail from it, your server won't be able to receive bounces, so handle it deliberately.

TLS and Authentication

That's what allows the server to offer STARTTLS. Everything a client said before the handshake is discarded afterwards, including who it claimed to be, because none of it was protected.

Authentication needs one handler, and a second one for the mechanisms that prove a password without sending it:

on_password is what makes CRAM-MD5 possible. Checking the proof means calculating it again, which means knowing the password. A server that can't provide the password doesn't advertise the mechanism. Without on_auth, the server doesn't advertise any authentication at all.

PLAIN and LOGIN are only advertised once the connection is encrypted. require_auth rejects mail from a client that hasn't authenticated, and require_tls rejects mail on a connection that isn't encrypted.

Limits

Option Default What it does
max_size 35 MB The largest message to accept
max_recipients 100 The number of recipients a single message can have
timeout 300000 How many milliseconds a client can stay silent

A client that declares a size over the limit is rejected at MAIL, before it uploads anything. A client that doesn't declare a size is rejected when it goes over the limit. After ten invalid commands in a row, the connection is dropped.

Running an IMAP Server

ImapServer runs the session state machine and answers every command from a MailStore. Which mail exists and where it's kept is up to the store:

The server implements IMAP4rev1, along with UNSELECT, MOVE, IDLE, LITERAL+, SASL-IR and ID. It advertises exactly what it implements, so a client that reads the capability list and trusts it won't run into problems.

Where the Mail Is Stored

Two stores are included. MemoryStore keeps everything in memory and forgets it when the process exits. That's what a test needs, and also what a server embedded in a larger program needs when the mail itself isn't important:

MaildirStore implements the same interface on disk.

Maildir

Each account is a directory that holds its INBOX directly, with every other mailbox next to it under a name starting with a dot. This is the Maildir++ layout, which other mail tools understand. A mailbox written by this server can be read by other tools, and mail delivered by other tools shows up here.

Every mailbox consists of the three directories that Maildir defines. A message is first written into tmp, which nothing reads from, and only moved into place once it's complete, so a reader never sees half a message. new is where a delivery agent puts mail that nobody has looked at yet, and cur is where a message is kept once a client has seen the mailbox, with its flags recorded in the file name after :2,. Windows doesn't allow a colon in a file name, so there the flags come after ;2, instead, as they do in mbsync. An account on disk looks like this:

That compatibility is the reason to use it. A delivery agent can drop a message in, and the server finds it the next time it looks, without a shared database or any protocol between them.

IMAP needs a message number that stays the same when a file is renamed, and Maildir doesn't have one, so each mailbox keeps a small index file next to its directories that records which file has which number. When a message's file disappears, its number is retired instead of being reused, so a client that remembers the number is told the message is missing instead of being given a different one.

Mail is stored on disk, but accounts aren't:

Where an application keeps its passwords is up to the application, not the mail library. A store with an authenticator can't provide a password, so the server stops advertising the mechanisms that need one.

Writing Your Own Store

A store only has to implement the same methods. Nothing in the interface requires files:

Method Purpose
authenticate(username, password) Checks whether the credentials are correct
password_of(username) Returns the password, for the mechanisms that need it
has_passwords() Whether the store can provide passwords at all
mailboxes(username) Lists the mailboxes
exists, create, remove, rename Manage the mailboxes themselves
messages(username, mailbox) Returns every message in a mailbox, oldest first
append(username, mailbox, raw, flags, received) Adds a message
set_flags(username, mailbox, uid, flags) Changes a message's flags
expunge(username, mailbox) Removes the messages marked as deleted
counters(username, mailbox) Returns uidnext and uidvalidity

Subclass MailStore and implement these methods, and an ImapServer can serve whatever data is behind them.

Serving Several Connections

Both servers handle one connection until it ends before accepting the next. That suits the protocols, but it doesn't work for more than one client at a time. mail.pool puts a pool of isolates behind a single listening socket:

build runs inside each worker to create that worker's own server, because isolates don't share anything and each one needs its own server. It can be any function. Keeping it in a separate module is just a convenient place to put each worker's setup:

An IMAP connection can stay open for hours, so the pool size limits how many clients can be served at once, rather than how quickly they're served. Size the pool for the number of clients, not the rate of requests.

pool.start() does everything except running the accept loop. Use it when you need to know the address before the first connection, as you would in a test.

Verifying Where Mail Came From

A receiving server has no reason to trust a From header. With DKIM, the sending domain signs the message when it's sent, and the receiver checks the signature against a key published in that domain's own DNS.

Signing

The signature covers the body and the most important headers, and the header it adds goes at the top. Sign the message last, once nothing else about it will change. Changing a signed header afterwards breaks the signature. mail.send() sets the Message-ID and Date headers if they're missing, so either let it do that or set them yourself before signing.

Option Default What it does
algorithm rsa-sha256 The signing algorithm. The alternative is ed25519-sha256.
canonicalisation relaxed/relaxed The canonicalization for the headers and then the body
headers A sensible set Which headers to sign
expires_in None The number of seconds until the signature expires

relaxed tolerates the changes to whitespace and line folding that a mail server might make along the way. simple covers the exact bytes, so any change at all breaks the signature. Both are supported. relaxed/relaxed is what almost everyone uses, which is why it's the default.

The public key goes in DNS under the selector:

Verifying Signatures

You get one result for each signature, in the order they appear in the message. A message without any signatures gives an empty list. That isn't a failure, it just means nobody signed the message.

The key is looked up through net.resolver, unless you pass verify() something else to look it up with. That's useful for a program with its own resolver or its own cache:

A parsed message is verified against the bytes it was parsed from, because that's the only thing a signature can be checked against. If you change a parsed message and verify it again, the result describes the message as it arrived, not the one you now have.

What a Signature Does Not Say

A valid signature means the domain vouches for the message. It doesn't mean the message is wanted, that the From header matches the signing domain, or that the sender is who they appear to be to a human reader. Deciding how much a signature from a particular domain is worth is a separate question, and the answer is usually DMARC.

DNSSEC isn't validated. DNSSEC signatures are passed along when a server sends them and the dnssec option asks for them, but nothing here checks them. A program that needs a validated answer needs a validating resolver and a trusted connection to it, which is what the tls option of net.resolver provides.

Authentication Mechanisms

All three protocols use the same authentication mechanisms, and mail.sasl implements them once rather than three times. A client is given credentials and chooses the strongest mechanism that both sides support:

Mechanism What it does
SCRAM-SHA-256, SCRAM-SHA-1 Proves the password without sending it, and also proves that the server knew it
CRAM-MD5 Proves the password without sending it, but proves nothing about the server
XOAUTH2, OAUTHBEARER Sends a bearer token, which is what the large providers require
PLAIN, LOGIN Sends the password itself, so they're never used without TLS
EXTERNAL Sends nothing, because the client certificate already identifies the client

Mechanisms are preferred in the order of that table. Use SCRAM wherever a server supports it. The server stores something derived from the password rather than the password itself, the client never sends the password, and the exchange ends with the server proving that it knew the password too, which protects against a server that simply accepts everything.

Channel binding, the -PLUS variant of SCRAM, isn't supported. It needs a value from the TLS session that net.tls doesn't expose.

To use a specific mechanism instead of letting the client choose:

Errors

Every error is a MailError, so catching that catches every error the module raises itself.

Error Raised when
MessageError The bytes aren't a message, or the message contradicts itself
ProtocolError The server sent something the protocol doesn't allow
ConnectionClosed The connection closed in the middle of a conversation
AuthenticationError The credentials were rejected, or no usable mechanism was offered
StateError A command was used somewhere it doesn't make sense
MailboxError A mailbox doesn't exist or can't be created
SmtpError The SMTP server rejected something, with a reply code
ImapError The IMAP server responded with NO or BAD
Pop3Error The POP3 server responded with -ERR

The distinction worth designing a mail program around is the one SMTP makes:

A 4xx reply means the server couldn't accept the message right now, and the sender should try again later. A 5xx reply means it won't accept the message, and trying again won't change that. Queue messages that get the first and bounce messages that get the second. Treating them the same is how a mail queue either loses mail or sends it forty times.

SmtpError has a code, the three-digit reply code, and an enhanced code, the more detailed code from RFC 3463, when the server sends one. Only rely on the first digit of either.

ImapError has a status, which is NO when the server understood the command but refused it, and BAD when it didn't understand the command at all. BAD points to a problem with the client rather than with the request.

Design Limits

It never sends a password over an unencrypted connection. There's no option or flag to change this. If the only mechanisms available would send the password unprotected, the client raises an error instead. tls: 'disable' turns off TLS negotiation, but it doesn't turn off this check.

It never writes a character set it can't encode. Asking for a body in ISO 8859-1 raises an error, instead of writing UTF-8 bytes under a header that claims otherwise.

It doesn't validate DNSSEC. See What a Signature Does Not Say.

It doesn't implement a POP3 server. A POP3 server is an IMAP server with almost everything removed, and running mail.imap is the better option.

It doesn't decide whether mail is wanted. There's no spam filtering, reputation system or policy. DKIM tells you who signed a message, and what you do with that information is up to you.

Module Reference

The standard library reference documents every class and method. Here's an overview of the module:

Function Description
mail.message() Starts a new message
mail.parse(data) Parses a message
mail.send(url, note, options) Sends a message, handling the connection for you
mail.smtp(url, options) Connects to a server that sends mail
mail.imap(url, options) Connects to a server that stores mail
mail.pop3(url, options) Connects to a server that hands over mail
mail.parse_address(text) Parses a single address
mail.parse_address_list(text) Parses every address in a header
mail.format_addresses(people) Formats a list of addresses
mail.attachment(data) Starts a new attachment
mail.Attachment.from_file(path) Creates an attachment from a file on disk

Methods of an Attachment:

Methods Purpose
set_filename, set_content_type, set_encoding Describe what it is
set_disposition, set_cid, set_description Describe how it's presented
filename, content_type, disposition, cid, size, data Read these values back
to_part Returns the message part it becomes

Methods of a Message:

Methods Purpose
set_from, set_sender, set_reply_to Who it's from
add_to, add_cc, add_bcc, set_to, set_cc, set_bcc Who it's for
set_subject, set_text, set_html What it says
attach, embed What it carries, as an Attachment
set_header, add_header, set_date, set_message_id Everything else
set_in_reply_to, set_references Which conversation it belongs to
sender, to, cc, bcc, reply_to, recipients Read the addresses back
subject, text, text_body, html_body Read the contents back
parts, walk, find_part, attachments Work with the message tree
to_bytes, to_string Write it out

The protocol modules:

Module Contents
mail.smtp SmtpClient, SmtpServer, SmtpSession, Reply
mail.imap ImapClient, ImapServer, Mailbox, Envelope, BodyPart, MessageInfo
mail.imap MailStore, MaildirStore, MemoryStore, StoredMessage
mail.pop3 Pop3Client, Entry
mail.dkim Signer, Signature, Result, verify, is_signed
mail.sasl of, choose, and a class for each mechanism
mail.pool serve, start, Cluster

And the lower-level modules, for programs that need them directly:

Module Contents
mail.address parse, parse_list, parse_groups, format_list
mail.headers Headers, fold, unfold
mail.encoding The transfer encodings, encoded words and parameters
mail.content ContentType, ContentDisposition
mail.stream LineStream, connect, start_tls, endpoint
mail.imap.parser The IMAP grammar, for reading a response yourself

Chapter 19 · The Big Modules

Configuration and the Environment

Any program that works with other services needs to be told where they are: a database address, an API key, a port to listen on, or a flag that turns on verbose logging for an afternoon. None of that belongs in the source code. It changes between your laptop and the server, and some of it should never be committed to a repository at all.

The industry's standard answer is the process environment. Orchestrators, CI runners and shells all set environment variables, and every language can read them. What none of them handle is the first machine in the chain, which is yours. There's no orchestrator on your laptop, and nobody wants to type eight variable assignments in front of every command.

The env module fills that gap. It reads a .env file into the process environment when the program starts, and it reads values back out already converted to the number, boolean or list your program needs. The file is a convenience for development, while the environment is the real interface. A program written with env doesn't know or care where a value came from, which is what lets it run unchanged in both places.

  • Loading the File
  • Writing a .env File
    • Quoting
    • Comments
    • Values That Span Lines
  • Existing Variables Take Priority
    • Overriding
    • Empty Means Unset
  • References Between Values
    • Fallbacks and Required Values

  • Reading Values
  • Configuring a Load
    • Layering Files

  • Writing a File
  • Errors
  • Keeping Secrets Out of Git
  • Module Reference

Loading the File

It takes one call, which should go as early in the program as possible:

env.load() without an argument reads .env in the current working directory, which is what almost every program wants. The examples in this chapter write their file first and pass its name, so that you can run each one as it is.

The file is optional. If it doesn't exist, load() leaves the environment exactly as it was, and the program continues with whatever the shell already provided. That's intentional, so the same program runs on a laptop with a .env file and on a server without one.

Writing a .env File

Each line has a name, an = and a value:

A name is a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits and underscores, which is the same rule a shell uses. Anything else stops the load with a ParseError instead of being silently ignored, because a name that no shell could export is always a typo.

A leading export is allowed and ignored, so you can also load the same file into your shell with source when you want the variables there too.

Quoting

An unquoted value is everything up to the end of the line, with whitespace removed from both ends. If that's not what you want, put the value in quotes:

Each quoting style differs from the others in exactly one way:

Written Means
KEY=value Trimmed, and ends at a comment or the end of the line
KEY='value' Every character exactly as written, with nothing resolved
KEY=`value` The same, for values that contain both kinds of quotes
KEY="value" Backslash escapes are resolved, and $ references are expanded

Inside double quotes, \n, \r, \t, \f, \v, \b, \a, \e and \0 mean the same as they do in Zuri, and \xHH, \uHHHH and \u{H...} specify a code point. A backslash before any other character keeps both characters, so "C:\Users\me" gives you the path you meant, and you don't need to think about escaping.

Use single quotes for any value that's a secret. A generated password that contains $ or \ is kept exactly as it is, and nothing in it can accidentally refer to another variable.

Comments

A # starts a comment, either on a line of its own or after a value. Inside an unquoted value, it only starts a comment when it's at the start of the value or follows a space, which is why PASSWORD=hunter#2 above kept its #. If you'd rather not rely on that rule, quote the value, and the question doesn't come up.

Values That Span Lines

A quoted value continues until its closing quote, including any newlines. This is how you put a private key in the file:

Single quotes work the same way and don't resolve anything, which usually makes them the better choice for keys.

Existing Variables Take Priority

If a name is already set in the process environment, it's left as it is, and the file only fills in the rest:

This is the reason for the default. The file contains what a developer needs to run the program at all. In production, the real values are set through the shell, the orchestrator or the CI runner, and the file doesn't need to know anything about it.

load() returns a Result that accounts for every name and every file, so a program never has to guess whether its configuration was loaded. applied contains the variables the load set, skipped contains the ones that were already set, and values contains everything the file defined, either way. files lists the paths that were read, and missing lists the ones that didn't exist.

Overriding

When the file really should take priority, say so:

Empty Means Unset

Throughout the module, a variable set to an empty string is treated as unset. FLAG= in a file, an empty shell variable and a variable that was never set all mean the same thing, because that's what people mean by all three. A load fills in an empty variable, has() returns false for it, require() raises an error for it, and every typed reader returns its default value.

If you need to tell an empty value from a missing one, which is rare, use os.get_env(), which doesn't treat them the same.

References Between Values

A value can refer to another value, or to the surrounding environment, using the same syntax as a shell:

The split string in that example is because of Zuri, not .env files. A ${ written inside a Zuri string literal is an interpolation, so when you build .env text in source code, you have to keep the $ and the { apart. A file you write in an editor doesn't have this problem, as the dosini block above shows.

A reference resolves to the value the variable will have once the load has finished. That rule is what makes PORT=${PORT:-8080} mean what it looks like: the value from the environment if there is one, or 8080 if there isn't. This is true whichever line of the file the reference is on, and it changes with override() in the same way that priority does.

A definition can also refer to the value it's replacing, which is how you extend a path instead of overwriting it:

Fallbacks and Required Values

The three modifiers are the ones POSIX defines. Adding a colon in front of each one changes the test from "is it set" to "is it set to something":

Written Means
${NAME:-fallback} The value, or fallback if it's unset or empty
${NAME-fallback} The value, or fallback if it's unset
${NAME:+instead} instead if the value is set and not empty, and nothing otherwise
${NAME+instead} instead if the value is set, and nothing otherwise
${NAME:?reason} The value, or a MissingVariable error with reason as its message
${NAME?reason} The same, but an empty value counts as set

The text after a modifier is also expanded, so a fallback can have its own fallback:

:? is particularly useful. It lets the file itself document what a deployment requires, and if something is missing, the program fails when it starts, with the reason included:

Literal Dollar Signs

\$ is a dollar sign and nothing else. A $ that isn't followed by a name, as in PRICE=$5.00, already stands for itself. Values in single quotes or backticks are never expanded, so you don't need to worry about a secret that contains ${:

Reading Values

An environment variable is always text, but programs rarely want text. The typed readers convert the value, and reject anything that isn't what it claims to be:

Function Returns
get(name, default) The text, or the default
require(name, reason) The text, or raises a MissingVariable error
has(name) Whether the variable is set at all
int(name, default) A decimal integer, which can have a sign
float(name, default) A number, including one with an exponent
bool(name, default) True for 1, true, yes, y and on, and false for their opposites
list(name, separator, default) The value split into a list, with each item trimmed and empty items removed

A value that's set but can't be converted raises a ValueError that names the variable, instead of silently falling back to the default. PORT=eighty is a configuration mistake, and the right time to find out about it is when the program starts, not on the first request that needs a port.

These functions read the process environment, not the file. They give the same answer whether a value came from .env or from the shell, which is what lets one program run in both places without any special cases.

Most programs should use require() for at least one setting. For a setting that the code can't make up a default for, the program should stop right at the start, with the setting's name in the error message:

Configuring a Load

When the one-line form isn't enough, env.loader() returns a Loader. Every setting returns the loader, so you can write a whole configuration as a single expression. Running a loader doesn't change it, so you can keep one and use it again.

Layering Files

Sources are read in the order they're added, and the last source to define a name is the one whose value is used:

This combination is the one you'll use most often. .env contains what the whole team shares, and is worth committing as .env.example, while .env.local contains what's different on one particular machine, and isn't committed. A path can start with ~, which is expanded to the home directory.

Loading From Text

source() adds text instead of a path, so configuration that came from the network or a secret store goes through exactly the same parsing, expansion and priority rules as a file on disk:

Requiring the File

By default, a missing file isn't an error, and its path is recorded in Result.missing. When the file really is part of the deployment, mark it as required, so the load fails with a clear error if it's missing:

Reading Without Loading

read() does everything load() does except the final step. Nothing is written to the process environment, but $ references are still resolved as they would have been, so what you get back is exactly what load() would have set. It's how a tool can inspect a file, and how a test can check one without changing the environment of the process it's running in.

expand(false) turns off expansion completely, for a file of secrets where every value should be used exactly as written.

Writing a File

stringify() is the opposite of parse(), for a program that generates a .env file instead of reading one:

Values are written without quotes where that's unambiguous, and in double quotes where it isn't, and a $ inside a value is escaped so that loading the file again doesn't expand it. The output round-trips: passing it to parse() returns the same names and values.

Numbers, bigints, booleans and bytes are converted to text. Anything else raises a TypeError, because guessing how a list should look in an environment file is how configuration silently goes wrong.

Errors

Every error the module raises is an EnvError, and each subclass includes details that the message alone can't:

Class Raised when Includes
ParseError A source isn't a valid environment file line, column
MissingFile A required file doesn't exist path
MissingVariable A required variable isn't set name

Catching EnvError catches all three. A ValueError from a typed reader is an ordinary ValueError, so you can handle it in the same place as the rest of your validation errors.

Keeping Secrets Out of Git

A .env file holds the values that differ from one deployment to the next, which means it holds your secrets. Three lines in your .gitignore take care of that once and for all:

Commit a .env.example that lists every variable but contains no real values. It's the only documentation of what the program needs that can't get out of date, because as soon as someone adds a setting without adding it there, a fresh checkout stops working.

Avoid committing a .env.production alongside a .env.staging. Configuration varies by deployment, not by environment name, and as soon as there are two files, someone will edit the wrong one. Use one file per machine, and let required() and :? make it clear what that machine is still missing.

Module Reference

Here's everything the module provides:

Function Description
load(path) Reads a file into the process environment
loader() Returns a Loader, for loads that need more configuration
parse(source) Converts text into names and values, without changing the environment
stringify(values) Converts names and values back into text
is_name(name) Checks whether a name is a valid variable name

Reading values:

Functions Description
get, require, has Read the text, or check whether it's missing
int, float, bool, list Read the text and convert it, or raise a ValueError

The classes:

Class Members
Loader path, paths, source, override, expand, required, read, load
Result values, applied, skipped, files, missing
EnvError ParseError, MissingFile, MissingVariable

And the lower-level module, for programs that need it directly:

Module Contents
env.expand expand(value, resolve), the $ reference syntax on its own

Chapter 20 · The Big Modules

Parsing the Command Line

A program started from a shell receives a list of strings and nothing else. Whatever the user meant by -v, --output report.csv or commit -m "fix the thing" has to be worked out from that list, and that's where command-line programs tend to slowly fall apart. The first version reads os.args and checks a few positions. The second adds a flag, and the checks become a chain of conditions. By the fourth version, nobody can say what -vo does without trying it, the help text no longer matches the code that reads the flags, and a typo quietly does something else instead of reporting an error.

The args module takes a declarative approach instead. You declare which options exist, what type of value each one takes and which ones are required. The module works out what the user typed, converts and validates the values, generates the help text from the same declarations, and rejects anything that doesn't match.

  • A First Parser
  • What parse() Returns
  • Options
    • Passing a Value
    • Types
    • Defaults and Missing Options

    • Restricting the Allowed Values

A First Parser

It takes three lines of declarations and one call:

parse() without an argument reads the real command line, which is what a program normally does. Throughout this chapter, it's given an explicit list instead, because that's also how you test a parser, and because an example in a book can't depend on how you ran it.

What parse() Returns

It always returns a dictionary with three keys:

options holds every option that was given on the command line or has a default. command is nil, or the subcommand that was given. indexes holds the positional arguments, in the order they were declared. The three are independent, so a program can use one of them and ignore the others.

A declared positional argument that wasn't given and has no default stays in indexes as nil, so the argument after it is still at the index where it was declared, instead of moving down one place.

Options

An option is declared by its long name. The short name is optional, and so is everything else:

--output and -o are the same option.

Passing a Value

A long option takes its value either as the next argument or attached with =. The two forms mean the same thing:

The argument is split at the first =, so --output=a=b writes to a=b instead of losing half of the name, and --output= sets the value to an empty string instead of leaving it missing. The attached form is also the only way to pass a value that starts with a dash, because in --output -5, the parser reads -5 as an option:

A short option only takes its value as the next argument, as in -o out.csv, never -oout.csv or -o=out.csv. A short option token is a group of single-character flags, and neither = nor the letters of a value are flags.

Types

The type determines what the string is converted to, and whether the option takes a value at all.

Constant The option takes The result is
args.NONE Nothing true when the option is present
args.STRING A value The string itself
args.INT A value A whole number
args.NUMBER A value A number, which can have a fractional part
args.BOOL A value A boolean
args.LIST A value, and can be repeated A list of strings
args.CHOICE A value from a fixed set The string, or the value it maps to
args.OPTIONAL A value, if there is one The string, or true

NONE is the default, and it's a plain flag. BOOL takes an explicit value, and it accepts every spelling a user is likely to try:

1, true, yes, y and on all mean true, and 0, false, no, n and off all mean false.

Defaults and Missing Options

value is the option's value when it isn't given on the command line:

If an option has no default and isn't given on the command line, it isn't in the dictionary at all. That's how you tell a flag that was left out from one that was set to false, and it's why verbose is missing from the first line instead of being false. Use options.contains('verbose') to check, or give the option a default so you don't need to.

Requiring an Option

If the option is left out, the program stops with error: required option --output is missing, followed by the usage line, and exits with status 1. Nothing else runs.

Restricting the Allowed Values

CHOICE with a list only accepts the values in the list:

Any other value stops the program with error: --level must be one of quiet, normal or loud, not "shouty", which names the invalid value and lists the alternatives, without you having to write either.

If you pass a dictionary instead, the user types the key and the program receives the corresponding value. This is how you turn a short name on the command line into a more meaningful value inside the program:

Repeated Options

LIST collects a value every time the option appears:

Deprecating an Option

An option that you no longer want, but can't remove yet, keeps working and prints a warning:

The warning goes to standard error, so the person running the program sees it, but it doesn't end up in output that another program might be reading.

Positional Arguments

Positional arguments are declared with add_index, and they're filled in the order they were declared:

They accept type, choices, value, required and metavar, just as options do. A positional argument that wasn't declared is an error rather than being silently ignored, which means a mistyped flag fails with an error instead of being taken as a file name.

Subcommands

A program that does several different jobs can give each one a name and its own options:

add_command returns the command, so you can chain its options directly after it. A command's options are added to the same options dictionary as the global options, and command.name tells you which job the user asked for.

The order matters, and it's the same order every tool like this uses: the parser's own options come before the command name, and the command's options come after it. notes -v list works, but notes list -v doesn't, because after list, the parser is reading list's options, and -v isn't one of them.

Commands That Take a Value

A command can take a single value directly, in the way that git commit -m takes a message:

The value comes straight after the command name, before the command's own options. metavar is the word the help text shows in place of the value, so the usage line reads notes add <text> instead of notes add <value>.

Attaching an Action

A command can include the function that implements it, which is called after parsing with the options and the command's value:

This is worth using once you have more than two or three commands. Otherwise, you end up with a chain of comparisons on command.name that you have to keep in sync with the declarations yourself.

Command-Line Conventions

Users type things that the parser wasn't explicitly told about. These are the conventions it supports.

Combining Flags

You can put several flags after a single dash:

Every character in the group has to be a declared option. -vqz is an error, rather than -vq with the z silently ignored, so you find out about the typo now and not after the program has run.

Abbreviations

A long option can be shortened to any prefix that's still unambiguous:

Set parser.allow_abbrev = false to turn this off. That's worth doing for a program whose set of options is still growing, because a prefix that's unambiguous today stops being unambiguous as soon as someone adds --version, and any script written with the short form breaks.

End of Options

A -- on its own ends option parsing. Everything after it is a positional argument, even if it starts with a dash:

This is how a program can pass arguments on to another program without needing to understand them.

Reading Arguments From a File

An argument that starts with @ is replaced by the contents of that file, with one argument per line:

The file's contents are inserted in place, so any arguments after it still take priority. This is useful when a command line becomes too long for a shell to handle comfortably, and for arguments that a program would rather not put where ps can see them. Set parser.allow_atfile = false to turn it off, for a program that should treat a leading @ as ordinary text.

Help

The help text is generated from the declarations, so it always matches what the program accepts:

-h and --help are declared for you and work wherever they appear. After a command, they describe that command instead of the whole program. help() does the same thing when you call it directly. Both print the help text and exit with status 0.

Colors are used when standard output is a terminal and NO_COLOR isn't set, so output that's piped or redirected is plain text without escape codes. set_terminal_width() sets the width the text wraps at, which is what the example above does, so that the output is the same in every terminal. If you don't set it, the parser asks the terminal for its width, then falls back to COLUMNS, and then to 80.

If a parser's command line didn't match anything at all, it prints its help text and continues. An option with a default counts as a match, so this never happens for a parser with any defaults. To turn this behavior off completely, pass false as the second argument to args.Parser.

Errors

Every error is reported the same way: a line on standard error starting with error:, followed by the usage text, and an exit status of 1.

What happened The message
An option that wasn't declared unknown option: --color
An option that needs a value was the last argument option --name expects <name>
A required option was left out required option --output is missing
A value that isn't in choices --level must be one of quiet or loud, not "shouty"
A required positional argument was left out required positional argument <source> is missing
An argument that doesn't match anything unexpected argument: report.csv

None of these raise an exception. When a command-line program receives something it can't use, there's nothing useful left for it to do, and a stack trace in the user's terminal tells them less than a one-line message. The errors that do raise an exception are mistakes in the declarations, such as a duplicate option name, a short name that's already used, or choices that's neither a list nor a dictionary. Those are bugs in the program rather than mistakes by the user, so they raise an ArgsError or a TypeError from the add_option call that caused them.

Testing Command-Line Parsing

parse() accepts an explicit list, which is what makes it testable:

Create the parser in a function, so that each test gets a new one. A parser keeps the results of its last parse, so sharing one between tests makes them depend on the order they run in. To test the paths that end in os.exit(), which are help and every error above, you need to run a real subprocess, which is what os.exec() is for. Chapter 23 covers testing in more detail.

Module Reference

Creating a parser:

Method Description
Parser(name, default_help) Creates a new parser
add_option(name, help, opts) Adds an option, either globally or to a command
add_command(name, help, opts) Adds a subcommand and returns it, for chaining
add_index(name, help, opts) Adds a positional argument
parse(custom_args) Parses the command line, or the given list
help() Prints the help text and exits with status 0
set_terminal_width(width) Sets the width that text wraps at

Properties you can set after creating a parser:

Property Description
description, epilog Text shown before and after the options
allow_abbrev Whether unambiguous prefixes of long options are accepted. The default is true.
allow_atfile Whether @file arguments are expanded. The default is true.
terminal_width The width that text wraps at

Keys you can use in opts:

Key Description
short_name The single-character form of the option
type One of the type constants
value The value when the option isn't given
choices A list of allowed values, or a dictionary that maps keys to values
required Whether the program refuses to run without it
metavar The word the help text shows in place of the value
deprecated Prints a warning to standard error when the option is used
action For a command, the function to run after parsing

The type constants:

Constants Description
NONE, STRING, INT, NUMBER A flag, and the three plain value types
BOOL, LIST, CHOICE, OPTIONAL A yes or no answer, a repeated value, a value from a fixed set, and an optional value

Chapter 21 · Going Deeper

Metaprogramming and Reflection

Zuri programs have access to Zuri's own compiler. The zuri module provides the lexer, the parser and the bytecode compiler as ordinary functions, along with a reflection API for working with live functions, classes, modules and instances.

That's an unusual amount of the language to expose, so it's worth being clear about what it's for. These are the tools behind documentation generators, linters, plugin loaders, serializers, debuggers and editor tooling, which are all programs that work with other programs. They aren't meant for everyday code, and the chapter ends with the one thing they intentionally can't do.

Reflection and the Compiler API

The module is divided into two clear halves, and confusing them is the most common mistake:

Reflection The compiler API
Works with Objects that exist right now Source code
Entry points zuri.reflect.* tokenize(), parse(), compile()
Can tell you A function's arity, a class's fields, an instance's values A doc block, a comment, a line number, what the compiler produced
Can't tell you Anything about the source code it came from Anything about a running value

A function's arity is a run-time fact. The function object stores it, and reflection reads it. The same function's doc block is a fact about the source code. It only exists in the file, and only the parser can find it. No function bridges the two, which is why a documentation generator parses files instead of importing them.

A Common Structure

tokenize(), parse() and compile() all return results with the same structure: a flat list of small records, each tagged in the same way.

Function Returns Tag Data
tokenize(source) A list of Token kind value, text
parse(source) A list of Node kind fields
compile(source) A list of Instr op fields

There's a single Token class, a single Node class and a single Instr class, rather than one class for each kind of token, grammar rule or opcode. The grammar has about fifty node types and the instruction set has about sixty opcodes, so a class for each would mean more than a hundred nearly identical classes that would have to be kept in sync with the compiler forever.

The downside of this choice is real: nothing tells you which fields a particular kind has. Your editor can't autocomplete a Binary node's left, op and right. Instead, the module relies on a different habit, which is to run it and look:

Everything about that node is right there. It's a Stmt that wraps a Var, the initializer is a Binary node whose op is the string 'Plus', and the literal 1 is an Integer node rather than a generic literal. Each header shows where the node starts, and name_span shows exactly where the name total is. You didn't have to look anything up.

dump() is the quickest way to learn the structure of any node, and it's the first thing to try whenever you're unsure. zuri.dump_file(path) does the same for a whole file.

Runtime Reflection

Reflection answers questions about a value you have. Every reflection function is in zuri.reflect.

What Kind of Value Is This?

kind() is a more literal version of typeof(). Note the last line: a built-in native function reports 'function', as do closures and bound methods, because as far as the language is concerned, all three can be called in exactly the same way.

Functions

function_info() returns { name, arity, variadic, is_method, owning_class_name, source_path }. The last field is the only one that refers back to the source code, and it's a path, not the content. To read the function's doc block, you still have to parse that file.

Classes

Four things in that output are worth a closer look.

fields includes name, which was never declared with var. It was created by self.name = name inside @new. Reflection reports the class's actual structure, not just what the var lines said.

statics is separate from fields, because a static field belongs to the class, while a field belongs to each instance.

Decorated methods are listed under their @ names. @new and @to_json appear in methods alongside the ordinary methods.

_secret is listed. Reflection can see private members, as explained below.

Each entry in methods is a complete function_info, so info.methods.area.arity works without another call.

superclass_name is a string or nil, not a class:

Instances

get_props() lists the names of the fields an instance actually has. get_prop(), set_prop(), has_prop() and del_prop() read and write fields by a computed name. They're the reflection equivalents of the getprop family of built-in functions from Chapter 6.

They can't create a field. Classes are sealed, so set_prop() with a name that the class never declared returns false and doesn't change anything.

class_of() works in the other direction. Given an instance, it returns the class it was created from, as the class itself:

typeof() returns the class's name, and two classes with the same name declared in different modules return the same name. Only the class itself can tell them apart, and only the class can be called, passed to class_info() or used as a dictionary key. That's how a library can store something for each class. For example, sql.model stores each model's definition this way.

Looking Up Methods by Name

Three functions turn a method name into something you can call:

The difference between the last two is important. get_method() returns the unbound function, so you have to pass the instance yourself when you call it. bind_method() returns the method already attached to the instance, so it can be stored, passed around and called without anything extra. That's what makes a dispatch table of methods possible:

has_decorator() and get_decorator() do the same for methods whose names start with @. Pass the name without the @.

Reflection Can See Private Members

All of the functions above ignore the leading underscore rule:

This is intentional, and it's the same choice getprop() makes. A serializer has to see every field, or it writes an incomplete record, and a debugger has to see every field, or it shows misleading information. Hiding private fields would defeat the only purpose these functions have.

The lesson here is that reflection is for building tools, not for getting around encapsulation. If code uses get_prop() to read a private field it couldn't otherwise read, it hasn't found a clever loophole. It has written something the next person to read it won't expect.

Modules

module_info() returns a module's name, its path and the members it exports.

import takes its path exactly as written, so it can't import a file whose name the program only learns while it's running. zuri.import_file() can. It imports the module at a given path, just as an import naming that file would, and returns it:

That's how you build a plugin loader: import a directory of modules, check whether each one has a known function, and call the ones that do. A relative path is resolved from the working directory. The module comes from the same cache that import uses, so its top level only runs once, however many times and in whatever way it's imported, and two imports of the same file return the same module, which are equal (==) to each other. sql.migrate loads its migrations this way.

The Garbage Collector

The garbage collector runs automatically as a program allocates memory. gc() runs a full collection immediately:

Every unreachable object is freed before gc() returns, and anything that releases a resource when it's collected does so at that point. For example, an ffi pointer taken over with own() runs its destructor. The freed memory is also returned to the operating system before gc() returns. No program needs to call gc() to work correctly. It's for situations where timing matters, such as releasing native resources at a known point, or a test that checks what garbage collection does. A full collection visits every live object, so calling it in a loop is slow.

Tokens

tokenize() is the first stage. It takes source text and returns a flat list of tokens.

Nothing is filtered out. Comments, doc blocks and newlines are all returned as tokens, and the list always ends with a single Eof token. The parser skips comments and whitespace when it runs, but tokenize() reports everything the lexer saw, which is exactly what a formatter or a syntax highlighter needs.

Each Token has these fields:

Field Description
kind The lexer's own name for the token type, such as 'Identifier', 'Plus' or 'Comment'
line, column The position, starting from 1. column counts characters, not bytes.
start, end The character offsets of the token's exact text
text The exact source text, including any delimiters
value The token's data, where it has any, such as a literal's value, an identifier's name or a comment's content

start and end make it possible to edit source code. They let you recover or replace a token's original text without running the lexer again, which is how a rename tool or a code formatter works.

is_trivia() returns true for comments and doc blocks, so you can filter them out with a single call:

The Lexer Never Raises an Error

Invalid input doesn't raise an error. Instead, it produces a token of kind 'Error' that describes what went wrong:

That means tokenize() accepts any input at all, which makes it safe to use on a file you didn't write, or on a half-written buffer in an editor. Neither parse() nor compile() works like that. Both raise an error for invalid input, because neither can produce a meaningful result from it.

The Syntax Tree

parse() is the second stage. It turns tokens into a tree.

A Node has a kind, a position and a fields dictionary. The fields contain other nodes, plain lists, plain dictionaries or simple values and nothing else, so you can walk through the tree in the same way, whatever node you're looking at.

Node Positions

A node's position covers all of the source it was parsed from. start and end are character offsets, of the first character and of the character just after the last one, so slicing the source with them gives you the node's own text. line and col give the start of the node, and end_line and end_col give its end, all counted from 1:

A declaration starts at its keyword, so a function starts at def, and its name has its own name_span. That's everything a tool needs to underline a mistake, jump to a definition or select a whole statement.

Walking the Tree

walk_nodes(tree, visitor) visits every node, depth first:

That output is worth a second look, because it shows how much the parser makes explicit. The single parameter n, which has no annotation, still produced an Argument that wraps a TypeHint that wraps an Any. The absence of an annotation is represented in the tree rather than left out, so a tool that walks the tree never has to handle "no type was written" as a special case.

The visitor can also be a dictionary that maps node kinds to handlers, in which case only the matching nodes are passed to it:

find_nodes(tree, kind) is a shortcut for when you only want nodes of one kind:

Comments Are Kept

This is what makes documentation tools possible. Comments and doc blocks are kept in the tree, in their original positions, as nodes of their own:

A doc block is a sibling placed immediately before whatever it documents, so pairing them up takes a single pass with one variable of state. That's exactly what the example below does.

Most parsers throw comments away. Keeping them is what lets you build a formatter or a documentation generator on top of a parser, rather than only an interpreter.

Bytecode

compile() is the third stage. It turns the tree into VM instructions.

An Instr has an op, a line and a fields dictionary, which is the same structure a Node has, and walk_instrs() and find_instrs() work exactly like the tree walkers.

Notice the AddImm instruction. The compiler included the constant 2 in the add instruction instead of loading it separately. Questions like this can only be answered by the bytecode, and reading it is the most direct way to find out what the compiler actually did with your code:

The power comes before the multiplication, because ** binds more tightly than *. One line of bytecode settles a question that reading the expression might not.

Resolved Operands

Several opcodes only contain an index into the compiler's constant pool, which doesn't tell you much by itself. Instead of making every caller fetch and match up a table of constants, each of these fields comes with the resolved value next to the index:

const_idx is the index, value is the constant it refers to, and dst is the register the result is stored in. The same pairing appears on GetGlobal, GetField, Invoke and the other opcodes like them.

The resolved value of a Closure instruction is a nested function prototype ({ name, arity, variadic, instructions }), whose own instructions are wrapped in the same way, all the way down. So when you compile a file that contains functions, you can see their bodies too, not only the code around them.

Line Numbers Only, Not Columns

Every instruction records the source line it came from, but never a column, because the compiler only tracks lines. Both Token and Node have accurate column information from the lexer, but Instr doesn't.

Checking Source Without Running It

parse() and compile() raise an error at the first sign of invalid source, which is the right behavior for a tool that needs the complete program. A tool that works on source while it's being written, half a statement at a time, needs the opposite: everything that can be read, and a precise description of what's wrong.

parse_partial() reads as much as it can. When a statement fails, the parser reports it, skips ahead to the start of the next statement and continues, so each mistake only affects one statement and is reported once:

Each error is a Diagnostic, which has a message and the same six-part position that a node has, so you can underline it precisely. The statement that failed is still in the tree, with an empty string where its missing name should be.

check() goes one step further. Source that parses successfully is passed on to the compiler, which catches problems that the grammar can't see, such as a break outside a loop or a name declared twice in the same scope:

If check() returns an empty list, the source compiles. Neither function runs any code or raises an error for invalid source, so you can use both of them on whatever an editor's buffer contains at any moment.

Reading Files

Each of these functions has a _file version that reads a file first:

Source string File
tokenize(source) tokenize_file(path)
parse(source) parse_file(path)
compile(source) compile_file(path)
parse_partial(source) parse_partial_file(path)
check(source) check_file(path)

There's also one with no string version: dump_file(path) reads and parses a file, and returns the dump() of every top-level node. It's usually the quickest way to find out what's actually in a file.

Example: Extracting Documentation

Here's the technique that this book's own reference appendices are built with. It takes source code and returns every documented function in it, pairing each declaration with the doc block above it.

The key is that zuri.parse() keeps comments in the tree. A doc block is returned as a DocBlock node of its own, placed as a sibling immediately before whatever it documents. zuri.doc.attach() walks through a list of siblings and pairs each one with the doc block directly above it, and zuri.doc parses the contents of each block into its text and its @ tags:

undocumented doesn't appear in the output. attach() returns it with documented set to false, because there's no doc block above it.

There are several reasons to prefer this approach over scanning the text yourself.

The parser knows what a declaration is. A function named def_handler, a def inside a string literal and a doc block inside a block comment would all confuse a text scan, but none of them confuse the parser.

Parameter names and types come from the actual nodes. A parameter's type_hint node contains its types and whether it accepts nil, so a generated signature matches what the runtime will actually enforce, rather than what the source code seemed to say.

It stays up to date. When the grammar gains a new feature, so does the parser, and a tool built this way keeps working.

The tags are parsed for you. zuri.doc joins a tag's wrapped lines, reads its type and the name it documents, and treats @return as @returns. It's the same parsing that this book's own reference is generated with, so a block is read the same way here as it is there.

Example: A Linter

The other common use for this module is checking code rather than generating something from it. Here's the kind of rule a team builds up over time: report every function that has more than a certain number of parameters.

There are three reasons to do this with the parser rather than with a regular expression over the text.

It can't be fooled by text that looks like code. A function named def_handler, the word def inside a string literal and a commented-out declaration aren't Function nodes, so none of them are counted.

It reports the correct line. node.line comes from the lexer, so the message points to the declaration, however the code around it is formatted.

It keeps working. When the grammar gains a new feature, so does the parser, and a rule written this way doesn't silently stop matching.

The dictionary form of the visitor is important here. Only Function nodes are passed to the handler, so you don't need an if node.kind == ... check, and you can't accidentally match a kind you didn't mean to.

Serializing Without @to_json

Reflection is useful when you'd otherwise have to write the same method in every class:

A single function works for every class, and there's no method in each class to keep in sync with its fields. Note that this also reads private fields, which is right for a debugging dump but wrong for an API response. For an API response, either filter out names that start with an underscore, or write a real @to_json and let each class decide what to expose.

Telling Watch Mode Which Files a Program Reads

zuri run --watch restarts a program when a file it depends on changes. The runtime automatically reports every Zuri source file the program reads. A library that reads other files that affect the program's behavior declares each one with zuri.watch.depends_on(), which is how Wire gets its templates watched:

Outside watch mode, depends_on() does nothing and active() returns false, so a library can always call it. zuri.watch is a separate module from the rest of zuri, so importing it doesn't load the parser and the compiler.

Other Uses

Plugin systems. Load modules from a directory, check whether each one has the function your program expects, and call the ones that do. module_info() lets you check without having to import modules blindly and hope for the best.

Editor tooling. tokenize(), parse_partial() and check() never raise errors, so you can run them on a half-written buffer. Every token and node has start and end offsets, so a rename or reformat can rewrite exact ranges of text, and you can underline every problem check() finds exactly where it is.

Understanding the compiler. Calling zuri.compile() on a snippet is quicker than reading the compiler's source code, and it always matches the version of the compiler you're actually running.

Generating parts of this book. Appendices D and E are generated from libs/ using exactly the techniques described above, and the audit that checks those stubs works the same way.

What You Can't Do

There's no eval(). You can compile source code to bytecode and inspect it, but you can't run a string as code.

Zuri leaves it out for security reasons. eval() blurs the line between data and code, and sooner or later, every program that uses it runs a string it didn't intend to, such as a form field, a query parameter, a configuration value or a webhook payload. As soon as one of those reaches eval(), whoever provided it can run code with your program's full permissions. That code can read your files, open network connections and send your secrets wherever it likes. This is the most damaging class of vulnerability in dynamic languages, and it keeps happening because the dangerous call looks harmless in a code review: a single function, a few characters of input, and nothing in the language warns you.

So Zuri doesn't provide eval(), and every task people usually use it for has a better solution:

Instead of Use
Evaluating an expression entered by a user A dictionary of handlers keyed by the input
Calling a method whose name you computed zuri.reflect.bind_method()
Changing behavior at run time Pass in a function
Turning text into data json.decode()
