Each of these does the job with a fixed set of possible outcomes that you can review. That's the difference between a program that handles its input and a program that does whatever its input tells it to.

Classes are sealed, so reflection can't add a method to a class at run time either. Techniques from other languages that depend on monkey patching don't carry over to Zuri. Instead, express the variation as a subclass, or as a function that you pass in.

Chapter 22 · Going Deeper

Performance and the JIT

Zuri runs your bytecode in an interpreter until part of it becomes hot. It then compiles that part to machine code and runs the machine code instead. There are two compilers, a fast baseline compiler and a slower optimizing compiler. By default, hot functions are compiled by the optimizing compiler, and the baseline compiler handles the ones it turns down. All of this happens automatically, on background threads, without any annotations or flags.

Here's the difference it makes for a simple recursive Fibonacci function, measured on an idle machine:

That's more than three times faster, for a function that does nothing but add and compare, and you don't have to write anything to get it. The rest of this chapter explains how the compilers work, and covers the few cases where the way you write code determines whether you get that speedup.

The Two Compilers

Kebbi is the baseline compiler. It turns a function's bytecode into machine code one instruction at a time, keeps values in machine registers, and works out what it can about types before it compiles. For example, it knows that a parameter annotated as list is a list, and that a counter that starts at 0 and goes up by 1 is a whole number. Kebbi compiles quickly, and the code it produces runs several times faster than the interpreter.

Bayelsa is the optimizing compiler. It represents the whole function as a graph of typed values, and optimizes that graph before generating any machine code. It applies a fact it has proven once to every later use, moves checks that can't change out of loops, keeps loop counters as plain integers, inlines small functions into the functions that call them, and wherever nothing proves a type, speculates based on what the function has done so far. Bayelsa takes longer to compile, and the code it produces is the fastest that Zuri can generate.

Both compilers use Cranelift, and both run on background threads. A program never waits for a compilation. It keeps running in the interpreter, or in the code it already has, until the new code is ready.

How a Function Is Compiled

  1. The interpreter. Every function starts here. The interpreter counts how many times the function is called and how many times its loops repeat, and records what kinds of values each operation sees.
  2. Bayelsa (the default). Once a function is warm, Bayelsa compiles it directly, using the information the interpreter recorded. Small helper functions are inlined, checks on constants are moved out of loops, and variables are kept in CPU registers.
  3. Kebbi as a fallback. If Bayelsa turns down a function, for example because it contains a catch block, Kebbi compiles it instead.

If you set ZURI_JIT_TIERED=1, Zuri can also use a multi-tier pipeline. A warm function is first compiled by Kebbi with profiling instrumentation, and once that profiling code has done enough work, Bayelsa compiles the function using the information it gathered.

When Speculation Fails

Bayelsa compiles the code based on what it has seen. A loop that has only ever added whole numbers uses integer arithmetic. A module constant that held 10 is compared as the integer 10. An index operation that has only ever seen bytes reads a byte. Each assumption is checked at the point where it's made, and if a check fails, the frame is handed back to the interpreter at that exact instruction, with every variable as the compiled code left it. This is called deoptimization.

The place where the check failed is remembered, and the next compilation of the function doesn't make that assumption there. So a function is deoptimized at a particular place only once, not every time it gets there.

Functions That Stay in Kebbi

Bayelsa leaves a function to Kebbi in two cases:

  • The function contains a catch. Kebbi compiles it, including its handlers.
  • The function's hot operations are ones that Kebbi handles inline but Bayelsa would pass to the runtime, such as arithmetic on values that weren't always numbers, method calls on strings, and indexing lists and strings whose type can't be determined. In those cases, Kebbi's code is faster.

A function that's left in Kebbi is recompiled without its profiling code, so it runs at Kebbi's full speed.

How Functions Become Hot

Every function counts its own calls, and every loop counts how many times it repeats. When a counter reaches its threshold, a compilation job is sent to a background thread. When the machine code is ready, later calls use it.

The threshold isn't a fixed number. It depends on the size of the function:

A large function gets a low threshold, because it does more work per call, so compiling it pays off sooner. A getter with three instructions gets a high threshold, because compiling it is a gamble, and most tiny functions never run often enough to make it worthwhile.

Loops get their own, lower threshold, through on-stack replacement. A loop inside a function that's only ever called once still gets compiled, and execution jumps from the interpreter into the middle of the compiled version without unwinding anything. That's what makes a script that runs once fast. A loop's threshold follows the same curve, based on the length of the loop itself, so a short loop in a long function, such as setup code that goes through a small table, has to repeat many times before the function around it is compiled.

You can see it happen:

fib goes straight to Bayelsa, because by default, warm functions are compiled directly by the optimizing compiler. With Bayelsa turned off (ZURI_JIT_KEBBI=1), Kebbi compiles it instead, and the output lists what Kebbi was able to prove:

When Bayelsa leaves a function to Kebbi, the output includes a line explaining why:

You can also see what was and wasn't compiled:

Comparing calls with threshold tells you how close a function came to being compiled.

Use Errors Only for Errors

A function with a catch is compiled like any other. As long as no error is raised, a catch costs almost nothing: the handler is registered and removed around the body, and the body runs as compiled code.

What does cost something is an error that's actually raised. A raise hands the frame back to the interpreter at that instruction, and a caught error continues at its handler in the interpreter too. The function returns to compiled code the next time its loop repeats, or the next time it's called. That's a reasonable cost for a real failure, but not for an outcome that a loop runs into every few iterations:

Here are two hundred rounds of a thousand iterations, with one in ten failing:

Variant Time
raise, caught inside the loop 73ms
nil returned and checked 11ms

When failure is an expected outcome, such as input that might not parse or a key that might be missing, return a value that indicates it and check that value. Save raise for situations the caller can't reasonably recover from. A raise that never runs, such as a guard clause at the top of a function, doesn't slow down the compiled code.

Type Annotations Improve Performance

The JIT speculates based on the types it has seen. When you tell it the type instead, it doesn't need to guess, and the check disappears.

Here are twenty thousand rounds over a list of a thousand elements:

Variant Time
values: list 85ms
No annotation 150ms

Running the two variants in both orders gives the same result, which confirms that the difference comes from the annotation and not from warm-up.

Annotate the parameters of any function on a hot path. It costs one word per parameter, and it documents the function at the same time.

Keep Types Stable

Speculation works by assuming the future will look like the past. If a variable holds a number for ten thousand iterations and then a string on the next one, the code is deoptimized: the compiled code falls back to the interpreter, and the function might be recompiled with a weaker assumption.

A single deoptimization is cheap. But a loop that's deoptimized on every iteration is slower than if it had never been compiled at all.

In practice, this means:

  • Use each variable for one kind of value.
  • Use a list of numbers, not a list of numbers that sometimes contains strings.
  • A field that starts as nil and later holds a number has two types. Start it at 0 instead.

The last one is the most common case. A class field declared as var count is nil until the constructor runs, so every read of it in compiled code has to handle both types. var count = 0 doesn't have this problem.

Where to Put a Hot Loop

A loop that processes every element belongs in a standalone function with typed parameters, not in a method that reads a field:

This is slower, because every iteration reads self.pixels through a field check:

This is faster, because the loop only uses local variables with declared types:

The standard library's imagine module is written this way throughout, and the difference for a loop over every pixel is measured in multiples, not percentages.

Reading the Bytecode

When you want to know what the compiler actually did, ask it:

The AddImm instruction, rather than a separate load, tells you that the constant was included in the instruction itself. This is the quickest way to check whether a change to your code did what you hoped, and it's always accurate.

Measuring Performance Reliably

Every number in this chapter is a single measurement on a single machine. Treat them as ratios rather than numbers to reproduce, because your results will vary with your processor, your build and whatever else the machine is doing. These five rules make the difference between a measurement and a guess.

Warm up before you start timing. The first few hundred iterations run in the interpreter, and if your benchmark is short, that's all you've measured.

Run each variant separately. Two variants in the same process share warm-up state and a heap. Run them in both orders, and if the result changes, you've measured the order.

Keep an eye on the machine. A laptop under sustained load slows itself down, so a second run isn't comparable to the first. Check the load just before the timed run, not before the build that comes before it.

Change one thing at a time. If a fix changes three places, there are three possible explanations for its effect, and one of them is often a regression hidden by the other two.

Measure the real program. A microbenchmark of a single function tells you about that function on its own, with a warm cache and no other allocations competing with it. Running the real workload with ZURI_JIT_COVERAGE=1 tells you which function to look at in the first place, which is nearly always more useful.

Timing Code Yourself

time() returns the time in seconds since the epoch, with microsecond resolution, so a timing harness only takes four lines:

The elapsed time will be different on every run, but the length won't. Print both, so that if the length ever changes, you know the harness is broken, rather than thinking the code has become faster.

Choosing a Mode

By default, Bayelsa compiles functions directly, and falls back to Kebbi whenever it turns a function down. ZURI_JIT_KEBBI=1 (or ZURI_JIT_BAYELSA=0) turns off Bayelsa, so every hot function stays in Kebbi. ZURI_JIT_TIERED=1 turns on the multi-tier pipeline, where Kebbi profiles a function before Bayelsa compiles it.

Keep the default for anything that runs long enough for its speed to matter, such as servers, batch jobs, numeric work, and anything whose hot loops run for more than a moment. That's where Bayelsa's code pays back the cost of compiling it many times over.

Turn off Bayelsa (ZURI_JIT_KEBBI=1) when:

  • The program is short. A script that finishes in a fraction of a second spends a significant part of its run time compiling, and the faster code arrives too late to pay for itself.
  • CPU cores are limited. Bayelsa's compilations use more processor time than Kebbi's. On a machine or container limited to one core, or when every core is busy running isolates, that time comes out of the program's own.
  • Startup time is what matters. A command-line tool that's run over and over again, for a few milliseconds each time, gains nothing from code that's faster on its thousandth iteration.
  • Timings need to be consistent from the first run. Kebbi reaches its full speed sooner and stays there.

Measure both. The setting is a single environment variable, and running your real workload both ways answers the question for that workload.

Environment Variables

These variables are for measuring and debugging. Ordinary programs don't need any of them.

Variable Effect
ZURI_JIT=0 Turns off the JIT completely
ZURI_JIT_KEBBI=1 Compiles with Kebbi only (the same as ZURI_JIT_BAYELSA=0)
ZURI_JIT_TIERED=1 Turns on multi-tier mode, where Kebbi profiles before Bayelsa compiles
ZURI_JIT_LOG=1 Prints one line for each compilation attempt
ZURI_JIT_LOG_IR=1 Prints the Cranelift IR, and Bayelsa's own IR before it
ZURI_JIT_COVERAGE=1 Prints a table of what was compiled when the program exits
ZURI_JIT_NO_SPECIALIZATION=1 Compiles functions, but without speculating on types
ZURI_JIT_THREADS=n Sets the number of background compiler threads
ZURI_JIT_CALL_K, ZURI_JIT_OSR_K Set the constants for the warm-up curve
ZURI_JIT_TIERUP_K Sets how much profiling work comes before Bayelsa, in tiered mode
ZURI_GC_LOG=1 Prints garbage collector activity
ZURI_GC_NURSERY_MB=n Sets the starting and minimum size of the young generation, in megabytes
ZURI_OPCODE_PROFILE=1 Prints a histogram of the interpreter's opcodes
MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY=n Sets how many milliseconds freed memory waits before it's returned to the operating system. The default is 10.

ZURI_JIT=0 is the most useful one. Running a benchmark with and without it tells you straight away whether your hot path is being compiled at all, which is the first thing to check when something is slower than it should be.

Knowing When to Stop

The interpreter is fast, and the JIT works automatically. Most Zuri code doesn't need any performance work at all, and code that does usually needs just one of the three changes described in this chapter: return a value instead of raising an error for an expected outcome, annotate a parameter, or stop storing two types in one variable.

Only try anything more unusual after ZURI_JIT_COVERAGE has shown you which function is actually causing the problem.

Chapter 23 · Going Deeper

Testing

A test is a program that runs your program and tells you whether it did the right thing. The test module provides everything you need for this: a way to name and group tests, a way to state what you expect, and a report that tells you which expectation failed and where.

There's nothing to install. Just write import test and you can start.

A First Test

Run it the same way you run anything else:

There are three things to notice right away.

import test { * }. A test file needs describe, it, expect and the rest available directly, not behind a module name. import test on its own also works, and gives you test.describe, test.expect and so on. Use that form in code that isn't itself a test file.

Nothing tells the tests to run. describe and it don't run anything. They build a tree, which runs once the file has finished declaring it, through os.at_exit(). That separation is what lets the framework count the tests before the first one starts, focus on a single test, filter tests by name and run them in random order. run() exists for when you want to pass options or read the result, which Controlling a Run covers.

@{ ... } is a function. it('name', @{ ... }) gives the framework a body to call later, which is why the framework can also choose not to call it.

When a Test Fails

Change 850 to 900 and run the test again:

You get the message, the two values, the line number and the code around it. The process exits with status 1, which is what a CI system checks.

Grouping Tests

You can nest describe blocks as deeply as the thing you're describing needs:

The nesting appears in the report and in the name that a failure is reported under, such as Cart > add() > merges a duplicate SKU. Choose names that read as a sentence when they're joined together like that, because that's how you'll read them.

Expectations

expect(value) returns an object that has every matcher on it.

.not negates any matcher. The same implementation handles both directions, so to_contain and not.to_contain can never disagree about what "contains" means.

Matchers can be chained, because each one returns the object it was called on:

A second argument gives the value a name, which is useful as soon as the number on its own wouldn't tell you which number it was:

Choosing Between to_be and to_equal

to_be uses Zuri's == operator. That already compares lists, dictionaries and bytes by their contents, so it's the right matcher for most values:

However, it compares two instances by identity, unless their class defines @eq, because that's what == does:

to_equal compares structures. It goes through an instance field by field, treats NaN as equal to itself, and can handle a value that contains itself. Use it whenever the objects on both sides of the comparison are created separately.

Available Matchers

Group Matchers
Equality to_be, to_equal, to_be_same_as, to_be_close_to, to_be_within, to_match_object
Truthiness to_be_true, to_be_false, to_be_truthy, to_be_falsy, to_be_nil, to_be_defined
Types to_be_a, to_be_string, to_be_number, to_be_int, to_be_float, to_be_bigint, to_be_bool, to_be_list, to_be_dict, to_be_bytes, to_be_function, to_be_callable, to_be_iterable, to_be_class, to_be_instance, to_be_instance_of
Numbers to_be_greater_than, to_be_greater_than_or_equal, to_be_less_than, to_be_less_than_or_equal, to_be_between, to_be_positive, to_be_negative, to_be_zero, to_be_divisible_by, to_be_even, to_be_odd, to_be_nan, to_be_finite, to_be_infinite
Text to_contain, to_contain_ignoring_case, to_equal_ignoring_case, to_start_with, to_end_with, to_match, to_be_blank
Collections to_have_length, to_be_empty, to_contain_equal, to_contain_all, to_contain_any, to_contain_none, to_contain_exactly, to_have_key, to_have_keys, to_have_value, to_have_property, to_be_sorted, to_have_unique_items
Errors to_raise, to_raise_instance_of, to_raise_with_message, to_not_raise
Mocks to_have_been_called, to_have_been_called_times, to_have_been_called_with, to_have_been_last_called_with, to_have_been_nth_called_with, to_have_returned, to_have_returned_with, to_have_raised
Output to_print, to_print_exactly, to_print_nothing
Snapshots to_match_snapshot
Anything else to_satisfy

Each matcher's doc comment describes exactly how it behaves and what it rejects.

A few of them are worth pointing out.

to_be_close_to is how you compare anything that has gone through floating-point arithmetic. expect(0.1 + 0.2).to_be(0.3) fails, because the sum is 0.30000000000000004.

to_raise and the matchers like it take a function rather than a value, because the framework has to be the one that calls it:

to_have_property follows a dotted path through dictionaries, instances and list indexes alike, which is what a decoded response usually consists of:

to_satisfy is for when nothing else fits:

Failing a Test Explicitly

When the assertions are inside a callback that might never run, state how many assertions you expect:

If the callback ran once instead of twice, the test fails with Expected 2 assertions but 1 ran, instead of passing on a technicality. has_assertions() is a less strict version that requires at least one assertion.

Setup and Teardown

These are the rules:

  • before_all runs once, just before the first test in its suite that's actually going to run. If every test in a suite was filtered out, before_all never runs, so nothing connects to anything.
  • after_all runs after the last test, and only if before_all ran. It also runs if before_all raised an error, because a setup that failed partway through might already have opened a connection or started a server. Write it so that it can cope with however far the setup got.
  • before_each hooks run starting with the outermost suite, and after_each hooks run starting with the innermost, so teardown undoes setup in the reverse order.
  • after_each runs even when the test failed, which is exactly when you need it.

A hook that raises an error is reported as a hook failure for the test it was preparing, instead of stopping the whole run. If a before_all raises an error, every test in its suite fails, because none of them got the setup they depend on.

Focusing, Skipping and To-Do Tests

When you're working on one particular thing:

As soon as anything is marked with only, everything else is skipped, but still listed, so you can't forget that it's turned on.

A to-do is a test without a body, and it('name') with nothing after it means the same thing. It doesn't count towards anything, and appears in the report as a reminder that stays there after you commit it.

Two options change what a failure means:

failing: true makes the test pass when the body fails and fail when the body passes, so on the day someone fixes the bug, the test tells you. retries runs the body again if it fails, and a test that passes on a later attempt is reported as flaky instead of being quietly counted as a pass.

Running a Test With Several Inputs

Each row becomes a separate test, with its own name and its own entry in the report, so one bad row doesn't hide the others. $0, $1 and so on stand for the row's values, and $# for the row number. describe_each does the same for whole suites, which is how you run one set of tests against several implementations of the same interface.

Test Doubles

mock() gives you a function that records how it was called and does whatever you tell it to.

mock() returns a Mock, and mock.fn is the plain function that you pass to the code under test. The matchers accept either one, so expect(operation) and expect(operation.fn) mean the same thing.

Behavior is used in order. Everything you queue with a _once method runs first, one call each, and after that the standing behavior takes over.

Method Effect
returns(v) / returns_once(v) Returns v
raises(e) / raises_once(e) Raises e
implements(fn) / implements_once(fn) Runs fn with the actual arguments
reset() Forgets the recorded calls
clear_behaviour() Forgets the configured behavior

Spying on an Existing Function

spy_on replaces a function in place and gives you a Mock that both records calls and stands in for the original:

A spy calls the original function unless you tell it otherwise, and it's restored automatically after the test that installed it, even if the test failed partway through. You don't need to undo anything yourself.

It works on a dictionary entry, and on an instance property that holds a function. It doesn't work on a class method or a module function, because Zuri classes can't be changed after they're declared, and a module's members can't be assigned from outside the module. If you want to be able to substitute something in tests, have the code take its collaborators as arguments or store them in properties, which is a good design anyway.

Snapshots

For a value that's too large to write out by hand, record it once and compare against the recording from then on:

The first run writes the file and passes:

The file is saved next to the test file, in __snapshots__:

Commit it. Reviewing changes to that file in a pull request is the whole point of snapshot testing, because an unexplained change there is exactly what you want to notice.

When the value changes, you see the difference:

If the new value is correct, update the snapshots:

This also removes entries that are no longer used. In CI, where the CI environment variable is set, writing a new snapshot counts as a failure instead of quietly passing, because a snapshot that nobody has looked at doesn't test anything.

Testing What Something Prints

You can also capture the output and make your own assertions about it:

This works because the runtime can redirect everything Zuri writes to standard output. The same mechanism keeps output from passing tests out of the report. It's captured and only shown when a test fails. run({ verbose: true }) shows it either way, and run({ capture: false }) turns capturing off completely.

Running Several Files

A real project has a whole directory of test files:

zuri test runs all of them:

You don't need to write anything for this. The command finds the tests directory where you ran it, and exits with status 1 if anything failed, so a CI job doesn't need any extra setup either.

Each file runs in a separate process. That's more than an implementation detail, because it gives you several guarantees:

  • A file that loops forever is stopped, and the other files still run. Use --timeout 30s to set how long is too long.
  • A file that crashes, or calls os.exit() partway through, is reported as a file that didn't report back, instead of bringing down the whole run.
  • Global state, modules loaded for their side effects and changes to the working directory never leak from one file to the next.

Files are reported in the order they were found, whatever order they finish in, so --jobs 4 makes a large suite faster without the report jumping around.

A test file doesn't need anything special to run this way. It declares its tests, and you can still run it on its own.

Running a Single File

Give its name, with or without the .zu extension:

All three run tests/pricing.zu. A name is looked for under tests first, so a test keeps its own name even if something else in the project has the same name. If the name isn't found directly in that directory, Zuri looks for a file with that name anywhere under it, so a file in a subdirectory can still be found by its own name.

A directory works too, wherever it is:

Command-Line Flags

Flag What it does
-j, --jobs <count> The number of files to run at once. auto runs one per CPU. The default is 1.
-t, --timeout <duration> How long a single file can run before it's stopped, such as 500ms, 30s, 2m or 1h, or a plain number of milliseconds. By default, there's no limit.
-b, --bail [count] Stops after this many files have failed. Without a count, stops at the first failure.
-m, --match <pattern...> File name patterns to run, instead of *.zu
-i, --ignore <pattern...> File name patterns to skip, instead of _*, .* and index.zu
--no-recursive Only runs the files directly inside the directory
-e, --env <assignment...> Sets extra environment variables for every test process, written as KEY=VALUE
-l, --list Prints the files that would run, one per line, and stops

--bail and the two pattern flags take every word that follows them, so put the file name before them, or end the list with --:

For the same reason, a count for --bail has to be attached, as in --bail=3, because a count written as a separate word can't be told apart from a file name.

Running a Suite Yourself

conduct() is the function that zuri test is built on, and a project that wants to control the run itself can call it directly. When you pass a directory to zuri run, it runs that directory's index.zu, so a single file lets you run the suite with zuri run tests:

It accepts the same settings as the command-line flags, as a dictionary, and returns the run's results instead of only reporting them. conduct leaves index.zu out when it looks for test files, and never runs the script that called it, so the index can't end up running itself.

Controlling a Run

Call run() yourself when you want to change how the run behaves, or to read the results. It takes a dictionary of options, and calling it replaces the automatic run, so nothing runs twice.

These are the options you're most likely to use:

Option What it does
filter Only runs tests whose full name contains this text, or matches it as a regular expression
bail Stops after this many failures
shuffle / seed Runs the tests in random order, and lets you reproduce that order later
reporter One of spec, dot, tap, junit, json, ndjson or silent
exit Exits the process with the run's status when it finishes

You can also set filter and reporter with ZURI_TEST_FILTER and ZURI_TEST_REPORTER, which lets you point the same command at a single test without editing the file.

Shuffling is worth turning on deliberately. Tests that only pass because an earlier test left something behind are a real and common problem, and running them in a different order every time is how you find them:

The seed is printed along with the summary, and passing it back reproduces exactly the same order.

Running Tests in CI

You don't need to add anything. A test file exits with 0 when everything passed and 1 when something didn't, whether or not it called run().

If your CI system needs a machine-readable report, { reporter: 'junit' } writes JUnit XML to standard output, and { reporter: 'tap' } writes TAP version 14.

Writing Your Own Reporter

The runner doesn't know anything about output. It walks the tree of tests and calls methods on a reporter, and every method has a default that does nothing:

The objects passed to the reporter are the same ones the built-in reporters receive: Case, Suite, Failure and Summary, which are documented in test.result.

Two Things to Keep in Mind

A test's timeout is checked after the body returns. Zuri runs synchronously, so a test runs to completion and then its time is checked. That catches a test that has become too slow, but it can't stop one that hangs. Handling a hang needs a process boundary, which is exactly what conduct puts around each file, and why its timeout is the one that's enforced.

All the tests in a file share the same interpreter. Reset whatever you change in before_each, and use shuffle to find out whether you've missed anything.

Further Reading

The module's own documentation includes the full list of matchers, with the edge cases of each one, every option that run() and conduct() accept, and the format of snapshot files. Appendix F lists the submodules, and Chapter 24 explains what to do once a test has told you something is wrong.

Chapter 24 · Going Deeper

Debugging

Something isn't doing what you expected. This chapter is about tracking down why: reading what the runtime tells you, recognizing the few messages that cause most of the confusion, and the techniques that turn a vague "it's broken" into a line number.

Reading an Error Message

An uncaught error prints three things: what went wrong, where it went wrong, and how the program got there.

The error type and message come first, then the source code around the failure, with the line that failed marked, and finally the call stack, starting with the innermost call.

A deep stack is shortened in the middle, because the top and the bottom are the useful parts. The top shows where the error happened, the bottom shows where your program started, and two hundred identical recursive calls in between don't tell you anything.

The process exits with status 1.

Common Error Messages

Every message below is real output. If you run this, you'll see all of them:

Here's what each one usually means in practice:

Message What to look for
undefined global 'x' A typo, or a def that's declared below the top-level line that calls it
undefined key 'x' in dict A key that really isn't there. If it's allowed to be missing, use get(key, fallback).
undefined field 'x' on instance of 'C' A typo in a field name. Classes are sealed, so this can't create a new field.
undefined property 'x' on instance of 'C' Reading a field or method that the class never declared
undefined member 'x' on module m The module doesn't export it, or the import needs an @ to re-export it
object of type nil does not define method 'f' Something earlier in the code returned nil
operator '+' not defined for call signature (nil, number) The same problem, one step earlier
'x' is private and can only be accessed via 'self' or 'parent' A name with a leading underscore, used from outside the class
'x' is already declared in this scope Two var declarations with the same name in the same block
cannot assign to constant 'x' Assigning to a local const
module 'x' could not be found Usually a missing leading . on an import of a sibling module

The two messages about nil are worth remembering. Zuri can't tell you where a nil came from, because by the time it causes a problem, the value has already been passed along. When you see one, don't look at the line that failed. Look at whatever produced the value.

Debugging Techniques

Print the Value and Its Type

In a dynamically typed language, the surprise is almost always that a value isn't what you assumed:

A single typeof() would have cleared up the confusion on the third line.

Give Your Classes @to_string()

echo displays an instance using its class's @to_string() method, or as <instance of Point> if the class doesn't have one:

Define @to_string() on any class you expect to look at while debugging. It only takes a few minutes, and it pays off the first time you print a list of instances.

Encode Nested Data Instead of Printing It

A deeply nested dictionary printed with echo is a single unreadable line. json.encode() with compact turned off indents it for you:

Add Context to Errors

An error raised deep in a chain of calls says what failed, but not what the program was doing at the time. Catch it, add what you were doing, and raise it again:

"Not a number" is a fact. "While reading config.json: not a number" is a fact you can do something about.

Print the Stack Trace Yourself

The stack trace is a list on the error object, so a handler can log it without letting the program crash:

Check How the Compiler Read Your Code

When an expression doesn't behave the way you read it, the bytecode will tell you how the compiler read it:

Look at the order: the power is calculated before the negation. ** binds more tightly than unary minus, so -2 ** 2 means -(2 ** 2), which is -4, not the 4 you'd get from (-2) ** 2. One line of bytecode answers the question. Chapter 21 covers zuri.compile() and zuri.parse() in detail.

Narrow Down the Problem With assert

An assert states something you believe is true, and you can leave it in the code:

Without it, average([]) would have returned NaN, and the problem would have shown up somewhere else entirely, as a value that looks like a number.

Watch the Garbage Collector

ZURI_GC_LOG=1 reports what the garbage collector is doing. Use it when the problem is memory rather than logic:

Chapter 22 lists the runtime's other diagnostic settings, along with what each one measures.

Common Pitfalls

These behaviors produce a wrong result rather than an error, which makes them much harder to track down.

Zero is falsy. var n = count or 10 turns a real 0 into 10, and if index is false for the first position but true for -1, which means "not found". Compare values explicitly.

to_number() returns 0 for text it can't parse. 'eighty', '' and '12abc' all become 0, and so does ' 7 ' with its spaces. There's no NaN and no error to catch, so invalid input silently becomes a valid zero. Validate the text before you convert it.

[] and {} are truthy. if items is true for an empty list. Use is_empty() instead.

sort() changes the list, but reverse() doesn't. var s = items.sort() sorts items as well. If you need both orders, clone the list first.

The result of a string method was thrown away. name.trim() on its own does nothing. Strings are immutable, so you have to assign the result.

A nested def is local. A function declared inside another function is scoped to it, like a var, and nothing outside that scope can call it.

x++ evaluates to the new value, unlike in C and JavaScript.

Writing Code That's Easier to Debug

Three habits pay off the first time something breaks.

Keep decisions separate from side effects. A function that reads a file, parses it and makes a decision based on it is really three functions. Split them up, and you can test the parsing and the decision without needing a file system.

Pass dependencies in. A function that calls time() behaves differently every second, while a function that takes a timestamp as an argument behaves exactly the same every time you call it with the same number. That means you can reproduce a failure instead of waiting for it to happen again.

Return values instead of printing them. An echo inside a function is invisible to the code that called it, and useless to anything that wants to check the result. Return the string, and let the caller decide what to do with it.

Chapter 25 · The Capstone

A Full-Stack Task Board

In this chapter, we'll build a real web application: a shared task board with three columns, a browser interface and a JSON API over the same data.

It's about four hundred lines of Zuri, and it uses almost everything this book has covered: classes and inheritance for the domain model, custom errors for validation, the module system for structure, files and JSON for storage, the HTTP server for routing, middleware and static files, Wire for HTML rendered on the server, os for configuration and signals, and log for output.

There are no dependencies and nothing to install. Run zuri run taskboard and it starts.

What the Application Does

  • It has three columns: todo, doing and done.
  • A page at / shows the board, with forms for adding, moving and deleting tasks.
  • A JSON API under /api does the same things, for clients other than browsers.
  • A board.json file stores the state, and is written atomically.
  • A single error handler turns domain errors into the right status code, for both the HTML pages and the JSON API.

How This Chapter Is Organized

Each section builds one layer, starting from the inside:

  1. Laying Out the Project: the directory structure, and the reasons for it.
  2. The Storage Layer: the JSON file, and the board built on top of it.
  3. Validation and the Domain Model: the Task class, which owns every rule about what a task is.
  4. The JSON API: six routes for working with the board.
  5. Server-Rendered Pages with Wire: the templates, the forms and the redirect-after-post pattern.
  6. Middleware, Logging and Errors: the two pieces of shared behavior that every request goes through.
  7. Running It for Real: configuration, signals, and what changes when you want to use more than one core.
  8. Testing the Board: a test suite covering all three layers, and what the layered design makes possible.

Read the sections in order, because each one builds on the one before it.

25.1 · The Capstone

Laying Out the Project

Four design decisions are worth explaining, because they're what keep the rest of the code short.

First, here's the overall structure. Every dependency in this application points in the same direction:

routes depends on storage, storage depends on models, and models depends only on config. Nothing depends on anything in the other direction, which means you can read each layer on its own, and test it without the layers above it. Testing the Board is where that second benefit pays off.

config.zu is outside that chain. Every module can use it, and it doesn't use anything itself. It's the only module that can be used from anywhere, and that's acceptable because it contains no behavior at all.

One Package for Each Responsibility

models, storage and routes are packages, which means they're directories with an index.zu. The index.zu decides what's public:

That one line re-exports everything task.zu declares, so the rest of the application can write import .models { Task } without needing to know that task.zu exists. If you later split task.zu into two files, you only need to change that one line.

The @ is what makes it a re-export rather than a private import. Without it, models/index.zu could use Task itself, but nothing outside could get to it through models. The import would be local, and import .models { Task } elsewhere would fail. Re-exporting Imports covers this distinction, and this is the place where people most often get it wrong.

So the index.zu is an intentional list of what a package offers, which you can edit, rather than an accident of which files happen to exist.

The Underscore Matters

storage/_json_store.zu starts with an underscore, so no module outside storage can import it, and the compiler enforces that:

The point isn't to keep anything secret. It's that if you replace the JSON file with a database, you only have to rewrite one file, and the compiler guarantees that nothing else went around the Board to use it directly. It's not that you checked and nothing does. Nothing can, because any attempt fails to compile.

That guarantee is what turns a convention into a real boundary. A comment saying "internal, don't use" is only a suggestion, but a leading underscore is enforced.

app.zu and index.zu Are Separate Files

app.zu builds a fully configured server and returns it. index.zu starts it:

There are three things going on in that short file.

if __root__ == __file__ does most of the work. zuri run taskboard runs the directory, which runs index.zu, and the two values are equal, so the body runs and the server starts. If another program uses import .taskboard, the two values are different, because __root__ is that program's entry file. So nothing starts, and the other program can use app.build() however it likes. One file handles both cases, and Chapter 8 explains this pattern.

The signal handler is installed before the server starts. listen() doesn't return, so anything that needs to happen when the program stops has to be set up beforehand. os.on_signal('INT', ...) is what makes Ctrl+C shut the program down cleanly, instead of killing the process.

The log message comes before listen(), so the address is printed as soon as the process is ready, not after it stops. It's only one line, but it means you know the server started instead of having to guess.

Notice what index.zu doesn't do. It doesn't build or configure anything, and it doesn't know anything about boards, templates or routes. All of those decisions are in app.zu, which is why Middleware, Logging and Errors can go through a single function and cover how the whole application is put together.

Configuration With Defaults

There are four things to notice.

Every environment variable has a fallback, so the application runs without any configuration at all. You can run git clone and then zuri run taskboard, and it works. Nobody tries a program that needs six environment variables before it will start.

PORT is converted with to_number(). Environment variables are always strings, and a socket won't accept '8000' as a port. The conversion happens here, once, instead of wherever the port is used.

HERE is based on __file__, not os.cwd(). The templates and the stylesheet are stored next to the source code, so whoever runs the program doesn't need to be in the right directory. This is the rule from Chapter 9, and ignoring it causes the most trouble in a web application, where the program starts and serves a page, but only fails to find a template when someone requests it.

COLUMNS is defined here because it's the one piece of information that the model, the storage layer and the templates all share. _clean_column() validates against it, Board.columns() and Board.summary() loop over it, and the template renders one section for each entry. Adding a fourth column takes a one-line change in this file, and everything else follows.

That's how to decide whether something belongs in config.zu. Don't ask "is it a setting?" Ask "would changing it otherwise mean editing several files in the same way?"

25.2 · The Capstone

The Storage Layer

The storage layer consists of two files. One knows about the disk but nothing about tasks, and the other knows about tasks but nothing about the disk.

The JSON File

These fifty lines make four decisions.

A missing file isn't an error. On the first run, nothing has been saved yet, and the program should still start. A file that exists but can't be parsed is an error, because otherwise its contents would be overwritten with an empty board.

The error message includes the path. Whoever reads it is looking at a single line in a log.

The write is atomic. The data is written to a temporary file, which is then renamed into place. If the process is killed partway through a write, the previous board is left intact, because a rename within a directory either happens completely or not at all.

The file handle is opened explicitly. write() on a closed handle opens the file, writes to it and closes it again, so two write() calls in w mode would each truncate the file. Call open() first, then write, and then call close(). This is the rule from Chapter 9, and this is exactly the kind of code where it matters.

The Board

storage/index.zu is the layer above. It holds Task objects, answers questions about them and saves them using _json_store, and it's the only part of the application that knows a file is involved at all.

Instead of reading it as a hundred lines all at once, let's go through it one piece at a time.

The Error It Raises

This is a custom error class, and it's only four lines long, but it's worth it. Every layer above can check instance_of(error, NotFoundError) instead of matching against a message string, and the middleware in Middleware, Logging and Errors turns exactly this class into a 404 response. If get() raised a plain Error('not found'), that check would have to search the message text.

Notice the two lines inside @new. parent(message) lets the base constructor set message and record the stack trace, and self.type makes the class name appear in logs and in the message for an uncaught error. Both follow the pattern from Chapter 7.

Fields and Constructor

There are two fields, both declared with var, even though @new assigns both of them. The constructor could have declared them itself, but writing them out means you can see the shape of the class at the top without reading the constructor, and it becomes necessary as soon as any other method assigns to them.

The constructor does two things. It works out where the file is, and it loads what's in it.

directory or config.DATA_DIR is the pattern for optional parameters from Chapter 5. It's safe here because a directory can never sensibly be '' or 0, so the problem with falsy defaults doesn't apply to paths.

The map on the second line is the boundary between two worlds. read_all() returns plain dictionaries, because that's what JSON contains, and from_dict() turns each one into a real Task. Everything above this line works with objects, and everything below it works with dictionaries, and this is the only place where the two meet.

Reading From the Board

all() is a single line, and it returns the actual list instead of a copy. That's intentional, because every caller in this application only reads the list. If that ever changed, this is the line that would need a clone().

in_column() is just a call to filter(). It's a method rather than a loop in each place it's used, so that the question of which column a task is in is answered in one place.

Preparing Data for the Page

This is the method the HTML template uses, and it makes three decisions worth pointing out.

It loops over config.COLUMNS, not over the tasks. That means a column without any tasks still appears, as an empty column, which is how a board should look. Grouping by looping over the tasks would silently leave out empty columns, and would produce the columns in whatever order the data happened to be in.

It returns the results of to_view(), not Task objects. A view already contains the formatted date and the is_done flag, so the template doesn't have to calculate them. Server-Rendered Pages explains why that's particularly important for templates.

{ name, tasks } uses the shorthand syntax. Both keys have the same names as the variables that hold their values, so writing { name: name, tasks: tasks } would just add noise.

Finding a Single Task

The important decision here is that get() raises an error instead of returning nil.

That choice affects everything that calls it. Every caller either has a real task or gets an error, so none of the route handlers need an if task == nil check. If get() returned nil, that check would have to appear in five places, and sooner or later one of them would be forgotten, causing an error when a field is read from nil somewhere far away from the real cause.

The message includes the ID, because whoever reads the log only has the request to go on.

Changing the Board

All three methods follow the same pattern: change the list in memory, save it, and return what changed.

update() and remove() both start by calling get(), so an invalid ID raises a NotFoundError before anything is changed. There's no way for a change to be only half applied.

Each method returns the task it affected instead of returning nothing, which lets the JSON API respond with the created or updated record without looking it up again.

Using remove_at(index_of(task)) instead of remove(task) is intentional. The list's remove() compares by value, so two tasks with identical fields would make it ambiguous. Removing by position removes exactly the object that get() found.

Counting and Saving

summary() loops over the configured columns for the same reason columns() does: an empty column should be reported as 0, not left out.

_save() is the counterpart to the map in the constructor. Objects are written out as dictionaries using to_dict(), just as they were read in using from_dict(). The two methods go together, so if you add a field to Task, it has to appear in both, or it won't survive a restart.

_save() is private, and that's the most important property of this class. There's no public method that changes the board without saving it, because add, update and remove all call _save(), and nothing else can. A caller can't forget to save, because a caller never gets the choice.

The Trade-Off

The whole board is kept in memory and completely rewritten after every change.

For a board small enough for a team to read on one screen, that's the right trade-off. The code is simple enough to keep in your head, and rewriting a few kilobytes doesn't matter. But it's also the first assumption to revisit if the board ever needs to hold a hundred thousand tasks, and at that point, the answer is a real database, not a cleverer file format.

Concurrency

Board keeps the whole file in memory. If two processes wrote to the same board.json, each would overwrite the other's changes, and the atomic rename doesn't fix that. It guarantees that the file is never half written, but not that two writers agree.

This application only runs one server process, so the problem doesn't come up. Running It for Real is where it does.

25.3 · The Capstone

Validation and the Domain Model

Every rule about what a task is lives in a single class. Nothing above it checks a title again, and nothing below it stores a task that breaks a rule.

TaskError has a field as well as a message. That one extra value is what lets the API respond with {"error": "...", "field": "title"}, which in turn lets a form highlight the input that's wrong. Being able to carry more than a string is exactly why you'd write a custom error class.

The Class

Every field is declared with var and documented, even the ones the constructor sets. Classes are sealed, so this list is everything a task holds, and writing it out means the next person reading the code can see that without reading the constructor.

The constructor takes a required title, and an options dictionary for everything else. That's a pattern worth copying: a positional argument for the value that's always there, and named options for the rest, so you never see a call like Task('x', nil, nil, 'todo', nil).

It uses uuid.v7() instead of v4(), because version 7 includes a timestamp, so IDs sort by age. When an identifier is going to be used as a key in something ordered, you get that for free.

Changing a Task

update() uses contains() instead of checking for truthiness. That's the difference between a partial update that works and one that doesn't. A PATCH body of {"notes": ""} means "clear the notes", and if changes.notes would read it as "no change".

Both methods return self, so board.get(id).move_to('done') reads as a single action.

Converting a Task

There are two representations, and that's intentional. to_dict() is what gets stored, and it contains exactly what from_dict() needs to rebuild the task. to_view() is what gets displayed, and it adds values that are calculated rather than stored, such as a formatted date and a boolean that the template can check.

Keeping them separate means that changing how a task is displayed never changes the file format.

@to_json() lets you pass a Task straight to response.json(), and @to_string() makes echo show something useful when you look at a task while debugging.

Loading a Task From Storage

These four lines have one important property: they use the same constructor as everything else.

It would have been shorter to assign the fields directly. But because the constructor is used, a hand-edited board.json that contains an unknown column, or a task without a title, is rejected when the board loads, instead of becoming a task that nothing can display or fix.

The code uses data.get(key, nil) instead of data.key throughout, because a record saved by an older version of the program might not have every key. get() with a fallback turns a missing key into nil, which the constructor's defaults then handle, while data.column would raise an undefined key error.

It's also the exact opposite of to_dict(). The two methods go together, so a field added to Task has to appear in both, or it won't survive a restart. That's the kind of bug that only shows up the second time you run the program.

Where the Rules Are Defined

Look at the order of those three checks, because the order is the whole point of the function.

The type check comes first. A PATCH body of {"title": 42} reaches this function as a number, and 42.trim() would raise a TypeError about methods instead of a TaskError about titles. Checking the type first means the caller gets an error in the application's own terms.

The value is trimmed before checking whether it's empty, so ' ' is rejected. A title made of three spaces isn't a title, and calling title.is_empty() on the raw input would have accepted it.

The length is checked after trimming, so trailing whitespace doesn't count toward the limit.

And the function returns the cleaned-up value. It isn't a validator that answers yes or no. It either returns a valid, normalized value or raises an error. That's why the constructor can simply write self.title = _clean_title(title).

The message says what was wrong and what would have been right. unknown column "backlog", expected one of todo, doing, done tells the caller how to fix the problem, while invalid column doesn't.

Notice that the set of valid columns comes from config.COLUMNS instead of being written out here. Adding a column to the board is a one-line change in one file, and this check, columns() and summary() all follow it.

Each Helper Is Called From Two Places

Both helpers are private to the module, because of their leading underscore, so no other file can use them. Each one is called from exactly two places: the constructor and update().

That's the property this whole chapter is built on. There's no way to create or change a Task without going through them. from_dict() uses the constructor, move_to() calls _clean_column() itself, and a route handler can't use the private functions at all.

That means every layer above can assume that any Task it has is valid, which is why none of the route handlers in The JSON API check a title again.

Why Not Use the validate Module?

Zuri has a schema validator, and for a form with fifteen fields, it's exactly the right tool:

Here, though, the rules are three lines of Zuri that also normalize the value (with trim()), produce a domain error that includes a field, and live right next to the data they apply to. A schema would just be one more place to look.

Use validate when the problem is the shape of the input. Use methods on the class when the rules are part of what the object is.

25.4 · The Capstone

The JSON API

The API has six routes. Each one reads from or writes to the board and returns JSON, and none of them handle errors.

The Routes

The Structure of the File

register(server, board) takes the server and the board as arguments instead of importing them. That's what lets the same routes work with a different board, such as a temporary one in a test or one filled with sample data for a demo, and it keeps any decision about where the data is stored out of this file.

Listing Tasks, With an Optional Filter

A single route answers two questions: what are all the tasks, and what are all the tasks in a particular column?

query_param('column', nil) provides the fallback, and the check is column == nil instead of if column. That distinction matters, because a query string of ?column= produces an empty string, which is falsy but present, and an empty column name should be rejected by in_column(), not silently treated as "no filter".

The response includes summary alongside tasks, because a client that displays a board needs both, and making it ask separately would mean two requests for one screen.

Fetching a Single Task

This is a single line, and it can fail. board.get() raises a NotFoundError for an unknown ID, and this handler does nothing about it, for reasons explained in the section below.

Creating a Task

request.json_body() returns nil for a request with no body, or with a body that isn't JSON. or {} turns that into an empty dictionary, so body.get('title', nil) works either way, and a missing title becomes the model's problem, which is where the message about it already lives.

The 201 is the second argument to response.json(). A newly created resource shouldn't get a 200, and getting it right only takes one argument.

The handler returns task.to_view() rather than task, for the reason explained below.

Updating and Deleting Tasks

The PATCH handler passes the decoded body straight to board.update() without filtering it. That's safe, because update() only looks at the three keys it knows about, title, notes and column, using contains(). So a body containing {"id": "hacked"} doesn't change anything. The list of allowed keys is kept in the model, once, instead of in every route that accepts a body.

DELETE returns a body instead of an empty 204, so that a client that parses every response as JSON doesn't need a special case for one route.

Why the Handlers Don't Handle Errors

This is the main point of this section, and it's easiest to see if you count: there are six handlers, and not one catch block.

board.get() raises a NotFoundError for an unknown ID. board.add() and board.update() raise a TaskError for an invalid title or an unknown column. None of the handlers catch either error, and that's why each one is only one to five lines long.

The middleware in the next section catches both errors and turns them into a 404 and a 422. Only one place in this application knows which domain error corresponds to which status code, and it isn't a route.

Think about the alternative for a moment. Six handlers would each wrap their call to the board in a catch, choose a status code and format an error response. That's thirty or so lines of duplicated code, and a seventh route added next month would probably get one of those details slightly wrong.

Notice also the two imports at the top of the file. TaskError and NotFoundError are imported but never used again in this file. They're there because the module that catches them needs them to be re-exported through routes. That's the module system doing its job, and Chapter 8 explains why the @ matters there.

Using to_view() for Responses

Every response sends the result of to_view(), never the Task itself.

That one habit means the structure of the API is decided by Task, in a single method, instead of depending on however the object happens to be laid out internally. If you add a private field to Task tomorrow, the API still returns exactly what it returned yesterday.

It's also why the responses include created_on and is_done, which aren't stored anywhere. to_view() calculates them, so every client gets a formatted date and a boolean without having to work them out.

Trying the API

The last two requests are the interesting ones. You get a 422 with a field, and a 404 with a message, from handlers that never mention status codes at all.

25.5 · The Capstone

Server-Rendered Pages with Wire

The browser side of the application consists of two templates and four routes. Wire has its own chapter with the full reference, and this section uses the parts a real page needs.

The Layout

This is a valid HTML5 document. If you open it in a browser, you get a page with a heading and a paragraph. That's the whole idea behind Wire's design: the directives are attributes, so the template still looks like the page it renders.

x-slot="content" declares a region that an extending template can replace. The content inside it is the default, which is used when nothing replaces it.

The Page

Six directives make up the whole page.

x-for with x-value repeats an element once for each item and gives each item a name. The x-for="column.tasks" nested inside x-for="columns" is an ordinary nested loop, and the inner loop can still see columns from the outer one, which is how the dropdown for moving a task lists every column.

x-text replaces an element's children with escaped text, so nothing in a task's title can turn into markup.

x-attr takes a dictionary and adds its entries to the element as attributes, which is how a form's action is built from a task's ID.

x-if and x-not render an element only under a condition. x-not="column.tasks" shows the "Nothing here." line when the list is empty, because an empty list is falsy in Wire. That's not Zuri's rule, since [] is truthy in Zuri, but Wire uses its own rule, which is more convenient for templates.

{{ column.tasks|length }} is an interpolation with a filter. length is one of Wire's built-in filters, and it works on strings, lists, dictionaries and bytes.

The Routes

routes/pages.zu registers four routes: one that renders the board, and three that handle its forms. Let's go through it one piece at a time.

The Structure of the File

The whole file is a single register() function that takes its dependencies as arguments. Nothing here uses a global board or a global template engine, which is what makes the routes testable. Pass register() a board that uses a temporary directory, and the same code runs against it.

This is the "pass dependencies in" habit from Debugging, applied to the layer where it costs nothing and helps the most.

Rendering the Board

This route makes one call and contains no logic. Everything it passes to the template is either a constant or the result of a method call on the board. There's no loop, no formatting and no branching in this handler, because all of that has already been done somewhere better suited to it.

board.columns() does the grouping and _tagline() does the counting, while to_view(), in the domain model, has already formatted the dates. By the time the template runs, every value it needs is ready.

request.query_param('error', nil) is the other half of the redirect pattern described below. When a form fails, it redirects with ?error=..., and this is where the message comes back to be displayed.

Handling a Form

All three form handlers follow exactly this structure, so it's worth reading carefully once.

request.form() parses a URL-encoded body into a dictionary. The code uses form.get('title', nil) instead of form.title, because a browser can send a body with any fields at all, or none, and form.title would raise an undefined key error for a request that simply left it out. With get(), a missing field becomes nil, and _clean_title() turns that into a proper TaskError.

The catch wraps only the call to the board. response.redirect('/'), on the success path, is outside it, so a mistake in the redirect isn't reported as a validation failure. That's the "keep the catch block small" rule from Chapter 7.

The return inside the handler stops execution from continuing to the redirect on the success path. Without it, a failed add would send two redirects.

The Other Two Form Handlers

:id in the path is a route parameter, which request.param('id') reads.

Notice what these handlers don't do. Neither one checks that the ID belongs to a real task, because board.get() raises a NotFoundError and the catch handles it. Neither one validates the column, because _clean_column() does that. And neither one checks that the task exists before deleting it, because remove() calls get() first.

That's the benefit of putting the rules in the domain model. Each route handler is only four lines long, because there's nothing else left for it to do.

The Two Helper Functions

_tagline() turns the board's counts into the line shown under the heading. It's defined here rather than in Board because it's a presentation decision. A different front end would word it differently, and the board shouldn't care.

_escape() is more careful than it looks. The message is about to be put into a URL, so it removes everything except letters, digits, spaces and basic punctuation, and then replaces spaces with +.

There are two details in that one line. The first replace() uses a regular expression, and the second passes false as its third argument to turn pattern matching off, so the single space is matched literally instead of as a pattern. And removing characters instead of percent-encoding them is a deliberate choice. This is a message the program generated, not user input being sent back, so a conservative list of allowed characters is simpler than encoding, and it can't produce an invalid URL.

Redirecting After a Post

Every form handler ends with a redirect instead of rendering a page. This is the post/redirect/get pattern. It exists because if a browser displays a page in response to a POST, it submits the POST again when the user refreshes the page. Adding a task twice because someone pressed F5 isn't a bug you want to have to explain.

The failure path redirects too, passing the message as a query parameter, which the next GET displays in the error banner. Either way, the browser ends up on a plain GET /, which is safe to refresh, bookmark or go back to.

Why These Handlers Catch Errors and the API's Handlers Don't

The API handlers in The JSON API let errors propagate, because the middleware turns them into status codes. These handlers catch them, because a browser submitting a form doesn't want a 422 page. It wants the board back, with a message on it.

The same domain errors are presented in two different ways, and the choice is made by the layer that knows what kind of client it's talking to. Neither Board nor Task needs to know that a browser is involved.

The Stylesheet

server.serve_files('/static', config.STATIC_DIR) serves the directory. The static file handler takes care of content types, ETag headers, conditional requests and range requests by itself, so app.css is just a plain file:

The Result

The result is HTML rendered on the server, without any JavaScript, and with every value escaped by the template engine rather than by whoever wrote the template.

25.6 · The Capstone

Middleware, Logging and Errors

Two kinds of behavior apply to every request but don't belong in any handler: logging what happened, and turning a domain error into a status code. Both are implemented as middleware.

That one function puts the whole application together, and the order of its lines is the order of the application.

It creates the board first, because everything else needs it. Passing data_dir through, instead of letting Board find it, means that a test or a second instance can use a different directory without changing config.

auto_reload: true on the template engine reads a template again when its file changes, which is what you want while you're writing one. It's also the first setting to reconsider before you deploy, because it costs a file system check on every render.

port == nil ? config.PORT : port isn't the same as port or config.PORT. The difference matters here. Port 0 is a valid value that means "let the operating system choose a free port", but 0 is falsy, so the or version would silently replace it with the configured port. This is the problem with zero from Chapter 3, in a place where it would really cause trouble.

max_body_size is set explicitly. A server that accepts request bodies of any size can be exhausted by anyone with a single request. 64 KiB is plenty for a form that sends a title and a column.

Middleware is installed before the routes. Middleware runs from the outside in, so anything registered here wraps every route added afterwards, including /health and the static files below.

Routes are registered by passing each module what it needs. api.register(server, board) and pages.register(server, board, view) work the same way: each is a function that receives its dependencies and adds routes to the server. The page routes get the template engine, and the API routes don't, because they never render a template.

/health is defined here instead of in a route module, because it's about the process rather than about tasks. It reports the number of tasks, so that a monitoring check can confirm that the board actually loaded, not just that the server responds.

serve_files() comes last and maps /static to a directory. It's last because more specific routes should be registered before a route that matches a whole prefix.

And build() returns the server without binding a socket. Nothing here starts listening. That separation lets the entry point decide how to run the server, whether as a single process, with a pool of isolates, or in a test harness that never listens at all, and it's what makes the next section possible.

The Middleware

A middleware function takes three arguments: the request, the response and a next function. Calling next() runs everything that comes after the middleware, including the other middleware and finally the route handler itself.

That explains the structure of both functions here. Code before the call to next() runs on the way in, and code after it runs on the way out, once the handler has finished and the response has been filled in. So a middleware function covers two points in time, not just one, and the call in the middle separates them.

How the Logger Works

The time is recorded on the way in, before anything else runs. The log line is written on the way out, because that's the only point at which response.status is known. On the way in, nothing has set it yet.

That's why timing middleware works at all. The same function body runs at both ends of the request, and a local variable keeps its value in between.

How the Error Handler Works

This middleware doesn't do anything before or after next(). All of its work happens in the handler, and it catches every error raised anywhere after it, whether in a route, the board, the model or the store.

The whole application depends on this. A catch around next() catches errors from the routes, because next() is the routes.

Why the Logger Comes First

Middleware runs from the outside in, in the order it was added. So the logger wraps the error handler, which wraps the routes:

If you follow the order from the bottom up on the way out, the reason becomes clear. A request that failed is still logged, and it's logged with the status the error handler chose, rather than whatever the response contained when the error was raised.

If you swapped the two, a failed request would be logged before the error handler had set its status, or it wouldn't be logged at all if the error went past the logger first.

The Built-in Logger

http.middleware.logger() is a ready-made request logger, and in a real application, it's what you'd use:

It writes the Common Log Format with the response time added, which every log analysis tool already understands. It accepts a sink to send lines somewhere other than standard output, a format to build each line yourself, and trust_proxy to log the forwarded client address instead of the address of the connection.

The nine lines above are written out here because you learn more from a middleware you've read in full than from one you've only called. Once you understand what next() does, switch to the built-in one.

A Single Place for Status Codes

This is what you gain from defining NotFoundError and TaskError as real classes, instead of raising Error('not found') everywhere. instance_of() maps each domain error to a status code, in one place.

There are three details that matter.

Unknown errors become a 500 with a generic message, and the real message goes to the log. An error message can contain a path, a query or part of a file. It belongs where the people running the service can read it, not where users can.

The format of the response depends on the client. A request under /api, or one whose Accept header asks for JSON, gets a JSON response, and everything else gets HTML. request.wants_json() checks the header for you.

A response that a handler has already sent isn't overwritten, because the error handler only runs when next() raised an error.

The Output

log adds the time, the level and the module name to every line, and uses colors when the output is a terminal. The module name is based on where the call was made, so a message from routes/api.zu shows that without you having to say so.

The 409ms on the first GET / is the time Wire took to compile the two templates. Every later render uses the cached instruction tree, which is why the later lines show 1 to 3ms.

Other Useful Middleware

http.middleware has ready-made middleware for what every application eventually needs, such as CORS, compression, rate limiting and authentication. Each one is a function you pass to server.use(), at the position in the chain where you want it.

25.7 · The Capstone

Running It for Real

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000, and the board is there. Add a task, move it and delete it. Stop the server with Ctrl+C and start it again, and everything is still there.

The Entry Point

import @.app re-exports app, so another program can write import .taskboard { app } and build its own server. Because of the __root__ == __file__ check, importing this package doesn't start anything.

os.on_signal('INT', ...) handles Ctrl+C. This application saves after every change, so there's nothing left to write when it stops, but the handler is here because once the hook exists, it's the obvious place to finish whatever the program was doing.

Configuration

Every setting comes from the environment, and has a default:

Running it without any environment variables also works, which makes the first run easy.

Trying It Out

The HTML form and the JSON API work with the same board, through the same validation, and each reports failures in the form its own client understands.

What Gets Stored

The file is easy to read, edit and search. If you type an invalid column into it by hand, it's rejected the next time the board loads, because from_dict() uses the same constructor as everything else.

Running on a Single Process

server.listen() serves connections on a single isolate. For a team's task board, that's more than enough. The slowest part of any request is Wire compiling the templates for the first time, and every request after that takes a few milliseconds.

Zuri can serve requests on several cores, using http.serve(). It takes a setup function, calls it once inside each worker with that worker's own server, and runs the pool:

Doing that here would change one important thing: each isolate has its own heap, so each worker would have its own Board, its own copy of every task, and its own idea of what board.json should contain. If two workers saved at the same time, each would write a complete file, and one of them would win.

The board would have to stop being kept in memory. These are the usual options:

  • A database. Replace _json_store.zu with a real store that supports transactions. Nothing above it needs to change, which is why it's a single private file.
  • A single owner. Keep the board in one isolate, and have the workers send it messages over a channel. Every change becomes a message, and that one isolate processes them one at a time.
  • A lock. Protect the file with an advisory lock, and read it again before every write. This is the easiest to add, but every request then has to pay the cost of reading the file.

Which one is right depends on how many people use the board, and none of them is worth doing until the board can't keep up. The design already makes room for each of them, and that's the part worth getting right early.

What the Application Used

Almost everything.

Chapter What the application uses it for
3, 4 Every line
5 Anonymous handlers, closures over board, typed parameters
6 Task, Board, custom errors, @to_json, to_string
7 TaskError, NotFoundError, and a catch where forms are handled
8 Packages, index.zu, re-exporting with @, privacy with _, __file__
9 file(), atomic renames, os.join_paths, os.get_env
13 json, uuid, date, log
14 Wire: layouts, slots, loops, filters and escaping
15 The HTTP server, routing, middleware and static files
23 The test suite in Testing the Board
24 The request log, and error responses that make it easy to read

What it didn't use is just as telling. It doesn't use isolates, because one process is enough. It doesn't use validate, because the rules belong in the model. And it doesn't use binary data, compression or reflection. All of those are available, but using them here would have made the application longer without making it better.

Next Steps

These are the natural next steps, roughly in order of how much they teach you:

Authentication. Use bcrypt to hash passwords, a signed cookie for the session, and a middleware that rejects any request that isn't authenticated. There's already a place in the middleware chain for it.

Live updates. Use http.sse to send an event to the browser whenever the board changes, so that two people looking at the board see each other's changes.

A board for each user. Store one board.json per user, cache Board objects by user ID, and make path a parameter instead of a default.

A database. Replace _json_store.zu, without changing anything else, and see how much the underscore helps.

Search and filtering. Use filter() on the board, exposed through query parameters, with the same code serving both the HTML page and the API.

Each of these is a change to a single layer. That's what the layout was designed for, and Testing the Board shows how to make any of these changes with confidence.

25.8 · The Capstone

Testing the Board

The application works. This section is about keeping it working, and it's the final benefit of the layered design from Laying Out the Project.

Here's the structure again:
