That's also the order to test the layers in. models only depends on config, so its tests don't need anything. storage depends on models and a file, so its tests need a directory. routes depends on storage and a server, and takes both as arguments, so its tests need neither a socket nor a real board.

Each layer is tested against the real layer below it, and without the layer above it at all.

Where the Tests Go

That's all there is to it. You run the application with zuri run taskboard and its tests with zuri test, and you don't need to remember any file names. The command exits with status 1 if anything fails, which is all a CI system needs.

Each test file is an ordinary script that declares its tests and stops. Each one runs in its own process, which matters here for a specific reason: each of these files creates a Board, and a Board is a file on disk. Because each file runs in its own process, nothing one file leaves behind can affect another.

Testing the Model

models/task.zu doesn't depend on anything outside itself. There's no file, no network, and no clock that matters. Its tests are the fastest, and they're the ones to write first, because every rule about what a task is lives in this file, and nothing above it checks any of them again.

Four of these are worth a closer look.

expect(@{ task.update(...) }).to_raise_instance_of(TaskError), followed by expect(task.column).to_be('todo'). There are two assertions because there are two claims: that the update was rejected, and that it was rejected before anything was changed. A validator that raises its error after assigning the value is a bug you'll only find by checking the second claim.

to_equal, not to_be, for the round trip. from_dict() creates a new Task, so the identities will never match. What matters is whether the contents survived.

expect([first.id, second.id]).to_be_sorted() is the simplest way to check the reason uuid.v7() was chosen. If someone ever changes that line to v4(), this test will tell them.

The record without a column and notes. This is the case of a record saved by an older version of the program, which is why data.get(key, nil) is used. The test stops the next person from simplifying get() to .column and only finding out it was a mistake when it breaks someone's real board.json.

Testing the Storage Layer

A Board is a file, so its tests need a directory of their own. Each test gets one, created and removed by the hooks:

The most valuable test here is survives a restart. It creates a second Board using the same directory, and asks it for the task the first one created. It's the only test that uses _json_store, to_dict() and from_dict() together, and it's the test that fails when someone adds a field to Task and forgets to update one of the two methods.

after_each removes the directory whether or not the test passed, so a failed test doesn't leave anything behind for the next one to trip over. That's an important property, because teardown that only runs when a test succeeds isn't teardown you can rely on.

Notice that none of these tests read board.json directly. They ask the Board what it contains. The file format is the storage layer's concern, and a test that parsed the file would fail whenever the format changed, for reasons that have nothing to do with what the test was checking.

Testing the Routes

register(server, board) takes its two collaborators as arguments. The JSON API explained that this lets you run the routes with a board filled with sample data. Here's the other benefit.

A handler needs three things: something to register routes on, a request and a response. You can provide stand-ins for all three:

With three small classes, the routes become ordinary functions:

There are several things to say about this.

The board is real. Only the HTTP machinery is fake. A fake board would mean writing down what board.add() returns, and the test would keep passing from then on, whatever board.add() actually did. Fakes are for things that are slow, remote or awkward to set up, and a temporary file is none of those.

lets the model reject a bad body. As described in Why the Handlers Don't Handle Errors, the handler doesn't catch anything, so an invalid title comes out of the handler as a TaskError. The middleware depends on that behavior, and this test checks it directly instead of through the middleware.

ignores a key the model does not own tests the list of allowed keys in update(), at exactly the point an attacker would target. It's one line of test code for a property the code gets for free from contains(), and if someone ever "simplifies" that method, the test will fail.

Use a class, not a dictionary, for a fake. A dictionary already has its own get, add, set and keys methods, so fake.get('id') would call the dictionary's method instead of yours. A small class gives you exactly the names you intended.

What to Test Next

Two layers are intentionally left untested above.

The pages. routes/pages.zu renders templates. You can use the same fake server, and check the rendered HTML with expect(response.body).to_contain(...), or with to_match_snapshot(), which records the whole page once and compares against it from then on:

That stores the page in tests/__snapshots__/pages.zu.snap. The point is to review the changes when it changes. If a template edit changes more of the page than you meant it to, that's where you'll see it.

The whole application. You can start the real server on port 0, send real requests with the http client, and shut it down in after_all. That gives you a test that covers routing, middleware, templates and storage together. Write a few of these, not a hundred. They're your slowest tests, and they're the ones most likely to break for reasons that have nothing to do with what they're checking.

The Result

Run the tests:

That's twenty-five tests in under a second, without a server or a network. It's a direct result of the layered design: every dependency points in the same direction, and every layer takes its collaborators as arguments instead of importing them.

Laying Out the Project justified the layers by saying they make each layer readable on its own. This is the other half of that argument, and it's the half you'll notice every day.

Chapter 26 · Interoperability

Foreign Functions: C and Rust

The ffi module calls code written in C and Rust. It loads shared libraries, describes the functions in them and calls those functions with ordinary Zuri values. It turns Zuri functions into C function pointers so that a library can call back into your code. And it reads the declarations that a header file or a Rust crate already contains, so the description only has to be written once, by the people who wrote the library.

Every value that crosses the boundary is converted and checked against its C type. An integer that doesn't fit is a RangeError at the call, not a truncated argument inside the library. Memory allocated by the module knows its own size, and a read past its end is rejected before it happens. When a check isn't possible, because C returned an address without saying how much memory is behind it, the module tells you so instead of guessing.

You can use C libraries, Rust cdylib libraries, and static libraries written in either language. The layout of every struct, whether it's packed, over-aligned or full of bitfields, is the same as the platform's own compiler would give it.

Code blocks in this chapter that list several calls together are reference listings, not programs. They show the form of each call, not a sequence to run. Anything shown as a complete program runs as written. The programs that call the C runtime run on Linux as shown, and the ones that need a library of your own are shown but not run.

Following Along

Every machine has the C runtime library, so most of the examples below call it. ffi.LIBC names it for the platform the program is running on, and ffi.LIBM names the math library:

Some sections use a small library of your own. Save this as geometry.c:

Then build it as a shared library with the C compiler:

The Rust sections use a crate built with crate-type = ["cdylib"], which is shown where it's used.

Introduction

Sooner or later, every language needs to use code it didn't write, such as a database engine, a codec, a cryptography library, a scientific computing kernel, or a system call that the standard library doesn't wrap. That code already exists, it's fast and well tested, and it uses the C calling convention, which is the one convention every language agrees on, on every platform. Rust libraries can use it too, through extern "C".

Calling across that boundary means describing exactly what the other side expects: how wide each integer is, where each member of a struct is stored, and which register each value is passed in. The machine doesn't check any of this. A description that's off by a single byte silently corrupts memory, and the bug shows up later, somewhere unrelated.

ffi turns that description into a value your program can inspect. It builds the description from the source code the library's authors already wrote, lays out every type the same way the platform's compiler does, and checks every value against it as the value crosses the boundary:

The declarations are the same ones <stdlib.h> contains. The struct was returned as a dictionary, and the conversion rules were enforced for the arguments:

Loading a Library

ffi.open() loads a shared library and returns a Library. It accepts a path, a file name, or a bare name that it completes following the platform's conventions:

A bare name is looked for first in the directories given in paths, and then in the platform's own search order. On Linux, a library's unversioned libname.so file is usually only installed with its development package, so ffi.open() also asks the dynamic loader's cache for the versioned file that the runtime package installs, such as libsqlite3.so.0. On macOS, the name is tried as a .dylib and as a framework.

ffi.find() looks for a library the same way, without loading it:

Without a name, ffi.open() returns the running process, whose symbols include the C runtime library and everything else that's already loaded globally.

Two options change how a library is loaded. lazy: true resolves its symbols when they're first used, instead of all at once. global: true makes its symbols visible to libraries loaded after it, and to the process handle, which a plugin that relies on its host's symbols needs. Both options are Unix concepts and have no effect on Windows, where every loaded module is searched whenever the process is asked for a symbol.

If a library can't be found or loaded, ffi.open() raises a LoadError that includes the loader's own explanation, such as a missing dependency, a library built for a different architecture, or a file that isn't a library.

Symbols

A Library can tell you whether it exports a symbol, and where:

symbol() returns a Pointer to the symbol. On glibc, name@VERSION requests a particular version of a versioned symbol, for the rare program that needs to pin one.

Closing a Library

close() stops a library from being used, so every function bound from it raises a LoadError from then on. The code itself is only unloaded once nothing refers to the library anymore, including the functions bound from it, so a closed library is never unloaded while a call is still running.

Calling a Function

You bind a function by giving its name, its return type and its parameter types, and you get back an ordinary Zuri function:

You can store it, pass it to map(), spawn it in an isolate and call it like any other function. The number of arguments is checked just as it is for any function:

ffi.describe() describes a foreign function, and ffi.is_foreign() tells a foreign function apart from a Zuri one:

Binding one function at a time works well for a few functions. For more than that, you can read the declarations from a header, as the next sections show.

Types

Every C type is represented by a Type. The module exports the built-in types:

ffi.char, ffi.schar, ffi.uchar char, signed char, unsigned char 1

The module also exports Rust's names for the same types: ffi.i8 to ffi.u128, ffi.isize, ffi.usize, ffi.f32, ffi.f64, and ffi.rust_char for Rust's char. A Rust name and its C equivalent refer to the same type:

A type knows its size, alignment and kind on the current platform:

Building Types

Pointers, arrays, const and function types are built from other types:

ffi.type() reads the C name of a built-in type, which is often the shortest way to write one:

Structs, unions and enums are built member by member, as described in Structs, Unions and Arrays and Enums and Constants.

Numbers Across the Boundary

A Zuri number is a double, which can represent every integer up to 2^53 exactly, but no further. C integer types go up to 2^64, and with __int128, 2^128. So integers cross the boundary like this:

  • Going in, a number must be a whole number that fits in the type, and you can pass a bigint for any integer type. A fraction, a string or a bool passed for an integer raises a TypeError, and a value outside the type's range raises a RangeError. Values are never truncated or wrapped around.
  • Coming out, an integer is returned as a number if it's within 2^53 of zero, and as a bigint otherwise, so no value is ever rounded.

When a value could be either type, your program has to handle both, for example with is_bigint(value) or by comparing against a bigint, which also compares correctly with a number.

Floating-point types accept any number. long double is wider than a double on some platforms: it's 80-bit extended precision on x86-64 Linux and macOS, and 128-bit quad precision on Arm Linux. Values going in are converted exactly, and values coming out are rounded to the nearest double, as C's own conversion does.

bool accepts and returns a Zuri bool, and a C character type accepts a number or a one-character string:

A complex number is represented as a list of two numbers, [real, imaginary]. You can pass one by value wherever the C compiler supports _Complex, which is everywhere except Windows.

Declaring Functions From C

ffi.declare() reads C declarations and returns a Declarations object, which is a set of types, functions, variables and constants that isn't tied to any particular library. Binding it to a library produces a namespace:

Library.declare() does both steps at once, and it's what most programs use.

The namespace contains a function for each declared function, a Pointer for each declared variable, each constant, and each type that has a name of its own. You use it in the same way as a module. A tagged type without a typedef, such as struct stat, is accessed through the declarations instead, as in api.type('struct stat').

If a declared function isn't exported by the library, you get a SymbolError that names every missing function. With allow_missing: true, the other functions are bound and the missing ones are left out, which is useful for a header that describes several versions of a library.

What Is Read

Everything a header says about an API:

  • typedef, struct, union and enum, including forward declarations, self-referencing records, nested records, anonymous members, bitfields and flexible array members
  • Function prototypes, including variadic ones, and function pointer types nested to any depth
  • extern variables
  • _Static_assert, which is evaluated, so a header that checks its own assumptions checks them here too
  • __attribute__((packed)), aligned(n), ms_abi and sysv_abi, __declspec(align(n)), _Alignas, and asm labels that give a function a different symbol name. Other attributes are skipped.
  • extern "C" { ... }, as written in headers that are shared with C++

A function with a body, such as an inline helper in a header, is read but not bound, because the library doesn't have to export it.

The Preprocessor

Real headers contain a lot of preprocessor lines, so enough of the preprocessor is implemented to read them as they're written:

  • A #define of a value is expanded wherever the name appears, and also becomes a constant. Values can be numbers in any base with any suffix, floating-point numbers, character constants, strings, adjacent strings (which are joined), and expressions that use other constants. A value cast to a pointer type, as headers write sentinels such as ((void *) -1), becomes a Pointer of that type at that address, or nil when the address is zero. A macro can use a type that's declared after it, as C allows, since a macro only has a meaning where it's used.
  • #if, #ifdef, #ifndef, #elif, #else and #endif are evaluated, along with defined(), using the macros that the target platform's compiler predefines, such as __linux__, __APPLE__, _WIN32, __x86_64__, __aarch64__ and __LP64__. __has_include() and the other __has_ queries always return false.
  • #pragma pack applies to the records declared after it, exactly where it's written.
  • #undef removes a macro, and #error stops with its message.
  • Including a C standard header is allowed, because everything it declares is already known. Including <stdio.h> also declares FILE.

Two things are rejected, with the line and column of the problem. The first is including any other file, because declarations are read exactly as given and files are never fetched, so paste in the declarations the program needs. The second is using a function-like macro, which would require the preprocessor's full expansion rules. Defining a function-like macro is allowed and recorded, and only using one is an error.

Functions That Return Text

C has no way to say who owns a returned pointer, but it has a convention that's clear enough to follow. A function returning const char * returns text that it keeps, while one returning char * usually hands over memory to the caller. So a declared function that returns const char * returns a string, or nil for a null pointer, and one that returns char * returns a Pointer, which your program reads and then frees. The same applies to const wchar_t *.

In the real header, getenv is declared as char *getenv(const char *). Declaring it as const char * here is the program's way of saying that it won't free the result, which is correct.

Extending and Sharing Declarations

You add sources to a set one after another, and each one can see what came before it. A set can include another set and use its types without owning them, which is how two libraries can share one set of common types:

types(), functions(), variables() and constants() list what a set contains, and type() resolves any C type name against it, as in shapes.type('segment *[2]').

Declaring Functions From Rust

Rust libraries are called through the C ABI they export, meaning extern "C" functions and the #[repr(C)] types they use. ffi.declare_rust() reads those declarations the way a crate writes them, so you can pass it the crate's source code as it is. Given this lib.rs, built with crate-type = ["cdylib"]:

The Zuri side reads the same file:

Here's what's read and what's skipped:

  • Functions in extern "C" blocks (including unsafe extern "C" blocks), with #[link_name] for a different symbol name
  • extern "C" fn definitions marked with #[no_mangle] or #[export_name], with their bodies skipped. One without either attribute is rejected, because it's exported under a mangled name that nothing can look up.
  • #[repr(C)], #[repr(C, packed)], #[repr(C, align(N))] and #[repr(transparent)] structs, tuple structs and unions
  • Enums with #[repr(C)] or an integer #[repr], with or without fields
  • type aliases, const items and statics
  • #[cfg(...)], which is evaluated for the platform the program is running on
  • Everything else, from use statements to impl blocks, macros and private functions, is skipped

A type can be used before it's declared, as Rust allows. A struct without #[repr(C)] can only be used through a pointer, because Rust doesn't specify its layout. Rust in Depth explains how each Rust type crosses the boundary.

C and Rust declarations can go in the same set, and each can use the other's types, which suits a crate that includes a C header alongside its source code.

Pointers and Memory

A Pointer is an address, optionally with the type of the value it points to. You get memory from ffi.alloc(), which returns it zeroed and typed:

get() and set() read and write elements of the pointer's type, as ptr[i] does in C, and add() moves forward by a number of elements, as ptr + i does in C. read() and write() take their own type and a byte offset, and work on any pointer:

Memory is little-endian on every platform the module supports, as the third line shows. cast() gives a pointer a type, or removes its type.

Checked Access

Memory allocated by the module knows its size, and every access through a pointer into it is checked against that size before it happens:

If a write fails to convert its value, nothing is written, so a record is never left half updated. Freed memory rejects every access, and freeing memory twice raises an error instead of causing a double free.

A pointer returned by C code doesn't have a size, because C didn't say how much memory is behind it. The only thing that can be caught through such a pointer is a null pointer. How much memory is actually there depends on what the library's documentation says.

Passing Pointers as Arguments

A pointer parameter accepts more than just a Pointer. Each of these is converted for the duration of the call:

Passed Becomes
nil A null pointer
A Pointer Its address
A string A NUL-terminated copy, for a pointer to characters
Bytes The bytes' own storage, without copying
A list A temporary array of the target type, copied back after the call
A dictionary A temporary record, copied back after the call
A Zuri function A callback, for a function pointer
A Callback Its code
A foreign function Its address

A list or dictionary is only copied back when the pointer isn't to a const type, so you can use it as an output parameter:

Bytes are passed using their own storage, so a C function that fills a buffer fills the bytes directly:

A callback mustn't resize a bytes value that's been passed to a call while the call is running. Its storage is only guaranteed to stay in the same place as long as nothing changes its length.

Other Kinds of Allocation

ffi.alloc_bytes(size, align) allocates untyped memory. ffi.malloc() allocates memory from the C allocator, for memory you'll pass to C code that frees it with free(), so it's never freed when the pointer is garbage collected. ffi.at(address, type) creates a pointer from a known address. copy_from(), fill() and compare() are the equivalents of memmove, memset and memcmp for checked memory.

Strings and Text

A string passed where a pointer to characters is expected becomes a NUL-terminated copy for the duration of the call, using the encoding implied by the character type: UTF-8 for char, UTF-16 for char16_t, UTF-32 for char32_t, and the platform's own encoding for wchar_t, which is UTF-16 on Windows and UTF-32 everywhere else.

ffi.string and ffi.wstring are pointer types that also convert values coming back. A function declared to return one of them returns a Zuri string, or nil for a null pointer.

Text that needs to last longer than a call, because it's stored in a struct or kept by the library, has to be put in memory of its own with ffi.alloc_string():

read_string() reads up to the terminator, or exactly a given number of code units, in any of the four encodings, and raises a ValueError for text that isn't valid in its encoding. write_string() writes text followed by its terminator. If a read in a block of known size finds no terminator, it's rejected instead of reading past the end.

Structs, Unions and Arrays

A record is built one member at a time, and laid out in the same way the platform's C compiler lays it out:

A record is sealed the first time anything needs its size, including passing a value of that type, and can't be changed after that. set_packed() packs it as #pragma pack does, set_align() increases its alignment, and add_field() accepts a minimum alignment for a single member, as _Alignas does:

Record Values

A record value is represented as a dictionary of its members, both going in and coming out. A member that's missing from a dictionary going in is set to zero. Nested records are nested dictionaries, and array members are lists, except that an array of char is read as the string it contains, and an array of other bytes is read as bytes:

Through a pointer, get_field() and set_field() read and write a single member, as ptr->name does, and field() returns a pointer to a member, as &ptr->name does. fields() lists the members along with their offsets.

Bitfields

add_bitfield() adds a member with a given width in bits. Bitfields follow the platform's rules for packing them, which are GCC's and Clang's on Linux and macOS and MSVC's on Windows, including a zero-width bitfield that ends a storage unit:

Unions

A union value going in is a dictionary that holds a single member, the one to store. Coming out, it contains every member, each read from the same bytes, because only your program knows which one is meaningful:

A union that's been read back and passed in again is accepted as it is, because its members agree with each other. If the members disagree, a TypeError is raised.

Passing Records by Value

Records can be passed to and returned from functions by value, whatever their shape. Which registers a record is passed in depends on its size and the types of its members, and differs on every platform. Those rules are applied to the record's actual layout, including packed and over-aligned records and bitfields:

midpoint takes pointers to records, so the dictionaries were passed as temporary records. scale_all takes a pointer to an array of records, so a list of dictionaries was passed as a temporary array and copied back afterwards.

Enums and Constants

An enum is an integer type with named constants. A value of an enum type is a number, and wherever one is passed in, you can use a constant's name instead:

Declared enums include their constants. A declared enum is stored as an int unless its values need more space, it specifies a type (as in enum x : uint8_t), or GCC's packed attribute asks for the smallest possible type. Every enum constant, #define constant and Rust const becomes a constant of the declarations, and a member of the namespace they're bound to.

Callbacks

A Zuri function passed where a function pointer is expected becomes a C function pointer for the duration of that call:

The arguments are converted from their C types, with pointers becoming Pointer values and records becoming dictionaries, and the return value is converted to the callback's return type. A small integer is widened to a full register, the same way a C compiler returns one.

Long-Lived Callbacks

A library that stores a function pointer and calls it later, such as a signal handler, an event callback or a logging hook, needs a callback that lasts longer than the call that passed it. ffi.callback() creates one:

A long-lived callback lasts until you call release(). Nothing else frees it, because there's no way to know when the library has finished with the pointer, so a callback that's never released lasts as long as the program. After release(), the callback can no longer be passed anywhere, and C code must not call it again.

Errors Inside a Callback

A Zuri error can't unwind through C stack frames, because the C code in between expects to finish. So an error raised inside a callback is caught, C receives a zero (or the callback's error_value), and the error is raised again, unchanged, as soon as the C function returns:

The first error is the one that's raised. Any later calls to the callback during the same C call return the error value.

Callbacks and Threads

C libraries often run their own threads, and those threads can call callbacks. A Zuri isolate runs on a single thread, so a call from any other thread is passed to the isolate that created the callback, and the calling thread waits until the isolate has run it. The isolate responds at its next safepoint, which is the same point where it checks for signals, or immediately if it's inside a foreign call or in ffi.serve().

That covers a library whose threads call back while the program is busy with something else. It doesn't cover a function that blocks the isolate until its own threads have finished calling back. In that case, the isolate would be waiting for the function, the function for its threads, and the threads for the isolate. ffi.threaded() gives that kind of function a version that runs on a helper thread, while the isolate keeps responding to callbacks:

The callback ran on the isolate's own thread, partway through the threaded call. A program that has nothing else to do while it waits for calls from another thread can wait in ffi.serve(timeout), which handles whatever calls arrive and returns how many it handled.

Variadic Functions

A variadic function, such as printf and its relatives, takes its fixed parameters with declared types, followed by any number of other arguments. Each argument after the fixed ones is passed as the type its value suggests:

Value Passed as
A whole number that fits in an int int
A larger whole number long long
Any other number double
A bigint long long, or unsigned long long if necessary
A bool int
A string const char *
A pointer, bytes or nil void *

For anything else, give the value a type with Type.of(). C's usual promotions still apply on top of that, so a float is passed as a double, and a type narrower than int is passed as an int.

The second call shows why of() exists. %.1f with a plain 2 would pass an int, and printf would read a double that was never passed.

Errors and errno

All of the module's own errors are subclasses of FfiError:

Class Raised when
FfiError A type can't be used in the way requested, such as a record without a size passed by value, or a signature that libffi can't call
LoadError A library can't be found or loaded, or a function is called after its library was closed
SymbolError A library doesn't export a symbol
DeclarationError C or Rust source can't be read. line and column point to the problem.
PointerError Memory would be accessed out of bounds, through a null pointer or after being freed, or freed twice
CallbackError A released callback is used
LinkError A static library can't be linked

A value that can't be converted to its C type raises the usual TypeError or RangeError, the same errors any function raises for an invalid argument, and the message names the function, the argument and the type.

errno

C reports failures through errno, which anything that runs afterwards might change. So errno is cleared just before every foreign call and read just after it, and ffi.errno() returns the value that the most recent call on this isolate left there:

34 is ERANGE. On Windows, ffi.last_error() reports GetLastError() in the same way, and it's always zero on other platforms. ffi.set_errno() sets errno, for the rare function that reads it.

Ownership and Lifetimes

Three kinds of memory cross the boundary, and each one has a single owner.

Memory from ffi.alloc() belongs to the program. It's freed when the last pointer to it is garbage collected, or earlier, when you call free(). Pointers created from it with add(), offset(), cast() and field() share the same memory and keep it alive. The one rule to follow is that a pointer must stay reachable for as long as C code holds the address. If C was given some memory and Zuri lost track of it, that memory can be freed while C is still using it.

Memory from ffi.malloc() belongs to whoever frees it. It's never freed by the garbage collector, because the usual reason to allocate it is to pass it to C code that frees it with free(). Otherwise, call free() to release it.

Memory allocated by C belongs to C until your program takes ownership of it with own(), passing the function that releases it, or no function for memory that the C allocator's free() releases:

An owned pointer is released when it's garbage collected, or when you call free(), and every pointer derived from it rejects any access afterwards. A destructor can be any foreign function that takes a single pointer, such as sqlite3_close, png_destroy, or CString::from_raw wrapped in an extern "C" function. Only a pointer to the start of an allocation can free it.

The garbage collector runs destructors in the middle of its own work, when no Zuri code can run, so a destructor that calls a callback during garbage collection always gets zero back, or the callback's error_value. When you call free() yourself, the destructor runs from your program, where callbacks work as they do anywhere else.

Static Libraries

A static library is object code waiting for a linker, so nothing can load it at run time as it is. ffi.link() passes it to the platform's linker, which links every object in it into a shared library, and then loads the result:

On Linux and macOS, the linker is the C compiler, which is cc or whatever $CC names. On Windows, it's MSVC's link.exe, found through the Visual Studio installation. The result is cached under a name based on the contents of the archives and the options, in ffi.default_link_cache() or the directory given in the cache option, so the linker only runs once for a given input, and every time the program starts after that, it loads the cached library.

A Rust staticlib includes the Rust standard library, which in turn needs a few system libraries. An archive that contains Rust code is recognized and linked against them automatically.

On Windows, a static library's functions aren't marked for export, so the linked DLL exports every symbol the archives define with an unmangled name, or exactly the symbols listed in the exports option.

libraries, search_paths and flags pass extra libraries, their directories and raw arguments to the linker, and linker replaces the linker itself. A failure raises a LinkError that includes the linker's own output.

Isolates

Types, pointers, libraries, foreign functions, callbacks and declarations can all be passed to another isolate, and none of them are moved: both sides keep a working handle to the same thing. A type is a description, a library is a handle that the loader shares across threads, and a pointer is an address, so memory written by one isolate can be read by another:

Whatever is in that memory is shared without any synchronization, just as it is between C threads. A callback belongs to the isolate that created it, so if it's passed somewhere else, its calls still run on the original isolate.

Rust in Depth

Every Rust type that has a defined C ABI can cross the boundary, and every other type is rejected with an explanation.

Rust Crosses as
i8 ... u128, isize, usize Integers, including 128-bit integers passed by value
f32, f64 Numbers
bool A bool
char A one-character string, checked to be a Unicode scalar value
*const T, *mut T A Pointer, or nil for null
&T, &mut T, NonNull<T>, Box<T> A Pointer. Passing nil is rejected.
Option<&T>, Option<NonNull<T>>, Option<Box<T>> A Pointer or nil
extern "C" fn(...) A function pointer: a Zuri function or a Callback going in, and a callable value coming out
Option<extern "C" fn(...)> The same, or nil
NonZeroU32 and the other NonZero types A number. Zero is rejected.
Option<NonZeroU32> A number, or nil for None
[T; N] A list
#[repr(C)] struct A dictionary
#[repr(transparent)] struct Its single field
#[repr(C)] or #[repr(u8)] enum without fields A number, or a variant name going in
#[repr(C)], #[repr(C, u8)] or #[repr(u8)] enum with fields A dictionary with a variant key
MaybeUninit<T>, ManuallyDrop<T>, Cell<T> The same as T
PhantomData<T> Nothing, because it takes up no space

An enum with fields is laid out according to the rules for its representation. A value names its variant, and the rest of the dictionary holds its fields. The fields of a tuple variant are named '0', '1' and so on, and a variant without fields can be passed as just its name:

A slice crosses as the pointer and length that Rust's own FFI convention combines it into, and ffi.slice(type) builds that #[repr(C)] struct:

These are rejected, each with an explanation: &str, &[T], String, Vec and every other type without a stable layout, trait objects, tuples, generic types and functions, Option of a type without a niche, a function without #[no_mangle] or #[export_name], and the extern "Rust" ABI.

A panic that escapes from a function in a Rust library ends the process. A library that catches its panics at its own boundary, or keeps them on its own threads, returns normally. One that lets a panic escape ends the process, even when it's called from an isolate. An extern "C" function aborts immediately. An extern "C-unwind" function unwinds into Zuri, which can't catch a panic from another copy of Rust's runtime, so it aborts. A Rust library built with panic = "abort" ends the process on any panic. This is the only kind of panic that isn't contained within its isolate.

Platform Differences

The module runs on 64-bit little-endian platforms, x86-64 and Arm, on Linux, macOS and Windows, and it follows each platform's C compiler:

Linux x86-64 Linux Arm macOS x86-64 macOS Arm Windows x86-64
long 8 8 8 8 4
char Signed Unsigned Signed Signed Signed
wchar_t 4, signed 4, unsigned 4, signed 4, signed 2, unsigned
long double 80-bit 128-bit 80-bit 64-bit 64-bit
_Complex passed by value Yes Yes Yes Yes No
Enum values larger than int Wider type Wider type Wider type Wider type int, truncated
Bitfield rules GCC GCC Clang Clang MSVC

ffi.platform() reports these values for the running platform. A program that passes records between platforms through files or sockets gets the same layouts that the C compiler on each platform produces, which is what the C code on that platform expects.

Calling conventions follow the platform too: System V on Linux and macOS x86-64, AAPCS64 on Arm, with Apple's variations of it, and the Microsoft x64 convention on Windows. On x86-64, a function type or Library.function() can request abi: 'win64', or abi: 'sysv64' on Unix, for a function compiled for the other convention. Declarations read ms_abi and sysv_abi attributes, and Rust's extern "win64" and extern "sysv64".

128-bit integers can be passed by value, in both directions, under every one of these conventions. The Microsoft x64 convention passes them by reference and returns them in a vector register, the same way rustc, Clang and GCC compile them, so a callback that returns an i128 works there just as it does everywhere else.

What Is Checked

A foreign call runs code that the module can't see into, so its guarantees stop where the C code begins. Up to that point:

  • Every value is converted to its declared type, with integers checked against their range, and every other kind of value checked against its type.
  • Memory allocated by the module is checked against its bounds and rejects any use after free(). Freeing it twice is an error.
  • A null pointer is caught before anything is read or written through it.
  • A write that fails doesn't change anything.
  • A Zuri error inside a callback never unwinds through C code, and a Rust panic inside the module never reaches C code.
  • A callback called from any thread runs on its own isolate.

Beyond that, what C code does is up to C. A declaration that doesn't match the library, a pointer read beyond what the library says is there, a callback that C calls after it was released, or bytes resized by a callback while C writes to them are all undefined behavior in C, and they still are here. Reading declarations from the library's own header or crate, instead of writing them by hand, is the best way to avoid the first of these.

Design Limits

It doesn't run the full C preprocessor. Macros that define values and conditional blocks are evaluated, but including other files and expanding function-like macros aren't supported, and they're rejected where they appear.

It doesn't compile C code. Static libraries are linked by the platform's own linker, which needs a C toolchain on the machine that links them.

It doesn't guess who owns memory. A pointer returned by C isn't freed until your program says how, with own().

It doesn't free callbacks automatically. A callback lasts until you call release(), because only your program knows when the library has finished with it.

It doesn't unwind through foreign stack frames. Errors are caught and raised again once the C code has returned. A panic in a callback is held in the same way, and then continues and ends its isolate. A panic that escapes from a Rust library ends the process, as described in Rust in Depth.

Module Reference

The standard library reference documents every class and method. Here's an overview of the module:

Function Description
ffi.open(name, options) Loads a library, or the current process
ffi.find(name, paths) Finds where a library would be loaded from
ffi.link(archives, options) Links static libraries and loads the result
ffi.declare(source), ffi.declare_rust(source), ffi.declarations() Create sets of declarations
ffi.struct(name), ffi.union(name), ffi.enum(name, type) Build records and enums by hand
ffi.pointer(type, options), ffi.array(type, length), ffi.function_type(returns, params, options), ffi.slice(type), ffi.type(spelling) Build other types
ffi.alloc(type, count), ffi.alloc_bytes(size), ffi.malloc(size), ffi.alloc_string(text), ffi.at(address, type) Allocate or refer to memory
ffi.function(pointer, type), ffi.threaded(function), ffi.describe(function), ffi.is_foreign(value) Work with foreign functions
ffi.callback(function, type, options), ffi.serve(timeout) Work with callbacks
ffi.errno(), ffi.set_errno(n), ffi.last_error() Read and set error codes
ffi.platform(), ffi.default_link_cache() Report facts about the platform
ffi.LIBC, ffi.LIBM Name the C runtime and math libraries

Methods of a Library: function, variable, symbol, has, declare, declare_rust, bind, path, close, is_closed.

Methods of a Pointer: get, set, read, write, get_field, set_field, field, read_string, write_string, read_bytes, write_bytes, to_list, add, offset, cast, copy_from, fill, compare, own, free, is_owned, is_freed, address, is_null, type, size, equals.

Methods of a Type: name, kind, size, align, is_const, target, length, signature, pointer, array, as_const, of, equals. A StructType or UnionType also has add_field, add_bitfield, set_packed, set_align, fields, offset_of, has_field and variants, and an EnumType has add_constant, constants and value.

Methods of a Declarations: declare, declare_rust, include, type, constant, constants, types, functions, variables, bind.

Methods of a Callback: pointer, type, release, is_released.

Chapter 27 · Sharing and Shipping

Packages and Nyssa

A package is a Zuri project that other projects can use. Zuri installs, publishes and serves packages itself. The commands come with the runtime, and so does Nyssa, the package registry they talk to, so there's nothing else to install.

This chapter covers all of it:

  1. Projects and Versions: what goes in project.toml, how packages are named, and how to read version ranges.
  2. Installing Packages: adding, updating and removing dependencies, the lockfile, and the places packages can come from.
  3. Publishing Packages: accounts, tokens and publishing a version to a registry.
  4. Commands From Packages: packages that add zuri commands, and installing tools for your user.
  5. Bundles and Upgrades: shipping a program to machines without Zuri, and keeping Zuri itself up to date.
  6. Running Nyssa: hosting a registry for a team, a company or the public.

The Commands

Command What it does
zuri init Creates a project
zuri install Adds packages, or installs everything a project declares
zuri uninstall Removes packages, along with anything only they needed
zuri update Updates packages to newer versions
zuri restore Installs exactly what the lockfile lists
zuri info Describes the project's packages, or a package on a registry
zuri search Searches for packages on a registry
zuri account Signs in and manages tokens
zuri publish Publishes a version of a package
zuri yank Stops a version from being chosen
zuri owner Manages who can publish a package
zuri clean Frees the disk space used by downloads and installs
zuri bundle Packages a program together with a runtime
zuri upgrade Updates Zuri itself to a newer release
zuri serve Runs a Nyssa registry

Every command accepts --help, and every command that changes a project accepts --dry-run, which shows exactly what it would do.

Key Concepts

  • A project is a directory with a project.toml. Every command works on the project that contains the current directory, which it finds by searching upward, the same way imports do.
  • Packages are installed into the project. They go in .zuri/libs, which import searches before the standard library. Two projects on the same machine never share or conflict over an installed package.
  • Each package has a single version. Every requirement in the project has to be satisfied at the same time. If that's not possible, the install stops and tells you which requirements conflict. A package is never installed twice in two different versions.
  • The lockfile is the record. project.lock pins every package to an exact version, along with the checksum of what was downloaded, and zuri restore reproduces it anywhere.
  • Nothing is left half done. An install is prepared next to .zuri/libs and swapped in all at once, so if it fails or is interrupted, the project is left as it was.

27.1 · Sharing and Shipping

Projects and Versions

Starting a Project

zuri init creates a project that runs, with a test that passes and a project.toml that describes it. zuri init --help lists the questions it asks, and the options you can use to answer them in advance.

project.toml

Key Meaning
name The package's name, which is also the name it's imported by
version The version that gets published, as a semantic version
description A one-sentence description, shown in search results
authors, license, readme, homepage, repository, keywords Shown on the package's page. license is an SPDX expression.
zuri The versions of Zuri the package works with, as a range
include, exclude Which files are published, as glob patterns

[dependencies] lists what the project needs to run. [dev-dependencies] lists what you need to work on it, such as test fixtures, and they're never required by projects that depend on this one. Both sections are managed by the package commands, which keep any comments and blank lines already in the file.

Four more sections are described later in this chapter: [registries] in Installing Packages, [install] and [hooks] in Install Scripts, and [bundle] in Bundles and Upgrades.

Package Names

A package name consists of lowercase letters, digits, hyphens and underscores. It must start with a letter, end with a letter or digit, and be no longer than 64 characters. When you import a package, every hyphen in its name becomes an underscore:

Package Import
http-extra import http_extra
json-schema import json_schema
orm_lite import orm_lite

Because of this, two names that only differ in their hyphens and underscores refer to the same package, and a registry rejects the second one. A name that the standard library already uses, such as json or http, can't be used for a package, because the standard library module would always be imported instead.

Versions

A version has the form major.minor.patch, as described by Semantic Versioning:

  • Increase the patch version for fixes that don't change anything people rely on.
  • Increase the minor version for additions that don't break anything.
  • Increase the major version for any change that could break code written against the previous version.

A pre-release version, such as 2.0.0-rc.1, sorts before the release it leads up to, and build metadata after a + is ignored when comparing versions.

Version Ranges

A dependency specifies which versions it accepts:

Range Accepts
1.4.2 or ^1.4.2 >=1.4.2, <2.0.0, meaning any compatible version
^0.4.2 >=0.4.2, <0.5.0, because below 1.0, a minor version change can break things
^0.0.4 Exactly 0.0.4
~1.4.2 >=1.4.2, <1.5.0, meaning patch releases only
=1.4.2 Exactly 1.4.2
1.4 >=1.4.0, <2.0.0, which is a caret range, like any plain version
1.4.*, 1.4.x >=1.4.0, <1.5.0
* Any release
>=1.2, <1.8 Both conditions at once. Conditions can be separated by a comma or a space.
^1.2 || ^2.1 Either range

A plain version is treated as a caret range, so by default you get compatible updates without having to ask for them. Use = to pin an exact version.

A pre-release is only chosen for a range that itself names a pre-release of the same major.minor.patch version. So ^2.0.0-rc.1 accepts 2.0.0-rc.3, but ^1.4 doesn't accept any pre-release at all. If you asked for releases, you'll never get an unfinished version.

27.2 · Sharing and Shipping

Installing Packages

Adding a Dependency

The newest version is installed and recorded in project.toml as a caret range, such as http-extra = "^1.5.0". To choose a different version, give a range. Pass --exact to record =1.5.0 instead, or --dev to add a development dependency:

Everything the package needs is installed along with it, and every package goes in .zuri/libs under its import name:

zuri init tells git to ignore .zuri, except for .zuri/cmds, so installed packages are never committed. project.toml and project.lock are committed, and together they're enough to recreate the directory.

The Lockfile

project.lock records the exact version that every package was resolved to, whether it's a direct dependency or not, along with where it came from and the checksum of what was downloaded:

zuri restore installs exactly what the lockfile lists. It's what you run after a fresh checkout, and what a teammate or a build server runs:

A package whose download doesn't match its recorded checksum is rejected. --frozen stops with an error if the lockfile no longer matches project.toml, instead of resolving the dependencies again, which is what you want for a build that must install exactly what was reviewed. --production leaves out anything that only development dependencies need.

zuri install without a package name does the same as zuri restore after you've changed project.toml. It only resolves what changed, and keeps every other package at its locked version.

Conflicting Requirements

Every package gets exactly one version, chosen so that every requirement in the project is satisfied at the same time. When that's not possible, the install stops without changing anything, and explains the conflict step by step:

Read it from the bottom up: report-kit needs version 2 of json-schema, http-extra needs version 1, and a project can't have both. To fix it, use a newer version of http-extra that accepts version 2 of json-schema, if one exists, or stop using one of the two packages.

Updating Packages

current is the installed version, wanted is the newest version the declared range allows, and latest is the newest version available, marked when updating to it could break code written against the current version.

--latest changes the range in project.toml to the newest release, keeping an exact range exact, and points out every update to a new major version.

Removing Packages

Anything that was only installed because the package needed it is removed as well. A package that something else still needs is kept, and zuri uninstall tells you what needs it.

Getting Information About Packages

A package whose declared range, locked version and installed version don't agree is marked with one of these states: missing, drifted, unlocked or extraneous. With --verify, a package whose files have changed since it was installed is marked as modified.

You can also ask the registry for information:

Git and Local Packages

A package doesn't have to come from a registry:

The package's name is taken from its own project.toml. A git dependency is locked to the commit that its tag, branch or revision pointed to, and to the checksum of that commit's packaged files, so zuri restore installs the same files even after the branch has moved on. zuri update updates a branch dependency to its newest commit. A path dependency is copied again every time the project is installed, which suits a package that you're working on alongside the project that uses it.

A published package can only depend on packages from a registry, because a git or path dependency wouldn't mean anything on the machine of whoever installs it.

Other Registries

Packages are installed from the default registry, https://pub.zurilang.org, unless you say otherwise:

The dependency records which registry it came from, so everyone who installs the project gets it from the same place. A project that uses a registry often can give it a name once:

You can also define aliases in $ZURI_HOME/config.toml, for your own use in every project. Setting default there, or setting ZURI_REGISTRY in the environment, changes the registry that's used when none is named, although a project that defines its own default keeps using it.

A package is never installed from a different registry as a fallback. A package requested from one registry is only ever installed from that registry, so a package with the same name on another registry can never be substituted for it.

Install Scripts

A package can specify scripts to run before and after it's installed:

A script can do anything that the person running zuri install can do, so a dependency's scripts only run if the project allows that package by name:

The project's own scripts always run. --allow-hooks allows more packages for a single run, and --no-hooks doesn't run any scripts. A script runs with zuri run, from the package's directory, without a shell in between, and it has to finish within ten minutes with status 0. Its output goes to a log file under $ZURI_HOME/logs, which is named in the error if the script fails. ZURI_PACKAGE_NAME, ZURI_PACKAGE_VERSION, ZURI_PACKAGE_DIR and ZURI_PROJECT_DIR tell the script where it's running. If a script fails, the whole install is undone.

Working Offline, Caches and Disk Space

Downloads are kept in a cache, checked against their checksums, and shared by every project on the machine. --offline installs packages from the cache only, and if something's missing, it fails with an error that names what's missing instead of using the network.

Anything that zuri clean removes comes back automatically the next time it's needed, either downloaded again or restored from the lockfile.

Environment Variables

Variable What it does
ZURI_HOME Where your packages, settings and tokens are stored. The default is ~/.zuri.
ZURI_CACHE Where downloads are cached. The default is $ZURI_HOME/cache.
ZURI_REGISTRY The default registry, as an alias or an address
ZURI_TOKEN, ZURI_TOKEN_<ALIAS> A registry token, which takes priority over the saved one
HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, NO_PROXY The proxy used for every download
NO_COLOR Turns off colored output

27.3 · Sharing and Shipping

Publishing Packages

Creating an Account

To publish packages, you need an account on the registry. You don't need one to install packages.

This command asks for a username, an email address and a password, creates the account and signs in the command line. It also prints a recovery key, which is only shown once and is the only way back into the account if you lose the password. You can also create an account on the registry's website and sign in afterwards:

Signing in exchanges your password for a token, and every later command sends the token instead. The password itself is never stored. Tokens are stored in $ZURI_HOME/credentials.toml, one for each registry, in a file that only you can read.

Tokens

A token has scopes that limit what it can do:

Scope Allows
publish Publishing new versions
yank Yanking and restoring versions
owners Adding and removing a package's owners
account Issuing and revoking tokens

A token is only shown once, when it's issued, and the registry only stores a digest of it. It's valid for 365 days unless you set a different number with --days. zuri account logout revokes the saved token and removes it.

A build server should sign in with a token instead of a password. It can read the token from standard input, so that it never appears in the shell history or the process list, or take it from the environment:

Give it a token that only has the publish scope, so that even if the token leaks, it can't be used to yank versions, change owners or issue more tokens.

What Gets Published

A package consists of the project's files, packed into an archive. Inside a git repository, that means the files git tracks, or would track. Outside one, it means every file under the project. .git and .zuri are never included. include and exclude in [project] narrow or widen that selection with glob patterns, where * matches within one directory and ** matches across any number of directories:

Files that look like they contain secrets, such as .env, private keys and credential files, are left out, and the publish stops and lists them. If one of those files really is meant to be published, add it to include.

Check exactly what would be sent first. This project leaves out its tests with exclude = ["tests"]:

The last line counts how many of the public names in the package's modules have a doc comment, in the same way the registry counts them for the version's page, and lists the first few that don't have one. Publishing shows the same information before it sends anything.

The archive is built the same way every time, with sorted entries, fixed times and owners, and normalized permissions. The same files always produce the same bytes and the same checksum, on any machine.

Publishing a Version

Before anything is sent, the project must have a valid name and version, git must have no uncommitted changes (you can use --allow-dirty to publish anyway), and the package can contain at most 20,000 files, which can unpack to at most 256 MiB. A license that isn't a valid SPDX expression produces a warning. The registry then checks the archive again itself, and rejects anything that isn't safe to unpack.

A published version never changes. Publishing the same files again is reported as already published, and publishing different files under an existing version is rejected. To fix a version, publish the next one.

The first account to publish a package name owns it.

Each version's page on the registry has an API tab next to its README. It shows the package's API reference, generated from the doc comments in the published files in the same way zuri doc generate generates one, with a page for each public module (Chapter 30). You don't need to build or upload anything for it, because the registry reads the code without ever running it. Each name links to the line that declares it on the Source tab, where you can read every file in the version, and searching the registry's site for a name finds it in the newest version of each package. A name in braces that the package doesn't document itself, such as {http.Request}, links to the standard library reference, which the registry serves for the version of Zuri it runs on, or to the API of a package it depends on from the same registry.

Documentation in docs, built with zuri doc, is the package's guide. A registry that serves guides builds the guide when the version is published and links to it from the version's page. It only uses the package's own files, so everything the guide's doc.toml names and its pages include has to be part of the package (Packages' Guides).

Yanking a Version

A yanked version stays on the registry, and any project whose lockfile already lists it keeps installing it, so yanking never breaks an existing build. It's only left out when versions are chosen again. Yank a version that has a serious bug, but don't yank a version just to hide that it existed.

Package Owners

Every owner can publish, yank and change the owners of a package. A package always has at least one owner.

Using Another Registry

publish, yank, owner and account use the default registry unless --registry names a different one, either by address or by alias:

A dependency from another registry has to name that registry in project.toml, so that whoever installs the package can find it. A dependency that doesn't name a registry comes from the registry the package itself is published on.

27.4 · Sharing and Shipping

Commands From Packages

A package can add commands to zuri, written the same way as the runtime's own commands: a cmds directory in the package, with one command per .zu file or directory, as described in Appendix I.

When the package is installed in a project, its commands work from anywhere inside that project and appear in zuri --help, marked with the package they come from:

The runtime's own commands come first, followed by the project's own commands in .zuri/cmds, so a package can never replace either of them. If two installed packages provide the same command, the second one is rejected when you install it.

Installing Tools for Your User

--global installs a package into $ZURI_HOME instead of into a project, which is how you install a tool that you use everywhere:

The commands of a globally installed package work from any directory. Each one also gets a launcher in $ZURI_HOME/bin, so if that directory is on your PATH, you can run the command directly:

zuri install --global tells you if that directory isn't on your PATH. Globally installed packages can also be imported from any script, after the project's packages and the standard library.

27.5 · Sharing and Shipping

Bundles and Upgrades

Bundling a Program

zuri bundle packages a project together with a runtime, so that it can run on a machine that doesn't have Zuri installed:

A bundle contains the runtime, renamed after the program, the standard library it was built with, and the project along with the packages it needs in production. Running the bundle starts the project's index.zu, whatever directory it's started from, and its arguments are passed to the program in os.args. It doesn't use anything installed on the machine it runs on, such as a ZURI_ROOT or anything in a ZURI_HOME, so it behaves the same everywhere.

Format What it creates
archive A .tar.gz of the bundle directory, or a .zip for Windows. This is the default.
dir The bundle directory itself
exe A single file, which unpacks itself into the user's cache the first time it runs and starts from there afterwards
app A macOS application

Bundles are written to dist in the project, and named <name>-<version>-<platform>, unless you use --output and --name to choose otherwise.

What Goes Into a Bundle

The lockfile has to match project.toml, and every package it lists, except development dependencies, has to be installed at its locked version, so a bundle never includes packages that weren't resolved. zuri restore fixes either problem. A project without any dependencies doesn't need a lockfile at all. The project's files are selected in the same way as for publishing, so include and exclude apply here too.

Building for Other Platforms

A bundle for another platform is built using the release of the same Zuri version for that platform. It's downloaded once, checked against its published checksum and kept in $ZURI_HOME/runtimes. You can use --runtime to name an unpacked runtime to use instead. These are the supported platforms:

  • x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
  • aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
  • x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
  • aarch64-unknown-linux-musl
  • x86_64-apple-darwin
  • aarch64-apple-darwin
  • x86_64-pc-windows-msvc

A bundle runs anywhere its runtime does: a GNU bundle on glibc 2.28 or later, and a musl bundle on any musl system, including a bare Alpine installation.

You can build a single-file bundle for macOS on any machine. Its payload is stored inside the executable's image rather than after it, and the result is signed ad hoc, which is all an Apple silicon Mac needs to run it.

Signing for Distribution

A program downloaded onto a Mac only runs if it's signed with a Developer ID and notarized, and notarization requires the hardened runtime. With the hardened runtime, Zuri's JIT needs the com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit entitlement to create executable memory, so sign it with an entitlements file that grants it:

--force replaces the ad hoc signature. Sign an app bundle the same way, passing the .app directory instead of the executable.

macOS Applications

An app bundle needs an identifier, written in reverse domain name form. name is the name Finder shows, and icon is an .icns file in the project.

Upgrading Zuri

--check tells you whether a newer release is available, and exits with status 1 if there is one. zuri upgrade downloads the release for the current platform, checks it against its published checksum, unpacks it next to the installation and runs it to confirm the version it reports. Only then are the executable, the standard library and the included commands all replaced at once, and if any part of that fails, everything is put back.

A release without a published checksum is rejected, and so is an installation you don't have permission to write to, before anything is downloaded. --version chooses a particular release, --prerelease includes pre-releases, and installing an older release requires --allow-downgrade. Releases come from the project's GitHub releases. ZURI_RELEASES_URL points to another list of releases in the same format, such as a mirror, and GITHUB_TOKEN is sent along if it's set.

27.6 · Sharing and Shipping

Running Nyssa

Nyssa is Zuri's package registry, and any Zuri installation can run one. It provides the registry API that every package command talks to, and a website where you can find packages, read their READMEs and the API references generated from their doc comments, read the standard library reference, and manage your account and its tokens.

That's a working registry, without any setup. Point the package commands at it:

Settings

Every setting can be given as a flag, as a NYSSA_ environment variable, or as a line in nyssa.toml in the storage directory, in that order of priority:

Flag Variable Default
--host NYSSA_HOST 127.0.0.1
--port NYSSA_PORT 3000
--storage NYSSA_STORAGE $ZURI_HOME/nyssa
--config NYSSA_CONFIG nyssa.toml in the storage directory
--public-url NYSSA_PUBLIC_URL http://<host>:<port>
--workers NYSSA_WORKERS One per CPU core, up to 8
--database NYSSA_DATABASE SQLite in the storage directory
--signup NYSSA_SIGNUP open
--max-archive-size NYSSA_MAX_ARCHIVE_SIZE 10485760 bytes
--trust-proxy NYSSA_TRUST_PROXY Off
--read-only NYSSA_READ_ONLY Off
--tls-cert, --tls-key NYSSA_TLS_CERT, NYSSA_TLS_KEY None
--guides-url NYSSA_GUIDES_URL None, in which case packages' guides aren't built or served
NYSSA_NAME Nyssa, the name the site shows
NYSSA_MAIL_URL, NYSSA_MAIL_USERNAME, NYSSA_MAIL_PASSWORD, NYSSA_MAIL_FROM None

public_url is the address people use to reach the registry. It's used in links and emails, and package commands refer to the registry by it. Passwords belong in the environment, never in a flag, where they'd be visible in the process list. That means NYSSA_DATABASE for a connection string that contains a password, and NYSSA_MAIL_PASSWORD.

The Database

SQLite in the storage directory doesn't need any setup, and it can easily serve a registry for a team or a company. PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB can serve the same site, using the same connection strings the sql module accepts:

The schema is kept up to date by migrations, each written once for every database engine and applied when the registry starts, so starting a newer version of Zuri against an older database updates it. zuri serve migrate does the same and then exits, so you can prepare a database before a deployment. On PostgreSQL and SQLite, each migration runs in a transaction. MySQL and MariaDB commit on every schema change, so on those databases each migration runs outside a transaction and is recorded once it has finished. If several registries start at the same time against the same database, each migration is still only applied once.

Published archives are stored by checksum under the storage directory, so a backup needs to include the database and that directory.

Serving It Securely

Passwords and tokens are sent over the network whenever someone signs in or publishes, so a registry that can be reached from other machines must be served over HTTPS, in one of two ways:

The second way is for a registry behind a proxy that terminates TLS, such as nginx or a load balancer, and tells the registry to trust the client addresses that the proxy forwards. If the registry listens beyond the local machine without either, it prints a warning.

Packages' Guides

A package can include a guide, which is documentation built by zuri doc, in its docs directory (Chapter 30). If you give the registry a host to serve guides on, it builds each version's guide when the version is published, and links to it from the version's page:

A guide is the package's own HTML and scripts, so it's only served on the guides host, never on the registry's own host. There, its scripts run without access to anything that belongs to the registry, such as a session or a signed-in page. That's why the guides host must be different from the registry's host, even if the port is different, because a cookie applies to every port on its host. Point the guides host at the registry in the same way as the registry's own address, through the same proxy if there is one, and the registry responds to each request according to the host name it was sent to. A guide is available at /<package>/<version>/ on that host, and /<package>/ shows the guide for the newest version.

A guide is built using only the package's own files. Everything its doc.toml names and its pages include has to be inside the package, or the guide isn't built, and the package's own page template is never used, because a template runs code. Guides for versions published before guides were turned on are built in the background the next time the registry starts.

Accounts

With signup = "open", anyone can create an account. A private registry turns off sign-up and creates accounts itself:

Command What it does
zuri serve admin create <username> Creates an account, whether or not sign-up is open
zuri serve admin promote <username> Makes the account an administrator
zuri serve admin demote <username> Makes it an ordinary account again
zuri serve admin suspend <username> Suspends the account and revokes all of its tokens
zuri serve admin restore <username> Lifts a suspension

An administrator can yank any version and change the owners of any package, which is how a malicious release is stopped or an abandoned package is handed over to someone else. Only a package's owners can publish new versions. Every change is recorded in the audit log, along with who made it and where it came from.

If mail is configured, a new account has to confirm its email address before it can publish, and a lost password can be reset by email. Without mail, the account's recovery key is the only way back in.

Maintenance

Back up a PostgreSQL or MySQL database with its own tools, such as pg_dump or mysqldump. Read-only mode keeps a registry running during maintenance, or while a migration happens somewhere else.

Running It as a Service

On Linux, systemd can keep it running:

secrets.env contains NYSSA_DATABASE and NYSSA_MAIL_PASSWORD, and only the service's user can read it. When the service is stopped, every request that's already running is allowed to finish first.

Security Measures

  • Passwords are hashed with Argon2id. Tokens and recovery keys are only stored as digests, and every token has scopes and an expiry date.
  • After five failed sign-ins, an account is locked for fifteen minutes. The failures are counted in the database, so every worker sees them. Each worker also allows an address 30 attempts a minute to sign in, sign up or recover an account.
  • Every form includes a token that only the site's own pages have, pages are sent with a content security policy that doesn't allow scripts to run, and HTML in READMEs is sanitized before it's displayed.
  • Every archive is checked before it's stored, including its checksum, its size, every path in it, and whether its project.toml names the package and version it was published as. Anything that couldn't be unpacked safely is rejected.
  • A name that only differs from a published name in case, hyphens or underscores is rejected, so that no package can pretend to be another.
  • When something fails, the visitor sees a plain error page, and the full error, including the stack trace, goes to standard error for whoever runs the registry.

The API

The package commands use version 1 of a JSON API, which any client can use. Every error response has the form { "error": { "code", "message" } }, with a status code that describes the error, and the code values don't change.

Request What it does
GET /api/v1/config Describes the registry and what it accepts
GET /api/v1/index/:name Lists every version of a package, with checksums and dependencies
GET /api/v1/packages/:name Returns a package as its page shows it
GET /api/v1/packages/:name/:version/archive Downloads an archive
GET /api/v1/search?q= Lists packages that match a query, with sort, page and per_page
PUT /api/v1/packages Publishes a version, as a multipart upload
POST, DELETE /api/v1/packages/:name/:version/yank Yanks a version, or restores it
GET, PUT /api/v1/packages/:name/owners Lists the owners, or adds one
DELETE /api/v1/packages/:name/owners/:username Removes an owner
POST /api/v1/accounts Creates an account
POST, GET /api/v1/tokens Signs in or issues a token, or lists tokens
DELETE /api/v1/tokens/:id Revokes a token. Use current for the token sent with the request.
GET /api/v1/me Returns the account that the token belongs to
GET /healthz Responds with 200 while the registry is running

A request that changes anything sends its token in the header Authorization: Bearer nys_....

Chapter 28 · Talking to Other Programs

JSON-RPC

The rpc module implements JSON-RPC 2.0, for both the calling side and the answering side, over any kind of transport: in the body of an HTTP request, over a WebSocket, a TCP or TLS socket, a Unix domain socket or a pipe to a child process, or over any other stream of bytes. It's written in Zuri, on top of json, http, isolate and net, and it follows the specification exactly.

JSON-RPC is a remote procedure call protocol, and a small one. One program sends the name of a method and its parameters, and the other runs the method and sends back the result or an error. That's very nearly all there is to it, and the small size is deliberate. The protocol doesn't say anything about what the methods are, how the two programs are connected or which of them is in charge, so it works wherever two programs need to call each other. Services use it to call each other over HTTP. Blockchain nodes expose their whole API through it, over HTTP for calls and over WebSockets for the updates they push to subscribers. Mining pools, wallets, trading systems, editors and their tools, and plugin hosts use it over sockets and pipes.

The module follows the same approach. A service only answers messages, so the same service can answer whatever transport delivered the message. Serving it from an HTTP route, a WebSocket or a socket server only takes a few lines of code around it.
