Following Along

A service declares which methods it answers, and answers one message at a time:

The message went in as JSON text, and the answer came out the same way, without using the network at all. Everything else in this chapter is about how a message reaches a service and how its answer gets back, whether that's in the body of an HTTP request, over a WebSocket or a socket, or between two isolates in the same program.

Introduction

JSON-RPC has three kinds of message. Each one is a small JSON object whose jsonrpc member is "2.0".

A request names a method, and includes its params and an id. The other side has to answer it, and the answer includes the same id.

A notification is a request without an id. Nothing answers it, not even when it fails. Notifications are for things the sender wants done but doesn't need to hear back about, such as a log message, a progress report, or a change the other side should know about.

A response includes the id of the request it answers, and exactly one of result and error.

Parameters are either a list, which is matched to the method's parameters by position, or a dictionary, which is matched by name. Nothing else is allowed, so a call to square(4) sends [4], never 4.

Messages can also be sent together as a batch, which is a JSON array of messages. The requests in a batch are answered together, as an array of responses, each one matched to its request by id.

The protocol doesn't have its own transport, and it can be carried in two different ways. In an exchange, such as an HTTP request and its response, one message or batch goes in each direction and then the exchange is over. On a connection, such as a WebSocket or a socket, messages flow in both directions for as long as the connection stays open, and neither side is the client. Either side can send requests and notifications at any time, even while it's in the middle of answering one. On a stream of bytes, both sides also have to agree on where one message ends and the next one starts. That agreement is called the framing.

The module has a layer for each of these parts:

Layer What it contains
Messages Request, Notification, Response, RpcError, and encode(), decode() and read()
Services Service, and the Context passed to its handlers
HTTP http_handler() to serve a service, and HttpClient to call one
Framing HeaderFraming, LineFraming and MessageFraming
Transports StdioTransport, SocketTransport, ProcessTransport, WebSocketTransport, ChannelTransport and pipe()
Endpoints Endpoint, a service on a connection
Servers serve(), which creates an endpoint for every connection to a listening socket

import rpc gives you access to all of it.

Messages

Requests and Notifications

You build a message from its contents, and rpc.encode() writes it out in the form JSON-RPC sends:

An id is a string or a number, and the sender can choose whatever value it wants to match the answer with. An endpoint numbers its own requests starting from 1.

Setting params to nil leaves the member out of the message, which the specification allows for a method that doesn't take any parameters. Anything other than a list, a dictionary or nil is rejected when the message is built, before it can be sent:

Responses

Response.success() answers a request with its result, and Response.failure() answers it with an error:

A response's id is only nil when it answers a message whose id couldn't be read, such as a message that wasn't valid JSON at all. A result of nil is a result like any other, and is sent as null.

Errors and Error Codes

An error is an RpcError, which has a code, a short message, and optional data containing anything else the other side needs to know.

The specification reserves the codes from -32768 to -32000, and defines these:

Constant Code Meaning
PARSE_ERROR -32700 The message isn't valid JSON
INVALID_REQUEST -32600 The JSON isn't a valid message
METHOD_NOT_FOUND -32601 The method doesn't exist
INVALID_PARAMS -32602 The method can't accept these parameters
INTERNAL_ERROR -32603 The method failed while it was running
SERVER_ERROR_MIN to SERVER_ERROR_MAX -32099 to -32000 Errors defined by an implementation for its own use

An application's own errors can use any code outside the reserved range. Choose your codes once, document them and don't change them. The other side's program checks the code, while the message is for whoever reads the log.

RpcError is a subclass of Error, so you raise and catch it like any other error. When a request handler raises one, it becomes the answer.

Reading and Writing JSON

rpc.decode() reads a message from JSON text and checks it against every rule in the specification:

It returns a Request, a Notification or a Response, distinguished in the same way the specification distinguishes them. A message with a method and an id is a request, one with a method but no id is a notification, and one with a result or an error is a response.

Anything that breaks a rule is rejected with an RpcError that has the code it would be answered with:

rpc.read() does the same for a value that has already been decoded from JSON, for programs that get the JSON from somewhere that has already decoded it. rpc.encode() works in the other direction, for any message or list of messages.

Batches

A list of messages is encoded as a batch:

A batch is decoded into a list. Each entry is read separately, so one bad entry doesn't affect the others. In its place is an RpcError describing what's wrong with it, ready to be sent as an answer.

An empty batch, [], isn't a message at all, and decoding one raises INVALID_REQUEST.

Services

A Service holds the handler for every method that a program answers. answer() takes a single message or a batch, as JSON text or as bytes, and returns the JSON text of the answer, or nil if there's nothing to answer.

Answering Requests

on_request() sets the handler for a method. The handler is called with the request's params and a Context, and whatever it returns is sent back as the result:

The Context gives the request's id and method, the endpoint handling it, and the request it arrived in, which for a message sent over HTTP is the HTTP request. A handler that doesn't need the context can leave it out, as add does. A request for a method without a handler is answered with METHOD_NOT_FOUND, as mul is.

To replace a handler, call on_request() again with the same method name. The specification reserves method names that start with rpc., so on_request() rejects them.

A message that isn't valid UTF-8 or valid JSON is answered with PARSE_ERROR and an id of nil, because its id can't be read.

Reporting Errors

A handler fails a request by raising an error. An RpcError is sent back exactly as it is, including its code, message and data. Any other error is sent back as an INTERNAL_ERROR that includes the error's message:

An error that isn't an RpcError is also passed to the service's on_error() handler, since it indicates a failure in the program rather than a deliberate refusal. If a handler mustn't let the messages of its errors reach the other side, it should catch them and raise its own RpcError instead.

On the calling side, an error answer is raised by request() as the RpcError that the other side sent.

Notifications

on_notification() sets the handler for a notification. It's called in the same way, with the params and a Context, and whatever it returns is ignored, since nothing is sent back:

A notification for a method without a handler is dropped, and a notification handler that raises an error doesn't send anything back either. Instead, the error is passed to on_error(). That's the rule the specification sets, and it makes sense: the sender asked not to be answered.

Methods Without a Handler

on_unhandled() sets a fallback for every request and notification whose method doesn't have its own handler. It's called like any other handler, and context.method tells you which method it's handling:

It's useful for a group of methods that are all answered in the same way, for a proxy that passes calls on, and for logging requests that nothing answers. Raising METHOD_NOT_FOUND from it rejects a method, just as a service without a fallback would. Methods whose names start with rpc. never reach it.

Batches and the Batch Limit

A batch is answered with a batch. Each request in it gets an answer, in the same position, and each notification gets no answer. A batch that only contains notifications has no answer at all:

A single message containing a million requests is still a single message, and a service that accepted it would do the work of a million calls for it. A batch with more than batch_limit() messages, which is 1000 by default, is rejected completely, before any of it runs:

set_batch_limit(nil) accepts batches of any size, for a service that only receives calls from programs it trusts.

JSON-RPC Over HTTP

Over HTTP, each message or batch is the body of a POST request, and its answer is the body of the response. Each exchange stands on its own: nothing is framed, and no connection is kept between calls, apart from what HTTP keeps itself. This is how services usually call each other, and it's how most JSON-RPC traffic is sent.

Serving a Service

rpc.http_handler() turns a service into a route handler for an http server. Here, the server runs on its own isolate, and the client calls it:

In production, the service is created in the setup function that each http worker runs, and the server spreads requests across a pool of isolates:

Everything http provides for a route applies to this one too, including middleware, TLS, HTTP/2, compression, body size limits and the rest of Chapter 15.

A request that arrives over HTTP is answered in the response to that HTTP request, so its handler answers by returning a value. context.defer() raises an error there, because there's no connection to send a later answer on.

Calling a Service

rpc.HttpClient calls a service at a URL. Each call is a single POST request:

request() returns the result, or raises the RpcError that the service answered with. notify() doesn't expect anything back. request_batch() sends every call in a single POST and returns the answers in the same order as the calls, whatever order the server sent them in, with an RpcError in place of each call that failed.

The options are headers, which are sent with every call, timeout, the maximum number of seconds to wait for an answer, and client, the http.HttpClient to send requests through, for its proxy, TLS and connection settings. Each call can also have its own timeout.

Status Codes

The HTTP status codes follow common practice:

Status When
200 There's an answer, whether it's a result or a JSON-RPC error
204 There's nothing to answer, because the body was a notification or a batch of them
405 The request used a method other than POST. The response includes an Allow: POST header.
415 The body isn't application/json in UTF-8

A JSON-RPC error never changes the status code, so a METHOD_NOT_FOUND error is sent as a 200 response whose body says so. The http server's own limits apply before the service sees anything, so a body larger than its max_body_size gets a 413. If you register the handler with server.any(), every method other than POST gets a 405, and with server.post(), they get the server's 404.

On the calling side, any other status raises an RpcHttpError that includes the status and the body. Some servers send a JSON-RPC error with a status other than 200, as older drafts of JSON-RPC over HTTP required. When the body of such a response is a JSON-RPC answer, HttpClient reads it as one, and the error is raised as the RpcError it is.

Identifying the Caller

Every handler receives the HTTP request as context.request, so it can read headers, the client's address, or anything a middleware has stored in the request's context. Authentication belongs in a middleware, which rejects a request before the service sees it:

Framing

A stream of bytes doesn't have any boundaries. A program reading from a socket receives bytes in whatever chunks the network delivers them, so two messages might arrive in one chunk, or one message in ten. A framing marks where each message ends, so the reader can put the messages back together.

All the framings work in the same way. feed() takes the next bytes, in whatever chunks they arrive, and returns every message they complete. frame() works in the opposite direction, turning a message's text into the bytes to send.

Content-Length Headers

HeaderFraming puts a short block of headers in front of each message, giving its length in bytes:

The header block is ASCII text: lines of the form Name: value, each ending in \r\n, followed by a blank line, and then exactly as many bytes as Content-Length specifies. The length counts bytes rather than characters, so messages in any language are framed correctly.

When reading, the input can be split at any point at all:

The first chunk contained all of one message and the start of the next. feed() returned the complete message and kept the rest, and pending() tells you how many bytes it's keeping. The second chunk completed the second message.

Header names are case-insensitive. Content-Length is required. Content-Type is optional, and if it specifies a charset, the charset must be UTF-8. Any other header is ignored.

One Message per Line

LineFraming ends each message with a line break instead. This framing is known as newline-delimited JSON:

A line can end in \n or \r\n, and empty lines are skipped. json.encode() never writes a raw line break, because a line break inside a string is escaped, so each line always contains exactly one message. A peer that pretty-prints its JSON over several lines can't use this framing.

One Message per Read

MessageFraming doesn't add any framing at all. It's for transports that keep messages separate themselves, most notably WebSockets, where every read returns exactly one message. feed() treats each chunk as one complete message, and frame() returns the text unchanged.

A transport that needs this framing says so with its own framing() method, and an endpoint on that transport uses that framing unless you tell it otherwise. rpc.websocket() does exactly this.

Choosing a Framing

Both sides have to use the same framing, so the choice is usually made by whatever is on the other side. An endpoint uses its transport's own framing if it has one, and HeaderFraming otherwise, unless you specify something else:

When the choice is up to you, HeaderFraming is the more robust option. The reader knows how much data is coming before it arrives, and can reject a message that's too large without reading it.

Limits

Every framing rejects a message larger than max_size(), which is 64 MiB by default, and HeaderFraming rejects a header block longer than 8 KiB. Without these limits, a peer could make a reader use any amount of memory by never finishing a message.

The message is rejected as soon as its header arrives, before any of the message is read.

A framing that can't read its stream raises an RpcFramingError. Whatever the reason, the result is the same: nothing after that point in the stream can be read, because the reader no longer knows where the next message starts. At that point, the connection is over.

Transports

A transport carries the bytes. It can be any object with these three methods:

  • read(max) returns the next bytes that arrive, up to max bytes, waiting until at least one byte arrives. Once the stream has ended, it returns empty bytes.
  • write(data) sends all of data.
  • close() closes the stream in the direction it writes.

A transport can also have a can_listen() method, which returns true when another isolate can read from it while the isolate that created it writes to it. That's what listen() needs. Without the method, the answer is false.

Standard Streams

rpc.stdio() communicates over the program's own standard input and output. It's the transport for a program that's started by another program which then talks to it: the parent writes to the child's standard input and reads its standard output.

Standard output belongs to the protocol. Anything else the program prints there ends up in the middle of the stream and breaks it for the other side, so a program that serves over stdio should send everything else to standard error, as this one does with its log. Every write the transport makes is flushed immediately.

Sockets

rpc.socket() communicates over a connected TcpStream, UnixStream or TlsStream from net:

The server binds to port 0 so the system chooses a free port, and sends the address back over a channel for the client to connect to. It serves the one connection it accepts, and its serve() returns when the client closes its end.

A socket can only be used by one isolate at a time, so an endpoint on a socket reads with serve() and request() rather than listen().

This server handles a single connection and then ends. For a server that handles many clients at once, use rpc.serve(), which gives each connection its own endpoint.

Child Processes

rpc.process() communicates with a child process over its standard streams. Spawn the process with both stdin and stdout set to 'pipe':

Closing the endpoint closes the child's standard input. The calculator above treats that as the end of the connection, its serve() returns and the program ends, which is what wait() waits for. A child's streams belong to the isolate that spawned it, so this endpoint also reads with serve() and request().

WebSockets

rpc.websocket() communicates over a WebSocket from http.websocket, either one accepted by a route or one opened with websocket.connect(). Each JSON-RPC message is a single WebSocket message, so an endpoint on a WebSocket uses a MessageFraming automatically.

A WebSocket is a two-way connection, so either side can call the other whenever it likes. That makes it the best transport for a server that pushes updates to its clients, such as a node that streams new blocks to its subscribers:

The route accepts the WebSocket and serves an endpoint on it for as long as the client stays connected. When asked for a total, the server asks the client for a price before it answers. A WebSocket can only be used by one isolate at a time, so an endpoint on a WebSocket reads with serve() and request().

Between Isolates

rpc.pipe() returns two transports connected to each other, so that what one writes, the other reads. Each end is a ChannelTransport over a pair of isolate channels, and channels can be passed between isolates, so you can pass either end to another isolate and use it there.

A pipe is the natural way to give one part of a program a JSON-RPC interface to another part, and it's the easiest way to test an endpoint. The server and its test communicate exactly as they would over a socket, without anything listening on the network.

Writing Your Own Transport

Any object with the three methods is a transport. This one wraps another transport and counts how many bytes it sends:

Endpoints

An endpoint is a service on a connection. rpc.endpoint(transport) creates one, and everything in Services applies to it, including its handlers, its fallback, its batch limit and its errors. The connection adds the other direction: an endpoint can call the other side, and a handler on an endpoint can send its answer after it returns.

Calling the Other Side

request() sends a request and waits for the answer:

It returns the result, raises the RpcError that the other side answered with, or raises an RpcClosedError if the connection ends first. While it waits, it handles everything else that arrives, just as serve() would, including other answers, notifications and requests from the other side.

notify() sends a notification and returns as soon as it's been sent:

send_request() sends a request and returns immediately with the request's id. The answer is passed to a callback when it arrives:

The callback is called with the result and nil, or with nil and the error. Callbacks run on the isolate that owns the endpoint, while it's reading. Here, while request() was waiting for its own answer, the answers to the two earlier requests arrived first and their callbacks ran. If the connection ends while a callback is still waiting, it's called with an RpcClosedError.

Sending a Batch

request_batch() sends several requests as a single batch and waits for all of the answers. Each call is a pair of a method and its parameters, and the answers come back in the same order as the calls, whatever order the other side sent them in:

A batch can partly succeed, so a failed call doesn't raise an error. Instead, its position in the list holds the RpcError it was answered with. Only a closed connection or a timeout raises an error, because in those cases no answer can be relied on to arrive.

Answering Later

A handler normally answers by returning a value. Sometimes, though, the answer depends on work that hasn't been done yet, such as a job on another isolate, a reply from a third program, or an event that hasn't happened yet. In that case, the handler calls context.defer(), keeps the context, and answers through it with reply() or fail() when the answer is ready:

Once a request has been deferred, whatever its handler returns is ignored. It's answered exactly once, so answering it a second time, or answering a request that was never deferred, raises a ValueError. If a handler raises an error after deferring, the request fails with that error, unless it has already been answered. A request deferred from inside a batch is answered separately, after the batch's other answers.

Calls in Both Directions

Either side can call the other at any time, even from inside a handler. Here, when the server is asked for an order's total, it first asks the client for a price:

The client's request('total') is waiting when the server's request for price_of arrives. It answers that request while it waits, and then carries on waiting for its own answer. You don't need to set anything up for this, because every wait handles whatever arrives.

Reading the Connection

An endpoint reads from its transport in one of two ways, and either way, every handler runs on the isolate that owns the endpoint.

Serving Requests

serve() reads and answers messages until the connection ends, stop() is called or the endpoint is closed. For a server that only answers requests, as every server so far in this chapter has, it's all you need.

A message that isn't valid UTF-8 or valid JSON is answered with PARSE_ERROR and an id of nil, because its id can't be read. A stream whose framing can't be read makes serve() raise an RpcFramingError.

Listening While Doing Other Work

A program that also waits for other things can't simply stay inside serve(). listen() reads the transport on its own isolate, decodes each message there, and returns a Channel of the messages that arrive. The program takes items from the channel when it's ready, alongside its other channels, and passes each one to dispatch():

The server defers each request and passes the work to a worker. Its loop waits on both the connection and the worker's results, and handles whichever is ready first, so the endpoint never stops answering while work is in progress.

The reader isolate handles the framing and the JSON decoding, so a large message costs the owning isolate nothing until it's dispatched. Everything is still sent from the owning isolate, and every handler still runs there.

You can only listen to a transport that another isolate can read from, which means stdio and pipes. Sockets, WebSockets and child processes can only be used by one isolate at a time, and calling listen() on one of them raises a ValueError. Set the framing before you call listen(), because the reader isolate takes the framing with it.

serve() and request() also work on a listening endpoint, taking whatever arrives from the same channel.

Reading the Transport Yourself

A program that reads from the transport itself, such as one that polls many connections at once, passes each chunk it reads to feed(). It handles every message the bytes complete, just as serve() would, and empty bytes end the connection. rpc.serve() handles every connection it holds in this way.

Timeouts

request() and request_batch() accept a timeout in seconds:

A timeout only works if the endpoint is listening. An endpoint that reads its transport itself is stuck inside the transport's read while it waits, so it waits for as long as the read does. Over a socket, the socket's own set_read_timeout() sets the limit, and a read that times out raises the socket's error.

An answer that arrives after its request has timed out has nothing waiting for it, so it's passed to on_error().

Stopping and Closing

stop() makes serve() return once it has finished handling the current message, which lets a handler end the conversation:

close() closes the transport. After that, nothing more can be sent, and trying to send raises an RpcClosedError. Every send_request() callback that's still waiting is called with an RpcClosedError. is_closed() returns true once the endpoint has been closed, or the other side has ended the connection.

Serving Many Connections

rpc.serve() binds a listening socket and gives every connection it accepts its own endpoint, spread across a pool of worker isolates. Each worker polls the connections it holds instead of blocking on one, so a quiet client only costs a file descriptor rather than a thread, and a single worker can serve hundreds of long-lived connections side by side.

setup runs inside a worker for every connection, with the connection's endpoint and the client's address, and sets up the endpoint's handlers. Workers don't share anything with each other, so setup should be a function in a module, or a function that only uses its own imports, and it should create whatever the connection needs. Each endpoint is a full peer, so its handlers can call the client back, and it can send the client notifications whenever it has something to report.

Option Meaning Default
host The address to listen on '127.0.0.1'
port The port to listen on. 0 chooses a free port. 8000
path A Unix domain socket to listen on, instead of host and port nil
workers The number of worker isolates that serve connections The number of CPUs
backlog How many accepted connections can wait for a worker workers * 4
framing 'header' for Content-Length headers, or 'line' for one message per line 'header'
max_message_size The largest message accepted, in bytes 64 MiB
max_connections_per_worker The maximum number of connections each worker holds 256
idle_timeout How many seconds a connection can stay silent before it's closed nil, meaning never
read_timeout How many seconds a read can wait once a message has started 30
write_timeout How many seconds a write can wait 30
cert_chain, private_key PEM strings that put every connection behind TLS nil
on_ready A function called once the socket is bound, with the address and a stop function nil
max_connections The number of connections after which the server stops accepting new ones nil, meaning never

on_ready is called on the isolate that called serve(), once the socket is bound. Calling the stop function it receives stops the server from accepting connections. Every worker then finishes the message it's handling, closes its connections and ends, and serve() returns. That's what a signal handler should call to shut a server down cleanly. Reaching max_connections also stops the server from accepting connections, but the connections already accepted are served until each one closes, which is what the example above relies on.

Each worker uses a thread from the isolate pool for as long as the server runs. If serve() is the first thing in a program to use an isolate, it sizes the pool itself. Otherwise, call isolate.configure() at the very start, as the example does, with enough room for the workers and anything else the program runs.

With cert_chain and private_key, every connection uses TLS, and a client that fails the handshake is disconnected before it reaches a worker's handlers. With path, the server listens on a Unix domain socket, which is how local daemons provide an API to other programs on the same machine. The socket file is removed when the server stops. Unix domain sockets need a platform that supports them, which you can check with net.unix.is_supported().

A handler that calls its client with request() keeps its worker busy until the answer arrives, and every other connection on that worker has to wait too. For a call that might take a while, use send_request() with a callback instead, which keeps the worker free.

Watching the Conversation

on_trace() sees the text of every message, both as it's sent and as it arrives:

on_error() sees every problem that the other side isn't told about: an error raised by a notification handler, an error other than an RpcError raised by a request handler, an error raised by a callback, a response that nothing was waiting for, and a connection that failed. It's called with the error and the message it relates to, as a dictionary, or nil when no single message is to blame:

Without an on_error() handler, these problems are silently dropped. A server without one has no way to find out that its handlers are failing, so always set it.

Errors

Every error the module raises is one of these:

Error Raised when
RpcError A JSON-RPC error, with a code. It's either the other side's answer, or a message that broke the rules.
RpcHttpError An HTTP status arrived without a JSON-RPC answer. It includes the status and the body.
RpcFramingError The stream's framing can't be read, and nothing after that point can be read either
RpcClosedError The connection ended before an answer arrived, or the endpoint has been closed
RpcTimeoutError A request's timeout expired before its answer arrived
ValueError The calling program made a mistake, such as passing parameters that aren't structured, using a reserved method name or answering a request twice

The first one is the error a program handles as part of its normal work. The next four are about the transport, and the last one is a bug to fix.

Design Limits

It never sends parameters that aren't a list or a dictionary. The specification doesn't allow anything else, so a message that breaks this rule is rejected when it's built, not when the other side receives it.

It never accepts a message that breaks the specification. A missing or incorrect jsonrpc member, a method that isn't a string, an id that isn't a string, a number or null, or a response with both a result and an error are each rejected with the code the specification assigns, without any guessing.

It only reads text in UTF-8. JSON is always UTF-8, so a message that isn't is answered with PARSE_ERROR instead of being read with its invalid bytes replaced. A header block must be ASCII, and an HTTP body that declares a different charset is rejected with a 415.

It never answers a response. An invalid response is passed to on_error() and never sent back to the peer, so two endpoints can never get stuck answering each other's errors forever.

It doesn't let handlers use reserved names. Method names that start with rpc. belong to the specification, and on_request(), on_notification() and on_unhandled() won't answer them.

It never does an unlimited amount of work for a single message. A batch over the service's limit is rejected completely, and a framing rejects an oversized message based on its header, before reading any of it.

It doesn't defer a request that has nowhere to send its answer. A request that arrived over HTTP is answered in its HTTP response, so calling defer() on it raises an error, instead of leaving the client waiting for an answer that can never arrive.

It doesn't listen to a transport that only one isolate can use. A socket, a WebSocket or a child process is read where it's held, so calling listen() on one raises an error instead of trying to read it from somewhere it can't be read.

Module Reference

The standard library reference documents every class and method. Here's an overview of the module:

Function Description
rpc.Service() Creates a service, with handlers and answer()
rpc.http_handler(service) Creates an http route handler that answers with a service
rpc.HttpClient(url, options) Creates a client that calls a service over HTTP
rpc.endpoint(transport) Creates an Endpoint on a transport
rpc.serve(setup, options) Creates an endpoint for every connection to a listening socket
rpc.stdio() Uses the program's own standard streams
rpc.socket(stream) Uses a connected net stream
rpc.process(child) Uses a child process's standard streams
rpc.websocket(socket) Uses a WebSocket from http.websocket
rpc.pipe() Creates two transports connected to each other
rpc.encode(message) Encodes a message, or a list of messages, as JSON text
rpc.decode(text) Decodes JSON text into a message or a batch of messages
rpc.read(value) Reads a decoded value as a message or a batch of messages

The message classes and constants:

Name Description
Request(method, params, id) A call that expects an answer
Notification(method, params) A call that doesn't expect an answer
Response(id, result, error) An answer, which can also be created with Response.success() and Response.failure()
RpcError(code, message, data) An error, with to_dict()
PARSE_ERROR, INVALID_REQUEST, METHOD_NOT_FOUND Error codes defined by the specification
INVALID_PARAMS, INTERNAL_ERROR The remaining codes defined by the specification
SERVER_ERROR_MIN, SERVER_ERROR_MAX The range reserved for implementations

Methods of a Service, and therefore also of an Endpoint:

Methods Purpose
on_request, on_notification, on_unhandled Set what it answers
on_error, on_trace Set what it reports
set_batch_limit, batch_limit Set or get the maximum number of messages in a batch, which is DEFAULT_BATCH_LIMIT by default
answer Takes a message or batch and returns its answer

Additional methods of an Endpoint:

Methods Purpose
set_framing Sets how its messages are separated
request, request_batch, send_request, notify Call the other side
send, handle Send and handle messages as they are
serve, stop Read on the isolate that calls them
listen, dispatch Read on a separate isolate
feed Handles data the program read itself
close, is_closed End the connection

Methods of an HttpClient: request, request_batch, notify and send.

Members of a Context:

Members Purpose
endpoint, id, method, request What's being handled, where, and what it arrived in
is_notification Whether an answer will be sent
defer, is_deferred Take over answering the request
reply, fail, is_answered Answer a deferred request

Methods of the framings, HeaderFraming, LineFraming and MessageFraming:

Method Purpose
feed(data) Returns the messages that the next bytes complete
frame(message) Returns the bytes that send a message
set_max_size(size), max_size() Set or get the largest message accepted
pending() Returns how many bytes are held for an unfinished message

The transports, StdioTransport, SocketTransport, ProcessTransport, WebSocketTransport and ChannelTransport, each have read(max), write(data), close() and can_listen(), and WebSocketTransport also has framing().

Chapter 29 · Tooling

Editor Support

Zuri includes a language server. zuri lsp implements the Language Server Protocol, so any editor that supports the protocol gets completion, navigation, diagnostics as you type, refactoring, formatting and test running for Zuri, from the same server that comes with the runtime. The server is written in Zuri and uses the zuri module's own parser and compiler, so what it reports matches what the runtime would do with the same code.

There's an extension for Visual Studio Code that sets everything up for you. Neovim, Helix, Sublime Text and Emacs each need a few lines of configuration, which are shown at the end of this chapter.

  • Emacs
  • Troubleshooting

Features

Writing Code

Completion suggests what you can write at the cursor:

  • After a ., the members of the receiver's type. That includes an instance's fields and methods, including inherited ones and ones added by extensions, a class's static members, a module's exports, a built-in type's methods, and the keys of a dictionary written out where its variable was declared.
  • Anywhere else, the names in scope, the built-in globals, and the keywords that can start what you're writing.
  • After import, module paths, and between an import's braces, what the module exports.
  • At the start of a class member, @new and the operator decorators the class doesn't have yet, as method skeletons.
  • After the : of a type hint, the type names.
  • Inside a doc comment, its tags after @, and the names of the parameters it documents after @param.

A name exported by another module is offered along with the import it needs, either as import json and json.encode for a standard library module or a package, or as import .shapes { Point } for a module in the project.

Signature help follows a call while you write its arguments. It highlights the parameter at the cursor and shows its documentation, follows a constructor call to its @new, and stays on a variadic parameter for every argument it receives.

Hover shows a declaration as a line of Zuri, its documentation formatted in the same way as the standard library reference, the type inferred for a variable, the value of a constant, and an overview of a module.

Inlay hints show the name of the parameter each literal argument is passed to, and, if you turn them on, the type inferred for each variable.

Navigating Code

Go to definition follows an imported name back to the module that declares it, and a built-in name to the stub that documents it. Go to declaration stops at the import that brings a name into the file, and go to type definition goes to the class of the value a name holds. Go to implementation lists the methods in subclasses that override a method, or the subclasses of a class.

Find references and the highlighting of the current name use what each name resolves to, never its spelling, so a distance method in one class is never confused with another class's distance method.

The call hierarchy shows what calls a function and what it calls, and the type hierarchy shows the classes above and below a class. Each file has an outline, and the workspace symbol search finds declarations whose names contain the letters you type in order, so hrq finds HttpRequest. Each import links to the file it loads, and each class, function and method shows how many times it's used.

Diagnostics

Every error the server reports is either an error the compiler reports, or a failure that the runtime is certain to raise when the code runs:

  • A syntax error. The rest of the file is still checked after recovering from it.
  • An error from the compiler, such as break outside a loop.
  • An import of a module that doesn't exist, or of a name its module doesn't have.
  • module.name for a name the module doesn't have.
  • A name that nothing declares.
  • self.name = value outside @new, for a field that no class in the inheritance chain declares.
  • A literal argument of the wrong type, or a missing argument, for a typed parameter, with the runtime's own message.

A member that an instance of a fully known class doesn't have is reported as a warning, because an extension the server hasn't read could add it. Unused imports and declarations, and code after a return, raise, break or continue, are shown faded. Uses of anything documented as @deprecated are shown with a strikethrough.

The server never guesses. A value whose type can't be determined, a module whose wildcard imports lead to modules it hasn't read, and a class whose superclass can't be found never cause a diagnostic. Argument counts aren't checked either, because Zuri doesn't enforce them.

Quick fixes can add the import a missing name needs, correct a misspelled name or member, remove an unused import, and declare a field that's assigned outside @new.

Changing Code

Rename changes a declaration and every use of it throughout the workspace. A { name } dictionary entry keeps its key and becomes { name: renamed }. A rename is refused, with an explanation, when the new name is a keyword, when it's already declared somewhere the declaration or one of its uses would see it, when it would make something private that's used from outside, and for anything declared by the standard library or a package. A member used through a receiver whose type can't be determined is left unchanged, and the editor is told where.

Extract and inline refactorings are only offered where they don't change what the program does:

  • Extract variable moves an expression into a var just before its statement. It never moves an expression out of a loop's condition, the right side of and or or, a branch of ?:, a when label or an else if condition, and never past something with a side effect that runs first. When the expression has no side effects, every identical copy of it in the block can share the variable.
  • Extract function turns complete statements from one block into a function. The outer local variables they use become its parameters, and any values they set that are read afterwards are returned, either directly for a single value or in a dictionary for several. Statements that use self or parent become a private method.
  • Inline variable replaces each use of a var that's assigned once and never changed with its value.
  • Inline function replaces a call to a function whose body is a single return with that expression, and removes the function once every call has been inlined.

Formatting runs zuri fmt on a file or a selection, and only sends back the lines that changed. A file with a syntax error is left as it is.

Renaming or moving a file updates the relative imports that refer to it, both in the files that import it and in the moved file itself.

Running Tests

The server finds the tests that every file in the workspace declares with the test module, meaning each describe and it, along with their _only, _skip, _todo and _each forms, whose names are written as strings. A code lens above each one runs it, and one above the first test runs the whole file.

A test runs in the same way zuri test would run it: with zuri run on its file, in a separate process, from the root of the project. Each result is sent to the editor as soon as it's available, and each failed assertion is shown on the line where it failed, until the file changes or its tests run again.

Highlighting

Semantic highlighting colors each name according to what it resolves to, whether that's a class, a function, a method, a parameter, a variable, a field, a module or a decorator, and marks anything defined by the standard library. It works with any editor theme that supports semantic tokens.

How the Server Reads a Project

The server reads every .zu file in the workspace folders the editor opens. It does this in the background, on its own isolates, so it can respond while it's reading. Inside a git working tree, it reads the files git tracks or would track, so .gitignore is respected. Anything under .git, .zuri or node_modules is skipped, along with anything zuri.exclude lists.

Imports are resolved in exactly the same way the runtime resolves them: a relative import against the importing file, then the project's .zuri/libs, then the standard library, then the native modules, and finally the packages installed for the user in ZURI_HOME/libs. The standard library is read from the Zuri installation the server belongs to, or from zuri.root, or from ZURI_ROOT. A module imported by the workspace is read the first time it's needed.

Settings

The server reads its settings from the zuri section of the editor's configuration, either as nested objects or as dotted names, and picks up changes as soon as they're made.

Setting Default What it does
root '' The installation whose standard library is read. If empty, the server uses ZURI_ROOT, or the installation that zuri belongs to.
exclude [] Glob patterns, relative to a workspace folder, for files that are never read
index.workers 2 The number of isolates that read the workspace in the background
diagnostics.enable true Whether problems are reported at all
diagnostics.scope 'openFiles' 'openFiles', or 'workspace' to check every file in the workspace
diagnostics.delay 300 How many milliseconds to wait after a change before checking a file
diagnostics.unusedHints true Whether unused declarations are shown faded
inlayHints.parameterNames 'literals' Which arguments are labeled with parameter names: 'none', 'literals' or 'all'
inlayHints.variableTypes false Whether inferred variable types are shown
codeLens.references true Whether declarations show how many times they're used
completion.autoImport true Whether names from modules that haven't been imported yet are suggested
completion.callParentheses false Whether completing a function also adds its parentheses
testing.codeLens true Whether suites and tests show code lenses that run them

Starting the Server

Editors start the server themselves, and communicate with it over its standard input and output:

--stdio names the only way the server communicates, and it's accepted because editors pass it. --log writes the server's log to a file, as well as sending it to the editor. --log-level sets how much is logged: error, warn, info (the default), debug or trace, which also writes every message exchanged between the editor and the server to the log file.

The server exits with status 0 when the editor shuts it down properly, and with 1 if the connection ends without that, or if the editor that started it has exited.

Visual Studio Code

Install the Zuri extension from the marketplace, or from a downloaded package:

The extension starts the server for every workspace that contains a .zu file. Its settings are the server's settings, under zuri., plus two of its own: zuri.path, the zuri executable to run, and zuri.trace.server, which records the messages between the editor and the server in the Zuri Language Server output panel. Tests appear in the Test Explorer, and the commands Zuri: Restart Language Server, Zuri: Show Language Server Output and Zuri: Check Zuri Installation are available in the command palette.

Neovim

Neovim 0.11 has built-in support for configuring language servers:

To show inlay hints, use vim.lsp.inlay_hint.enable(), and to run a code lens, use vim.lsp.codelens.run().

Helix

Add the language and its server to languages.toml:

Sublime Text

With the LSP package installed, add a client to its settings:

The selector names the syntax that Zuri files are opened with. The Visual Studio Code extension's grammar, zuri.tmLanguage.json, is a TextMate grammar with the scope source.zuri, and the Convert command in PackageDev turns it into a .tmLanguage file for Sublime Text.

Emacs

Eglot, which is built into Emacs 29, needs a mode for Zuri files and the command that starts the server:

Settings go in eglot-workspace-configuration:

Troubleshooting

The server sends whatever it logs at its --log-level and above, which is info by default, to the editor's log for language servers. While the editor requests a trace, it also sends everything down to debug. Starting it with --log and --log-level debug writes all of this to a file, and --log-level trace also includes every message exchanged.

If nothing works at all, the editor probably can't start zuri. Run zuri --version in a terminal to check whether it's on your PATH. If your editor lets you set a path, as zuri.path does in Visual Studio Code, you can give it the location of the executable directly.

If the standard library can't be found, the server reports it in its log. To fix it, set zuri.root, or ZURI_ROOT for the editor, to the Zuri installation.

Chapter 30 · Tooling

Documenting a Project

zuri doc turns a directory of Markdown files into a website, with a page for each chapter and a table of contents next to it, a search box, a page that prints everything at once, light and dark themes, and syntax highlighting for every code block. It can also generate an API reference from the doc comments in a project's code. This book is built with it, and so is the standard library reference.

The output is a directory of plain files. Any web server can serve it, GitHub Pages can publish it as it is, and a browser can open it straight from disk.

  • Starting Documentation
  • The Table of Contents
  • Writing Pages
    • Links and Files
    • Code
    • Including Files
  • Building and Serving
  • Generating an API Reference
  • Nested Documentation
  • Settings
  • Customizing the Appearance
  • Publishing

Starting Documentation

Inside a project, zuri doc init starts documentation in its docs directory:

The documentation uses the project's name as its title, unless you give it a different one with --title. Outside a project, it's created in the current directory, and if you name a directory, it's created there instead, as in zuri doc init manual.

Documentation is organized like this:

Every command finds the documentation in the same way. It uses the directory named on the command line, or otherwise the current directory if it contains a doc.toml, or otherwise the docs directory of the project you're in, or failing that its docs/reference. That means zuri doc build works from anywhere inside the project.

The Table of Contents

src/SUMMARY.md lists the pages in reading order. A page that isn't listed there isn't part of the documentation.

  • The first heading is the title of the summary itself, and isn't shown. Every other heading starts a part, which is a titled group of chapters that the table of contents marks with its own color.
  • A link in a list is a numbered chapter. A list nested inside its item contains its sections, which are numbered beneath it as 1.1, 1.2 and so on.
  • A link outside any list is an unnumbered chapter, such as an introduction before the numbered chapters or a changelog after them.
  • A link without an address, like [Alerts](), is a draft. It's listed, grayed out, until it has a page.
  • --- draws a line across the table of contents.
  • {.unnumbered} after a part's heading leaves that part's chapters unnumbered, which suits appendices. After a single link, as in [Settings](settings.md){.unnumbered}, it does the same for that chapter and its sections.

Each page is written to the same place as its Markdown file, with .html instead of .md, so getting-started/installing.md becomes getting-started/installing.html. A README.md becomes its directory's index.html. The front page, index.html, is the first chapter.

Writing Pages

Pages are written in CommonMark, with GitHub's extensions: tables, task lists, strikethrough, footnotes, automatic links, emoji shortcodes such as :rocket:, and alerts written as > [!NOTE], > [!TIP], > [!IMPORTANT], > [!WARNING] or > [!CAUTION]. You can also write HTML directly in a page.

Every heading gets an ID: the heading in lowercase, with each space replaced by a dash and other punctuation removed, so ## Running in Production becomes #running-in-production, the same ID GitHub gives it. A heading that repeats an earlier one gets -1 added to it, then -2, and so on. Braces after a heading let you give it an ID of your own choosing, and classes:

When you hover over a heading, a § appears that links to it, and the headings on a page are listed next to it under "On this page".

The [markdown] table in doc.toml changes how pages are read. Its keys are the options of the standard library's markdown module, so smart = true gives you curly quotes and proper dashes, and math = true reads $...$ as mathematics and typesets it on the page. The markdown page of the library reference lists all of the options.

Links and Files

To link to another page, link to its Markdown file, as you would on GitHub: [the units](settings.md#units). The link is updated to point to the page when the site is built, so it works both on GitHub and on the site.

Images, and any other files in src that aren't Markdown, are copied into the site next to the pages, at the same paths, so an image written as ![a chart](images/rain.png) appears in both places too.

Building the site checks every link within the documentation, and reports any link that leads to a page not listed in SUMMARY.md, to a heading that doesn't exist on the page, or to a file that doesn't exist, along with the line it's on.

Code

Code blocks are highlighted when the site is built, so a page looks the same with JavaScript turned off. The first word of the fence names the language:

Language Fence
Zuri zuri
A REPL session zuri-repl
HTML and Wire html, wire
XML xml, svg
JSON json
Shell scripts sh, bash, shell
Terminal sessions console, terminal
TOML toml
INI and .env files ini, env
JavaScript and CSS js, css

Anything after the first word is ignored, so a block fenced as zuri,ignore is highlighted as Zuri. A block in any other language is shown as plain text, labeled with the name given in its fence.

In a console block, a line starting with a $ prompt is a command, and is highlighted as one. Every other line is the output of the commands. A console block without any prompt is a program's output on its own, and when it comes directly after a code block, the two are shown joined together, as the code and the output it printed. Every example in this book is written this way, as a zuri block followed by a console block:

A paragraph that only contains <span class="filename">Filename: main.zu</span>, written just before a code block, becomes a caption on the block that names the file it shows.

Every code block has a button that copies it. On a terminal session, it only copies the commands, without their prompts or their output.

Including Files

{{#include path}} is replaced by the contents of the file at path, relative to the page. When it's the only line inside a code block, the block shows that file, so an example always matches the file it comes from, and can't get out of sync with code that's tested elsewhere:

A colon after the path selects part of the file: forecast.zu:12 is line 12 on its own, forecast.zu:5:20 is lines 5 to 20, forecast.zu:5: is line 5 to the end, and forecast.zu::20 is up to line 20. A name instead of numbers, as in forecast.zu:today, selects the lines between two comments in the file that mark them, so the file can still be a complete program that runs:

The marker lines themselves are never included, whichever part of the file you select.

{{#title text}} sets the title shown in the browser tab for a page, instead of the one the table of contents gives it. To write either of these literally, put a backslash in front, as in \{{#include x}}.

Building and Serving

zuri doc build builds the site:

When a link within the documentation doesn't lead anywhere, it tells you where the link is:

Without --strict, the warnings are printed and the build succeeds. With it, the command fails, which is how a CI job can make sure the links stay valid. --out writes the site somewhere other than the location in doc.toml, and --open opens it in a browser once it's built.

--external also requests every http and https address the pages link to, once for each address, however many pages link to it, and warns about any address that responds with an error or can't be reached, after trying once more. A response asking it to slow down counts as a successful response. Addresses are requested a few at a time, so it takes seconds rather than minutes, but it needs network access, so it only runs when you ask for it rather than on every build:

With --strict as well, a broken address also fails the build.

While you're writing, zuri doc serve builds the site, serves it on your machine, and rebuilds it every time the documentation changes:

A page that's open in a browser reloads itself after every rebuild. If a build fails, it tells you why and keeps the last working version of the site, and the next save tries again. --port serves the site on a port other than 3000, --host 0.0.0.0 lets other machines access it, and --open opens it in a browser.

zuri doc clean removes the built site.

Generating an API Reference

zuri doc generate creates a reference for the project from its doc comments, with a page for every public module, showing each function, constant and class it contains, what they accept and what they return, with links between them.

The reference is documentation like any other, with its own doc.toml, in docs/reference unless you name a different directory. Its pages are Markdown files in src, which are written again from scratch on every run, so its .gitignore excludes them along with the site. zuri doc build and zuri doc serve regenerate them before building, and serve rebuilds whenever a module changes, so the reference is never out of date with the code. Edit the doc comments, never the generated pages.

Every .zu file in the project is treated as a module, except:

  • A file with any part of its path starting with an underscore, which the compiler keeps private.
  • Tests, meaning *.test.zu files, and the tests, docs, examples, benchmarks and cmds directories at the top level of the project.
  • Anything that [project] include and exclude in project.toml leave out of the package, and anything that .gitignore ignores.

A module is named the way it's imported. The project's index.zu is the package itself, such as weather, app/index.zu is weather.app, and app/forecast.zu would be weather.app.forecast. Each name is documented on the page for the file that declares it, and written with the path a reader would use to reach it. When index.zu re-exports app with import @.app { * }, the greet function in app is documented as weather.greet. A package's own page also lists every public name that can be reached through it, wherever it's declared.

A module's description is its doc comment tagged with @module, or if there isn't one, the doc comment at the top of the file, if an import comes after it. The tags in a declaration's doc comment become the sections of its entry: @param, @returns, @throws, @note, @deprecated and @see. A name in braces in the text, such as {Forecast} or {greet()}, links to where that name is documented, and @internal leaves a declaration out of the reference completely.

The [reference] table in doc.toml is what makes a set of documentation a reference:

Key Default Description
modules The project containing doc.toml The directory of modules to document
package The project's name, with each - replaced by _ The name the modules are imported under, or "" for none
exclude [] Patterns for files to leave out, relative to modules
intro None A Markdown file to show at the start of the front page, instead of the description
groups None Parts of the table of contents, each with a title, a description and its modules

Without groups, all the modules are shown in a single list, each one under the module it belongs to. With groups, each group becomes a part of the table of contents:

A module that isn't in any group is listed at the end, under Other Modules, with a warning, and --strict fails the build because of it, so a new module can't silently go missing from the table of contents. The standard library reference is generated this way.

Nested Documentation

A directory next to src that contains its own doc.toml is also documentation, and it's built along with the documentation around it, into the directory of the site with the same name. The most common case is the reference that zuri doc generate writes to docs/reference. If there's also a guide in docs, zuri doc build builds both,

and zuri doc serve serves both, rebuilding whenever a page or a module changes.

The top of every page then links to each set of documentation, and highlights the one the page belongs to. The outer documentation is labeled Docs, a reference is labeled API Reference, and anything else is labeled with its title. You can set a different label with label in a site's own [site] table:

Any of the logo, favicon, repository, [site.home], [[site.links]], css and js that a nested site doesn't set itself are taken from the site around it, so the whole thing reads as a single site, and its url is the outer url with the directory's name added. If you build it on its own, as in zuri doc build docs/reference, it's a separate site and doesn't inherit any of these settings.

A link from one set of documentation to another is written the same way it would be on GitHub, as the path from one Markdown file to the other. From docs/src/guide.md, [greet](../reference/src/weather-app.md#greet) links to the heading for greet() on the reference page for weather.app. The link is updated to point to the page that file becomes, and the build checks it along with all the others, naming the documentation it leads into if it doesn't lead anywhere.

Settings

doc.toml has five tables, and every key in them is optional. A key that a table doesn't support, or a value of the wrong type, stops the build with an error that names the key.

[documentation] describes the documentation:

Key Default Description
title The directory's name The title, shown at the top of every page
description None A one-sentence description, for search engines
authors None The authors' names
language "en" The language it's written in
source "src" The directory that contains the pages
output "site" Where the site is written
create-missing false Whether to create an empty page for a chapter whose file is missing, instead of stopping

[site] describes how the site looks and where it's published:

Key Default Description
url None The address the site is published at
repository None The source code repository, linked from every page
edit None An address for editing a page, with {path} standing for the page's file
logo None An image shown next to the title
favicon None The icon shown in the browser tab
theme "system" How a page first looks: "system", "light" or "dark"
fold false How many levels of the table of contents are expanded at first. false expands every level.
numbers true, or false for a reference Whether chapters are numbered
search true Whether the site can be searched
print true Whether the site has a page that prints everything at once
css [] Stylesheets added to every page
js [] Scripts added to every page
cname None The domain that GitHub Pages serves the site at
label "Docs", "API Reference" or the title What the links at the top call this site when it's built with others

The table of contents is always expanded as far as the current page, whatever fold is set to. [site.home] adds a link back to a parent site next to the title, and each [[site.links]] entry adds a link to the top of every page. An address that isn't absolute is relative to the front page. [markdown] is described in Writing Pages, [reference] in Generating an API Reference, and [redirects] keeps an old address working by redirecting it to a new one.

Every path in the file is relative to the directory that contains it.

Customizing the Appearance

Readers can choose light or dark mode, or follow their system setting, from the menu at the top of every page, and their choice is remembered. The theme setting only decides how a page looks before they've chosen.

Every page is rendered from a single Wire template, page.html, styled by doc.css, with its behavior provided by doc.js. A directory called theme next to doc.toml can replace any of these three files with a file of the same name. The versions that zuri doc uses are in cmds/doc/theme next to the zuri executable, and a copy of one of them is a good place to start. The css and js settings add to them instead of replacing them, which is usually all you need:

Publishing

The site is a directory of plain files without anything to run, so publishing it just means copying it somewhere a web server can read it.

GitHub Pages can serve it as it is. zuri doc writes the .nojekyll file that stops GitHub from leaving out files it doesn't expect, and a CNAME file when cname is set. Set url as well. It gives every page its canonical address, generates a sitemap.xml for search engines, and lets 404.html, the page shown for a missing address, work at any depth of the site, not only at the top level.

You can use every site without a mouse. /, s, or Ctrl+K (⌘K on a Mac) opens the search box, the up and down arrow keys move through the results, and the left and right arrow keys go to the previous and next chapter.

Appendices

Appendix A: Keywords

Zuri reserves 31 words. None of them can be used as the name of a variable, function, class or parameter.

Keyword What it does Covered in
and Logical "and", with short-circuiting Operators
as Binds an error in catch, or renames an import Errors, Modules
assert Raises an AssertError when its condition is falsy Control Flow
break Exits the innermost loop Control Flow
catch Runs a block and handles any error it raises Errors
class Declares a class, or with >, an extension to a class Classes, Extensions
const Declares a name that can't be reassigned Variables
continue Skips to the next iteration Control Flow
def Declares a function, named or anonymous Functions
default The branch of a using that runs when nothing else matches Control Flow
do Starts a do/while loop Control Flow
echo Prints a value followed by a newline Hello, World!
else The alternative branch of an if Control Flow
false The boolean value false Data Types
for Iterates over anything iterable Control Flow
if A conditional branch Control Flow
import Loads a module Modules
in Separates a for loop's variables from what it iterates over Control Flow
iter The counting loop Control Flow
nil The absence of a value Data Types
or Logical "or", with short-circuiting Operators
parent The parent class's constructor, or a parent class's method Inheritance
raise Raises an error Errors
return Returns from the current function Control Flow
self The current instance, inside a method Classes
static Attaches a field or method to the class rather than to its instances Classes
true The boolean value true Data Types
using A multi-way branch on a single value Control Flow
var Declares a variable Variables
when One branch of a using Control Flow
while The conditional loop Control Flow

Names That Aren't Keywords

These are ordinary global names rather than reserved words, so nothing stops you from shadowing them. But doing so is a good way to confuse whoever reads your code next:

The built-in error classes are global names too: Error, TypeError, ValueError, NumericError, ArgumentError, NotImplementedError, RangeError, AccessError, AssertError, PropertyError, UndefinedError and ModuleNotFoundError.

Names Reserved by Convention

Two module-level names are provided by the runtime instead of being declared by you: __file__ and __root__. See Modules.

The lexer never produces names that start with $, which is how the compiler can generate loop variables that never clash with yours.

A leading underscore marks something as private, for both class members and module members, and the compiler enforces it in both cases.

Appendices

Appendix B: Operators and Precedence

Precedence

The table lists operators from highest to lowest precedence. Operators on the same row have equal precedence and associate from left to right, except for **, which associates from right to left.

Level Operators Notes
1 Literals, (...), [...], {...}, self, parent
2 .. Only binds primary expressions
3 . () [] Member access, calls, indexing and slicing
4 ++ -- Postfix only
5 ** Right-associative. The exponent can have a unary operator.
6 ! - ~ Unary operators
7 * / // %
8 + -
9 << >> >>>
10 &
11 ^
12 |
13 < <= > >= == !=
14 and
15 or
16 ? :
17 = and the compound assignment operators

Some consequences to keep in mind:

  • 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512, because ** is right-associative.
  • 2 * 3 ** 2 is 18, because ** has higher precedence than *.
  • -2 ** 2 is -4, because ** binds more tightly than unary minus. Write (-2) ** 2 to raise a negative number to a power.
  • 2 ** -1 is 0.5, because the exponent can have its own sign.
  • 1 + 2..5 means 1 + (2..5), so put parentheses around ranges whose endpoints are calculated.

Arithmetic Operators

Operator Meaning Decorator
+ Addition, and string and list concatenation @add
- Subtraction @sub
* Multiplication, and string and list repetition @mul
/ Division, always floating point @div
// Floor division, which rounds toward negative infinity @floordiv
% Remainder, with the sign of the left operand @mod
** Exponentiation @pow
- (unary) Negation @neg

Comparison Operators

Operator Meaning Decorator
== Equal. Compares numbers, strings, lists and dictionaries by value, and everything else by identity. @eq
!= Not equal, the opposite of == @eq
< Less than, for numbers only @lt
<= Less than or equal to @lte
> Greater than @gt
>= Greater than or equal to @gte

@eq only runs when both operands are objects, so x == nil and x == 5 never call it.

Logical Operators

Operator Meaning
and True if both sides are truthy. Returns one of the operands, not a bool.
or True if either side is truthy. Returns one of the operands, not a bool.
! Logical negation, which always returns a bool
? : The conditional expression

Bitwise Operators

Operator Meaning Decorator
& And @and
| Or @or
^ Exclusive or @xor
~ Complement @not
<< Left shift @lshift
>> Arithmetic right shift @rshift
>>> Logical right shift, which fills with zeros @urshift

Assignment Operators

Operator Equivalent to
= Assignment
+= -= *= /= //= **= %= x = x op y
&= |= ^= ~= <<= >>= >>>= x = x op y
++ -- Increment and decrement. Postfix only, and evaluates to the new value.

Access Operators

Syntax Meaning
x.name A member of an object, dictionary or module
x[key] Index with a computed key
x[a, b] Slice from a up to but not including b
x[, b] Slice from the start
x[a, ] Slice to the end
a..b A range
...x A variadic parameter, only in a parameter list

Negative indexes count back from the end, for strings, lists and bytes.

Truthiness

These values are falsy: false, nil, 0, 0.0, -0.0, NaN, 0n, '' and bytes(0).

Everything else is truthy, including negative numbers, [], {} and '0'.

Operators Zuri Doesn't Have

There's no in operator for checking membership, so use contains() instead. There's no optional chaining with ?., and no null coalescing with ??, but or covers that, with the truthiness caveat described above. There's no comma operator, and no prefix ++ or --.

Appendices

Appendix C: Decorated Methods

A method whose name starts with @ is called by the runtime when a particular piece of syntax is used with an instance of its class. Apart from that, decorated methods are ordinary methods: they can be inherited, overridden and called by name.

See Decorated Methods for a full explanation, and Class Extensions for adding one to a class you didn't write.

Construction

Decorator Called by Signature
@new ClassName(...) @new(...args)

@new is the only place where self.x = value can declare a field that wasn't declared with var.

Arithmetic

Decorator Operator Signature
@add a + b @add(other)
@sub a - b @sub(other)
@mul a * b @mul(other)
@div a / b @div(other)
@floordiv a // b @floordiv(other)
@mod a % b @mod(other)
@pow a ** b @pow(other)
@neg -a @neg()

Bitwise

Decorator Operator Signature
@and a & b @and(other)
@or a | b @or(other)
@xor a ^ b @xor(other)
@not ~a @not()
@lshift a << b @lshift(other)
@rshift a >> b @rshift(other)
@urshift a >>> b @urshift(other)

@not is bound to ~, the bitwise complement. ! is logical negation, and it can't be overridden. An instance is always truthy, so !instance is always false.

Comparison

Decorator Operator Signature
@eq a == b, a != b @eq(other)
@lt a < b @lt(other)
@lte a <= b @lte(other)
@gt a > b @gt(other)
@gte a >= b @gte(other)

!= is the opposite of @eq. @eq only runs when the right operand is also an object, so x == nil never calls it, and it must return a bool. Lists, dictionaries, contains() and index_of() compare instances by identity, whether or not their class defines @eq.

Iteration

Decorator Called by Signature
@key for ... in @key(previous)
@value for ... in @value(key)

@key(previous) receives the previous key, starting with nil, and returns the next key, or nil when there are no more. @value(key) returns the value stored under that key.

Defining both methods makes is_iterable() return true for the class.

Display

Decorator Called by Signature
@to_string echo, print() @to_string()

@to_string() returns the text displayed for the instance, including when it appears inside a list or dictionary that's being displayed, as a key or as a value. It must return a string, and returning anything else raises a TypeError. Without it, an instance is displayed as <instance of ClassName>.

Serialization

Decorator Called by Signature
@to_json json.encode() @to_json()

Returns whatever should be encoded in place of the instance, which lets you decide exactly what gets sent.

to_string() Isn't a Decorated Method

to_string() doesn't have an @. It's a regular method that every value already has, and a class can override it.

Nothing calls it automatically. String interpolation and + display an instance as <instance of ClassName>, and echo and print() use @to_string().

Which Method Is Called

The left operand decides. a + b only looks for @add on the class of a. If a is a number and b is an instance of your class, the operation raises a TypeError, rather than calling b's @add.

An operator without a matching decorated method raises a TypeError that shows the exact combination of types:

file()

Returns an open file handle to the file specified in the path in the specified mode. If the mode is not specified, the file will be opened in the read only mode.

Valid modes include:

x and x+ create the file and fail when anything already exists at the path. The check and the creation are one step, so of two programs creating the same path in x mode, exactly one succeeds. That makes it the mode for lock files. The failure comes on the first read, write or open(), since creating the handle touches nothing.

Module Variables

Every file also has these variables, which describe the file itself, not anything it declares.

__file__

The path of the file in which it's used. In the file that the program was started from, it's the path the program was started with. In an imported module, it's the module's full path.

Type string

__root__

The path of the file that the program was started from. It's the same in every module and every isolate of a single run, so __root__ == __file__ is only true in that one file. That's how a file can work both as a module that other files import and as a program by itself:

__root__ and __file__ are both set when a file runs. The REPL doesn't run a file, so it defines neither.

Type string

Appendix E: Built-in Type Methods

Every method of every built-in type, with its signature, what it returns, and its edge cases. This appendix is the reference. For an introduction, see the chapters in Text, Numbers and Collections.

Methods are called with a dot, on the value itself:

Type Methods Page
string 41 String Methods
number 43 Number Methods
bigint 26 Bigint Methods
bool 1 Boolean Methods
list 40 List Methods
dict 21 Dictionary Methods
range 9 Range Methods
bytes 25 Bytes Methods
file 27 File Methods
function 6 Function Methods

What Is Not Listed Here

@key and @value exist on every iterable built-in type, which is what makes for ... in work on them. They are documented as a protocol in Appendix C rather than repeated on every page.

to_string() exists on every value, nil included.

Class instances carry whatever their class declares, plus to_string(). See Classes and Objects.

Module members are not methods. See Appendix F.

Conventions in These Pages

A parameter written name: ?type is optional. A parameter written ...name is variadic. A parameter with no type shown takes any value.

A method that mutates its receiver says so. Where a type has both, the distinction matters: list.sort() mutates and returns the list, while list.reverse() returns a new list and leaves the original alone.

trim()

Returns a copy of the string with characters removed from both ends.

Without an argument, whitespace is removed: spaces, tabs (\t), line feeds (\n), vertical tabs, form feeds and carriage returns (\r). Other Unicode spaces, such as the no-break space, are kept.

With chars, every character in it is removed instead, in any order and any number of times, until a character that isn't in chars is reached at each end. chars is a set of characters, not a prefix or suffix, so 'xyax'.trim('xy') is 'a'. An empty chars removes nothing.

The original string is never changed. If there's nothing to remove, the result is an equal copy.

For example:

Parameters

  • chars (?string): The characters to remove. Defaults to whitespace.

Returns string

to_bigint()

Returns the integer in the string as a bigint, or 0n if the string doesn't contain one.

This is to_number() for integers too large for a number. A number is only exact up to 2^53, and beyond that, digits are lost. An ID or a BIGINT UNSIGNED value read from a database often goes beyond it. Here, every digit is kept, however many there are.

The number is found in the same way as for to_number(): it's the first number in the string, and any text around it is ignored. No fractional part is read, because the result is an integer, so '12.5'.to_bigint() is 12n.

Parameters

  • base (number): The base of the digits, from 2 to 36. Defaults to 10.

Returns bigint

Raises RangeError if base is outside 2 to 36.

match()

If str is a plain string, this returns true if the string contains str, and false otherwise.

If str is a regular expression, this returns false if there's no match. Otherwise, it returns a dictionary describing the first match: the whole match under the key 0, each capture group under its number, and each named group under its name as well. A group that isn't part of the match is nil. When several groups share a name, which the J modifier allows, the name refers to the one that's part of the match.

If offset is given, matching starts at that position in the string.
