replace()

Returns a copy of the string with every occurrence or match of str replaced by replacement.

If str is a regular expression, replacement can refer to capture groups as $index. Group 0 is the whole match, so $0 inserts the whole match.

To write a literal $ in replacement, put two backslashes (\\) before it.

For example:

Parameters

  • str (string): The string or regular expression to replace.
  • replacement (string): The replacement string.
  • use_regex (?bool): Whether str can be treated as a regular expression. Defaults to true.

Returns string

Note: When the third parameter, use_regex, is false, str is never treated as a regular expression, even if it looks like one.

replace_with()

Returns a copy of the string with every match of regex replaced by what callback returns. The callback is only called when there's a match.

The callback looks like this:

Its arguments are:

  • match: the matched text, which is the same as $0.

  • p1, p2, …, pN: the text matched by each capture group, including named groups, which is the same as $1, $2 and so on. For example, if the pattern is /(\a+)(\b+)/, p1 is the match for \a+, and p2 is the match for \b+. If a group is one side of an alternation, as in "abc".replace_with('/(a)|(b)/', replacer), the side that didn't match is nil.

  • offset: the position of the match in the whole string. For example, if the whole string is 'abcd' and the match is 'bc', this is 1.

  • string: the whole string being searched.

The number of arguments depends on the number of capture groups in the regular expression.

For example:

Here's an example with a capture group:

Parameters

  • regex (string): The regular expression to match.
  • callback (function): The function to call for each match.

Returns string

ascii()

Reinterprets the string as raw bytes: each byte of its UTF-8 encoding becomes a separate character, with a code point from 0 to 255, as in Latin-1. Normally, length(), each() and indexing work on the decoded Unicode characters instead.

The result is still a valid string, because every code point from 0 to 255 is valid UTF-8, so it can be used anywhere a normal string can. But if the string contained multi-byte characters, they can't be recovered from the result, and its length() is the original number of bytes, not the original number of characters.

This is for the rare case where code needs to go through a string one byte at a time, instead of one character at a time, for example for a string that came from a byte stream that was never meant to be decoded as Unicode.

Returns string

case_fold()

Returns a copy of the string case-folded for case-insensitive comparison, using full Unicode case folding instead of plain conversion to lowercase. This matters for characters whose folded form isn't just their lowercase form. For example, the German ß folds to ss.

Two strings that are equal when case is ignored always give the same result from case_fold(), so it's the right method for case-insensitive comparison. lower() isn't a substitute for it.

Returns string

compare()

Compares the string with another string.

Parameters

  • other (string): The string to compare with.

Returns number: A negative number if this string comes before other, zero if the two are equal, or a positive number if this string comes after other.

Raises Error if other isn't a string.

is_empty()

Returns true if the string is empty, and false otherwise.

Returns boolean

contains()

Returns true if the string contains str, and false otherwise.

Parameters

  • str (string): The string to look for.

Returns boolean

lines()

Returns the lines of the string as a list, as if the string were split at each line break.

Returns list

each_line()

Iterates over each line of the string, calling the provided callback function with the line and its index.

Parameters

  • callback (function): A function that takes two arguments: the line and its index.

Returns void

Raises Error if the callback is not a function.

each()

Iterates over each character of the string, calling the provided callback function with the character and its index.

Parameters

  • callback (function): A function that takes two arguments: the character and its index.

Returns void

Raises Error if the callback is not a function.

capitalize()

Returns a new string with the first character capitalized and the rest in lowercase.

Returns string

title()

Returns a new string with each word capitalized.

Returns string

to_string()

Returns the string itself.

Returns string

Note: Only an exact integer can be converted to a bigint, so a fractional number, Infinity and NaN all raise an error, instead of being rounded or clamped. A number above 2^53 is already imprecise as a double, so converting it gives the exact integer that the double holds, not the decimal literal it was written as.

int()

Truncates the number to its integer part, discarding anything after the decimal point. Unlike floor(), this rounds toward zero, not toward negative infinity, so the result for a negative number is different from floor().

max()

Returns the larger of the number and other.

A NaN never wins: when one of the two is NaN, the other is returned, and only two NaNs give NaN. -0 counts as smaller than 0, so (-0.0).max(0) is 0 whichever side the zeros are on.

Returns the smaller of the number and other.

A NaN never wins: when one of the two is NaN, the other is returned, and only two NaNs give NaN. -0 counts as smaller than 0, so 0.min(-0.0) is -0 whichever side the zeros are on.

sign()

Returns the sign of the number: 1 if it is positive, -1 if it is negative, and 0 (with its own original sign preserved) if it is zero.

Returns number

Returns the smallest whole number greater than or equal to the number.

Rounds the number to the nearest whole number. A value exactly halfway between two whole numbers rounds away from zero.

is_nan()

Returns true if the number is NaN (not a number), such as the result of 0/0, and false otherwise.

is_finite()

trunc()

Truncates the number toward zero, discarding anything after the decimal point. For a value that fits in a 64-bit integer, this gives the same result as int(). Unlike int(), trunc() works entirely in floating point, without converting to an integer, so it doesn't overflow for a number too large for a 64-bit integer.

Returns number

fraction()

Returns the digits after the decimal point as a whole number, not as a fraction. This isn't the same as (n - n.int()): 1.92.fraction() is 92, not 0.92.

Returns number

fixed()

Returns the number rounded to n decimal places, with a half rounding away from zero the same way round() does.

A number already shorter than n places is returned unchanged, and so are NaN and the infinities. Beyond 17 places an f64 has no digits left to round, so a larger n behaves as 17.

to_string()

Returns the decimal digits of the bigint, with a leading - if it's negative and without the trailing n. Pass radix to use another base, with lowercase letters for digits above nine.

Returns string

Raises RangeError if radix is outside 2 to 36.

Note: The n that echo and string interpolation show is part of how a bigint is displayed, not part of the conversion. to_string() never includes it.

to_number()

Converts the bigint to a number.

Returns number

Note: This loses precision for anything above 2^53, because the result is the nearest double. A value beyond the range of a double becomes inf or -inf, instead of wrapping around or becoming zero. Check bits() first if that matters.

to_bool()

Converts the bigint to a boolean, by the same rule if uses. 0n is false, and every other bigint, negative ones included, is true.

Returns boolean

to_bytes()

Returns the bigint as bytes in two's complement, which includes the sign, so the bytes convert back to the same value. The result is the shortest byte string that can hold the value, and it's never empty: zero is a single 0x00 byte.

Parameters

Returns bigint

Raises TypeError if other is not a bigint.

modpow()

Returns (self ** exponent) % modulus without computing the full power, so it works with the very large exponents that cryptography uses.

Parameters

  • exponent (bigint)
  • modulus (bigint): Must not be zero.

Returns bigint

Raises TypeError if either argument isn't a bigint.

Raises RangeError if modulus is zero, or if exponent is negative and there's no modular inverse.

Note: The remainder is floored, not truncated, so the result has the sign of modulus, not of the receiver. A negative exponent is only allowed if the receiver has an inverse modulo modulus.

modinv()

Returns the modular multiplicative inverse, which is the x for which self * x == 1 (mod modulus).

Parameters

  • modulus (bigint): Must not be zero.

Returns bigint|nil

Raises TypeError if modulus isn't a bigint.

Raises RangeError if modulus is zero.

Note: If the receiver and modulus aren't coprime, this returns nil instead of raising an error, because having no inverse is an ordinary result, not a mistake by the caller. The result has the sign of modulus.

bits()

Returns how many bits the magnitude occupies, ignoring the sign. Zero occupies none.

Returns number

bit()

Returns whether the bit at index is set, counting from the least significant bit, which is at index 0.

Parameters

  • index (number): A non-negative integer.

Returns boolean

Raises RangeError if index is negative or fractional.

Note: The bigint is read as two's complement, so a negative bigint reports true for every index above its magnitude, instead of running out of bits.

Returns a new bigint with the bit at index set or cleared. The original bigint isn't changed.

Parameters

  • index (number): A non-negative integer.

Returns bigint

trailing_zeros()

Returns the count of least-significant zero bits, which is the largest power of two dividing the bigint.

Returns number|nil

Note: Returns nil for zero, which has no largest such power and would otherwise have to report an arbitrary number.

Returns whether the bigint is zero.

Returns boolean

is_even()

Returns whether the bigint is even. Zero is even.

Returns boolean

is_odd()

Returns whether the bigint is odd.

Returns boolean

sort()

Sorts the items in the list in place, and returns the sorted list. Items of different types are sorted by type, in this order:

nil, booleans, numbers, strings, ranges, lists, dictionaries, files, bytes, functions, classes and modules.

Items of the same type are sorted by value, so the number 5 comes before 8.

For example:

The boolean comes before the number, the number comes before the string, and the string comes before the list. Lists inside the list are sorted too.

Sorting by something else

Pass a comparator to choose the order yourself. It's called with two items, and returns a negative number to put the first item first, a positive number to put the second item first, or zero to leave them as they are:

The sort is stable, so items that the comparator treats as equal keep the order they were in. That means you can sort a list by one thing and then by another to order it by both:

This leaves people of the same age in order of name.

Parameters

  • comparator (function)

Returns list

Note: A comparator only sorts the list it's given. Lists inside the list, which sort() sorts without a comparator, are left as they are, because only the comparator knows what the order should be.

Note: A comparator that contradicts itself produces some order, not an error, because no order could satisfy it.

close()

Closes the stream to an opened file. You'll rarely ever need to call this method yourself in most use cases.

For example:

open()

Opens the stream to a file for the operation originally specified on the file object during creation. You may need to call this method after a call to read() if the length isn't specified or write() if you wish to read or write again as the file will already be closed.

For example:

Returns void

read()

Reads from the open file, up to length bytes, and returns a string, or bytes if the file was opened in a binary mode. Without a length, it reads to the end of the file.

In text mode, the data must be valid UTF-8, and anything else raises an error, instead of being silently replaced. To read arbitrary bytes, open the file in a binary mode, such as 'rb'. io.stdin is already binary.

The file must be open in a mode that allows reading, which includes the default mode. If you read the whole file, it's closed for you. Otherwise, call close() when you've finished.

Parameters

  • length (?int)

Returns string|bytes

Returns string|bytes

write()

Writes a string or bytes to an opened file at the current insertion point. When the file is opened with the a mode enabled, write will always start from the end of the file. If the seek() method has been previously called, write will begin from the seeked position, otherwise it will start at the beginning of the file.

An example has been given above.

Every key above is present on every platform, so reading size or mtime needs no check of which one you are on.

Note: Windows keeps a different set of facts about a file, and the ones it has no answer for read as 0: dev, ino, uid and gid, with nlink always 1. mode is assembled from the file's type and its read-only attribute, so it carries the right file-type bits and either 0o444 or 0o666, widened by 0o111 for a directory or a name PATHEXT says the shell would run. ctime is the file's creation time there, Windows having no equivalent of a Unix inode-change time.

Returns the file handle as a string, naming its path and the mode it was opened in.

Returns string

Function Methods

Every method of the built-in function type, with its signature, what it returns, and any behavior you might not expect.

Method Returns Summary
name() string The function's declared name.
arity() number How many parameters the function declares, counting a variadic one as a single parameter.
is_variadic() bool Whether the last parameter is variadic (...name).
call(...args: list) any Calls the function with the given arguments, and returns its result.
apply(args: list) any Calls the function with the arguments in a list, and returns its result.
to_string() string The function rendered for display, as <function NAME(ARITY)>, with a trailing ... on the arity when the function is variadic.

name()

The function's declared name. An anonymous function is named @anon followed by a number, in the order the compiler found it. A bound method reports the method's own name, not its class's name.

Returns string

arity()

How many parameters the function declares, counting a variadic one as a single parameter.

A method read off an instance counts the instance as its first parameter, so a method declaring two parameters reports 3. A foreign function from ffi has no receiver and reports its C parameter list.

Returns number

is_variadic()

Whether the last parameter is variadic (...name).

Returns bool

call()

Calls the function with the given arguments, and returns its result. This is the same as calling it directly. It can make the code clearer when the function is stored in a variable.

Parameters

  • args (...any): the arguments to call it with

Returns any: Whatever the function returns.

Raises anything the called function raises.

apply()

Calls the function with the arguments in a list, and returns its result. call() takes the arguments separately, and this method takes them in a list.

If the list is shorter than the number of parameters, the remaining parameters are nil, just as when you call the function directly with too few arguments. If it's longer, the extra arguments go into a variadic parameter, or are discarded if there isn't one.

Parameters

  • args (list): the arguments to call it with, in order

Returns any: Whatever the function returns.

Raises TypeError if args isn't a list, and anything the called function raises.

to_string()

The function rendered for display, as <function NAME(ARITY)>, with a trailing ... on the arity when the function is variadic.

Returns string

Appendix G: The Error Hierarchy

Every error in Zuri is an instance of a class, and all of them inherit from Error. They're declared in ordinary Zuri and use the same class machinery as your own code, which is why subclassing one works exactly like subclassing anything else.

Fields

Every error has three fields:

Field What it holds
message The error message. The default is 'An unexpected error has occurred'.
type The name of the error's class, as a string
stacktrace A list of stack frames, starting with the innermost one

When Each Error Is Raised

Class Raised when
Error The base class, for general failures with nothing more specific to report
TypeError An operation received a value of the wrong type, such as an operator used with unsupported types, a method called on nil, or the wrong kind of value passed to an annotated parameter
ValueError The type was right, but the value wasn't
NumericError An arithmetic operation failed
ArgumentError A call passed the wrong number of arguments to a native function
NotImplementedError A method that should have been overridden wasn't
RangeError An index or bound was outside what the value allows
AccessError A permission or access check failed
AssertError An assert condition was falsy
PropertyError Code read a member that doesn't exist, such as a missing dictionary key, an undeclared field or a module member that wasn't exported
UndefinedError Code read an undefined global name
ModuleNotFoundError An import couldn't be resolved

Catching Errors

catch catches every error raised inside its block. To handle one kind of error and let the others through, check the error and raise it again if it isn't the kind you want:

instance_of() checks the whole inheritance chain, so checking against Error matches every error.

A parameter annotated as Error accepts any error, which makes a handler easy to read:

Defining Your Own Errors

There are two things to get right. Call parent(message) so that the base constructor sets message and records the stack trace. And set self.type, so that the class name appears in logs and in the message for an uncaught error.

Give the error whatever information its handler needs. Being able to carry more than a string is the reason to write an error class at all. The capstone project's TaskError includes the name of the field that failed validation, which is what lets its API respond with {"error": "...", "field": "title"}.

Uncaught Errors

An error that nothing catches prints its type, its message, the source code around the failure and the stack trace, and the program then exits with status 1:

A deep stack trace is shortened in the middle, because the top and the bottom are the useful parts.

There's No finally

Code after a catch statement runs whether or not the block raised an error, because the handler either recovers from the error or raises it again. Error Handling describes the patterns to use instead of finally.

Appendices

Appendix H: Coming From Another Language

The places where Zuri is most likely to surprise you are the places where it looks most familiar. This appendix lists them.

For Everyone

You might expect What Zuri does
x++ only as a statement x++ is postfix only, and inside an expression it evaluates to the new value. ++x doesn't parse.
[] to be falsy [] and {} are truthy. Use is_empty().
finally There isn't one. Code after the catch statement runs either way.
try The keyword is catch, and it takes the block that might fail: catch { ... } as e { ... }.
new Thing() Call the class instead: Thing().
switch and case with fall-through using and when, which only run the first match, with no break
A main function The top level of a file is the program.
Declarations to be hoisted They aren't. A def must come before the top-level line that calls it.
Overloading by number of arguments There's no overloading. Two def declarations with the same name in the same scope are a compile error.
Reopening a class class Ext > Target adds methods to an existing class, everywhere. See Extensions.
Comparing strings with < < only works with numbers. Use compare(), which returns -1, 0 or 1.
x in collection There's no membership operator. Use contains().
?. and ?? Neither exists. or covers the most common case, with the truthiness caveat above.
eval() There isn't one, on purpose. See Metaprogramming.

Coming From Python

  • Blocks use braces, not indentation, and every control flow statement needs them.
  • def declares functions and class declares classes, but there's no self parameter. self is available automatically inside a method, and you have to use it for every field access.
  • The constructor is @new, not __init__. Python's dunder methods are decorated methods that start with @, such as @add, @lt, @key and @to_json.
  • __eq__ is @eq, and != is always its opposite. It only runs when the other side is also an object, so x == nil never calls it. Without it, instances are compared by identity.
  • There are no list comprehensions. map(), filter() and reduce() are methods of lists.
  • len(x) is x.length(), str(x) is x.to_string(), and int(x) is x.int() or x.to_number().
  • Slices are written s[a, b], with a comma, not s[a:b].
  • elif is else if.
  • As in Python, modules run once and are cached. Circular imports work in the same way, with the same caveat.
  • if __name__ == '__main__' is written if __root__ == __file__.

Coming From JavaScript

  • var is block-scoped and behaves like let. const prevents a name from being reassigned, and it's enforced in local scopes.
  • == never converts types, so '1' == 1 is false. There's no ===.
  • Arrow functions are written @(x) => x * 2 or def(x) => x * 2, and @ is the more common form.
  • You don't have to worry about this being rebound, because self is always the instance.
  • Objects and dictionaries are the same thing, but a class instance isn't a dictionary. Classes are sealed, so you can't add a property to an instance, although a class Ext > Target declaration can add a method to the class.
  • null and undefined are both nil.
  • There's no async/await and no event loop. Concurrency uses isolates, which are real threads with separate heaps that communicate by copying values.
  • JSON.stringify is json.encode, and compact defaults to true.
  • Template literals are written '${expr}', in ordinary single or double quotes.

Coming From Ruby

  • There are no implicit returns. A function without a return returns nil.
  • There are no blocks or yield. Pass an anonymous function instead.
  • nil is the only nil-like value, and false is separate from it.
  • Method names don't end in ? or !. Predicates are named is_*, and whether a method changes its receiver is documented rather than indicated by punctuation.
  • each passes the value first and the index second to its callback, while for gives you the key first and the value second.
  • There's no method_missing. You can add methods to an existing class, but only through an explicit class Ext > Target declaration, not by reopening the class.
  • Modules are files, not a language construct, and there's no include or extend.

Coming From Go

  • Zuri is dynamically typed, with optional annotations on parameters that are checked on every call.
  • Errors are raised and caught, not returned, so there's no err != nil pattern.
  • Isolates aren't goroutines. They're operating system threads with separate heaps, and values passed between them are copied. That's the whole concurrency model, and it's why there are no mutexes.
  • Channels are bounded queues and behave the way you'd expect, including select().
  • There are no interfaces. A parameter annotated as Error accepts any subclass of Error, and that, together with inheritance, is all there is to polymorphism.
  • There's no equivalent of defer. Close what you opened on both the success path and the error path.

Coming From Java or C#

  • There's no static typing, no generics, no interfaces, and no packages as namespaces. A module is a file.
  • There's only single inheritance, and no abstract keyword. The usual approach is a base method that raises NotImplementedError.
  • Instead of public and private, a leading underscore marks something as private, and this is enforced at compile time for both class members and module members.
  • There's no overloading. Each name refers to one method, and declaring it a second time is a compile error.
  • equals() is @eq, and == calls it.
  • toString() is to_string(), and nothing calls it for you. What echo shows for an instance comes from @to_string().

Coming From C

  • Numbers are doubles. There's no integer type, and / never truncates. // is floor division.
  • As in C, the result of % has the sign of the left operand. // rounds toward negative infinity, which C's / doesn't.
  • There are no pointers and no manual memory management. A generational garbage collector manages the heap.
  • bytes is the buffer type, and struct is how you read and write binary layouts.
  • switch is using, and there's no fall-through.

Things That Can Save You an Hour

Interpolation doesn't call to_string(). '${thing}' gives you <instance of Thing>, so call the method yourself. echo displays an instance using @to_string(), which is a separate method.

list.sort() changes the list and returns it, while list.reverse() returns a new list and leaves the original unchanged. This difference is the most common cause of list bugs in Zuri code.

A def is scoped like a var. At the top level of a file, it creates a module-level name. Anywhere else, it creates a local in the block where it's written, and that local disappears when the block ends.

Imports are private by default. If your module imports something and a third file can't see it through your module, add the @.

To import a module in the same directory, write import .sibling, not the full path from the project root.

A conditional expression can be split across lines either way. ? and : can each end a line or start the next one, so both cond ? at the end of a line and a line starting with ? or : parse correctly.

Appendices

Appendix I: Custom Commands

zuri fmt, zuri init and zuri test are Zuri programs. The runtime includes them in a cmds directory next to itself, and when the first word after zuri isn't run, it looks for that word there and runs the script it finds. A project can add its own commands in the same way, in its .zuri/cmds directory, and they're run, listed and documented exactly like the commands that come with Zuri.

This is the place for scripts that a project keeps running by hand, such as a release checklist, a data import or a code generator. As a command, each one can be run by name from anywhere in the project, appears in zuri --help with a line describing what it does, and parses its own arguments with the same args module as everything else.

Where Commands Are Found

zuri <name> looks in these places, in order, and runs the first match:

Where What it contains
$ZURI_ROOT/cmds, or cmds next to the executable if ZURI_ROOT isn't set The commands that come with the runtime
.zuri/cmds in the project The project's own commands
cmds in each package in the project's .zuri/libs Commands provided by the project's packages
cmds in each package in $ZURI_HOME/libs Commands provided by the packages installed for your user

The project is the nearest directory above the working directory that contains a project.toml, so a project's commands can be run from anywhere inside it. If there's no project, .zuri in the working directory is used.

The commands that come with Zuri are checked first, so a project can't replace one of them. A project command named test is never run, and zuri --help leaves it out of the list. A project's own commands come before any provided by packages, and the project's packages come before your user's packages.

If two packages in the same place provide the same command, Zuri reports an error instead of choosing one at random. zuri <name> names both packages and runs neither, and zuri --help marks the command as provided twice. zuri install won't let you create the conflict in the first place.

zuri init writes a .gitignore that ignores everything under .zuri except .zuri/cmds, so a project's commands are committed along with the rest of its code, while the tools that store state in .zuri don't leave it in the repository.

Writing a Command

A command is either a single .zu file or a directory with an index.zu:

zuri greet runs greet.zu, and zuri release runs release/index.zu. If a directory and a file have the same name, the directory is used. The directory form is for a command that has grown too big for a single file. Its index.zu imports the other files with relative imports, as any package does, such as import .notes.

The name of a command is its file or directory name. It's always a single name, never a path, so zuri tools/greet is rejected as an unknown command before anything is looked up.

A name starting with _ is private, just as an identifier starting with one is. _notes.zu and _shared/index.zu are never treated as commands, so zuri --help leaves them out, and zuri _notes is an unknown command. That's where to put code shared by several commands, which each of them imports with a relative import, such as import .._shared.notes from release/index.zu.

Naming and Describing a Command

The first doc comment in the file describes the command. @command gives the name it's run by, and @description is the line that zuri --help shows next to it:

The doc comment has to start within the first 16 KiB of the file, which in practice means at the top. A description that's longer than a line continues on the indented lines below the tag, and ends at a blank line or the next tag. A command without a description is still listed, with just its name. @command is the first thing someone reading the file sees, and it names the file's own command. The runtime lists and runs a command by its file or directory name, so keep the two the same.

Arguments and the Exit Status

Everything after the command's name, including --help, belongs to the command, which reads it with the args module. Create a parser named after the command and call parse() without arguments. It reads the real command line, converts and validates each value, responds to --help based on the declarations, and rejects anything that isn't declared with a message and exit status 1. That's what gives every command, whether it comes with Zuri or not, the same flags, the same help layout and the same error messages:

The raw list is also available. os.args has the same structure for a command as for zuri run: the executable, the command's own file and then whatever the user typed, so the command's arguments are os.args[2,]. But reading that list by hand is how argument checks and help text get out of sync, which is exactly what the parser is designed to prevent, so a command should use args rather than os.args.

A command exits with status 0 when it runs to the end. An uncaught error prints its stack trace and exits with status 1, and os.exit() exits with any other status. A command that checks something, as zuri fmt --dry-run checks formatting, should exit with a non-zero status when the check fails, so that a shell script or a CI job can act on it.

The Working Directory

A command runs in the directory that zuri was started in, so os.cwd() is the user's directory, and for a project command, that's the project's root. __file__ is the command's own file, which is how a command can find files stored next to it:

Testing a Command

Create the parser in a function, as the greet command above does, and you can test the argument handling by passing a list to parse(), as described in Chapter 20. Everything else is ordinary Zuri, so keep the command's logic in functions and files next to index.zu, and test those.

The commands that come with Zuri keep their tests in a tests directory inside the command, and a project command can do the same. zuri test can run a directory anywhere in the project:
